title: Intego discovers undetected OSX/Adload decompiled Python adware
content:
## Snapshot
Researchers at Intego released a report detailing an Adload variant that may be a threat to Mac users.

## Description
Adload is a persistent adware threat to Mac users, historically spread via Trojan horse tactics, such as fake Flash Player installers, and later through UpdateAgent and WizardAgent. Recent variants show that while Adload’s compiled Mach-O files are detected by about one-third to one-half of antivirus engines on VirusTotal, its decompiled Python code goes entirely undetected by all 60+ engines on the platform. According to Intego, this suggests that many security solutions may not effectively detect Adload until it executes on a system. Additionally, the infection vector’s domain is flagged as malicious by only one of 96 reputation tools on VirusTotal, indicating that Adload can easily bypass common security measures and infect Macs with minimal effort from its developers.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
Threats to macOS have made OSINT headlines in recent months for using evolving attack techniques as threat actors increasingly adapt and expand their cyber targeting to include Mac users. Once considered a haven from malware, Mac users now face a growing array of sophisticated attacks. Microsoft has drawn on recent reporting of threats to macOS from across the security community to highlight observed trends and provide recommendations for defenders. To learn more, read [Recent OSINT Trends in Threats to MacOS](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/3d13591e).

## Recommendations
Apply these mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations.

- Use [Microsoft Defender Antivirus](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/microsoft-defender-antivirus-windows?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to protect from this threat.
- Turn on  and automatic sample submission on Microsoft Defender Antivirus. These capabilities use artificial intelligence and machine learning to quickly identify and stop new and unknown threats.
- Educate users about [protecting personal and business information](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/security-101/what-is-email-security?ocid=magicti_ta_abbreviatedmktgpage) in social media, filtering unsolicited communication, identifying lures in spear-phishing email and watering holes, and reporting reconnaissance attempts and other suspicious activity.
- Educate users about [preventing malware infections,](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/security-101/what-is-malware?ocid=magicti_ta_abbreviatedmktgpage) such as ignoring or deleting unsolicited and unexpected emails or attachments sent through instant messaging applications or social networks.
- Turn on [tamper protection for macOS](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/tamperprotection-macos?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint to prevent malicious changes to security settings.
- Encourage users to practice good [credential hygeine](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/security-101/what-is-login-security?ocid=magicti_ta_abbreviatedmktgpage) and turn on the Microsoft Defender Firewall to prevent malware infection and stifle propagation.
- Take immediate action to address malicious activity on the impacted device. If malicious code has been launched, the attacker has likely taken complete control of the device. Immediately isolate the system and perform a reset of credentials and tokens. Investigate the device timeline for indications of lateral movement activities using one of the compromised accounts. Check for additional tools that attackers might have dropped to enable credential access, lateral movement, and other attack activities.
- To protect against initial compromise, enable [Safe Links](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-office-365/safe-links-about?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) and [Safe Attachment](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-office-365/safe-attachments-about?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) policies in Defender for Office 365
- Enable [real-time protection for macOS](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/mac-preferences?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#enforcement-level-for-antivirus-engine) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus.
- Enable [real-time behavior monitoring for macOS](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/mac-preferences?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#enabledisable-behavior-monitoring) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus.
- Run endpoint detection and response [(EDR) in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus does not detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach.

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects threat components as the following malware:
 
- [TrojanDownloader:MacOS/SAgnt](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=TrojanDownloader:MacOS/SAgnt.C!MTB)
- [Adware:MacOS/Adload](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Adware:MacOS/Adload.K!MTB)
- [Adware:MacOS/Multiverze](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Adware:MacOS/Multiverze)

## References
[Intego discovers undetected OSX/Adload decompiled Python adware](https://www.intego.com/mac-security-blog/intego-discovers-undetected-osx-adload-decompiled-python-adware/). Intego (accessed 2025-02-14)

title: Unraveling the Many Stages and Techniques Used by RedCurl/EarthKapre APT
content:
## Snapshot
In January 2025, eSentire’s Threat Response Unit (TRU) discovered that the RedCurl espionage group, also known as EarthKapre, was using a legitimate Adobe executable (ADNotificationManager.exe) to sideload its malware.

## Description
The attack targeted an organization within the legal services industry, leveraging a phishing email with an Indeed-themed PDF that linked to a zip file containing an ISO image. When opened, the ISO mounted a drive displaying a single file (“CV Applicant \*.scr”), which, when executed, sideloaded the malware.
 
Once active, EarthKapre conducted reconnaissance using tools like AD Explorer, encrypted stolen data with 7-Zip, and exfiltrated it via PowerShell to a cloud service. The first-stage malware, a simple downloader, retrieved the next stage using a decryption routine based on SHA256 and AES keys. It also created a scheduled task disguised as a Google Corporation entry to ensure persistence.
 
Subsequent stages decrypted strings dynamically, checked for internet access via msn.com, and gathered system information. The malware used XOR encryption and base64 encoding to disguise data before exfiltration. Finally, it retrieved and executed the third-stage payload while deleting traces to evade detection.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
Active since at least 2018, [RedCurl](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1039/) is a threat actor known for engaging in corporate espionage targeting organizations across diverse industries, including finance, construction, consulting, retail, insurance, law, and travel. According to research from [Group-IB](https://www.group-ib.com/media-center/press-releases/red-curl/), RedCurl is Russian-speaking but lacks a definitive geographic connection to any specific region. Its victims are geographically distributed across countries such as Russia, Germany, Ukraine, the United Kingdom, Slovenia, Canada, Australia, and the United States.

RedCurl typically gains initial access to organizations with spear phishing emails, then executes discovery and collection commands and scripts to locate data of interest. The group then exfiltrates files to C2 servers controlled by the actor.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat.
 
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/linux-preferences) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown threats.
- Run [EDR in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode?view=o365-worldwide?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus does not detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach.
- Allow [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations?view=o365-worldwide?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in full automated mode to allow Microsoft Defender for Endpoint to take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.
- [Enable](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-controlled-folders) controlled folder access.
- Ensure that [tamper protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection#how-do-i-configure-or-manage-tamper-protection) is enabled in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Enable [network protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-network-protection) in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Follow the credential hardening recommendations in the [on-premises credential theft overview](https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/9382203e-5155-4b5e-af74-21562b1004d5/analystreport) to defend against common credential theft techniques like LSASS access.
- [Enable](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-credential-stealing-from-the-windows-local-security-authority-subsystem) LSA protection.

title: Storm-2372 conducts device code phishing campaign
content:
#### Targeted Geolocations
- North America  
- Eastern Europe  
- Western Europe  
- North Africa  
- Sub-Saharan Africa  
- Middle East



#### Targeted Industries
- Defense Industrial Base  
- Education  
- Communications Infrastructure  
- Government Agencies & Services  
- Healthcare & Public Health  
- Non-Government Organization  
- Information Technology  
- Energy



## Snapshot
Microsoft Threat Intelligence discovered an active and successful device code phishing campaign by a threat actor we track as Storm-2372. Our ongoing investigation indicates that this campaign has been active since August 2024 with the actor creating lures that resemble messaging app experiences including WhatsApp, Signal, and Microsoft Teams. Storm-2372’s targets during this time have included government, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), information technology (IT) services and technology, defense, telecommunications, health, higher education, and energy/oil and gas in Europe, North America, Africa, and the Middle East. Microsoft assesses with medium confidence that Storm-2372 aligns with Russian interests, victimology, and tradecraft. 

In device code phishing, threat actors exploit the device code authentication flow to capture authentication tokens, which they then use to access target accounts, and further gain access to data and other services that the compromised account has access to. This technique could enable persistent access as long as the tokens remain valid, making this attack technique attractive to threat actors. 

Microsoft Threat Intelligence Center continues to track campaigns launched by Storm-2372, and, when able, directly notifies customers who have been targeted or compromised, providing them with the necessary information to help secure their environments. Microsoft is also tracking other groups using similar techniques, including those documented by Volexity in their [recent publication](https://www.volexity.com/blog/2025/02/13/multiple-russian-threat-actors-targeting-microsoft-device-code-authentication/).

## Activity Overview
The identified phishing attack masquerades as Microsoft Teams meeting invitations delivered through email. When targets click the meeting invitation, they are prompted to authenticate using a threat actor-generated device code. The actor then receives the valid access token from the user interaction, stealing the authenticated session.

A device code authentication flow is a numeric or alphanumeric code used to authenticate an account from an input-constrained device that does not have the ability to perform an interactive authentication using a web flow and thus must perform this authentication on another device to sign-in. In device code phishing, threat actors exploit the device code authentication flow. 

During the attack, the threat actor generates a legitimate device code request and tricks the target into entering it into a legitimate sign-in page. This grants the actor access and enables them to capture the authentication—access and refresh—tokens that are generated, then use those tokens to access the target’s accounts and data. The actor can also use these phished authentication tokens to gain access to other services where the user has permissions, such as email or cloud storage, without needing a password. The threat actor continues to have access so long as the tokens remain valid. The attacker can then use the valid access token to move laterally within the environment.

![Diagram illustrating the device code phishing attack flow, where a threat actor tricks a victim into entering a device code into a legitimate sign-in page to capture authentication tokens.](https://cdn-riq-ti.azureedge.net/616161d1-b295-4c9c-aa83-f729bb187ef6)
 
*Device code phishing attack cycle*

**Storm-2372 phishing lure and access**

Storm-2372’s device code phishing campaign has been active since August 2024. Observed early activity indicates that Storm-2372 likely targeted potential victims using third-party messaging services including WhatsApp, Signal, and Microsoft Teams, falsely posing as a prominent person relevant to the target to develop rapport before sending subsequent invitations to online events or meetings through phishing emails.

![Screenshots of a phishing conversation where the attacker poses as a researcher inviting the target to a videoconference on security in Europe.](https://cdn-riq-ti.azureedge.net/0fdb4954-ac98-46c7-b7ae-49f46c8f02f8)
 
*Sample messages from the threat actor posing as a prominent person and building rapport on Signal*

These invitations lure the user into completing a device code authentication request emulating the experience of the messaging service, which provides Storm-2372 initial access to victim accounts and enables Graph API data collection activities, such as email harvesting.

![A fake Microsoft Teams meeting invitation used by threat actors to lure users into completing a device code authentication request.](https://cdn-riq-ti.azureedge.net/be7cf3ea-7633-4712-a134-98867885a052)
 
*Example of lure used in phishing campaign*

On the device code authentication page, the user is tricked into entering the code that the threat actor included as the ID for the fake Teams meeting invitation.

**Post-compromise activity**

Once the victim uses the device code to authenticate, the threat actor receives the valid access token. The threat actor then uses this valid session to move laterally within the newly compromised network by sending additional phishing messages containing links for device code authentication to other users through intra-organizational emails originating from the victim’s account.

![Microsoft authentication page prompting the user to enter a code to allow access.](https://cdn-riq-ti.azureedge.net/e576e46e-040b-4e3d-a6fa-5f80f2efc778)
 
*Legitimate device code authentication page*
 
Additionally, Microsoft observed Storm-2372 using Microsoft Graph to search through messages of the account they’ve compromised. The threat actor was using keyword searching to view messages containing words such as username, password, admin, teamviewer, anydesk, credentials, secret, ministry, and gov. Microsoft then observed email exfiltration via Microsoft Graph of the emails found from these searches. 

As of February 14, 2025, Microsoft has [observed](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/) Storm-2372 shifting to using the specific client ID for Microsoft Authentication Broker in the device code sign-in flow. Using this client ID enables Storm-2372 to receive a refresh token that can be used to request another token for the device registration service, and then register an actor-controlled device within Entra ID. With the same refresh token and the new device identity, Storm-2372 is able to obtain a Primary Refresh Token (PRT) and access an organization’s resources. We have observed Storm-2372 using the connected device to collect emails.

The actor has also been observed to use proxies that are regionally appropriate for the targets, likely in an attempt to further conceal the suspicious sign-in activity.   

While many of the mitigations and queries listed below still apply in this scenario, alerts involving anomalous token or PRT activity surrounding close-in-time device registrations may also be a useful method for identifying this shift in technique. Additionally, [enrollment restrictions](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity/devices/manage-device-identities)—limiting the user permissions that can enroll devices into your Microsoft Entra ID environment—can also help to address this attack behavior.

## Attribution
The actor that Microsoft tracks as Storm-2372 is a suspected nation-state actor working toward Russian state interests. It notably has used device code phishing to compromise targets of interest. Storm-2372 likely initially approaches targets through third-party messaging services, posing as a prominent individual relevant to the target to develop rapport before sending invites to online events or meetings. These invites lure the user into device code authentication that grants initial access to Storm-2372 and enables Graph API data collection activities such as email harvesting.

Storm-2372 targets include government, NGOs, IT services and technology, defense, telecommunications, health, higher education, and energy/oil and gas in Europe, North America, Africa, and the Middle East.

## MITRE ATT&CK Techniques observed
Storm-2372 has exhibited use of the following attack techniques. For standard industry documentation about these techniques, refer to the [MITRE ATT&CK framework](https://attack.mitre.org/).

**Initial Access**
 
- [T1566 Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/) | Use of links and attachments referencing Microsoft Teams chats

**Persistence**

- [T1134.001 Access Token Manipulation: Token Impersonation/Theft](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1134/001/) | Acquire access token through device code phishing
- [T1078.004 Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078/004/) | Persist as legitimate cloud identities and access resources available to that identity.

**Exfiltration**

- [TA0010 Exfiltration](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0010/) | Exfiltration of emails

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations.
 
- Only allow device code flow where necessary. Microsoft recommends [blocking device code flow wherever possible](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity/conditional-access/policy-block-authentication-flows). Where necessary, configure Microsoft Entra ID’s [device code flow](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity/conditional-access/concept-authentication-flows) in your Conditional Access policies.
- Educate users about common phishing techniques. Sign-in prompts should clearly identify the application being authenticated to. As of 2021, Microsoft Azure interactions prompt the user to confirm (Cancel or Continue) that they are signing in to the app they expect, which is an option frequently missing from phishing sign-ins.
- If suspected Storm-2372 or other device code phishing activity is identified, [revoke the user's refresh tokens by calling *revokeSignInSession*s](https://learn.microsoft.com/graph/api/user-revokesigninsessions). Consider [setting a Conditional Access Policy to force re-authentication](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity/conditional-access/policy-all-users-persistent-browser#create-a-conditional-access-policy) for users.
- [Implement a sign-in risk policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/identity-protection/howto-identity-protection-configure-risk-policies) to automate response to risky sign-ins. A sign-in risk represents the probability that a given authentication request isn't authorized by the identity owner. A sign-in risk-based policy can be implemented by adding a sign-in risk condition to Conditional Access policies that evaluates the risk level of a specific user or group. Based on the risk level (high/medium/low), a policy can be configured to block access or force multi-factor authentication. 
    - When a user is a high risk and [Conditional access evaluation is enabled](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity/conditional-access/concept-continuous-access-evaluation), the user’s access is revoked, and they are forced to re-authenticate.
    - For regular activity monitoring, use [Risky sign-in reports](https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_AAD_IAM/SecurityMenuBlade/~/RiskySignIns), which surface attempted and successful user access activities where the legitimate owner might not have performed the sign-in.
- Require [multifactor authentication (MFA)](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/admin/security-and-compliance/set-up-multi-factor-authentication). While certain attacks such as device code phishing attempt to evade MFA, implementation of MFA remains an essential pillar in identity security and is highly effective at stopping a variety of threats.
    - Leverage [phishing-resistant authentication methods](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity/authentication/concept-authentication-methods) such as FIDO Tokens, or [Microsoft Authenticator](https://www.microsoft.com/security/mobile-authenticator-app) with passkey. Avoid telephony-based MFA methods to avoid risks associated with SIM-jacking.
    - Block [legacy authentication with Microsoft Entra by using Conditional Access](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity/conditional-access/block-legacy-authentication). Legacy authentication protocols do not have the ability to enforce MFA, as legacy MFA (per-user MFA prompts) is susceptible to abuse.
- Centralize your organization’s identity management into a single platform. If your organization is a hybrid environment, integrate your on-premises directories with your cloud directories. If your organization is using a third-party for identity management, ensure this data is being logged in a SIEM or connected to Microsoft Entra to fully monitor for malicious identity access from a centralized location. The added benefits to centralizing all identity data is to facilitate implementation of [Single Sign On (SSO)](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/manage-apps/plan-sso-deployment) and provide users with a more seamless authentication process, as well as configure Entra ID’s machine learning models to operate on all identity data, thus learning the difference between legitimate access and malicious access quicker and easier. It is recommended to [synchronize all user accounts](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/hybrid/connect/how-to-connect-password-hash-synchronization) except administrative and high privileged ones when doing this to maintain a boundary between the on-premises environment and the cloud environment, in case of a breach.
- [Secure accounts with credential hygiene](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/architecture/security-operations-introduction): practice the [principle of least privilege](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/roles/delegate-by-task) and audit privileged account activity in your Entra ID environments to slow and stop attackers.

## Detections/Hunting Queries
**Microsoft Entra ID Protection**

The following Microsoft Entra ID Protection risk detections inform Entra ID user risk events and can indicate associated threat activity, including unusual user activity consistent with known attack patterns identified by Microsoft Threat Intelligence research: 
 
- [Activity from Anonymous IP address](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/id-protection/concept-identity-protection-risks) (RiskEventType: anonymizedIPAddress)
- [Microsoft Entra threat intelligence (sign-in)](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/id-protection/concept-identity-protection-risks) (RiskEventType: investigationsThreatIntelligence)

### Microsoft Defender for Office 365
The following alerts might indicate threat activity associated with this threat. These alerts, however, can be triggered by unrelated threat activity and are not monitored in the status cards provided with this report. 
 
- This email has traits consistent with phishing
- This HTML has traits consistent with phishing

## Microsoft for XDR Advanced Hunting
**NOTE**: The following sample queries let you search for a week's worth of events. To explore up to 30 days’ worth of raw data to inspect events in your network and locate potential related indicators for more than a week, go to the **Advanced hunting** page > **Query** tab, select the calendar dropdown menu to update your query to hunt for the **Last 30 days**.    

**Device code phishing attempts**

The following query can help identify possible device code phishing attempts. [Run query](https://security.microsoft.com/v2/advanced-hunting?query=H4sIAE6Gr2cAA81Wy07bQBS960r9B5cVkQKESqiqEIs0sIjUVhWEbpGbmCRgJ5FtSKmqfjvnnpnJ2LGTmFatKmvsedz344xjiSSXQDJ5wFjIVIYYc66uMSJJpScx9--xDuQMI5EQXHo2xUxPf2C1D44UK09_IY_Yn4E2k9fyCpzm-YmxlAklRJh3QZ1T70wG8gQ7dHeKVQCpewWJXcxi0C1BMcJJGxR7Vu8VKELw9DG-YGcuY8rP8JQpL_DW8xR0IaginLRwrjsB-LOCRtUzgK0pozLGLJA3jMKedDC2-eXiMYEW443OMrmhnU_Wu4SaVH6GcYtIHGI9x_4RdEeIoZ5H9HtMOc4bv3NYI0WjGfM0Kkg034SnR3iH8CqHXW_XtLl9jcy6j5F8Z_5n4DDZGzI6mulrZG9m60RtcNlK4WsdZVX6gl7cgWfI2vS5GOCbMLIq3a0yUIWYLRiVulpq1-RC9z6z-pfM-718srViKqIP3zxfe4OfLTml_Ud4esy82hkg_qaWLqErw47m-grzMXgOWKGuvnNyaQdOyJNzz_m5JNWIMVQ9se3XKW2IbH3nrFLXr1kpB007e1sdqw8z8KoejXMOf5pmc0TunBabfNbxnZa8q7PZRU9jtwuHunjOSxxFJPpALeFWjz1C9PAe2ZpTnZ2dSFbtBfX9F7u9Sd6qMSxqcBX1kb2qqHAObSklj0s-ewQ9htVawSf2q-vOP-_rO1AYi-5tVZ_xO6OUl9xBc0qp07otcvs1iBGgG-sQRm-DbxYdIkZE-Q-Akon14RBPIO_sejeK1aPVJXYWtu8d4lSt2YQ-7RfVQ5sYZDDO4KPT2Mc92MV8tLovPfKpX0WU-2o7bWR7L2B813tFK-1Y3uMxWFi8tTWyTzbfQ941GbNq4nrCvtb5g5Xv0dB3zyOt8DjrUPTB1kvb5l7jOLG6xsT1jBgQgF9zFFoOU9NGw4Kavczhyqtb-pkUzhbUkfGt8Q6IkHrDxDvxupwLjwKbcbuMgf8XYk9WVVzOUdHmLk68Rese_z00_x1U3pSd7ehcd284FPYYbDqjKklznjAOqfW-TmIxXvp_ekPbcmio0rZW3bYJP3qkT4kc4erPySFDFS9e5r3a6v95Y_Zsk0g0q0GHS816pXlVqI1_VtEteQZGMzOKWg0AAA&timeRangeId=week)

`let suspiciousUserClicks = materialize(UrlClickEvents`

title: Multiple Russian Threat Actors Targeting Microsoft Device Code Authentication
content:
## Snapshot Multiple Russian threat actors have been conducting social engineering and spear-phishing campaigns to compromise Microsoft 365 accounts using Device Code Authentication phishing. Volexity has identified three distinct threat groups—CozyLarch (tracked by Microsoft as [Midnight Blizzard](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/d825313b053efea45228ff1f4cb17c8b5433dcd2f86353e28be2d484ce874616)), UTA0304, and UTA0307—leveraging this technique in targeted attacks since mid-January 2025. ## Description These campaigns primarily involve impersonating officials from organizations like the U.S. Department of State, the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense, and the European Parliament to deceive victims into granting account access. Attackers often establish trust through real-time communication on secure messaging apps like Signal and Element before directing victims to phishing emails containing links to Microsoft's Device Code Authentication workflow. Unlike traditional phishing attempts, these emails do not contain malicious links or attachments; instead, they direct users to legitimate Microsoft infrastructure, making detection by both users and automated security solutions more difficult. Once victims enter the provided code, attackers gain persistent access to their accounts, enabling data exfiltration and further espionage activities. Threat actors have varied their engagement tactics, including initiating Microsoft Teams meetings, granting access to external Microsoft 365 applications, and luring targets into secure chatrooms. CozyLarch has been observed sending phishing emails from Gmail accounts, using proxy IP addresses from U.S. mobile networks, and leveraging legitimate Microsoft URLs to facilitate authentication. UTA0307, in contrast, employs a more patient approach, waiting for engagement before sending a phishing link that generates a new Microsoft Device Code. When victims enter the code, attackers seize control of the M365 account and register multi-factor authentication to an app they control. ## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context Microsoft is also tracking other groups using similar techniques. Also in February, [Microsoft Threat Intelligence Center discovered](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/) an active and successful device code phishing campaign by a threat actor we track as Storm-2372. Our ongoing investigation indicates that this campaign has been active since August 2024 with the actor creating lures that resemble messaging app experiences including WhatsApp, Signal, and Microsoft Teams. Storm-2372’s targets during this time have included government, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), information technology (IT) services and technology, defense, telecommunications, health, higher education, and energy/oil and gas in Europe, North America, Africa, and the Middle East. Microsoft assesses with medium confidence that Storm-2372 aligns with Russian interests, victimology, and tradecraft.   In device code phishing, threat actors exploit the device code authentication flow to capture authentication tokens, which they then use to access target accounts, and further gain access to data and other services that the compromised account has access to. This technique could enable persistent access as long as the tokens remain valid, making this attack technique attractive to threat actors. Device code phishing is particularly effective because it removes traditional red flags such as malicious links or attachments, allowing adversaries to bypass automated security filters and deceive even cautious users. Malicious activity leveraging legitimate services remains a persistent and formidable challenge for defenders. Cybercriminals and state-sponsored actors increasingly exploit trusted platforms to evade detection, making it difficult for security tools and end users to distinguish between benign and malicious activity. For example, in January 2025, [Sophos X-Ops researchers identified](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/cfccd682) two threat actor groups, STAC5143 and STAC5777, abusing Microsoft Office 365 functionalities to infiltrate organizations. These attackers initiated chats or meetings through Microsoft Teams, taking advantage of default configurations to establish initial contact. Their techniques ranged from exploiting built-in Teams remote control and side-loading DLLs to deploying Python-based backdoors and leveraging Microsoft Quick Assist for persistence and credential theft. With state-sponsored threat actors and financially motivated cybercriminals alike adopting these techniques, the exploitation of both cloud-based and on-premises authentication mechanisms is an escalating threat that demands greater vigilance and adaptive defenses. ## Recommendations Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat.  - Only allow device code flow where necessary. Microsoft recommends [blocking device code flow wherever possible](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity/conditional-access/policy-block-authentication-flows). Where necessary, configure Microsoft Entra ID’s [device code flow](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity/conditional-access/concept-authentication-flows) in your Conditional Access policies. - Educate users about common phishing techniques. Sign-in prompts should clearly identify the application being authenticated to. As of 2021, Microsoft Azure interactions prompt the user to confirm (“Cancel” or “Continue”) that they are signing in to the app they expect, which is an option frequently missing from phishing sign-ins. - If suspected Storm-2372 or other device code phishing activity is identified, [revoke the user’s refresh tokens by calling *revokeSignInSessions*](https://learn.microsoft.com/graph/api/user-revokesigninsessions). Consider [setting a Conditional Access Policy to force re-authentication](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity/conditional-access/policy-all-users-persistent-browser#create-a-conditional-access-policy) for users. - [Implement a sign-in risk policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/identity-protection/howto-identity-protection-configure-risk-policies) to automate response to risky sign-ins. A sign-in risk represents the probability that a given authentication request isn’t authorized by the identity owner. A sign-in risk-based policy can be implemented by adding a sign-in risk condition to Conditional Access policies that evaluates the risk level of a specific user or group. Based on the risk level (high/medium/low), a policy can be configured to block access or force multi-factor authentication. - When a user is a high risk and [Conditional access evaluation is enabled](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity/conditional-access/concept-continuous-access-evaluation), the user’s access is revoked, and they are forced to re-authenticate. - For regular activity monitoring, use [Risky sign-in reports](https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_AAD_IAM/SecurityMenuBlade/~/RiskySignIns), which surface attempted and successful user access activities where the legitimate owner might not have performed the sign-in. - Require [multifactor authentication (MFA)](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/admin/security-and-compliance/set-up-multi-factor-authentication). While certain attacks such as device code phishing attempt to evade MFA, implementation of MFA remains an essential pillar in identity security and is highly effective at stopping a variety of threats. - Leverage [phishing-resistant authentication methods](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity/authentication/concept-authentication-methods) such as FIDO Tokens, or [Microsoft Authenticator](https://www.microsoft.com/security/mobile-authenticator-app) with passkey. Avoid telephony-based MFA methods to avoid risks associated with SIM-jacking. - Block [legacy authentication with Microsoft Entra by using Conditional Access](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity/conditional-access/block-legacy-authentication). Legacy authentication protocols do not have the ability to enforce MFA, as legacy MFA (per-user MFA prompts) is susceptible to abuse. - Centralize your organization’s identity management into a single platform. If your organization is a hybrid environment, integrate your on-premises directories with your cloud directories. If your organization is using a third-party for identity management, ensure this data is being logged in a SIEM or connected to Microsoft Entra to fully monitor for malicious identity access from a centralized location. The added benefits to centralizing all identity data is to facilitate implementation of [Single Sign On (SSO)](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/manage-apps/plan-sso-deployment) and provide users with a more seamless authentication process, as well as configure Entra ID’s machine learning models to operate on all identity data, thus learning the difference between legitimate access and malicious access quicker and easier. It is recommended to [synchronize all user accounts](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/hybrid/connect/how-to-connect-password-hash-synchronization) except administrative and high privileged ones when doing this to maintain a boundary between the on-premises environment and the cloud environment, in case of a breach. - [Secure accounts with credential hygiene](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/architecture/security-operations-introduction): practice the [principle of least privilege](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/roles/delegate-by-task) and audit privileged account activity in your Entra ID environments to slow and stop attackers. ## Detections/Hunting Queries The following query can help identify possible device code phishing attempts: | `let suspiciousUserClicks = materialize(UrlClickEvents`

`    ``| where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed", "UrlScanInProgress", "UrlErrorPage") or IsClickedThrough != "0"`

`    ``| where UrlChain has_any ("microsoft.com/devicelogin", "login.microsoftonline.com/common/oauth2/deviceauth")`

`    ``| extend AccountUpn = tolower(AccountUpn)`

`    ``| project ClickTime = Timestamp, ActionType, UrlChain, NetworkMessageId, Url, AccountUpn);`

`//Check for Risky Sign-In in the short time window`

`let interestedUsersUpn = suspiciousUserClicks`

`    ``| where isnotempty(AccountUpn)`

`    ``| distinct AccountUpn;`

`let suspiciousSignIns = materialize(AADSignInEventsBeta`

`    ``| where ErrorCode == 0`

`    ``| where AccountUpn in~ (interestedUsersUpn)`

`    ``| where RiskLevelDuringSignIn in (10, 50, 100)`

`    ``| extend AccountUpn = tolower(AccountUpn)`

`    ``| join kind=inner suspiciousUserClicks on AccountUpn`

`    ``| where (Timestamp - ClickTime) between (-2min .. 7min)`

`    ``| project Timestamp, ReportId, ClickTime, AccountUpn, RiskLevelDuringSignIn, SessionId, IPAddress, Url`

`);`

`//Validate errorCode 50199 followed by success in 5 minute time interval for the interested user, which suggests a pause for the code which the user provided from the phishing email`

`let interestedSessionUsers = suspiciousSignIns`

`let shortIntervalSignInAttemptUsers = materialize(AADSignInEventsBeta`

`    ``| where ErrorCode in (0, 50199)`

`    ``| summarize ErrorCodes = make_set(ErrorCode) by AccountUpn, CorrelationId, SessionId`

`    ``| where ErrorCodes has_all (0, 50199)`

title: China-linked Espionage Tools Used in Ransomware Attacks
content:
## Snapshot
Researchers at Symantec identified a ransomware attack against an Asian software and services company involving tools typically used by China-linked espionage actors.

## Description
The attack, which occurred in late 2024, utilized RA World ransomware and a number of tools that have previously been associated with espionage, not cybercrime. These tools include a a malicious DLL named toshdpapi.dll and a variant of PlugX, which were used to compromise the Foreign Ministry of two countries in southeastern Europe, the government ministry in two Southeast Asian countries, and a telecommunications operator between July 2024 and January 2025.

The ransomware attack, which occurred in November 2024, leveraged the same malicious DLL and PlugX malware variant as the identified espionage attacks. Machine's on the victim's network were encrypted with RA World ransomware and attackers demanded a $2 million ransom payment. 
 
According to Symantec, evidence suggests that the attacker may have prior experience with ransomware. [Palo Alto](https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/ra-world-ransomware-group-updates-tool-set/) linked other RA World ransomware attacks to Bronze Starlight (Emperor Dragonfly), a China-based group known for deploying various ransomware strains. The attacker also used NPS, a proxy tool previously associated with Bronze Starlight. [SentinelOne](https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/chinese-entanglement-dll-hijacking-in-the-asian-gambling-sector/) has reported Bronze Starlight’s involvement in attacks using LockFile, AtomSilo, NightSky, and LockBit ransomware. Bronze Starlight is tracked by Microsoft as [Cinnamon Tempest](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/a4c0819b0cc1c75cd05538cc22746e21cd5c0cecefd7cec09bced6e202fdfa39). 
 
Symantec notes that it remains unclear why an actor linked to espionage would conduct a ransomware attack. Unlike North Korean threat groups, Chinese espionage actors have not historically engaged in financially motivated cybercrime. One theory suggests that the ransomware was used as a cover-up for espionage activities, but this seems unlikely given the ineffective obfuscation of forensic evidence and the seemingly random target.
 
The attacker also engaged in ransom negotiations, indicating a genuine intent to profit rather than simply misdirect investigators. Symantec assesses the most plausible explanation is that an individual within a state-sponsored espionage group leveraged their access and tools for personal financial gain.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
First observed in April 2023, [RA World ransomware](https://thesecmaster.com/blog/ra-world-ransomware) leveraged Babuk ransomware source code to develop its payload. Initially, the operators behind RA World focused their attacks on the United States and South Korea before expanding their targeting to include organizations in Germany, India, Taiwan, and Latin America. The group typically employs a double-extortion model, exfiltrating data before encryption and threatening to publicly release it if ransom demands are not met.

## Recommendations
Apply these mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations.

- Educate users about [preventing malware infections](https://www.microsoft.com/security/business/security-101/what-is-malware?ocid=magicti_ta_abbreviatedmktgpage"%20\t%20"_blank), such as ignoring or deleting unsolicited and unexpected emails or attachments sent through instant messaging applications or social networks as well as suspicious phone calls.
- Invest in advanced anti-phishing solutions that monitor incoming emails and visited websites. [Microsoft Defender for Office 365](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender/microsoft-365-security-center-mdo?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) brings together incident and alert management across email, devices, and identities, centralizing investigations for email-based threats.
- Apply Microsoft’s [security best practices for Microsoft Teams](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/MicrosoftTeams/teams-security-best-practices-for-safer-messaging) to safeguard Teams users.
- Consider [blocking or uninstalling](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/client-management/client-tools/quick-assist#disable-quick-assist-within-your-organization) Quick Assist and other remote monitoring and management tools if these tools are not in use in your environment. Apply mitigations listed in [Microsoft’s technique profile on abuse of remote monitoring and management tools](https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/44b8f927-5ab5-46bb-bb79-7ca2d4e30156/overview).
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a huge majority of new and unknown variants.
- Turn on [tamper protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) features to prevent attackers from stopping security services.
- Run [EDR in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus doesn’t detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach.
- Enable [network protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-network-protection?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to prevent applications or users from accessing malicious domains and other malicious content on the internet.
- Enable [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in full automated mode to allow Microsoft Defender for Endpoint to take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.
- Use [device discovery](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/device-discovery?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to increase your visibility into your network by finding unmanaged devices on your network and onboarding them to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Refer to [Microsoft’s human-operated ransomware overview](https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/05658b6c-dc62-496d-ad3c-c6a795a33c27/analystreport) for general hardening recommendations against ransomware attacks.

Microsoft Defender XDR customers can turn on [attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to prevent common attack techniques used in ransomware attacks. Attack surface reduction rules are sweeping settings that are effective at stopping entire classes of threats:

- Ransom and lateral movement stage:
    - [Block process creations originating from PsExec and WMI commands](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-process-creations-originating-from-psexec-and-wmi-commands)
    - [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion)
    - [Use advanced protection against ransomware](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#use-advanced-protection-against-ransomware)
    - [Block credential stealing from the Windows local security authority subsystem (lsass.exe)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-credential-stealing-from-the-windows-local-security-authority-subsystem)
- Common techniques:
    - [Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-execution-of-potentially-obfuscated-scripts)
    - [Block JavaScript or VBScript from launching downloaded executable content](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-javascript-or-vbscript-from-launching-downloaded-executable-content)
- Common entry vectors:
    - [Block all Office applications from creating child processes](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-all-office-applications-from-creating-child-processes)
    - [Block Office communication application from creating child processes](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-office-communication-application-from-creating-child-processes)
    - [Block Office applications from creating executable content](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-office-applications-from-injecting-code-into-other-processes)
    - [Block Office applications from injecting code into other processes](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-office-applications-from-injecting-code-into-other-processes)

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects threat components as the following malware:
 
- [Trojan:Win32/Wacatac](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:Win32/Wacatac.B!ml)

## References
[China-linked Espionage Tools Used in Ransomware Attacks](https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/chinese-espionage-ransomware). Symantec (accessed 2025-02-13)

title: You've Got Malware: FINALDRAFT Hides in Your Drafts
content:
## Snapshot
Elastic Security Labs identified a new malware family named FINALDRAFT, which targets a foreign ministry with a custom loader called PATHLOADER and a backdoor.

## Description
FINALDRAFT is a 64-bit C++ malware that specializes in data exfiltration and process injection, with capabilities for advanced post-exploitation. It uses Microsoft's Graph API for command and control (C2) communications, abusing Outlook mail service for command requests and responses, which are Zlib compressed, AES encrypted, and Base64 encoded.

The malware registers 37 command handlers for process injection, file manipulation, and network proxy capabilities, and can inject into running processes or create hidden processes for injection. It also has the ability to proxy data to C2 via UDP and TCP listeners and a named pipe client, and employs file manipulation techniques that include overwriting data before deletion and copying files at the NTFS cluster level if standard methods fail. The malware includes several modules, such as a network enumeration module that mimics the ipconfig command, a PowerShell execution module that bypasses ETW logging and anti-malware scans, and a custom Pass-the-Hash toolkit for lateral movement.

An ELF variant of FINALDRAFT was also discovered, which supports more transport protocols but has fewer features, suggesting it is under development. This variant can execute shell commands and resolve the path of the currently running executable for self-deletion. An older FINALDRAFT PE sample was identified, which supports fewer commands and includes an HTTP transport channel.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat.
 
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/linux-preferences) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown threats.
- Run [EDR in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode?view=o365-worldwide?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus does not detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach.
- Allow [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations?view=o365-worldwide?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in full automated mode to allow Microsoft Defender for Endpoint to take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.
- [Enable](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-controlled-folders) controlled folder access.
- Ensure that [tamper protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection#how-do-i-configure-or-manage-tamper-protection) is enabled in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Enable [network protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-network-protection) in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Follow the credential hardening recommendations in the [on-premises credential theft overview](https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/9382203e-5155-4b5e-af74-21562b1004d5/analystreport) to defend against common credential theft techniques like LSASS access.
- [Enable](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-credential-stealing-from-the-windows-local-security-authority-subsystem) LSA protection.

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects threat components as the following malware:
 
- Trojan:Win64/SpyLoader.AB!MTB
- Trojan:Linux/Multiverze

title: From South America to Southeast Asia: The Fragile Web of REF7707
content:
#### Targeted Geolocations
- South America  
- Southeast Asia



#### Targeted Industries
- Government Agencies & Services



## Snapshot
Elastic Security Labs identified a campaign by threat actors, dubbed REF7707, targeting a South American foreign ministry with connections to other compromises in Southeast Asia. The campaign utilized novel malware families including finaldraft, guidloader, and pathloader.

## Description
The initial infiltration involved the use of Microsoft's certutil application to download malicious files after the attackers had obtained valid network credentials, which they then used for lateral movement. Finaldraft, a sophisticated remote administration tool, was executed via a renamed Windows-signed debugger and maintained in memory through Scheduled Tasks. This malware is capable of accepting add-on modules, using Microsoft’s Graph API for command and control, and operating across different operating systems with both Windows and ELF binary versions.

The attackers also used the diskshadow.exe utility to extract sensitive Registry hives and the Active Directory database, compressing them with 7zip. They gathered system and domain information and established persistence through Scheduled Tasks. The malware's command and control infrastructure also included several domains with servers in Southeast Asia, using Cloudflare-issued TLS certificates.

Despite the campaign's technical competence, poor operational security led to the exposure of additional adversary-owned infrastructure. The investigation revealed that finaldraft and associated loaders use third-party services like Google's Firebase, Pastebin, and a Southeast Asian University to host encrypted payloads. The geographic distribution of related samples and infrastructure suggests a focus on Southeast Asia and South America, with significant operational security failures providing insights into the adversary's tactics and infrastructure.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat:
 
- Enforce MFA on all accounts, remove users excluded from MFA, and strictly [require MFA](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/identity-protection/howto-identity-protection-configure-mfa-policy?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) from all devices, in all locations, at all times.
- Enable passwordless authentication methods (for example, Windows Hello, FIDO keys, or Microsoft Authenticator) for accounts that support passwordless. For accounts that still require passwords, use authenticator apps like Microsoft Authenticator for MFA. Learn [what authentication and verification methods are available in Microsoft Entra ID](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/authentication/concept-authentication-methods).
- For MFA that uses authenticator apps, ensure that the app requires a code to be typed in where possible, as many intrusions where MFA was enabled still succeeded due to users clicking “Yes” on the prompt on their phones even when they were not at their [devices](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/how-to-mfa-number-match?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc).
- Encourage users to use Microsoft Edge and other web browsers that support [SmartScreen](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/web-protection-overview?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc), which identifies and blocks malicious websites, including phishing sites, scam sites, and sites that host malware.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus, or the equivalent for your antivirus product, to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown variants.

Microsoft Defender customers can [turn on attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to prevent common attack techniques used in infostealer infections. Attack surface reduction rules are sweeping settings that stop entire classes of threats including, infostealers, credential theft, and ransomware. The following bullet points offer more guidance on specific mitigation advice: 

- [Turn on PUA protection in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/detect-block-potentially-unwanted-apps-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc)
- [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion)
- [Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-execution-of-potentially-obfuscated-scripts)

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects threat components as the following malware:
 
- [Trojan:Win64/SpyLoader.AB!MTB](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:Win64/SpyLoader.AB!MTB)

title: BTMOB RAT: Newly Discovered Android Malware Spreading via Phishing Sites
content:
## Snapshot
Researchers at Cyble Research and Intelligence Labs (CRIL) have identified a new Android malware named BTMOB RAT, which has evolved from the SpySolr malware.

## Description
BTMOB RAT is being distributed through phishing sites that mimic legitimate streaming services, such as the Turkish platform iNat TV, and fake mining platforms. The malware leverages Android’s Accessibility Service to perform a variety of malicious activities, including keylogging, screen capturing, and automated credential theft. It communicates with a command-and-control (C&C) server via WebSocket, enabling real-time data theft and remote execution of commands.

BTMOB RAT supports a range of harmful actions, such as live screen sharing, file management, audio recording, and web injections to steal sensitive information. The malware has been actively marketed on Telegram by its developers, who offer paid licenses and regular updates, suggesting an ongoing effort to refine its capabilities.

CRIL’s analysis indicates that the malware’s latest version, BTMOB RAT v2.5, retains structural similarities to SpySolr, reinforcing its lineage. It has been observed executing various commands, including stealing login credentials, manipulating screen activity, and unlocking infected devices. The threat actor behind BTMOB RAT appears to be monetizing the malware while continuously updating its features, making it a persistent risk to Android users.

## Recommendations
- Only install applications from trusted sources and official stores.
- If a device is no longer receiving updates, strongly consider replacing it with a new device.
- Use mobile solutions such as [Microsoft Defender for Endpoint on Android](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/microsoft-defender-endpoint-android?view=o365-worldwide)to detect malicious applications
    - Always keep Install unknown apps disabled on the Android device to prevent apps from being installed from unknown sources.
- Evaluate whether [Microsoft Defender for Internet of Things (IoT)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/defender-for-iot/organizations/overview) services are applicable to your IoT environment.

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects threat components as the following malware:

title: NetSupport RAT Delivered via ClickFix Technique for Initial Access
content:
## Snapshot
Researchers at eSentire Threat Response Unit (TRU) have detected a significant increase in incidents involving the NetSupport Remote Access Trojan (RAT) since early January 2025.

## Description
This RAT, originally a legitimate IT support tool known as NetSupport Manager, has been repurposed by cybercriminals to gain comprehensive control over victims' systems. It allows for real-time screen monitoring, keyboard and mouse manipulation, file transfers, and execution of malicious commands. The surge in NetSupport RAT incidents is attributed to the "ClickFix" Initial Access Vector (IAV), a social engineering method that deceives users into executing malicious PowerShell commands, which in turn download and run the RAT.

The [ClickFix](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/67d03ba9) technique involves a fake CAPTCHA page on compromised websites that prompts users to copy and paste PowerShell commands, leading to the installation of the [NetSupport RAT](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/bfa5316082cf01926a5507fa0a9f1771394bf3bf803e332de4aa62af8c55fb44). The payloads are often disguised within URLs that appear to be image files, with paths containing ".png," and the RAT's Command-and-Control (C2) gateway URLs frequently include "fakeurl.htm." Cybercriminal groups such as TA569 and SmartApe SG have been known to use the NetSupport RAT in their operations, which can result in ransomware attacks, data breaches, and significant business disruptions.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
[ClickFix](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/67d03ba9) was initially used by the threat group TA571 and the [ClearFake](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/c75089e9) cluster, and has since been adopted by various attackers impersonating well-known software and services. It uses fake error message dialogue boxes that trick users into copying and pasting commands, leading to malware downloads like [AsyncRAT](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/e9216610feb409dfb620b28e510f2ae2582439dfc7c7e265815ff1a776016776), [Lumma Stealer](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/33933578825488511c30b0728dd3c4f8b5ca20e41c285a56f796eb39f57531ad), and NetSupport. The technique bypasses browser security features, making it a stealthy tool for infiltrating systems, particularly in sectors like [transportation and logistics](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/f51acbdb). In [July 2024](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/85fea057), McAfee researchers reported its global use in July 2024, with incidents in the US, Canada, Mexico, Australia, Brazil, and China.

NetSupport Manager is a legitimate remote administration tool for IT support, but when misused by cybercriminals, it becomes a Remote Access Trojan (RAT), known as NetSupport RAT. This malware allows attackers to take control of compromised devices, record keystrokes, capture audio and video, transfer files, and execute commands. Its stealthy nature and ability to operate without elevated privileges make it difficult to detect, making it a popular choice for data theft and maintaining persistent access. NetSupport RAT is typically spread through phishing campaigns or bundled with other malware.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations.
 
- Use [Windows Defender Application Control or AppLocker](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/windows-defender-application-control/wdac-and-applocker-overview?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc)to create policies to block unapproved IT management tools
    - Both solutions include functionality to block specific software publisher certificates: WDAC [file rule levels](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/windows-defender-application-control/select-types-of-rules-to-create?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#windows-defender-application-control-file-rule-levels) allow administrators to specify the level at which they want to trust their applications, including listing certificates as untrusted. AppLocker’s [publisher rule condition](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/windows-defender-application-control/applocker/understanding-the-publisher-rule-condition-in-applocker?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) is available for files that are digitally signed, which can enable organizations to block non-approved remote monitoring and management (RMM) instances that include publisher information.
    - Microsoft Defender for Endpoint also provides functionality to block specific signed applications using the [block certificate action](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/t5/microsoft-defender-for-endpoint/indicators-enhancements-allow-block-by-certificates-amp-more/ba-p/1377586).
- Block connections to RMM software distribution sites via network blocking such as perimeter firewall rules if not in use in your environment. 
    - Organizations can use the [Configuration Manager to configure firewall and port settings](https://learn.microsoft.com/mem/configmgr/core/clients/deploy/windows-firewall-and-port-settings-for-clients?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc).
- For approved RMM systems used in your environment, enforce security settings where possible to implement MFA
- Consider searching for unapproved RMM software installations (Microsoft Threat Intelligence’s [Advanced hunting queries are available on GitHub](https://github.com/jischell-msft/RemoteManagementMonitoringTools)). If an unapproved installation is discovered, reset passwords for accounts used to install the RMM services. If a system-level account was used to install the software, further investigation may be warranted.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a huge majority of new and unknown variants.
- Turn on the following [attack surface reduction rule](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/overview-attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to block or audit activity associated with this threat. These rules, which can be configured by all Microsoft Defender Antivirus customers and not just those using the EDR solution, offer significant hardening against attacks.  

    - [Use advanced protection against ransomware](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#use-advanced-protection-against-ransomware).
    - [Block process creations originating from PsExec and WMI commands](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-process-creations-originating-from-psexec-and-wmi-commands). Some organizations may experience compatibility issues with this rule on certain server systems but should deploy it to other systems to prevent lateral movement originating from PsExec and WMI.
    - Assess rule impact before deployment: You can assess how an attack surface reduction rule might impact your network by opening the [security recommendation](https://security.microsoft.com/security-recommendations?ocid=magicti_ta_tvmsecreco) for that rule in threat and vulnerability management. In the recommendation details pane, check the user impact to determine what percentage of your devices can accept a new policy enabling the rule in blocking mode without adverse impact to user productivity.

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects threat components as the following malware:
 
- [TrojanDownloader:JS/NetSupport](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=TrojanDownloader:JS/NetSupport!MTB)
- [Trojan:VBS/NetSupportRat](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:VBS/NetSupportRat!MTB)

### Microsoft Defender for Endpoint
Alerts with the following titles in the security center can indicate threat activity on your network:
 
- Possible NetSupport Manager activity

The following alerts might also indicate threat activity associated with this threat, if Microsoft Defender for Endpoint is set to block mode.

- An active 'Netsupport' malware was blocked
- 'Netsupport' malware was detected
- 'NetSupport' malware was detected during a scheduled scan
- 'Netsupport' malware was prevented
- 'NetSupport' malware was prevented on a domain controller

## References
[NetSupport RAT Delivered via ClickFix Technique for Initial Access](https://www.esentire.com/security-advisories/netsupport-rat-clickfix-distribution#new_tab). eSentire (accessed 2025-02-11)
 
[NetSupportRAT](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/bfa5316082cf01926a5507fa0a9f1771394bf3bf803e332de4aa62af8c55fb44). Microsoft (accessed 2025-02-11)
 
[Security Brief: ClickFix Social Engineering Technique Floods Threat Landscape](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/67d03ba9). Microsoft (accessed 2025-02-11)
 
[AsyncRAT](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/e9216610feb409dfb620b28e510f2ae2582439dfc7c7e265815ff1a776016776). Microsoft (accessed 2025-02-11)
 
[Lumma Stealer](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/33933578825488511c30b0728dd3c4f8b5ca20e41c285a56f796eb39f57531ad). Microsoft (accessed 2025-02-11)
 
[From Clipboard to Compromise: A PowerShell Self-Pwn](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/c75089e9). Microsoft (accessed 2025-02-11)
 
[ClickFix Deception: A Social Engineering Tactic to Deploy Malware](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/85fea057). Microsoft (accessed 2025-02-11)
