title: Sandworm APT Targets Ukrainian Users with Trojanized Microsoft KMS Activation Tools in Cyber Espionage Campaigns
content:
## Snapshot
Researchers at EclecticIQ have identified a cyber espionage campaign orchestrated by Sandworm APT (Similary activity tracked by Microsoft as Seashell Blizzard) targeting Ukrainian Windows users.

## Description
The campaign, which has been active since late 2023, leverages pirated Microsoft Key Management Service (KMS) activators and counterfeit Windows updates to distribute the BACKORDER loader. This loader then deploys Dark Crystal RAT (DcRAT) for data exfiltration and espionage.

The attackers have exploited the widespread use of cracked software in Ukraine, including within government institutions, to facilitate large-scale espionage and network compromise. The campaign utilizes trojanized files, such as a ZIP file named “KMSAuto++x64\_v1.8.4.zip,” to deliver the malware, which establishes a remote connection to command-and-control servers and exfiltrates sensitive data. The BACKORDER loader, which is compiled in GO, creates scheduled tasks to maintain persistent access and uses Living Off the Land Binaries (LOLBAS) for defense evasion. Additionally, a new RDP backdoor named Kalambur has been discovered, which uses TOR for stealth and includes functionalities for system information gathering, OpenSSH deployment, and RDP backdoor setup.

The campaign's infrastructure is linked through shared registrars and email addresses, indicating a coordinated operation by Sandworm members. The group's activities, including the use of trojanized pirated software distributed through Ukrainian-speaking forums, have been linked to unauthorized access to a Ukrainian utility company's systems, aligning with Russia's strategy of destabilizing Ukraine's critical infrastructure.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
Microsoft tracks some Sandworm APT activity as [Seashell Blizzard. Read more about them here.](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/cf1e406a16835d56cf614430aea3962d7ed99f01ee3d9ee3048078288e5201bb)

Seashell Blizzard, a Russian state-sponsored threat actor, has a long history of cyber-enabled sabotage, espionage, and destructive attacks, particularly against Ukrainian infrastructure. The recent Sandworm APT campaign, which leverages trojanized Microsoft KMS activation tools to target Ukrainian users, aligns with Seashell Blizzard’s broader operational patterns. Known for attacks like NotPetya (2017) and FoxBlade (2022), Seashell Blizzard frequently exploits trusted software and supply chains to infiltrate targets. This latest campaign reinforces the group's strategy of weaponizing legitimate tools to establish persistent access, likely in support of intelligence gathering or pre-positioning for future disruptive operations. Organizations should remain vigilant against compromised software deployments and enhance defenses against advanced cyber threats.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations.

To harden networks against the Seashell Blizzard activity listed above, defenders can implement the following:

**Strengthen operating environment configuration**
 
- Utilize a vulnerability management system, such as [Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-vulnerability-management/defender-vulnerability-management), to manage vulnerabilities, weaknesses, and remediation efforts across your environment's operating systems, software inventories, and [network devices](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/network-devices).
- Require [multifactor authentication (MFA)](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/admin/security-and-compliance/set-up-multi-factor-authentication). While certain attacks such as AiTM phishing attempt to circumvent MFA, implementation of MFA remains an essential pillar in identity security and is highly effective at stopping a variety of threats.
    - Leverage [phishing-resistant authentication methods](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity/authentication/concept-authentication-methods) such as FIDO Tokens, or [Microsoft Authenticator](https://www.microsoft.com/security/mobile-authenticator-app) with passkey. Avoid telephony-based MFA methods to avoid risks associated with SIM-jacking.
- Implement Entra ID [Conditional Access authentication strength](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/concept-authentication-strengths) to require phishing-resistant authentication for employees and external users for critical apps.
- Encourage users to use Microsoft Edge and other web browsers that support [Microsoft Defender SmartScreen](https://learn.microsoft.com/deployedge/microsoft-edge-security-smartscreen), which identifies and blocks malicious websites, including phishing sites, scam sites, and sites that host malware.
- Organizations can also use [Microsoft Defender External Attack Surface Management (EASM)](https://www.microsoft.com/security/business/cloud-security/microsoft-defender-external-attack-surface-management) , a tool that continuously discovers and maps digital attack surface to provide an external view of your online infrastructure. EASM leverages vulnerability and infrastructure data to generate Attack Surface Insights, reporting that highlights key risks to a given organization.
- Enable [Network Level Authentication](https://learn.microsoft.com/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-server-2008-R2-and-2008/cc753488%28v=ws.11%29) for Remote Desktop Service connections.
- Enable [AppLocker](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/application-security/application-control/windows-defender-application-control/applocker/applocker-overview) to restrict specific software tools prohibited within the organization, such as reconnaissance, fingerprinting, and RMM tools, or grant access to only specific users.

**Strengthen Microsoft Defender for Endpoint configuration**

- Ensure that [tamper protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection#how-do-i-configure-or-manage-tamper-protection) is enabled in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Enable [network protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/enable-network-protection) in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Turn on [web protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/web-protection-overview).
- Run [endpoint detection and response (EDR) in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus does not detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach.
- Configure [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations) in full automated mode to let Microsoft Defender for Endpoint take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.
- Microsoft Defender XDR customers can turn on the following [attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction)to prevent common attack techniques used by threat actors.
    - [Block executable content from email client and webmail](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-executable-content-from-email-client-and-webmail)
    - [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion)
    - [Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-execution-of-potentially-obfuscated-scripts)
    - [Block JavaScript or VBScript from launching downloaded executable content](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?block-javascript-or-vbscript-from-launching-downloaded-executable-content)
    - [Block process creations originating from PSExec and WMI commands](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference%22%20/l%20%22block-process-creations-originating-from-psexec-and-wmi-commands)

**Strengthen Microsoft Defender Antivirus configuration**

- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus, or the equivalent for your antivirus product, to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown variants.
- Turn on Microsoft Defender Antivirus scanning of [downloaded files and attachments](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-advanced-scan-types-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc%22HYPERLINK%20%22https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-advanced-scan-types-microsoft-defender-antivirus?view=o365-worldwide).
- Turn on Microsoft Defender Antivirus [real-time protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/configure-real-time-protection-microsoft-defender-antivirus).
- [Turn on PUA protection in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/detect-block-potentially-unwanted-apps-microsoft-defender-antivirus) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus

**Strengthen Microsoft Defender for Office 365 configuration**

- Turn on [Safe Links](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-office-365/safe-links-about) and [Safe Attachments](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-office-365/safe-attachments-about) in Microsoft Defender for Office 365.
- Turn on [zero-hour auto purge (ZAP)](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-office-365/zero-hour-auto-purge) in Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to quarantine sent mail in response to newly acquired threat intelligence and retroactively neutralize malicious phishing, spam, or malware messages that have already been delivered to mailboxes.
- Invest in [advanced anti-phishing](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-office-365/anti-phishing-protection-about#additional-anti-phishing-protection-in-microsoft-defender-for-office-365) solutions that monitor incoming emails and visited websites. [Microsoft Defender for Office 365](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender/microsoft-365-security-center-mdo) merges incident and alert management across email, devices, and identities, centralizing investigations for email-based threats.
- Configure Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to [recheck links on click](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-office-365/safe-links-about).
- Use the [Attack Simulator](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-office-365/attack-simulation-training-get-started) in Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to run realistic, yet safe, simulated phishing and password attack campaigns. Run spear-phishing (credential harvest) simulations to train users against clicking URLs in unsolicited messages and disclosing credentials.

**Strengthen Microsoft Defender for Identity configuration**

- Prevent [clear text credential exposure](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-for-identity/security-assessment-clear-text#what-information-does-the-prevent-clear-text-security-assessment-provide).
- Reduce [lateral movement paths](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-for-identity/understand-lateral-movement-paths) that may be used by attackers.
- Identify [legacy components](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-for-identity/security-assessment) that may introduce security vulnerabilities.

## References
[Sandworm APT Targets Ukrainian Users with Trojanized Microsoft KMS Activation Tools in Cyber Espionage Campaigns](https://blog.eclecticiq.com/sandworm-apt-targets-ukrainian-users-with-trojanized-microsoft-kms-activation-tools-in-cyber-espionage-campaigns) EclecticIQ (Accessed 2025-02-12)
 
[Seashell Blizzard](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/cf1e406a16835d56cf614430aea3962d7ed99f01ee3d9ee3048078288e5201bb) Microsoft (Accessed 2025-02-12)

title: Apple fixes zero-day exploited in 'extremely sophisticated' attacks
content:
## Snapshot
Apple has released emergency security updates to patch a zero-day vulnerability that has been exploited in targeted and "extremely sophisticated" attacks, with the company acknowledging reports of exploitation against specific individuals. The vulnerability can be triggered by a physical attack that disables USB Restricted Mode on a locked device. USB Restricted Mode, introduced in iOS 11.4.1 nearly seven years ago, is a security feature that blocks USB accessories from establishing a data connection if the device has been locked for over an hour. This feature is intended to prevent forensic tools like GrayKey and Cellebrite from extracting data from locked iOS devices. In November, Apple also introduced an "inactivity reboot" feature that automatically restarts iPhones after prolonged idle periods to re-encrypt data and further hinder extraction efforts. The patched zero-day vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2025-24200 and reported by researchers at Citizen Lab, is an authorization issue that has been addressed with improved state management in iOS 18.3.1 and iPadOS 18.3.1. Affected devices include the iPhone XS and later, as well as various iPad models such as the iPad Pro 13-inch, iPad Pro 12.9-inch (3rd generation and later), iPad Pro 11-inch (1st generation and later), iPad Air (3rd generation and later), iPad (7th generation and later), and iPad mini (5th generation and later), and users are strongly advised to install the updates immediately. In 2023 and 2024, Apple patched multiple critical zero-day vulnerabilities exploited in the wild, including two disclosed by Citizen Lab (CVE-2023-41061 and CVE-2023-41064) that were used in the BLASTPASS zero-click exploit chain to infect fully patched iPhones with NSO Group's Pegasus spyware, as well as the first zero-day of the current year (CVE-2025-24085) fixed last month.

## Recommendations
Apple recommends users upgrade to mitigate this threat:
 
- iPadOS 17.7.5
- iOS 18.3.1
- IpadOS 18.3.1

[Apple fixes zero-day exploited in 'extremely sophisticated' attacks](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/apple/apple-fixes-zero-day-exploited-in-extremely-sophisticated-attacks/). Bleeping Computer (accessed 2025-02-11)

title: NanoCore RAT Attack Windows Using Task Scheduler to Captures keystrokes, screenshots
content:
## Snapshot
Cybersecurity researchers reported on the persistent threat posed by NanoCore, a notorious Remote Access Trojan (RAT) targeting Windows systems. Known for its espionage capabilities and modular design, NanoCore continues to evolve with sophisticated techniques for data theft and system control.

## Description
NanoCore ensures persistence by copying itself into hidden directories and modifying the Windows registry to execute its payload during startup. It also uses the Windows Task Scheduler to create tasks that reinforce its presence on the system. The malware is designed to steal data and conduct espionage by capturing keystrokes, screenshots, and clipboard content, which it stores locally before sending to a Command-and-Control (C2) server. It communicates with a C2 server at simpletest.ddns.net over port 9632 and uses Google DNS for connectivity checks. Its modular plugin system, including a plugin named "SurveillanceEx," allows for real-time monitoring of user activity. To avoid detection, NanoCore employs obfuscation techniques, with analysts using tools like de4dot to deobfuscate and analyze its internal logic.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
This analysis highlights the growing trend of attackers abusing legitimate Windows features to maintain persistence and evade detection through Living off the Land (LotL) techniques. Threat actors increasingly leverage tools like Windows Task Scheduler and Registry Run Keys to execute malicious code and secure long-term access without raising immediate security alarms. In fact, [Microsoft's analysis of recent trends in OSINT cyber threats](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/db42e801) revealed that Scheduled Task/Job Manipulation was the top persistence technique, based on articles published by threat researchers across the security community between October and December 2024 (Q4). Since these features are integral to normal system operations and commonly used by administrators, they are often overlooked by traditional security controls, complicating detection and response efforts. As a result, organizations must adopt robust monitoring practices to detect suspicious use of native system utilities and implement strict controls over administrative functions.

## Recommendations
Recommendations to protect against Information Stealers: Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of [Information Stealer](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/2296d491ea381b532b24f2575f9418d4b6723c17b8a1f507d20c2140a75d16d6)  threats.
 
- Check your Office 365 email filtering settings to ensure you block spoofed emails, spam, and emails with malware. Use [Microsoft Defender for Office 365](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/defender-for-office-365?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for enhanced phishing protection and coverage against new threats and polymorphic variants. Configure Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to [recheck links on click](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-links-about?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) and [delete sent mail](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/zero-hour-auto-purge?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in response to newly acquired threat intelligence. Turn on [safe attachments policies](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-attachments-policies-configure?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to check attachments to inbound email.
- Encourage users to use Microsoft Edge and other web browsers that support [SmartScreen](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/web-protection-overview?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc), which identifies and blocks malicious websites, including phishing sites, scam sites, and sites that host malware.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus, or the equivalent for your antivirus product, to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown variants.
- Enforce MFA on all accounts, remove users excluded from MFA, and strictly [require MFA](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/identity-protection/howto-identity-protection-configure-mfa-policy?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc)  from all devices, in all locations, at all times.
- Enable passwordless authentication methods (for example, Windows Hello, FIDO keys, or Microsoft Authenticator) for accounts that support passwordless. For accounts that still require passwords, use authenticator apps like Microsoft Authenticator for MFA. Learn [what authentication and verification methods are available in Microsoft Entra ID.](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/authentication/concept-authentication-methods)
- For MFA that uses authenticator apps, ensure that the app requires a code to be typed in where possible, as many intrusions where MFA was enabled still succeeded due to users clicking 'Yes' on the prompt on their phones even when they were not at their [devices](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/how-to-mfa-number-match?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) .
- For information on password management for Microsoft Edge read ["Microsoft Edge password manager security."](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/deployedge/microsoft-edge-security-password-manager-security)

Microsoft Defender customers can [turn on attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc)  to prevent common attack techniques used in infostealer infections. Attack surface reduction rules are sweeping settings that stop entire classes of threats including, infostealers, credential theft, and ransomware. The following bullet points offer more guidance on specific mitigation advice:

- [Turn on PUA protection in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/detect-block-potentially-unwanted-apps-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc)

title: Massive brute force attack uses 2.8 million IPs to target VPN devices
content:
## Snapshot
The Shadowserver Foundation has reported a large increase in brute force attacks targeting VPNs and firewalls, with up to 2.8 million unique IP addresses involved daily.

## Description
The large-scale attack primarily targets networking devices from Palo Alto Networks, Ivanti, and SonicWall. According to Shadowserver, the campaign has been ongoing since last month, with most attacking IPs originating from Brazil, followed by Turkey, Russia, Argentina, Morocco, and Mexico. The attackers are leveraging compromised routers and Internet of Things (IoT) devices from manufacturers such as MikroTik, Huawei, Cisco, Boa, and ZTE to conduct the attacks. Their goal is to compromise edge security devices—including firewalls, VPNs, and gateways—that are often exposed to the internet for remote access. Successful credential compromise could allow attackers to hijack devices or infiltrate networks.
 
Shadowserver notes that the attack scale has recently increased, with many attacking IPs likely part of a botnet or residential proxy network. These proxies mask malicious traffic as normal user activity, making detection more difficult. Additionally, attackers may use compromised gateway devices as proxy exit nodes, routing malicious traffic through an organization's network.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
[Microsoft has highlighted emerging botnet threats](https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/b3cab684-574c-4f5b-a658-d78ba1d4e570/overview) based on incidents and observations from the security community. In 2024, botnet activity surged by 25%, contributing to an estimated $600 billion in cybercrime-related economic impact. Attackers are increasingly using evasion techniques, versatile payloads, and expanding their targets—particularly across Linux and Internet of Things (IoT) systems—exploiting systemic security gaps. Botnets facilitate ransomware, financial fraud, and politically motivated attacks. Linux and IoT devices are prime targets due to their widespread use, minimal security configurations, and role in critical infrastructure. Threat actors exploit vulnerabilities in these environments to build large-scale botnets for malicious activities. The low visibility and limited security investment in these systems make them attractive to adversaries seeking scalable and persistent threats.

## Recommendations
- Separate privileged roles: Admin and user accounts should be distinct. Use [Privileged Identity Management](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/privileged-identity-management/pim-configure) or separate accounts for privileged tasks, limiting accounts with excessive permissions. Apply MFA and [Conditional Access](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/conditional-access/overview), especially for accounts with elevated roles.
- Passwords and MFA Implement: [Complex and long passwords](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/device-security/security-policy-settings/password-policy) provide the necessary first level of security against brute-force attacks. Ensure comprehensive use of [MFA](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/tutorial-enable-azure-mfa), particularly for accounts with virtual machine contributor privileges. Discourage password reuse. A full list of cloud security recommendations can be found in [Security recommendations – a reference guide](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/defender-for-cloud/recommendations-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc).
- Use risk-based sign-in behaviors and conditional access policies: Monitor high Azure Active Directory risk scores and correlate risky behavior with subsequent activity. Implement conditional access policies for multifactor reauthentication, device compliance, password updates, or blocking authentication.
- Detect login anomalies: Employ standard anomaly detection methods for identifying unusual login patterns, such as proxy usage, anomalous locations, and user agents. Utilize Microsoft 365 Defender for detecting suspicious activities performed by risky users.  Activity can be identified and investigated with [Microsoft Defender for Identity](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender/microsoft-365-security-center-mdi?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc).
- Monitor external Azure IP addresses: Authentication from non-tenant IP addresses should be considered anomalous. Use the [az vm list-ip-addresses](https://learn.microsoft.com/cli/azure/vm?view=azure-cli-latest#az-vm-list-ip-addresses) command to identify allocated IP addresses within the tenant.
- Monitor quota increases: Watch for unexpected quota increases, especially across multiple regions or for rarely used resources, as they may indicate resource abuse attacks. Quota increase detections can be refined by focusing on commonly abused core types.
- Protect user accounts from attacks with Microsoft Entra [smart lockout](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/authentication/howto-password-smart-lockout), which blocks bad actors attempting to guess passwords or use brute-force methods.
- Regularly update and patch software to protect against known vulnerabilities, using [Microsoft Defender vulnerability management dashboard](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-vulnerability-management/tvm-dashboard-insights).
- [Allow investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations?view=o365-worldwide%3Focid%3Dmagicti_ta_learndoc) in full automated mode to allow Microsoft Defender for Endpoint to take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.

## References
[Massive brute force attack uses 2.8 million IPs to target VPN devices](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/massive-brute-force-attack-uses-28-million-ips-to-target-vpn-devices/). BleepingComputer (accessed 2025-02-11)
 
[Recent OSINT trends in botnet threats](https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/b3cab684-574c-4f5b-a658-d78ba1d4e570/overview). Microsoft (accessed 2025-02-11)

title: FinStealer
content:
## Snapshot
Researchers at CYFIRMA have uncovered a malware campaign exploiting the brand of a major Indian bank through fraudulent mobile applications.

## Description
Distributed via phishing links and social engineering tactics, these fake apps mimic legitimate banking applications to steal user credentials, financial data, and personal information. The malware employs advanced evasion techniques, including XOR encryption, Telegram-based command-and-control (C2) servers, and runtime behavior modifications to bypass security measures. Attackers leverage stolen credentials for unauthorized transactions, identity theft, and selling banking data on darknet forums.

The malware, built using Kotlin, requests excessive permissions such as reading and sending SMS messages to intercept one-time passwords (OTPs). A high-severity SQL injection vulnerability (CVE-2011-2688) was also found in the attackers’ infrastructure, potentially allowing unauthorized access to stored credentials. The malware’s communication infrastructure includes IP-based C2 servers and Telegram bots for flexible command execution. Additionally, WebView exploitation allows the attackers to redirect users to phishing sites designed to harvest sensitive data.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations.

- Check your Office 365 email filtering settings to ensure you block spoofed emails, spam, and emails with malware. Use [Microsoft Defender for Office 365](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/defender-for-office-365?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for enhanced phishing protection and coverage against new threats and polymorphic variants. Configure Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to [recheck links on click](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-links-about?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) and [delete sent mail](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/zero-hour-auto-purge?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in response to newly acquired threat intelligence. Turn on [safe attachments policies](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-attachments-policies-configure?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to check attachments to inbound email.
- Encourage users to use Microsoft Edge and other web browsers that support [SmartScreen](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/web-protection-overview?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc), which identifies and blocks malicious websites, including phishing sites, scam sites, and sites that host malware.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus, or the equivalent for your antivirus product, to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown variants.
- Enforce MFA on all accounts, remove users excluded from MFA, and strictly [require MFA](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/identity-protection/howto-identity-protection-configure-mfa-policy?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) from all devices, in all locations, at all times.
- Enable passwordless authentication methods (for example, Windows Hello, FIDO keys, or Microsoft Authenticator) for accounts that support passwordless. For accounts that still require passwords, use authenticator apps like Microsoft Authenticator for MFA. [Refer to this article](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/concept-authentication-methods?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for the different authentication methods and features.
- For MFA that uses authenticator apps, ensure that the app requires a code to be typed in where possible, as many intrusions where MFA was enabled still succeeded due to users clicking “Yes” on the prompt on their phones even when they were not at their [devices](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/how-to-mfa-number-match?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc). Refer to [this article](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/concept-authentication-methods?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for an example.
- Remind employees that enterprise or workplace credentials should not be stored in browsers or password vaults secured with personal credentials. Organizations can turn off password syncing in browser on managed devices using [Group Policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/deployedge/microsoft-edge-enterprise-sync#sync-group-policies?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc).

Microsoft Defender customers can [turn on attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to prevent common attack techniques used in infostealer infections. Attack surface reduction rules are sweeping settings that stop entire classes of threats including, infostealers, credential theft, and ransomware. The following bullet points offer more guidance on specific mitigation advice:

- [Turn on PUA protection in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/detect-block-potentially-unwanted-apps-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc)
- [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion)
- [Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-execution-of-potentially-obfuscated-scripts)

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus

title: Chinese-Speaking Group Manipulates SEO with BadIIS
content:
## Snapshot
Throughout 2024, researchers from Trend Micro observed the deployment of BadIIS, a malware campaign targeting Internet Information Services (IIS) servers.

## Description
This malware is used for SEO fraud and injecting malicious content into legitimate web traffic. Once installed on a compromised IIS server, BadIIS can alter HTTP responses, redirecting users to illegal gambling sites or attacker-controlled servers hosting malware and phishing schemes. The campaign has impacted multiple countries, including India, Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines, Singapore, Taiwan, South Korea, Japan, and Brazil and spans industries including government agencies, universities, technology firms, and telecommunications providers. 

BadIIS modifies web traffic by checking user-agent and referrer fields, redirecting search engine traffic to fraudulent sites to manipulate SEO rankings. It also operates in injector mode, embedding obfuscated JavaScript into responses, which further redirects users to malicious websites. The malware's command-and-control (C2) infrastructure relies on encrypted communication, with attackers using simplified Chinese in code, suggesting a Chinese-speaking threat group is responsible for the activity.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat.
 
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/linux-preferences) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown threats.
- Run [EDR in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode?view=o365-worldwide?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus does not detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach.
- Allow [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations?view=o365-worldwide?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in full automated mode to allow Microsoft Defender for Endpoint to take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.
- [Enable](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-controlled-folders) controlled folder access.
- Ensure that [tamper protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection#how-do-i-configure-or-manage-tamper-protection) is enabled in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Enable [network protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-network-protection) in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Follow the credential hardening recommendations in the [on-premises credential theft overview](https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/9382203e-5155-4b5e-af74-21562b1004d5/analystreport) to defend against common credential theft techniques like LSASS access.
- [Enable](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-credential-stealing-from-the-windows-local-security-authority-subsystem) LSA protection.
- Microsoft Defender XDR customers can turn on the following [attack surface reduction rule](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction) to prevent common attack techniques used for ransomware.

- - [Block](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-executable-content-from-email-client-and-webmail) executable content from email client and webmail
    - [Block](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion) executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion

Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects threat components as the following malware:
 
- Trojan:Win32/IIStealer

title: Hackers exploit Cityworks RCE bug to breach Microsoft IIS servers
content:
## Snapshot
Hackers are actively exploiting a high-severity deserialization vulnerability in Trimble Cityworks software, identified as CVE-2025-0994, to execute remote commands on Microsoft Internet Information Services (IIS) servers and deploy Cobalt Strike beacons for initial network access.

## Description
Trimble Cityworks, a GIS-centric asset management software used by local governments and public works, is compromised when authenticated users exploit this flaw to perform remote code execution (RCE) attacks. The vulnerability affects Cityworks versions prior to 15.8.9 and Cityworks with office companion versions before 23.10. Trimble has released updates to address the issue and recommends that on-premise deployments apply the security update immediately, while cloud-hosted instances will be updated automatically. The company also advises administrators to correct overprivileged IIS identity permissions and attachment directory configurations. Indicators of compromise released by Trimble reveal that attackers are using tools like WinPutty and Cobalt Strike beacons for remote access.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
According to CISA, CVE-2025-0994, [rated 8.6 on the CVSS scale](https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2025-0994), can be exploited remotely with low complexity despite requiring high-level privileges. Overprivileged IIS identities and misconfigured attachment directories further elevate the risk, potentially leading to a significant loss of confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Confirmed to be actively exploited in the wild and listed in CISA’s  [Known Exploited Vulnerability (KEV) catalog](https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog) as of February 7, 2025, organizations are urged to apply patches by February 28, 2025.
 
As stated in the original article, this vulnerability was leveraged to gain RCE in this attack, and the adversaries used [Cobalt Strike](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/fd8511c1d61e93d39411acf36a31130a6795efe186497098fe0c6f2ccfb920fc) as the initial access vector.
 
Originally designed as a commercial penetration testing tool, Cobalt Strike can provide attackers with a stealthy, persistent foothold within the compromised system. This foothold can be used to facilitate subsequent stages of the attack, including lateral movement, credential theft, and privilege escalation, ultimately threatening full system compromise. Microsoft has tracked threat actors that have used Cobalt Strike for diverse operations, including Midnight Blizzard, Brass Typhoon, Diamond Sleet, and Pistachio Tempest.

## Recommendations
Trimble recommends the following actions to mitigate the impact of this vulnerability:
 
- Apply Security Patch: Update to Cityworks 15.8.9 or 23.10 immidiately
- Review IIS permissions: Ensure IIS is not running with local or domain administrative privileges.
- Secure attachment directories: Limit configurations to only necessary folders.

Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations.

> 
> 
> Enable [tamper protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection) to prevent attacks from stopping or interfering with Microsoft Defender Antivirus.
> 
> 
> Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/microsoft-defender-antivirus/enable-cloud-protection-microsoft-defender-antivirus) and automatic sample submission on Microsoft Defender Antivirus. These capabilities use artificial intelligence and machine learning to quickly identify and stop new and unknown threats.
> 
> 
> Utilize the Windows Defender Firewall and your network firewall to [prevent RPC and SMB communication along endpoints](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/topic/preventing-smb-traffic-from-lateral-connections-and-entering-or-leaving-the-network-c0541db7-2244-0dce-18fd-14a3ddeb282a) whenever possible. This limits lateral movement as well as other attack activities.
> 
> 
> Run [Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus doesn’t detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach.
> 

Microsoft Defender customers can turn on [attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to prevent common attack techniques used in ransomware attacks:

> 
> 
> [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc "https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion")
> 
> 
> [Use advanced protection against ransomware](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction#use-advanced-protection-against-ransomware?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc "https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction#use-advanced-protection-against-ransomware")
> 
> 
> [Block credential stealing from the Windows local security authority subsystem (lsass.exe)](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction#block-credential-stealing-from-the-windows-local-security-authority-subsystem?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc "https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction#block-credential-stealing-from-the-windows-local-security-authority-subsystem")
> 
> 
> [Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction#block-execution-of-potentially-obfuscated-scripts?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc "https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction#block-execution-of-potentially-obfuscated-scripts")
>

## Detections/Hunting Queries

title: Rat Race: ValleyRAT Malware Targets Organizations with New Delivery Techniques
content:
#### Targeted Geolocations
- China



## Snapshot
Researchers at Morphisec released a report detailing the infection chain of ValleyRAT, a multi-stage remote access trojan (RAT) often attributed to the threat group Silver Fox.

## Description
The attack begins with victims downloading a fake Chrome browser from a phishing site, leading to the execution of a malicious Setup.exe file. This file requests administrative privileges and downloads additional payloads, including DLL files and an executable disguised as the Chinese version of TikTok (Douyin).

A key component, sscronet.dll, is injected into the svchost.exe process to evade detection and maintain persistence via Windows registry modifications. Attackers also use DLL side-loading techniques with Douyin.exe and manipulate the nslookup process to execute malicious code stealthily.

The malware deploys a keylogger, captures screen activity, and injects itself into interactive Windows sessions to monitor user inputs. It includes anti-VM checks to evade analysis by security researchers and hooks system functions to bypass security defenses. Persistence is further achieved by creating a disguised executable, GFIRestart64.exe. Finally, ValleyRAT connects to command-and-control (C2) servers for further exploitation and data exfiltration.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
[Silver Fox](https://intezer.com/blog/malware-analysis/weaponized-software-targets-chinese/) is a group known to conduct cybercrime and espionage campaigns, often targeting Chinese-speaking individuals and organizations. The group is known to conduct phishing activities and to deploy malware like ValleyRAT and Gh0st RAT to deploy additional payloads and monitor victim activities.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat.
 
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/linux-preferences) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown threats.
- Run [EDR in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode?view=o365-worldwide?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus does not detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach.
- Allow [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations?view=o365-worldwide?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in full automated mode to allow Microsoft Defender for Endpoint to take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.
- [Enable](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-controlled-folders) controlled folder access.
- Ensure that [tamper protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection#how-do-i-configure-or-manage-tamper-protection) is enabled in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.

title: Scalable Vector Graphics files pose a novel phishing threat
content:
## Snapshot
Since mid-January, researchers at Sophos have noted an increase in email-based phishing attacks that leverage Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) files to bypass security measures.

## Description
Unlike traditional image formats, SVG files can contain embedded hyperlinks and scripts, allowing attackers to direct users to phishing sites. These malicious SVG files are often attached to emails with deceptive subject lines, such as fake voicemail notifications or legal document requests, to lure victims into clicking the links.

When opened, the SVG file launches a web browser and displays a seemingly legitimate page, often mimicking well-known services like DocuSign, SharePoint, or Google Voice. Many phishing pages are protected by CAPTCHA gates, making them harder to detect through automated security scans. Some variants also use JavaScript to automatically load phishing pages without user interaction.

In more advanced cases, attackers embed base64-encoded ZIP archives within SVG files, which contain malware capable of logging keystrokes. Additionally, phishing sites often prefill login forms with the victim’s email address, harvested from the original email link. Sophos researchers observed that these attacks continue to evolve, incorporating new techniques to evade detection and trick users into divulging their credentials.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. 
 
- Educate users about [protecting personal and business information](https://www.microsoft.com/security/business/security-101/what-is-email-security) in social media, filtering unsolicited communication, identifying lure links in phishing emails, and reporting reconnaissance attempts and other suspicious activity.
- Turn on [Zero-hour auto purge (ZAP)](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-office-365/zero-hour-auto-purge) in Defender for Office 365 to quarantine sent mail in response to newly-acquired threat intelligence and retroactively neutralize malicious phishing, spam, or malware messages that have already been delivered to mailboxes.
- Educate users about [preventing malware infections](https://www.microsoft.com/security/business/security-101/what-is-malware), such as ignoring or deleting unsolicited and unexpected emails or attachments.
- Invest in advanced anti-phishing solutions that monitor incoming emails and visited websites. [Microsoft Defender for Office 365](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-xdr/microsoft-365-security-center-mdo) brings together incident and alert management across email, devices, and identities, centralizing investigations for email-based threats.
- Encourage users to use Microsoft Edge and other web browsers that support [Microsoft Defender SmartScreen](https://learn.microsoft.com/deployedge/microsoft-edge-security-smartscreen), which identifies and blocks malicious websites, including phishing sites, scam sites, and sites that host malware.
- Implement [Conditional Access authentication strength](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity/authentication/concept-authentication-strengths) to require phishing-resistant authentication for employees and external users for critical apps.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/enable-cloud-protection-microsoft-defender-antivirus) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a huge majority of new and unknown variants.
- Enable [network protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/enable-network-protection) to prevent applications or users from accessing malicious domains and other malicious content on the internet.
- Turn on [tamper protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection) features to prevent attackers from stopping security services.
- Enable [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations) in full automated mode to allow Defender for Endpoint to take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.
- Run [endpoint detection and response (EDR) in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode), so that Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus doesn’t detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts detected post-breach.

Microsoft Defender XDR customers can turn on [attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction) to prevent common attack techniques:

- [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion)
- [Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-execution-of-potentially-obfuscated-scripts)
- [Block JavaScript or VBScript from launching downloaded executable content](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-javascript-or-vbscript-from-launching-downloaded-executable-content)

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects threat components as the following malware:
 
- Trojan:HTML/Adobe.GN!MTB
- [Trojan:Script/Wacatac](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:Script/Wacatac.B!ml)

## References
[Scalable Vector Graphics files pose a novel phishing threat](https://news.sophos.com/en-us/2025/02/05/svg-phishing/). Sophos (accessed 2025-02-06)

title: Critical RCE bug in Microsoft Outlook now exploited in attacks
content:
## Snapshot
CISA added CVE-2024-21413 to the Known Exploited Vulnerability Catalog.

## Description
A researcher at Check Point originally discovered a critical Microsoft Outlook remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability, tracked as [CVE-2024-21413](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/CVE-2024-21413). This vulnerability is now being exploited in attacks prompting CISA to issue a warning to U.S. federal agencies about ongoing attacks. CISA has added the vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, indicating active exploitation, and has given federal agencies a three-week deadline until February 27 to secure their networks. The agency has also advised private organizations to prioritize patching this vulnerability to prevent attacks.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
[CVE-2024-21413](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/CVE-2024-21413) is a remote code execution vulnerability in Microsoft Outlook. The affected products include Office 2016, Office 2019, Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise, and Office LTSC 2021. This vulnerability allows threat actors to bypass Office’s Protected View by leveraging the Preview Pane, causing potentially malicious content to open in editing mode rather than read-only mode. Successful exploitation can lead to the leakage of local NTLM credentials and full remote code execution, severely compromising system confidentiality, integrity, and availability. The vulnerability does not require any prior privileges for exploitation

## Recommendations
Microsoft released [security updates](https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/en-US/advisory/CVE-2024-21413) to fix this vulnerability on February 13, 2024. Customers who have not patched are urged to do so as soon as possible for their organization’s security. Customers using Microsoft Office 2016 (32- bit and 64-bit editions) build number 16.0.5435.1001 should apply all necessary updates included in this security update. While Microsoft Defender XDR has deployed heuristics-based detections to protect against this vulnerability, further steps can be taken to protect against exploitations of this vulnerability.
 
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations.

- Apply necessary [security updates](https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/en-US/advisory/CVE-2024-21413) released by Microsoft to affected devices.
- Secure your environment by following the [principle of least privilege](https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/9382203e-5155-4b5e-af74-21562b1004d5/analystreport) to prevent user interaction with malicious links.
- Microsoft Defender customers can enable [attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference) to further harden customer environments:
    - [Block Office applications from creating executable content](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference)

## References
[Critical RCE bug in Microsoft Outlook now exploited in attacks](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/critical-rce-bug-in-microsoft-outlook-now-exploited-in-attacks/). Bleep Computer (accessed 2025-02-07).

title: Hackers exploit SimpleHelp RMM flaws to deploy Sliver malware
content:
## Snapshot
Cybersecurity firm Field Effect has confirmed that hackers are exploiting vulnerabilities in SimpleHelp Remote Monitoring and Management (RMM) clients to create unauthorized administrator accounts, install backdoors, and potentially prepare for ransomware attacks. The vulnerabilities, identified as CVE-2024-57726, CVE-2024-57727, and CVE-2024-57728, allow threat actors to download and upload files on devices and escalate privileges to administrative levels.

## Description
The attackers begin by exploiting the SimpleHelp RMM client vulnerabilities to establish a connection to a target endpoint from an Estonian-based server from IP address 194.76.227\[.\]171. They then execute discovery commands to gather information about the system, network, users, and security suites like CrowdStrike Falcon. The attackers create a new administrator account named "sqladmin" for persistent access and install the [Sliver](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/7b3299451d6740a9ce460a67156d8be84c0308fd6e5ccafccdb368da9f06c95c) post-exploitation framework as well as a backdoor called agent.exe to serve as an alternative persistence access mechanism in case the RMM access was lost. Armed with the information discovered during the discovery phase, the attackers then compromised the Domain Controller using the same SimpleHelp RMM client, creating another admin account "fpmhlttech" and installing a Cloudflare Tunnel disguised as Windows svchost.exe for stealthy access. 

Field Effect's report also mentions signs of Akira ransomware attacks, although there is not enough evidence for a high-confidence attribution.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
The vulnerabilities exploited in this attack—CVE-2024-57726, CVE-2024-57727, and CVE-2024-57728—were originally discovered and disclosed by Horizon3 researchers in mid-January. These flaws allow attackers to upload and download files, escalate privileges, and gain persistent access to compromised systems. In response, SimpleHelp released security patches between January 8 and 13 in product versions 5.5.8, 5.4.10, and 5.3.9. However, as of January 28, threat monitoring group Shadowserver Foundation reported that 580 vulnerable instances remain exposed online, with the majority (345) located in the United States.  

This latest research builds on findings from Arctic Wolf, which reported on January 22 that it had observed unauthorized access attempts against devices running SimpleHelp RMM software. While Arctic Wolf did not definitively attribute these attacks to the recently disclosed vulnerabilities, it assessed with medium confidence that they were linked to Horizon3’s findings. The latest evidence further corroborates this connection by demonstrating that attackers are actively exploiting these flaws to establish persistent access and deploy post-exploitation frameworks.

This campaign underscores a growing trend of attackers abusing legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) tools like SimpleHelp to facilitate cyber intrusions. Both cybercriminals and nation-state actors increasingly leverage RMM software to maintain access, conduct reconnaissance, and deploy malware—including ransomware—without triggering security alerts. Because these tools are widely used by IT administrators, managed service providers (MSPs), and enterprise support teams, they are often whitelisted in security environments, making detection and mitigation more challenging. As a result, organizations must implement strict controls over the use of RMM tools and continuously monitor for signs of abuse. Read about [Recent OSINT trends in abuse of remote monitoring and management tools](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/687fdb34). For more extensive recommendations on hunting for and defending against RMM abuse, see our [technique profile](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/9782a9ef).

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. 
 
- Use [Windows Defender Application Control or AppLocker](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/windows-defender-application-control/wdac-and-applocker-overview) to create policies to block unapproved IT management tools
    - Both solutions include functionality to block specific software publisher certificates: WDAC [file rule levels](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/windows-defender-application-control/select-types-of-rules-to-create?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#windows-defender-application-control-file-rule-levels) allow administrators to specify the level at which they want to trust their applications, including listing certificates as untrusted. AppLocker’s [publisher rule condition](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/windows-defender-application-control/applocker/understanding-the-publisher-rule-condition-in-applocker) is available for files that are digitally signed, which can enable organizations to block non-approved RMM instances that include publisher information.
    - Microsoft Defender for Endpoint also provides functionality to block specific signed applications using the [block certificate action](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/t5/microsoft-defender-for-endpoint/indicators-enhancements-allow-block-by-certificates-amp-more/ba-p/1377586).
- For approved RMM systems used in your environment, enforce security settings where possible to implement multifactor authentication (MFA).
- Consider searching for unapproved RMM software installations (see the Advanced hunting section). If an unapproved installation is discovered, reset passwords for accounts used to install the RMM services. If a system-level account was used to install the software, further investigation may be warranted.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/cloud-protection-microsoft-defender-antivirus) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a huge majority of new and unknown variants.
- Turn on the following [attack surface reduction rule](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/overview-attack-surface-reduction) to block or audit activity associated with this threat:
    - [Use advanced protection against ransomware](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#use-advanced-protection-against-ransomware)
    - [Block process creations originating from PsExec and WMI commands](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-process-creations-originating-from-psexec-and-wmi-commands). Some organizations may experience compatibility issues with this rule on certain server systems but should deploy it to other systems to prevent lateral movement originating from PsExec and WMI.

## Detections/Hunting Queries
Because organizations might have legitimate and frequent uses for RMM software, Microsoft recommends using advanced hunting queries to locate RMM software that has not been endorsed by your organization for further investigation. In some cases, these investigations might show benign activity from legitimate users. Regardless of use case, all newly installed RMM instances should be scrutinized and investigated. If a system-level account was used to install the software, further investigation might be warranted.
 
If any queries have high fidelity for discovering unsanctioned RMM instances in your environment and do not detect benign activity, you can create a [custom detection rule](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender/custom-detection-rules) from the advanced hunting query in the Microsoft Defender XDR portal.
 
[Advanced hunting queries are available on GitHub](https://github.com/jischell-msft/RemoteManagementMonitoringTools).

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects threat components as the following malware sometimes used at part of an attack chain exploiting RMM tools:
 
- [Ransom:Win32/Akira](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Ransom:Win32/Akira.A!ibt&threatId=-2147119980)
- [Ransom:Win64/Akira](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Ransom:Win64/Akira.PB!MTB&threatId=-2147122925)
- [Backdoor:Linux/Sliver](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Backdoor:Linux/Sliver.A!MTB&ThreatID=2147899857)
- [Trojan:Linux/Sliver](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:Linux/Sliver.A!MTB&threatId=-2147142453)
- [Trojan:Win64/Sliver](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:Win64/Sliver.D&threatId=-2147161988)

## References
[Hackers exploit SimpleHelp RMM flaws to deploy Sliver malware](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-exploit-simplehelp-rmm-flaws-to-deploy-sliver-malware/) BleepingComputer (accessed 2025-02-07)
 
[Not-so-SimpleHelp exploits enabling deployment of Sliver backdoor](https://fieldeffect.com/blog/field-effect-mitigates-not-so-simplehelp-exploits-enabling-deployment-of-backdoors) Field Effect Security Intelligence (accessed 2025-02-07)
 
[Arctic Wolf Observes Campaign Exploiting SimpleHelp RMM Software for Initial Access](https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog-uk/arctic-wolf-observes-campaign-exploiting-simplehelp-rmm-software-initial-access/) Arctic Wolf (accessed 2025-02-07)

title: University site cloned to evade ad detection distributes fake Cisco installer
content:
## Snapshot
Malvertisers are using fake identities or stolen ones to distribute malicious ads, with a recent campaign targeting users searching for Cisco AnyConnect.

## Description
The attackers created a fake ad that appeared in Google search results, leading to a domain registered less than a day before the ad's appearance. Clicking on the ad triggers server-side checks to differentiate between potential victims and non-targets such as bots or VPNs. The campaign cleverly used content stolen from the Technische Universität Dresden to create a decoy website, which inadvertently revealed the attackers' likely Russian origin due to a browser language leak. Victims who clicked on the ad were redirected to a phishing site and presented with a fake Cisco AnyConnect installer. This installer was digitally signed and delivered the NetSupport RAT, a remote access Trojan, which upon execution, connected to two IP addresses, granting attackers remote access to the victim's machine.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
NetSupport Manager has been commercially available for remote device administration since 1989 and is commonly used for managing and controlling systems across a network. It supports various features like file transfer, remote screen sharing, chat functions, and system monitoring. While these features are useful for IT administrators, they also make NetSupport Manager an attractive tool for threat actors when repurposed as a remote access trojan (RAT). NetSupport RAT operates using a client-server architecture, where the server component is installed on the attacker’s machine and communicates with infected systems. The client component, or agent, is installed on the victim’s machine, allowing the attacker to remotely control the system.

Read more [about NetSupport RAT here.](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/bfa5316082cf01926a5507fa0a9f1771394bf3bf803e332de4aa62af8c55fb44)

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations.
 
- Use [Windows Defender Application Control or AppLocker](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/windows-defender-application-control/wdac-and-applocker-overview?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to create policies to block unapproved IT management tools
    - Both solutions include functionality to block specific software publisher certificates: WDAC [file rule levels](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/windows-defender-application-control/select-types-of-rules-to-create?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#windows-defender-application-control-file-rule-levels) allow administrators to specify the level at which they want to trust their applications, including listing certificates as untrusted. AppLocker’s [publisher rule condition](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/windows-defender-application-control/applocker/understanding-the-publisher-rule-condition-in-applocker?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) is available for files that are digitally signed, which can enable organizations to block non-approved remote monitoring and management (RMM) instances that include publisher information.
    - Microsoft Defender for Endpoint also provides functionality to block specific signed applications using the [block certificate action](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/t5/microsoft-defender-for-endpoint/indicators-enhancements-allow-block-by-certificates-amp-more/ba-p/1377586).
- Block connections to RMM software distribution sites via network blocking such as perimeter firewall rules if not in use in your environment.
    - Organizations can use the [Configuration Manager to configure firewall and port settings.](https://learn.microsoft.com/mem/configmgr/core/clients/deploy/windows-firewall-and-port-settings-for-clients?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc)
- For approved RMM systems used in your environment, enforce security settings where possible to implement MFA.
- Consider searching for unapproved RMM software installations (Microsoft Threat Intelligence’s [Advanced hunting queries are available on GitHub](https://github.com/jischell-msft/RemoteManagementMonitoringTools)). If an unapproved installation is discovered, reset passwords for accounts used to install the RMM services. If a system-level account was used to install the software, further investigation may be warranted.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a huge majority of new and unknown variants.
- Turn on the following [attack surface reduction rule](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/overview-attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to block or audit activity associated with this threat. These rules, which can be configured by all Microsoft Defender Antivirus customers and not just those using the EDR solution, offer significant hardening against attacks.
    - [Use advanced protection against ransomware](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#use-advanced-protection-against-ransomware).
    - [Block process creations originating from PsExec and WMI commands](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-process-creations-originating-from-psexec-and-wmi-commands). Some organizations may experience compatibility issues with this rule on certain server systems but should deploy it to other systems to prevent lateral movement originating from PsExec and WMI.
    - Assess rule impact before deployment: You can assess how an attack surface reduction rule might impact your network by opening the [security recommendation](https://security.microsoft.com/security-recommendations?ocid=magicti_ta_tvmsecreco) for that rule in threat and vulnerability management. In the recommendation details pane, check the user impact to determine what percentage of your devices can accept a new policy enabling the rule in blocking mode without adverse impact to user productivity.

title: CISA orders agencies to patch Linux kernel bug exploited in attacks
content:
## Snapshot
CISA has added a high-severity Linux kernel flaw, [CVE-2024-53104](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/cves/CVE-2024-53104/), to the Known Exploited Vulnerability catalog.

## Description
The vulnerability is an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the USB Video Class (UVC) driver within the Linux kernel version 2.6.26. CVE-2024-53104 allows for physical escalation of privilege without requiring additional execution privileges on unpatched devices. The issue arises from the driver's inability to accurately parse UVC\_VS\_UNDEFINED frames, leading to frame buffer size miscalculations and potential out-of-bounds writes. [GrapheneOS](https://x.com/GrapheneOS/status/1886639593430376958) has suggested that this USB peripheral driver vulnerability may be one of the bugs exploited by forensic data extraction tools. Google released a [security patch](https://source.android.com/docs/security/bulletin/2025-02-01#spl-details) for Android users for this vulnerability on February 5, 2025. Additionally, CISA added the vulnerability to the [Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog](https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog?search_api_fulltext=CVE-2024-53104&field_date_added_wrapper=all&field_cve=&sort_by=field_date_added&items_per_page=20&url=) after it was exploited in the wild. Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are required to patch the vulnerability by February 26, 2025 but CISA encourages all organizations patch the affected devices immediately in order to mitigate this threat.

## References
[CISA orders agencies to patch Linux kernel bug exploited in attacks](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisa-orders-agencies-to-patch-linux-kernel-bug-exploited-in-attacks/) Bleeping Computer (accessed on 2025-02-07).
