title: Hackers spoof Microsoft ADFS login pages to steal credentials
content:
## Snapshot
Abnormal Security identified a phishing campaign targeting organizations' Microsoft Active Directory Federation Services (AD FS), using spoofed login pages to steal credentials and bypass multi-factor authentication (MFA).

## Description
The campaign primarily impacts the education, healthcare, and government sectors, with at least 150 targets. Attackers aim to gain access to corporate email accounts for internal phishing or business email compromise (BEC) attacks. The phishing emails impersonate the victim's IT team, urging recipients to log in to update security settings or accept new policies. Victims are redirected to a phishing site that mimics their organization's AD FS login page, where they are prompted to enter credentials and MFA codes or approve fraudulent push notifications.
 
The phishing templates are tailored to the organization's MFA settings, including Microsoft Authenticator, Duo Security, SMS verification, and other methods. Once attackers gain access, they steal data, create email filter rules, and conduct lateral phishing. They also use Private Internet Access (PIA) VPN to obscure their location and appear geographically closer to the target organization. While these attacks do not directly compromise AD FS, they exploit users' trust in familiar login processes.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
BEC is a social engineering attack in which threat actors impersonate trusted sources to manipulate victims. Common BEC tactics include financial fraud, email thread hijacking, vendor and user impersonation, mass credential harvesting, and email laundering. Attackers use techniques like phishing, spoofed domains, impersonation, fake MFA prompts, and inbox manipulation to deceive employees into making unauthorized transfers or disclosing sensitive information.
 
BEC attacks have a significant impact, often leading to financial losses and business disruptions. Industries that heavily rely on email communication and financial transactions are frequent targets.
 
For more information on BEC, read [Business Email Compromise - Financial fraud](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/7933f885) and [Business Email Compromise - Mass Credential Harvest](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/49bf5e52).

## Recommendations
[Microsoft highly recommends](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/ad-fs/ad-fs-overview) migrating to [Microsoft Entra ID](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/fundamentals/whatis). For more information, see [**Resources for decommissioning AD FS**](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/ad-fs/ad-fs-decommission)

Recommendations to protect against phishing attacks: Implement multifactor authentication (MFA) to mitigate credential theft from phishing attacks. MFA can be complemented with the following solutions and best practices to protect organizations:

- Activate conditional access policies. [Conditional access](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/conditional-access/overview?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc)  policies are evaluated and enforced every time an attacker attempts to use a stolen session cookie. Conditional access policies evaluate sign-in requests using additional identity-driven signals like user or group membership, IP location information, and device status, among others, and are enforced for suspicious sign-ins. Organizations can protect themselves from attacks that leverage stolen credentials by enabling policies such as compliant devices or trusted IP address requirements.
- Configure [continuous access evaluation](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/conditional-access/concept-continuous-access-evaluation?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc)  in your tenant.
- Invest in advanced anti-phishing solutions that monitor incoming emails and visited websites. [Microsoft Defender for Office](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender/microsoft-365-security-center-mdo?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc)  365 brings together incident and alert management across email, devices, and identities, centralizing investigations for threats in email. Organizations can also leverage web browsers that automatically [identify and block malicious websites](https://learn.microsoft.com/deployedge/microsoft-edge-security-smartscreen?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) . To build resilience against phishing attacks in general, organizations can use [anti-phishing policies](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/set-up-anti-phishing-policies?view=o365-worldwide)  to enable mailbox intelligence settings, as well as configure impersonation protection settings for specific messages and sender domains. Enabling [SafeLinks](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-links?view=o365-worldwide)  ensures real-time protection by scanning at time of delivery and at time of click.
- Continuously monitor for suspicious or anomalous activities, and search for sign-in attempts with suspicious characteristics (for example location, internet service provider \[ISP\], user agent, and use of anonymizer services). Activity can be identified and investigated with [Microsoft Defender for Identity](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender/microsoft-365-security-center-mdi?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) , which contributes identity-focused information into incidents and alerts, providing key context and correlating alerts from other products within Microsoft 365 Defender. This ensures all alerts are available in one place, and the scope of a breach can be determined faster than before.

Defenders can also complement MFA with the following solutions and best practices to further protect their organizations from such attacks.

- Use [security defaults](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/fundamentals/concept-fundamentals-security-defaults?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc)  as a baseline set of policies to improve identity security posture.
- Block phishing websites and other malicious URLs and domains in the browser through [Microsoft Defender SmartScreen](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/operating-system-security/virus-and-threat-protection/microsoft-defender-smartscreen/) , as well as the detection of suspicious and malicious behavior on endpoints.

title: Take my money: OCR crypto stealers in Google Play and App Store
content:
## Snapshot
Researchers have identified a malware campaign named "SparkCat" that has been active since late 2024, targeting both Android and iOS users through official app stores like Google Play and the App Store, as well as unofficial ones. The malware was embedded in various applications, including a food delivery app called "ComeCome," which had over 10,000 downloads on Google Play alone, contributing to a total of over 242,000 installations across different apps.

## Description
The malware leveraged a malicious SDK/framework designed to steal recovery phrases for cryptocurrency wallets by scanning the device's image gallery for keywords related to these mnemonics. It utilized the TextRecognizer interface of Google's ML Kit library for OCR to recognize text in images and exfiltrate data to a command-and-control (C2) server. The malware's communication with the C2 server was also sophisticated, using an unidentified protocol implemented in Rust and multiple encryption and compression techniques, including AES-GCM-SIV and RSA.

The Android malware module employed an OCR plug-in built with Google's ML Kit library, while the iOS module was obfuscated with HikariLLVM and contained classes for downloading configurations, sending device data, searching for, and uploading photos. The malware requested access to the image gallery under the guise of legitimate functionality, such as attaching images to support chats, and was capable of uploading photos to Amazon's cloud storage or the attackers' server.

The investigation suggested that the campaign likely originated from Chinese-speaking developers and targeted users in Europe and Asia, with potential implications for other regions. Analysis of the Android apps showed Chinese comments within the word processor code and error descriptions, suggesting the developer is fluent in Chinese. The malware retained debugging symbols, which revealed paths and usernames from the framework creators' devices. Characteristics of "SparkCat"  include its cross-platform nature, use of Rust, and obfuscation.

## Recommendations
Recommendations to protect against Mobile Malware 
 
- Never click on unknown links received through ads, SMS messages, emails, or similar untrusted sources.
- Use mobile solutions such as [Microsoft Defender for Endpoint](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/microsoft-defender-endpoint-android?view=o365-worldwide) on Android to detect malicious applications
- Always keep Install unknown apps disabled on the Android device to prevent apps from being installed from unknown sources.
- Avoid granting SMS permissions, notification listener access, or accessibility access to any applications without a strong understanding of why the application needs it. These are powerful permissions that are not commonly needed.
- If a device is no longer receiving updates, strongly consider replacing it with a new device.

## References
[Take my money: OCR crypto stealers in Google Play and App Store](https://securelist.com/sparkcat-stealer-in-app-store-and-google-play/115385/). Secure List (accessed 2025-02-06)

title: NOVA: blast from the past
content:
## Snapshot
Researchers from the BI.ZONE Threat Intelligence team have observed a large-scale campaign leveraging NOVA stealer impacting Russian organizations across a variety of industries.

## Description
NOVA stealer, a commercial fork of SnakeLogger, is distributed via phishing emails containing malicious contract-themed attachments. The malware is offered under a Malware-as-a-Service (MaaS) model, with subscriptions starting at $50, allowing threat actors to focus on spreading the malware rather than developing it.

Once executed, NOVA employs steganography to extract hidden data, replicates itself in the AppData\Roaming directory, and modifies Microsoft Defender settings to evade detection. It gains persistence through the Windows Task Scheduler and injects its payload into a child process. The stealer harvests saved credentials, logs keystrokes, captures screenshots, and extracts clipboard data, which it then exfiltrates via SMTP. NOVA also attempts to disable security tools such as Microsoft Defender, Task Manager, and CMD, though some of these functions appear incomplete. The malware queries external services to obtain IP and location data of compromised systems, aiding attackers in refining their operations.

Since August 2024, the stealer has been actively promoted and sold via a dedicated Telegram group, with additional offerings including a cryptor for obfuscating payloads. According to BI.ZONE, the affordability and accessibility of NOVA stealer highlight the growing threat posed by MaaS platforms, enabling a wider range of cybercriminals to execute credential theft and espionage campaigns.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
First observed in late 2020, [SnakeLogger](https://www.splunk.com/en_us/blog/security/under-the-hood-of-snakekeylogger-analyzing-its-loader-and-its-tactics-techniques-and-procedures.html) (also known as SnakeKeylogger and KrakenKeylogger) is a malware with both information stealing and keylogging capabilities. Developed in .NET, the malware has the ability to harvest stored credentials, capture screenshots, log keystrokes, and conduct system and network reconnaissance.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations.

- Check your Office 365 email filtering settings to ensure you block spoofed emails, spam, and emails with malware. Use [Microsoft Defender for Office 365](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/defender-for-office-365?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for enhanced phishing protection and coverage against new threats and polymorphic variants. Configure Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to [recheck links on click](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-links-about?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) and [delete sent mail](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/zero-hour-auto-purge?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in response to newly acquired threat intelligence. Turn on [safe attachments policies](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-attachments-policies-configure?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to check attachments to inbound email.
- Encourage users to use Microsoft Edge and other web browsers that support [SmartScreen](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/web-protection-overview?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc), which identifies and blocks malicious websites, including phishing sites, scam sites, and sites that host malware.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus, or the equivalent for your antivirus product, to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown variants.
- Enforce MFA on all accounts, remove users excluded from MFA, and strictly [require MFA](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/identity-protection/howto-identity-protection-configure-mfa-policy?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) from all devices, in all locations, at all times.
- Enable passwordless authentication methods (for example, Windows Hello, FIDO keys, or Microsoft Authenticator) for accounts that support passwordless. For accounts that still require passwords, use authenticator apps like Microsoft Authenticator for MFA. [Refer to this article](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/concept-authentication-methods?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for the different authentication methods and features.
- For MFA that uses authenticator apps, ensure that the app requires a code to be typed in where possible, as many intrusions where MFA was enabled still succeeded due to users clicking “Yes” on the prompt on their phones even when they were not at their [devices](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/how-to-mfa-number-match?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc). Refer to [this article](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/concept-authentication-methods?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for an example.
- Remind employees that enterprise or workplace credentials should not be stored in browsers or password vaults secured with personal credentials. Organizations can turn off password syncing in browser on managed devices using [Group Policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/deployedge/microsoft-edge-enterprise-sync#sync-group-policies?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc).

Microsoft Defender customers can [turn on attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to prevent common attack techniques used in infostealer infections. Attack surface reduction rules are sweeping settings that stop entire classes of threats including, infostealers, credential theft, and ransomware. The following bullet points offer more guidance on specific mitigation advice:

- [Turn on PUA protection in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/detect-block-potentially-unwanted-apps-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc)
- [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion)
- [Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-execution-of-potentially-obfuscated-scripts)

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects threat components as the following malware:
 
- [Trojan:MSIL/SnakeLogger](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:MSIL/Snakelogger.AMMB)

## References
[NOVA: blast from the past](https://bi-zone.medium.com/nova-blast-from-the-past-ccac0c3e6160). BI.ZONE (accessed 2025-02-03)

title: Flesh Stealer: Unmasking the Blue Masked Thief

Flesh Stealer employs multiple evasion techniques, including anti-debugging, anti-VM checks, and Base64 obfuscation to evade detection.

title: Beyond the Chatbot: Meta Phishing with Fake Live Support
content:
## Snapshot
Trustwave researchers investigate a sophisticated phishing campaign targeting Meta/Facebook users by impersonating live support chat services.

## Description
The attack begins with a phishing email warning of unusual API activity on the victim's Facebook account, using urgent subject lines to drive action. The email contains a disguised link hosted on a Salesforce-owned domain, leading to a phishing site with a Cloudflare CAPTCHA check for legitimacy. Victims are prompted to enter personal details, including email and name, under the guise of an appeal ticket process. The scheme has evolved from pop-ups to inline forms requesting additional details like phone numbers.
 
A chatbox interface, featuring a fake representative named “Joseph Turner,” engages victims and requests screenshots of Facebook pages and even account passwords. Attackers likely use a Telegram API for chat interactions and collect sensitive data—including passwords and OTPs—via POST requests.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
[In January 2022](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/66570457), Trustwave published a blog detailing how threat actors exploit Facebook Messenger’s chatbot feature for phishing attacks. By leveraging its widespread use in digital marketing and customer support, attackers create the illusion of legitimacy. Trustwave researchers identified a phishing campaign that deceived users by mimicking Meta’s own services, making the social engineering tactics more effective and reducing the likelihood of users questioning the authenticity of the messages.
 
Since then, phishing attack social engineering tools have continued to evolve, with CAPTCHAs becoming an increasingly common technique. The [Microsoft Digital Defense Report 2024](https://cdn-dynmedia-1.microsoft.com/is/content/microsoftcorp/microsoft/final/en-us/microsoft-brand/documents/Microsoft%20Digital%20Defense%20Report%202024%20%281%29.pdf) mentions the use of CAPTCHA services by threat actors in phishing campaigns to bypass detection. Captchas often appear in multi-step redirection processes, preceding phishing landing pages to create legitimacy and evade security filters. By integrating captchas with other legitimate services, attackers make it more difficult for both automated systems and human analysts to detect and block these threats.

## Recommendations
Trustwave highlights that legitimate support channels typically advise users not to share their passwords, as doing so could compromise account security.

Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat.

Implement multifactor authentication (MFA) to mitigate credential theft from phishing attacks. MFA can be complemented with the following solutions and best practices to protect organizations:  

- [Help prevent social engineering attacks](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/security-insider/emerging-threats/feeding-from-the-trust-economy-social-engineering-fraud?ocid=magicti_ta_blog) by not blending personal accounts with work emails or work-related tasks. Avoid opening emails, attachments, and links, including links from social networks, from suspicious sources. Ask yourself if the sender is who they say they are before clicking anything. Be wary of senders as well as offers that are too good to be true. Do a search to determine if the offer is legitimate or a trap.
- Activate conditional access policies. [Conditional access](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/conditional-access/overview?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) policies are evaluated and enforced every time an attacker attempts to use a stolen session cookie. Conditional access policies evaluate sign-in requests using additional identity-driven signals like user or group membership, IP location information, and device status, among others, and are enforced for suspicious sign-ins. Organizations can protect themselves from attacks that leverage stolen credentials by enabling policies such as compliant devices or trusted IP address requirements.
- Configure [continuous access evaluation](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/conditional-access/concept-continuous-access-evaluation?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in your tenant.
- Invest in advanced anti-phishing solutions that monitor incoming emails and visited websites. [Microsoft Defender for Office](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender/microsoft-365-security-center-mdo?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) 365 brings together incident and alert management across email, devices, and identities, centralizing investigations for threats in email. Organizations can also leverage web browsers that automatically [identify and block malicious websites](https://learn.microsoft.com/deployedge/microsoft-edge-security-smartscreen?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc). To build resilience against phishing attacks in general, organizations can use [anti-phishing policies](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/set-up-anti-phishing-policies?view=o365-worldwide) to enable mailbox intelligence settings, as well as configure impersonation protection settings for specific messages and sender domains. Enabling [SafeLinks](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-links?view=o365-worldwide) ensures real-time protection by scanning at time of delivery and at time of click.
- Continuously monitor for suspicious or anomalous activities, and search for sign-in attempts with suspicious characteristics (for example location, internet service provider \[ISP\], user agent, and use of anonymizer services). Activity can be identified and investigated with [Microsoft Defender for Identity](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender/microsoft-365-security-center-mdi?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc), which contributes identity-focused information into incidents and alerts, providing key context and correlating alerts from other products within Microsoft 365 Defender. This ensures all alerts are available in one place, and the scope of a breach can be determined faster than before.

Defenders can also complement MFA with the following solutions and best practices to further protect their organizations from such attacks.  

- Use [security defaults](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/fundamentals/concept-fundamentals-security-defaults?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) as a baseline set of policies to improve identity security posture.
- Block phishing websites and other malicious URLs and domains in the browser through [Microsoft Defender SmartScreen](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/operating-system-security/virus-and-threat-protection/microsoft-defender-smartscreen/), as well as the detection of suspicious and malicious behavior on endpoints.

title: Analyzing ELF/Sshdinjector.A!tr with a Human and Artificial Analyst
content:
## Snapshot
Researchers at Fortinet released an analysis into malware used during the Lunar Peek campaign attributed to the DaggerFly espionage group.

## Description
The malware, referred to as ELF/Sshdinjector.A!tr by Fortinet, targets Linux-based network appliances or IoT devices for data exfiltration. It consists of a dropper, a malicious SSH library (libsshd.so), and multiple persistence mechanisms.

The dropper ensures the system is infected before deploying the payload, which replaces critical system binaries like ls, netstat, and crond. Once established, the malware modifies the SSH daemon to exfiltrate system data and establish communication with a command-and-control (C2) server. It collects details such as MAC addresses, running processes, and user credentials from /etc/shadow. 

The malware also allows attackers to execute commands remotely, list directories, transfer files, and open shell terminals. Communication with the C2 server is facilitated through a custom protocol with hard-coded identifiers. Notably, the malware includes references to Chinese-language terms within its function names.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
[MITRE](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1034/) lists Daggerfly, also known as Evasive Panda and Bronze Highland, as a China-based advanced persistent threat group that primarily targets individuals and organizations in government, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), and the telecommunications industry primarily in Asia and Africa. Active since at least 2012, Daggerfly is also known for its exclusive use of [MgBot](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1146/), a modular malware with data exfiltration capabilities. 

Daggerfly [made OSINT headlines](https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/daggerfly-espionage-updated-toolset) in July 2024 as the group employed a new Windows backdoor, dubbed Suzafk by Symantec, alongside updated versions of its MgBot framework and a macOS backdoor named Macma. The group's activities targeted organizations in Taiwan and a US-based NGO operating in China.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations.
 
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/linux-preferences) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown threats.
- Run [EDR in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode?view=o365-worldwide?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus does not detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach.
- Allow [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations?view=o365-worldwide?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in full automated mode to allow Microsoft Defender for Endpoint to take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.
- [Enable](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-controlled-folders) controlled folder access.
- Ensure that [tamper protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection#how-do-i-configure-or-manage-tamper-protection) is enabled in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Enable [network protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-network-protection) in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Follow the credential hardening recommendations in the [on-premises credential theft overview](https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/9382203e-5155-4b5e-af74-21562b1004d5/analystreport) to defend against common credential theft techniques like LSASS access.
- [Enable](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-credential-stealing-from-the-windows-local-security-authority-subsystem) LSA protection.

title: Stealers on the Rise: A Closer Look at a Growing macOS Threat
content:
## Snapshot
Researchers at Palo Alto have identified a significant increase in macOS infostealers, with Poseidon, Atomic, and Cthulhu Stealers being particularly prevalent. These infostealers are distributed through various methods including malvertising, Trojanized installers, and Google ads, stealing a variety of personal and financial information.

## Description
Information stealers are malware designed to steal sensitive information, including financial details, credentials, and files. These malware variants are indiscriminate, aiming to maximize data collection for profit, exposing organizations to risks like data leaks and enabling further attacks, such as ransomware deployment. MacOS infostealers often exploit the AppleScript framework, using social engineering to trick victims into revealing credentials or disabling security controls. 

Research has revealed three prominent macOS infostealers: Atomic Stealer, Poseidon Stealer, and Cthulhu Stealer. Atomic Stealer, or AMOS, is offered as malware-as-a-service on hacker forums and Telegram, and is distributed through malvertising, capable of stealing browser data, cryptocurrency wallets, and instant messaging data. Poseidon Stealer is spread via Trojanized installers and Google ads, leveraging encoded AppleScript files to obtain system information and passwords. The infostealer Cthulhu Stealer, sold on Telegram by the "Cthulhu Team," also uses malicious installers and AppleScript to steal a variety of information, including gaming credentials, and stores it in a directory before uploading to a command-and-control server.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
[Information stealers](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/2296d491ea381b532b24f2575f9418d4b6723c17b8a1f507d20c2140a75d16d6) are malware designed to steal sensitive data from browsers, such as session tokens, passwords, credit card information, cryptocurrency wallets, and credentials for systems like VPNs, RDP, and identity providers. These malware types can also deploy additional malicious software into the compromised environment.
 
As commodity malware, infostealers are widely used to extract information from targeted devices and send it to the attacker. Their growing popularity has fostered the development of an infostealer ecosystem, giving rise to a new class of threat actors who exploit these tools to carry out their attacks.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations.
 
- Check your Office 365 email filtering settings to ensure you block spoofed emails, spam, and emails with malware. Use [Microsoft Defender for Office 365](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/defender-for-office-365?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for enhanced phishing protection and coverage against new threats and polymorphic variants. Configure Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to [recheck links on click](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-links-about?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) and [delete sent mail](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/zero-hour-auto-purge?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in response to newly acquired threat intelligence. Turn on [safe attachments policies](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-attachments-policies-configure?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to check attachments to inbound email.
- Encourage users to use Microsoft Edge and other web browsers that support SmartScreen, which identifies and blocks malicious websites, including phishing sites, scam sites, and sites that host malware.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus, or the equivalent for your antivirus product, to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown variants.
- Enforce MFA on all accounts, remove users excluded from MFA, and strictly [require MFA](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/identity-protection/howto-identity-protection-configure-mfa-policy?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) from all devices, in all locations, at all times.
- Enable passwordless authentication methods (for example, Windows Hello, FIDO keys, or Microsoft Authenticator) for accounts that support passwordless. For accounts that still require passwords, use authenticator apps like Microsoft Authenticator for MFA. [Refer to this article](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/concept-authentication-methods?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for the different authentication methods and features.
- For MFA that uses authenticator apps, ensure that the app requires a code to be typed in where possible, as many intrusions where MFA was enabled still succeeded due to users clicking “Yes” on the prompt on their phones even when they were not at their [devices](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/how-to-mfa-number-match?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc). Refer to [this article](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/concept-authentication-methods?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for an example.
- Remind employees that enterprise or workplace credentials should not be stored in browsers or password vaults secured with personal credentials. Organizations can turn off password syncing in browser on managed devices using [Group Policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/deployedge/microsoft-edge-enterprise-sync#sync-group-policies?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc).

Microsoft Defender customers can [turn on attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to prevent common attack techniques used in infostealer infections. Attack surface reduction rules are sweeping settings that stop entire classes of threats including, infostealers, credential theft, and ransomware. The following bullet points offer more guidance on specific mitigation advice:

- [Turn on PUA protection in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/detect-block-potentially-unwanted-apps-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc)
- [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion)
- [Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-execution-of-potentially-obfuscated-scripts)

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects threat components as the following malware:
 
- [Trojan:MacOS/Multiverze](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:MacOS/Multiverze)
- [Trojan:MacOS/RealstStealer.B!MTB](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:MacOS/RealstStealer.B!MTB)

title: AsyncRAT Abusing Python and TryCloudflare For Stealthy Malware Delivery
content:
## Snapshot
Forcepoint's X-Labs research team has uncovered a new malware campaign leveraging AsyncRAT, Python scripting, and TryCloudflare tunnels for payload delivery.

## Description
The campaign begins with phishing emails containing Dropbox URLs that distribute a ZIP file with a .URL internet shortcut. This shortcut redirects victims to a TryCloudflare-hosted malicious link, leading to a .LNK file that triggers PowerShell scripts to download an obfuscated JavaScript file. A batch file then retrieves another ZIP archive containing a Python script and additional components. The Python script, central to the attack, uses the ctypes library to allocate memory, create processes, and inject code.
 
The attackers utilize the "Early Bird APC Queue" injection technique to execute malicious code during the initialization phase of legitimate processes, thus evading detection. The payload then establishes communication with command-and-control (C2) servers over non-standard ports such as 3232 and 4056, enabling data exfiltration and remote command execution while bypassing conventional security monitoring.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
[AsyncRAT](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/e9216610feb409dfb620b28e510f2ae2582439dfc7c7e265815ff1a776016776) is a remote access trojan (RAT) written in .NET that enables attackers to control infected Windows machines while evading detection. It is typically distributed through phishing emails and establishes an encrypted connection to a command and control (C2) server using protocols like HTTP, HTTPS, and DNS. Once connected, attackers can execute commands, capture keystrokes, take screenshots, and exfiltrate files while operating in the background. AsyncRAT employs multiple evasion techniques, including code obfuscation, encrypted network traffic, and disabling security features like Windows Defender.

Active since at least 2019, AsyncRAT has been used to target financial institutions, healthcare, government, and education sectors. Proofpoint recently reported AsyncRAT being delivered in [tax-themed](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/e3cac3e6) and [ClickFix](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/67d03ba9) campaigns, and the AhnLab Security Intelligence Center (ASEC) reported its [distribution through Scalable Vector Graphic (SVG) files](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/2758cf39). Notably, [Forcepoint reported](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/bf7946e8) observing AsyncRAT being delivered via TryCloudflare tunnel infrastructure in August 2024 to execute the payload.

## Recommendations
Implement multifactor authentication (MFA) to mitigate credential theft from phishing attacks. MFA can be complemented with the following solutions and best practices to protect organizations:
 
- Activate conditional access policies. [Conditional access](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/conditional-access/overview?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc)  policies are evaluated and enforced every time an attacker attempts to use a stolen session cookie. Conditional access policies evaluate sign-in requests using additional identity-driven signals like user or group membership, IP location information, and device status, among others, and are enforced for suspicious sign-ins. Organizations can protect themselves from attacks that leverage stolen credentials by enabling policies such as compliant devices or trusted IP address requirements.
- Configure [continuous access evaluation](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/conditional-access/concept-continuous-access-evaluation?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc)  in your tenant.
- Invest in advanced anti-phishing solutions that monitor incoming emails and visited websites. [Microsoft Defender for Office](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender/microsoft-365-security-center-mdo?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc)  365 brings together incident and alert management across email, devices, and identities, centralizing investigations for threats in email. Organizations can also leverage web browsers that automatically [identify and block malicious websites](https://learn.microsoft.com/deployedge/microsoft-edge-security-smartscreen?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) . To build resilience against phishing attacks in general, organizations can use [anti-phishing policies](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/set-up-anti-phishing-policies?view=o365-worldwide)  to enable mailbox intelligence settings, as well as configure impersonation protection settings for specific messages and sender domains. Enabling [SafeLinks](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-links?view=o365-worldwide)  ensures real-time protection by scanning at time of delivery and at time of click.
- Continuously monitor for suspicious or anomalous activities, and search for sign-in attempts with suspicious characteristics (for example location, internet service provider \[ISP\], user agent, and use of anonymizer services). Activity can be identified and investigated with [Microsoft Defender for Identity](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender/microsoft-365-security-center-mdi?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) , which contributes identity-focused information into incidents and alerts, providing key context and correlating alerts from other products within Microsoft 365 Defender. This ensures all alerts are available in one place, and the scope of a breach can be determined faster than before.

Defenders can also complement MFA with the following solutions and best practices to further protect their organizations from such attacks.

- Use [security defaults](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/fundamentals/concept-fundamentals-security-defaults?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc)  as a baseline set of policies to improve identity security posture.
- Block phishing websites and other malicious URLs and domains in the browser through [Microsoft Defender SmartScreen](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/operating-system-security/virus-and-threat-protection/microsoft-defender-smartscreen/) , as well as the detection of suspicious and malicious behavior on endpoints.

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
- [Trojan:MSIL/AsyncRAT](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:MSIL/AsyncRAT)
- [Trojan:XML/AsyncRAT](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:XML/AsyncRat)
- [Trojan:VBS/AsyncRAT](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:VBS/AsyncRAT)
- [Backdoor:Win32/AsyncRAT](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Backdoor:Win32/Asyncrat)
- [Backdoor:MSIL/AsyncRAT](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Backdoor:MSIL/AsyncRAT&threatId=0)
- [TrojanDownloader:PowerShell/AsyncRAT](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=TrojanDownloader:PowerShell/AsyncRat.C!MTB&threatId=-2147066591)

## References

[AsyncRAT Reloaded: Using Python and TryCloudflare for Malware Delivery Again](https://www.forcepoint.com/blog/x-labs/asyncrat-reloaded-python-trycloudflare-malware). Forcepoint (2025-02-06)
 
[Security Brief: Threat Actors Take Taxes Into Account](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/e3cac3e6). Microsoft (2025-02-06)
 
[Security Brief: ClickFix Social Engineering Technique Floods Threat Landscape](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/67d03ba9). Microsoft (2025-02-06)
 
[Warning Against Malware in SVG Format Distributed via Phishing Emails](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/2758cf39). Microsoft (2025-02-06)

title: CVE-2025-0411: Ukrainian Organizations Targeted in Zero-Day Campaign and Homoglyph Attacks
content:
## Snapshot
The Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) Threat Hunting team discovered a zero-day vulnerability, [CVE-2025-0411](https://www.zerodayinitiative.com/advisories/ZDI-25-045/), in 7-Zip that was exploited in the wild to deploy the SmokeLoader malware. The exploit was linked to Russian cybercrime groups targeting Ukrainian governmental and non-governmental organizations, likely for cyberespionage purposes.

## Description
The attackers initiated the campaign through spear-phishing emails sent from compromised Ukrainian government and business accounts, delivering 7-Zip archives containing disguised malicious files. 7-Zip is a free, open-source file archiver software that supports various compression formats, including its high-compression 7z format, and is widely used for creating and extracting compressed archives. The attack used a nested archive structure to exploit the CVE-2025-0411 vulnerability, with the inner ZIP archive deploying a homoglyph attack to mimic a .doc file, which led to the execution of malicious JavaScript, Windows Script, and Windows Shortcut files without triggering Windows Mark-of-the-Web protections. 

The campaign involved a two-layer archive strategy, with the outer zip archive named "Documents and payments" and an inner archive named "List," both using homoglyphs—where visually similar but distinct characters were used to disguise malicious file extensions—to deceive users. The inner archive contained a .url file that directed victims to an attacker-controlled server hosting another ZIP archive, which in turn contained an executable disguised as a PDF document. Upon execution, this file deployed the SmokeLoader payload, resulting in full system compromise. 

Affected Ukrainian entities included the State Executive Service, Zaporizhzhia Automobile Building Plant, and Kyiv Public Transportation Service. The vulnerability was subsequently patched in 7-Zip version 24.09 released on November 30, 2024.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
SmokeLoader is a modular malware loader that has been actively used in cyberattacks for over a decade, primarily for deploying additional payloads and facilitating financial fraud. Its adaptability and evasion techniques make it a persistent threat across industries. In September 2024, [FortiGuard Labs uncovered](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/c718d8cb) a phishing campaign in Taiwan that used SmokeLoader to directly deliver attacks via plugins, exploiting vulnerabilities in Microsoft Office (CVE-2017-0199 and CVE-2017-11882). The malware leveraged obfuscated scripts and multi-stage execution techniques, deploying plugins for credential theft, keylogging, and browser injection. Similarly, as of May 2024, [CERT-UA had observed](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/7bef5f52) increased activity from UAC-0006, a financially motivated threat actor using phishing emails with malicious ZIP archives to distribute SmokeLoader. Once installed, the malware downloads additional tools such as Taleshot and RMS, forming a botnet that CERT-UA warns could be leveraged for banking fraud. These incidents highlight SmokeLoader’s continued evolution and its role in cybercrime campaigns.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat.  

- Use Microsoft Defender Vulnerability management to identify and address [zero-day vulnerabilities](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-vulnerability-management/tvm-zero-day-vulnerabilities)

- Keep [software up to date](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/mem/configmgr/sum/) to prevent unauthorized access, using [Microsoft Intune](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/mem/intune/fundamentals/what-is-intune).

Use [Microsoft Defender for Office 365](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/defender-for-office-365?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for enhanced phishing protection and coverage against new threats and polymorphic variants. Configure Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to [recheck links on click](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-links-about?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) and [delete sent mail](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/zero-hour-auto-purge?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in response to newly acquired threat intelligence. Turn on [safe attachments policies](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-attachments-policies-configure?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to check attachments to inbound email.
- Encourage users to use Microsoft Edge and other web browsers that support [SmartScreen](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/web-protection-overview?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc), which identifies and blocks malicious websites, including phishing sites, scam sites, and sites that host malware.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus, or the equivalent for your antivirus product, to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown variants.
- Enforce MFA on all accounts, remove users excluded from MFA, and strictly [require MFA](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/identity-protection/howto-identity-protection-configure-mfa-policy?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) from all devices, in all locations, at all times.
- Enable passwordless authentication methods (for example, Windows Hello, FIDO keys, or Microsoft Authenticator) for accounts that support passwordless. For accounts that still require passwords, use authenticator apps like Microsoft Authenticator for MFA. Refer to [this article](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/concept-authentication-methods?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for the different authentication methods and features.
- For MFA that uses authenticator apps, ensure that the app requires a code to be typed in where possible, as many intrusions where MFA was enabled still succeeded due to users clicking “Yes” on the prompt on their phones even when they were not at their [devices](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/how-to-mfa-number-match?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc).
- Remind employees that enterprise or workplace credentials should not be stored in browsers or password vaults secured with personal credentials. Organizations can turn off password syncing in browser on managed devices using [Group Policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/deployedge/microsoft-edge-enterprise-sync#sync-group-policies?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc).

Microsoft Defender customers can turn on [attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to prevent common attack techniques used in infostealer infections. The following bullet points offer more guidance on specific mitigation advice:

- [Turn on PUA protection in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/detect-block-potentially-unwanted-apps-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc)

title: "Crazy Evil" Cryptoscam Gang: Unmasking a Global Threat in 2024
content:
## Snapshot
Researchers from Insikt Group have uncovered the activities of Crazy Evil, a highly flexible Russian-speaking cybercriminal group that specializes in identity fraud, cryptocurrency theft, and information stealer malware.

## Description
Crazy Evil operates through a network of traffers, who are social engineering experts that redirect legitimate traffic to malicious phishing pages. The group is organized into six subteams—AVLAND, TYPED, DELAND, ZOOMLAND, DEFI, and KEVLAND—each running scams tailored to specific victim profiles. 
 
Crazy Evil primarily targets cryptocurrency users, influencers, and gaming personalities by creating highly convincing spearphishing campaigns. The group uses infostealer malware such as Stealc, Atomic macOS Stealer (AMOS), and Angel Drainer to compromise victims' devices and steal digital assets. Their phishing scams have been linked to major attacks on social media, often exploiting platforms like Telegram and Discord to distribute malicious links.
 
Since its emergence in 2021, Crazy Evil has generated millions of dollars in illicit revenue and has infected tens of thousands of devices globally. The group actively promotes its services on dark web forums like Lolz.Guru and YouHack, offering training and resources to aspiring traffers. Their methods include hardware wallet attacks, address poisoning, and fully undetectable (FUD) malware deployment.
 
Insikt Group reports that Crazy Evil has remained undetected for nearly four years, continuously adapting its techniques. The group has expanded beyond targeting job seekers to exploiting the decentralized finance (DeFi) ecosystem, making it a growing threat to cryptocurrency security. Their ability to rapidly adjust to security measures and recruit new affiliates suggests their operations will persist, posing a significant risk to individuals and organizations in the digital asset space.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations.

- Check your Office 365 email filtering settings to ensure you block spoofed emails, spam, and emails with malware. Use [Microsoft Defender for Office 365](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/defender-for-office-365?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for enhanced phishing protection and coverage against new threats and polymorphic variants. Configure Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to [recheck links on click](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-links-about?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) and [delete sent mail](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/zero-hour-auto-purge?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in response to newly acquired threat intelligence. Turn on [safe attachments policies](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-attachments-policies-configure?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to check attachments to inbound email.
- Encourage users to use Microsoft Edge and other web browsers that support [SmartScreen](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/web-protection-overview?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc), which identifies and blocks malicious websites, including phishing sites, scam sites, and sites that host malware.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus, or the equivalent for your antivirus product, to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown variants.
- Enforce MFA on all accounts, remove users excluded from MFA, and strictly [require MFA](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/identity-protection/howto-identity-protection-configure-mfa-policy?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) from all devices, in all locations, at all times.
- Enable passwordless authentication methods (for example, Windows Hello, FIDO keys, or Microsoft Authenticator) for accounts that support passwordless. For accounts that still require passwords, use authenticator apps like Microsoft Authenticator for MFA. [Refer to this article](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/concept-authentication-methods?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for the different authentication methods and features.
- For MFA that uses authenticator apps, ensure that the app requires a code to be typed in where possible, as many intrusions where MFA was enabled still succeeded due to users clicking “Yes” on the prompt on their phones even when they were not at their [devices](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/how-to-mfa-number-match?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc). Refer to [this article](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/concept-authentication-methods?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for an example.
- Remind employees that enterprise or workplace credentials should not be stored in browsers or password vaults secured with personal credentials. Organizations can turn off password syncing in browser on managed devices using [Group Policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/deployedge/microsoft-edge-enterprise-sync#sync-group-policies?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc).

Microsoft Defender customers can [turn on attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to prevent common attack techniques used in infostealer infections. Attack surface reduction rules are sweeping settings that stop entire classes of threats including, infostealers, credential theft, and ransomware. The following bullet points offer more guidance on specific mitigation advice:

- [Turn on PUA protection in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/detect-block-potentially-unwanted-apps-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc)
- [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion)
- [Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-execution-of-potentially-obfuscated-scripts)

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects threat components as the following malware:
 
- [Spyware:Win32/Stealc](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Spyware:Win32/Stealc)
- [Spyware:Win64/Stealc](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Spyware:Win64/Stealc)

title: macOS FlexibleFerret | Further Variants of DPRK Malware Family Unearthed
content:
## Snapshot
Researchers at eSentire have identified a new variant of the macOS Ferret malware family, linked to North Korean cyber campaigns, called "FlexibleFerret."

## Description
This malware is part of the "Contagious Interview" campaign, where threat actors lure victims into installing malware under the guise of job interview software. Apple recently updated its XProtect malware signatures to block several Ferret variants, but the newly discovered FlexibleFerret remains undetected.
 
FlexibleFerret is distributed via an Apple Installer package named "versus.pkg," which contains multiple malicious components, including a fake Zoom binary and a persistence mechanism disguised as a system file. Once installed, the malware executes scripts that install additional payloads, log activity, and establish persistence on the infected system. It also attempts to trick users into believing a legitimate application has failed to run by displaying a fake error message.
 
Similar to other North Korean malware campaigns, FlexibleFerret uses Dropbox for data exfiltration and api.ipify.org to identify the host’s public IP address. Researchers found strong similarities between FlexibleFerret and previously identified Ferret malware, including shared code and overlapping indicators of compromise (IOCs). Additionally, the malware has been used to target developers on GitHub by embedding malicious links in fake issue reports.
 
According to eSentire, the discovery of FlexibleFerret highlights the continued evolution of North Korean cyber threats, as attackers adapt by signing their malware with legitimate Apple Developer credentials and exploring new infection vectors. While Apple has taken steps to block earlier Ferret variants, organizations should remain vigilant, as FlexibleFerret and similar threats continue to evade traditional defenses.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
The objectives of nation-state threat actors linked to North Korea are diverse, encompassing espionage, financial gain, and politically motivated disruption or destruction. Microsoft Threat Intelligence researchers have increasingly observed some of these threat actors widening their missions to encompass multiple goals within the same operation, blurring the lines between traditional intelligence operations and cybercrime.

Understanding the targeting and objectives of North Korean state-sponsored threat actors is essential for the organizations most at risk of being impacted. To learn more about the activities of North Korean state-sponsored threat actors, read Microsoft's [Threat overview: North Korea state-sponsored activity](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/c83adbd4) and Microsoft's compilation of [Recent OSINT trends of North Korean threat actors](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/87adc2a0).

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following to reduce the risk of these threats:
 
- [Require multifactor authentication (MFA)](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/identity-protection/howto-identity-protection-configure-mfa-policy?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc). [Refer to this article](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/concept-authentication-methods?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for the different authentication methods for MFA like Microsoft Authenticator. Remove users excluded from MFA. Don't enter MFA codes sent by any kind of unwanted messages. Many attacks where MFA was set up still worked because users clicked **Yes** on the prompt on their phones even when they weren't at their devices.
- Implement [conditional access authentication strength](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/concept-authentication-strengths?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to require phishing-resistant authentication for employees and external users for critical apps.
- Implement [conditional access app control in Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-cloud-apps/proxy-intro-aad?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for users connecting from unmanaged devices.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/enable-cloud-protection-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a huge majority of new and unknown variants.
- Turn on [tamper protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) features to prevent attackers from stopping security services.
- Run [endpoint detection and response (EDR) in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus doesn’t detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected after a breach.
- Enable [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc)  in full automated mode to allow Defender for Endpoint to take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.
- Additional layers of protection can be applied with intrusion detection and prevention systems ([IDPS](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/firewall/premium-features?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#idps)) using Azure Firewall Premium. [Perform network intrusion detection by using Azure Network Watcher and open-source tools](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/network-watcher/network-watcher-intrusion-detection-open-source-tools?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc). Use Azure Web Application Firewall ([WAF](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/web-application-firewall/overview?WT.mc_id=AZ-MVP-5000120)) to provide centralized protection of your web applications from common exploits and vulnerabilities.
- Check your Office 365 email filtering settings to ensure you block spoofed emails, spam, and emails with malware. Use [Microsoft Defender for Office 365](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/defender-for-office-365?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for enhanced phishing protection and coverage against new threats and polymorphic variants. Configure Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to [recheck links on click](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-links-about?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) and [delete sent mail](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/zero-hour-auto-purge?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in response to newly acquired Threat Intelligence. Turn on [safe attachments policies](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-attachments-policies-configure?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to check attachments to incoming emails. Keep [Microsoft Purview auditing](https://learn.microsoft.com/purview/audit-solutions-overview?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) set up so that audit records can be investigated when needed.
- Apply [security best practices for Microsoft Teams](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoftteams/teams-security-best-practices-for-safer-messaging?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc). Refer to the [security guide for Microsoft Teams](https://learn.microsoft.com/MicrosoftTeams/teams-security-guide?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc).
- Ransom and lateral movement stage:
    - [Block process creations originating from PsExec and WMI commands](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-process-creations-originating-from-psexec-and-wmi-commands). Some organizations may experience compatibility issues with this rule on certain server systems but should deploy it to other systems to prevent lateral movement originating from PsExec and WMI.
    - [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion)
    - [Use advanced protection against ransomware](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#use-advanced-protection-against-ransomware)

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects threat components as the following malware:
 
- [Trojan:MacOS/Multiverze](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:MacOS/Multiverze)
- Trojan:MacOS/NukeSpeed

title: Ongoing Email Bombing Campaigns leading to Remote Access and Post-Exploitation
content:
## Snapshot
eSentire has recently observed a surge in email bombing attacks, where threat actors flood victims' inboxes with spam emails before impersonating IT support via Microsoft Teams.

## Description
The attackers claim to offer assistance in resolving the email issue and request a remote session, during which they deploy malware to gain persistent access. This tactic has been linked to ransomware-related threat clusters tracked by [Sophos](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/cfccd682) as STAC5143 and STAC5777.
 
Once granted remote access, attackers use tools like Microsoft Quick Assist or Teams screen sharing to execute malicious payloads. In one case, they downloaded and combined files to create a malicious archive, which was extracted and used to deploy a harmful DLL file. The malware leveraged legitimate processes such as odbcconf.exe and OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe to evade detection. The attackers also added a registry key containing Command-and-Control (C2) server IPs, deleted evidence of their activities, and masked their operations with misleading success messages.
 
Other observed attack variations included PowerShell-based payload delivery, the use of TeamViewer for persistence, and the deployment of credential-stealing tools like XenArmor. Attackers also leveraged .NET DLL payloads to establish C2 connections and conduct network reconnaissance. eSentire assesses with high confidence that email bombing will remain an effective initial access technique, requiring organizations to implement robust security measures to mitigate this growing threat.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
Email Bombing attacks leverage social engineering by exploiting victims’ psychological responses to fear and urgency. When users receive an overwhelming flood of spam emails, they often panic, fearing their email account has been compromised or is malfunctioning. This sense of urgency makes them more susceptible to manipulation, as they seek immediate solutions to restore normalcy. Attackers then impersonate IT support via Microsoft Teams, offering assistance and gaining the victim’s trust.
 
By leveraging the authority of IT teams, threat actors manipulate employees into granting remote access without suspicion. Using familiar tools like Microsoft Quick Assist or Teams screen sharing, they reinforce the illusion of legitimacy. This combination of stress, urgency, and perceived authority makes the attack highly effective, allowing attackers to bypass security awareness defenses and compromise systems.
 
Microsoft has observed [Storm-1811](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/0a78394b205d9b9d6cbcbd5f34053d7fc1912c3fa7418ffd0eabf1d00f677a2b), a financially motivated cybercriminal group known to deploy Black Basta ransomware, use email bombing techniques and Microsoft Quick Assist in social engineering attacks leading to ransomware. Organizations can reduce the risk of attacks by [blocking or uninstalling](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/client-management/client-tools/quick-assist#disable-quick-assist-within-your-organization) Quick Assist and other remote management tools if the tools are not in use in their environment. Quick Assist is installed by default on devices running Windows 11. Additionally, [tech support scams](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/protect-yourself-from-tech-support-scams-2ebf91bd-f94c-2a8a-e541-f5c800d18435) are an industry-wide issue where scammers use scare tactics to trick users into unnecessary technical support services. Educating users on how to recognize such scams can significantly reduce the impact of [social engineering attacks](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365-life-hacks/privacy-and-safety/what-is-social-engineering.).

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following best practices to protect users and organizations from attacks and threat actors that misuse Quick Assist: 
 
- Consider [blocking or uninstalling](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/client-management/client-tools/quick-assist#disable-quick-assist-within-your-organization) Quick Assist and other remote monitoring and management tools if these tools are not in use in your environment. If your organization utilizes another remote support tool such as [Remote Help](https://www.microsoft.com/security/business/endpoint-management/microsoft-intune-remote-help), block or remove Quick Assist as a best practice. Remote Help is part of the [Microsoft Intune Suite](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/Microsoft-Intune) and provides authentication and security controls for helpdesk connections.
- Educate users about protecting themselves from [tech support scams](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/protect-yourself-from-tech-support-scams-2ebf91bd-f94c-2a8a-e541-f5c800d18435). Tech support scams are an industry-wide issue where scammers use scary tactics to trick users into unnecessary technical support services. Only allow a Helper to connect to your device using Quick Assist if you initiated the interaction by contacting Microsoft Support or your IT support staff directly.
- Don't provide access to anyone claiming to have an urgent need to access your device.
- If you suspect that the person connecting to your device is conducting malicious activity, disconnect from the session immediately and report the concern to your local authorities and/or any relevant IT members within your organization.
- Users who have been affected by a tech support scam can also use the [Microsoft technical support scam form](https://support.microsoft.com/windows/cfa4609a-92cc-4808-95e8-392b4ffd0753) to report it.

Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations.

- Educate users about [protecting personal and business information](https://www.microsoft.com/security/business/security-101/what-is-email-security?ocid=magicti_ta_abbreviatedmktgpage) in social media, filtering unsolicited communication, identifying lure links in phishing emails, and reporting reconnaissance attempts and other suspicious activity.
- Educate users about [preventing malware infections](https://www.microsoft.com/security/business/security-101/what-is-malware?ocid=magicti_ta_abbreviatedmktgpage), such as ignoring or deleting unsolicited and unexpected emails or attachments sent through instant messaging applications or social networks as well as suspicious phone calls.
- Invest in advanced anti-phishing solutions that monitor incoming emails and visited websites. [Microsoft Defender for Office 365](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender/microsoft-365-security-center-mdo?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) brings together incident and alert management across email, devices, and identities, centralizing investigations for email-based threats.
- Educate Microsoft Teams users to verify ‘External’ tagging on communication attempts from external entities, be cautious about what they share, and never share their account information or authorize sign-in requests over chat.
- Implement [Conditional Access authentication strength](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/concept-authentication-strengths) to require phishing-resistant authentication for employees and external users for critical apps.
- Apply Microsoft’s [security best practices for Microsoft Teams](https://learn.microsoft.com/MicrosoftTeams/teams-security-best-practices-for-safer-messaging) to safeguard Teams users.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/enable-cloud-protection-microsoft-defender-antivirus) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a huge majority of new and unknown variants.
- Enable [network protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/enable-network-protection?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to prevent applications or users from accessing malicious domains and other malicious content on the internet.
- Turn on [tamper protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection) features to prevent attackers from stopping security services.
- Enable [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations) in full automated mode to allow Defender for Endpoint to take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.
- Refer to [Microsoft’s human-operated ransomware overview](https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/05658b6c-dc62-496d-ad3c-c6a795a33c27/analystreport) for general hardening recommendations against ransomware attacks.

Microsoft Defender XDR customers can turn on [attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to prevent common attack techniques:

- [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion)
- [Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-execution-of-potentially-obfuscated-scripts)
- [Block process creations originating from PSExec and WMI commands](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?view=o365-worldwide#block-process-creations-originating-from-psexec-and-wmi-commands)
- [Use advanced protection against ransomware](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#use-advanced-protection-against-ransomware)

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects threat components as the following malware:
 
- [Trojan:Win32/Seheq](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:Win32/Seheq!rfn)
- [Trojan:Win32/CryptInject!MTB](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:Win32/CryptInject!MTB)

## References
[Ongoing Email Bombing Campaigns leading to Remote Access and Post-Exploitation](https://www.esentire.com/security-advisories/ongoing-email-bombing-campaigns-leading-to-remote-access-and-post-exploitation). eSentire (accessed 2025-02-03)
 
[Threat actors misusing Quick Assist in social engineering attacks leading to ransomware](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/f9b51b94). Microsoft (accessed 2025-02-03)
 
[Storm-1811](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/0a78394b205d9b9d6cbcbd5f34053d7fc1912c3fa7418ffd0eabf1d00f677a2b). Microsoft (accessed 2025-02-03)
