title: Operation Phantom Circuit: North Korea’s Global Data Exfiltration Campaign
content:
## Snapshot
Researchers at SecurityScorecard released a report detailing a campaign by the Lazarus group dubbed "Phantom Circut" targeting cryptocurrency and technology developers globally.

## Description
The operation involved the use of command-and-control (C2) servers active since September 2024, which not only delivered payloads but also maintained persistent communication with infected systems. A key discovery in the investigation was a hidden administrative layer within the C2 infrastructure, built using a React-based web platform and Node.js API, that enabled attackers to manage exfiltrated data, oversee compromised systems, and control payload delivery. Lazarus carried out a software supply chain attack by embedding obfuscated backdoors into legitimate software packages, tricking developers into deploying compromised applications. The campaign had a wide reach, infecting over 233 victims worldwide and routing stolen data back to North Korea.
 
To conceal their operations, the attackers used a sophisticated multi-layered obfuscation strategy, leveraging Astrill VPNs and proxy relays to disguise their geographic origin. Traffic was routed through intermediaries, including Sky Freight Limited in Russia and Oculus Proxy endpoints, before reaching the C2 infrastructure.
 
SecurityScorecard researchers identified six North Korean IP addresses directly linked to the C2 servers, confirming Lazarus's involvement. Further analysis revealed connections between the campaign’s infrastructure and past North Korean remote IT worker schemes. Activity associated with the North Korean remote IT worker threat is tracked by Microsoft as [Storm-0287](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/29ec3550).

- Run [endpoint detection and response (EDR) in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus doesn’t detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected after a breach.
- Enable [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc)  in full automated mode to allow Defender for Endpoint to take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.
- Additional layers of protection can be applied with intrusion detection and prevention systems ([IDPS](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/firewall/premium-features?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#idps)) using Azure Firewall Premium. [Perform network intrusion detection by using Azure Network Watcher and open-source tools](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/network-watcher/network-watcher-intrusion-detection-open-source-tools?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc). Use Azure Web Application Firewall ([WAF](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/web-application-firewall/overview?WT.mc_id=AZ-MVP-5000120)) to provide centralized protection of your web applications from common exploits and vulnerabilities.
- Check your Office 365 email filtering settings to ensure you block spoofed emails, spam, and emails with malware. Use [Microsoft Defender for Office 365](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/defender-for-office-365?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for enhanced phishing protection and coverage against new threats and polymorphic variants. Configure Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to [recheck links on click](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-links-about?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) and [delete sent mail](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/zero-hour-auto-purge?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in response to newly acquired Threat Intelligence. Turn on [safe attachments policies](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-attachments-policies-configure?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to check attachments to incoming emails. Keep [Microsoft Purview auditing](https://learn.microsoft.com/purview/audit-solutions-overview?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) set up so that audit records can be investigated when needed.
- Apply [security best practices for Microsoft Teams](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoftteams/teams-security-best-practices-for-safer-messaging?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc). Refer to the [security guide for Microsoft Teams](https://learn.microsoft.com/MicrosoftTeams/teams-security-guide?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc).
- Ransom and lateral movement stage:
    - [Block process creations originating from PsExec and WMI commands](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-process-creations-originating-from-psexec-and-wmi-commands). Some organizations may experience compatibility issues with this rule on certain server systems but should deploy it to other systems to prevent lateral movement originating from PsExec and WMI.
    - [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion)
    - [Use advanced protection against ransomware](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#use-advanced-protection-against-ransomware)

title: Persistent Threats from the Kimsuky Group Using RDP Wrapper
content:
#### Targeted Geolocations
- Korea



## Snapshot
According to research from the AhnLab Security Intelligence Center (ASEC), the Kimsuky group (tracked by Microsoft as [Emerald Sleet](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/07f48a46)) continues to conduct highly targeted spear-phishing attacks, distributing malicious shortcut files (.LNK).

## Description
These files often include the names of specific individuals and companies in their filenames and are disguised as Office documents to appear legitimate. When executed, they launch PowerShell or Mshta commands to download and deploy malware such as PebbleDash and a custom-built RDP Wrapper. The RDP Wrapper enables remote desktop access and is modified by the attackers to evade detection.
 
To maintain persistence, the group installs proxy malware to facilitate remote access even when infected systems are on private networks. Identified proxy variants include a launcher-based tool, a mutex-named proxy, and a Go-based revsocks tool. Additionally, Kimsuky deploys keyloggers in both PowerShell script and executable form, with recent variants modifying file storage locations.
 
The group also employs infostealer malware to extract credentials from web browsers. A newly observed tool, "forceCopy," copies browser configuration files using the NTFS Parser library instead of traditional API calls. New Loader and Injector malware variants have also emerged, enabling attackers to load payloads into memory or inject code into other processes.
 
ReflectiveLoader, an obfuscated PowerShell script based on an open-source tool, has been found alongside other PowerShell-based malware. These findings suggest a shift in Kimsuky's tactics, favoring RDP-based remote access over traditional backdoors while continuing to refine their methods for persistence and credential theft.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
The threat actor Microsoft tracks as [Emerald Sleet](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/07f48a46) is a North Korean state actor that has been active since at least 2013. The actor is known to primarily target individuals working in international affairs, with a special focus on those whose work relates to Northeast Asia, as well as non-government organizations, government agencies and services, and media in North America, South America, Europe, and East Asia. Emerald Sleet focuses on specific targets of interest to steal credentials and information that advance its agenda.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat:

**Strengthen Microsoft Defender for Endpoint configuration**
 
- Ensure that [tamper protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection) is enabled in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Enable [network protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/enable-network-protection) in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Turn on [web protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/web-protection-overview).
- Run [Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus does not detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach.
- Configure [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations) in full automated mode to let Microsoft Defender for Endpoint take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.
- Microsoft Defender XDR customers can turn on the following [attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction) to prevent common attack techniques used by threat actors.
    - [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference)
    - [Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference)
    - [Block process creations originating from PSExec and WMI commands](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference)

**Strengthen Microsoft Defender for Office 365 configuration**

- Turn on [Safe Links](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-office-365/safe-links-about) and [Safe Attachments](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-office-365/safe-attachments-about) for Office 365.
- Enable [Zero-hour auto purge (ZAP)](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-office-365/zero-hour-auto-purge) in Office 365 to quarantine sent mail in response to newly acquired threat intelligence and retroactively neutralize malicious phishing, spam, or malware messages that have already been delivered to mailboxes.
- Invest in [advanced anti-phishing](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-office-365/anti-phishing-protection-about) solutions that monitor incoming emails and visited websites. [Microsoft Defender for Office 365](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender/microsoft-365-security-center-mdo) merges incident and alert management across email, devices, and identities, centralizing investigations for email-based threats.
- Configure Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to [recheck links on click](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-office-365/safe-links-about).
- Use the [Attack Simulator](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-office-365/attack-simulation-training-get-started) in Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to run realistic, yet safe, simulated phishing and password attack campaigns. Run spear-phishing (credential harvest) simulations to train end-users against clicking URLs in unsolicited messages and disclosing credentials.

**Strengthen operating environment configuration**

- Require [multifactor authentication (MFA)](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/admin/security-and-compliance/set-up-multi-factor-authentication). While certain attacks such as adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing attempt to circumvent MFA, implementation of MFA remains an essential pillar in identity security and is highly effective at stopping a variety of threats.
    - Leverage [phishing-resistant authentication methods](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity/authentication/concept-authentication-methods) such as FIDO Tokens, or [Microsoft Authenticator](https://www.microsoft.com/security/mobile-authenticator-app) with passkey. Avoid telephony-based MFA methods to avoid risks associated with SIM-jacking.
- Implement Entra ID [Conditional Access authentication strength](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/concept-authentication-strengths) to require phishing-resistant authentication for employees and external users for critical apps.
- Encourage users to use Microsoft Edge and other web browsers that support [Microsoft Defender SmartScreen](https://learn.microsoft.com/deployedge/microsoft-edge-security-smartscreen), which identifies and blocks malicious websites, including phishing sites, scam sites, and sites that host malware.
- Enable [Network Level Authentication](https://learn.microsoft.com/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-server-2008-R2-and-2008/cc753488%28v=ws.11%29) for Remote Desktop Service connections.

## References

title: XE Group: From Credit Card Skimming to Exploiting Zero-Days
content:
## Snapshot
A recent joint investigation by Intezer Labs and Solis Security uncovered new tactics employed by XE Group, a sophisticated cybercriminal organization active since 2013.

## Description
Originally focused on credit card skimming, XE Group has shifted its operations toward targeted information theft and exploiting zero-day vulnerabilities. The group's latest campaigns involve long-term persistence strategies, such as reactivating webshells years after initial breaches.
 
In 2024, XE Group leveraged two previously undocumented vulnerabilities in VeraCore—an upload validation flaw and an SQL injection exploit—to gain unauthorized access to web applications. These vulnerabilities allowed attackers to install webshells, maintain stealthy access, and execute remote commands. Notably, an intrusion first traced back to 2020 remained undetected until the attackers re-engaged in 2024 using credentials stolen years earlier.
 
Their evolving tactics include obfuscating malicious files, automating data exfiltration, and integrating advanced techniques such as PowerShell scripting for stealthier payload delivery. Investigators also linked XE Group to past campaigns targeting Microsoft IIS servers, where they exploited vulnerabilities in Telerik UI components.
 
According to Intezer, XE Group’s persistent access to compromised systems highlights their ability to blend patience with technical expertise. Their recent activities emphasize the need for proactive vulnerability management and stronger detection mechanisms to mitigate long-term cyber threats.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations:
 
- Regularly update and patch software to protect against known vulnerabilities, using [Microsoft Defender vulnerability management dashboard](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-vulnerability-management/tvm-dashboard-insights).
- Keep [software up to date](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/mem/configmgr/sum/) to prevent unauthorized access, using [Microsoft Intune](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/mem/intune/fundamentals/what-is-intune).
- Additional layers of protection may be applied with intrusion detection and prevention systems ([IDPS](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/firewall/premium-features#idps)) using Azure Firewall Premium. [Perform network intrusion detection by using Azure Network Watcher and open-source tools.](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/network-watcher/network-watcher-intrusion-detection-open-source-tools) Use Azure Web Application Firewall ([WAF](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/web-application-firewall/overview?WT.mc_id=AZ-MVP-5000120)) to provide centralized protection of your web applications from common exploits and vulnerabilities.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus, or the equivalent for your antivirus product, to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown variants.
- Enforce MFA on all accounts, remove users excluded from MFA, and strictly [require MFA from all devices](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/identity-protection/howto-identity-protection-configure-mfa-policy?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc), in all locations, at all times.
- Practice the principle of least-privilege and maintain credential hygiene. Avoid the use of domain-wide, admin-level service accounts. Restricting local administrative privileges can help limit unwanted installations.
- Separate privileged roles. Admin and user accounts should be distinct. Use [Privileged Identity Management](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/privileged-identity-management/pim-configure) or separate accounts for privileged tasks, limiting accounts with excessive permissions. Apply [Conditional Access](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/conditional-access/overview), especially for accounts with elevated roles.  [Adaptive Protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/purview/insider-risk-management-adaptive-protection?tabs=purview-portal) can automatically apply strict security controls on high-risk users and minimize impact of potential data security incidents.

Microsoft Defender customers can turn on [attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to prevent common attack techniques

- [Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-execution-of-potentially-obfuscated-scripts)
- [Block Webshell creation for Servers](Block%20Webshell%20creation%20for%20Servers)
- Alerts for Linux machines: [Possible malicious web shell detected](Possible%20malicious%20web%20shell%20detected)

title: ClickFix vs. traditional download in new DarkGate campaign
content:
## Snapshot
In a recent malvertising campaign, attackers combined ClickFix with traditional phishing installers to deliver the DarkGate malware loader.

## Description
The first delivery method utilized PowerShell code via "ClickFix", and threat actors used a spoofed Google ad for the utility application Notion to lure victims to a fake “Verify you are human” page that mimicked Cloudflare Turnstile. The page’s obfuscated HTML deceived users into following steps that copied a malicious PowerShell command to their clipboard. When executed, this command decoded a Base64 string to download and run a binary containing an AutoIt script that ultimately deployed the DarkGate malware loader.

In the second delivery method, threat actors lured victims with a malicious ad that redirected them to a decoy site where a fake Notion installer was hosted on GitHub under the profile *herawtisabela1992.* The installer was digitally signed (now revoked) by KDL CENTRAL LIMITED, and much like the first delivery type, extracts an AutoIt payload configured with DarkGate. The same GitHub account was previously linked to distributing the Warmcookie (aka Badspace) backdo
 
The campaign's use of both ClickFix and traditional file downloads suggests that the threat actors are experimenting to determine which method is more effective for malware installation.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
Microsoft Threat Intelligence has also observed an unknown threat actor leveraging Notion branding to deploy DarkGate through the ClickFix Technique. Similar to the first delivery method mentioned by Malware Bytes, Microsoft observed the threat actor gain intial access to a victim's machine by using a fake Google ad for Notion that redirected to a fake verification page. The malicious code was then executed and downloaded DarkGate. The threat actor leveraged AutoIt to modify registry run keys, connect to a C2 server, and exfiltrate data. 

Recent OSINT reporting suggests that threat actors have been leveraging malicious Google ads and impersonating utility software to lure victims. Similar to this DarkGate campaign, an impersonation of Notion installer via a Google ads was utilized in a [SectopRAT](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/23c4c2dd67e084e3ee74068eed3cd1659ea7b2aacd21ccd13ea6bddddca9f787) campaign where AutoIt was [leveraged to distribute SectopRAT](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/93db57cc) malware as well as a campaign that utilized a malware loader, [FakeBat](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/f87ebe16), to distrubte [Lumma stealer](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/33933578825488511c30b0728dd3c4f8b5ca20e41c285a56f796eb39f57531ad).  ClickFix continues to be a common social engineering technque to distribute malware such as DarkGate, Danabot, Lumma Stealer, and NetSupport. By bypassing browser security features, ClickFix allows for undetected, effective infiltration. In [October 2024](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/cac6b305), GoDaddy security researchers identified over 6,000 WordPress sites compromised by a variant of the ClickFix technique that distributed via fake WordPress plugins. The fake plugins contained scripts that injected malicious JavaScript into the sites' HTML, ultimately displaying fake updates and error messages used to distribute information stealer malware.

## Recommendations
Organizations can mitigate some risks from malvertising by enabling Network Protection and [potentially unwanted program (PUA) application](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/detect-block-potentially-unwanted-apps-microsoft-defender-antivirus?view=o365-worldwide). By using the principle of least privilege and building credential hygiene, administrators can limit the destructive impact of malvertising attacks, even if the threat actors gain initial access to a system.
 
- Encourage users to use Microsoft Edge and other web browsers that support [Microsoft Defender SmartScreen](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/deployedge/microsoft-edge-security-smartscreen?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc), which identifies and blocks malicious websites, including phishing sites, scam sites, and sites that contain exploits and host malware.
- Turn on [network protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/enable-network-protection?view=o365-worldwide&ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to block connections to malicious domains and IP addresses.
- [Restrict privileged domain accounts and local accounts with administrator privileges](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2022/10/26/how-to-prevent-lateral-movement-attacks-using-microsoft-365-defender/?ocid=magicti_ta_blog). Randomize Local Administrator passwords with a tool like [Local Administrator Password Solution](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/laps/laps-overview) (LAPS) to prevent lateral movement using local accounts with shared passwords.
- Implement [Conditional Access App Control in Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-cloud-apps/proxy-intro-aad?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for users connecting from unmanaged devices.
- Enforce [multi-factor authentication (MFA)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/business-premium/m365bp-turn-on-mfa?view=o365-worldwide&tabs=secdefaults) on all accounts, remove users excluded from MFA, and always strictly require MFA from all devices, in all locations. Practice the principle of least privilege and maintain credential hygiene. Avoid the use of domain-wide, administrator-level service accounts. Restricting local administrative privileges can help limit installation of RATs and other unwanted applications.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus?view=o365-worldwide&ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block most new and unknown variants.
- Run [Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode?view=o365-worldwide&ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus doesn’t detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach.
- Enable [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations?view=o365-worldwide&ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in full automated mode to let Microsoft Defender for Endpoint take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.
- Turn on [tamper protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection?view=o365-worldwide&ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) features to prevent attackers from stopping security services.
- Refer to our [ransomware threat overview](https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/05658b6c-dc62-496d-ad3c-c6a795a33c27/analystreport) and how to protect yourself for recommendations on building strong credential hygiene and other robust measures to defend against ransomware.
- Turn on [Safe Links](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-office-365/safe-links-about) and [Safe Attachments](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-office-365/safe-attachments-about) for Office 365.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus, or the equivalent for your antivirus product, to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown variants.

Microsoft Defender XDR customers can turn on [attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?view=o365-worldwide&ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to prevent common attack techniques:

- [Turn on PUA protection in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/detect-block-potentially-unwanted-apps-microsoft-defender-antivirus?view=o365-worldwide&ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc)
- [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?view=o365-worldwide&ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion)
- [Use advanced protection against ransomware](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?view=o365-worldwide&ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#use-advanced-protection-against-ransomware)
- [Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?view=o365-worldwide&ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-execution-of-potentially-obfuscated-scripts)
- [Block use of copied or impersonated system tools](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-use-of-copied-or-impersonated-system-tools-preview)

## References
[ClickFix vs. traditional download in new DarkGate campaign](https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/cybercrime/2025/01/clickfix-vs-traditional-download-in-new-darkgate-campaign). Malware Bytes (2025-02-13)
 
[Large scale Google Ads campaign targets utility software.](https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/news/2024/10/large-scale-google-ads-campaign-targets-utility-software) Malware Bytes (2025-02-13)
 
[SectopRAT campaign pivoting to leverage AutoIt](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/93db57cc). Microsoft (2025-02-13)

title: X Phishing | Campaign Targeting High Profile Accounts Returns, Promoting Crypto Scams
content:
## Snapshot
SentinelLABS has identified an active phishing campaign targeting high-profile accounts on social media platforms, including those of U.S. political figures, journalists, technology and cryptocurrency organizations, and individuals with valuable usernames.

## Description
The campaign, which resembles a similar operation from the previous year, uses phishing emails with fake login notices or copyright violation themes to direct victims to credential phishing sites. The attackers have been exploiting Google's "AMP Cache" domain to bypass email detection and redirect users to phishing domains, ultimately leading them to fake websites where they are prompted to enter their account credentials.

Once an account is compromised, the attackers lock out the legitimate owner and use the account to post fraudulent cryptocurrency opportunities or links to external sites, aiming to lure more victims. The campaign's infrastructure shows a level of informality and flexibility, with domains registered through a Turkish hosting provider and hosted on an IP associated with a Belize-based VPS service. The attackers have also been observed using the FASTPANEL service to rapidly build and manage websites, which are often used as templates for phishing campaigns.

According to SentinelLABS, the campaign does not appear to be attributed to a specific country or widely-tracked threat actor, although past reports have suggested a connection to Turkish-speaking actors.  Additionally, the attackers have set up cryptocurrency-themed projects that may serve as placeholders for future attacks or direct pump-and-dump schemes. Some domains associated with the campaign have been used to deliver the DanaBot banking trojan.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. 
 
- Educate users about [protecting personal and business information](https://www.microsoft.com/security/business/security-101/what-is-email-security) in social media, filtering unsolicited communication, identifying lure links in phishing emails, and reporting reconnaissance attempts and other suspicious activity.
- Turn on [Zero-hour auto purge (ZAP)](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-office-365/zero-hour-auto-purge) in Defender for Office 365 to quarantine sent mail in response to newly-acquired threat intelligence and retroactively neutralize malicious phishing, spam, or malware messages that have already been delivered to mailboxes.
- Educate users about [preventing malware infections](https://www.microsoft.com/security/business/security-101/what-is-malware), such as ignoring or deleting unsolicited and unexpected emails or attachments.
- Invest in advanced anti-phishing solutions that monitor incoming emails and visited websites. [Microsoft Defender for Office 365](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-xdr/microsoft-365-security-center-mdo) brings together incident and alert management across email, devices, and identities, centralizing investigations for email-based threats.
- Encourage users to use Microsoft Edge and other web browsers that support [Microsoft Defender SmartScreen](https://learn.microsoft.com/deployedge/microsoft-edge-security-smartscreen), which identifies and blocks malicious websites, including phishing sites, scam sites, and sites that host malware.
- Implement [Conditional Access authentication strength](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity/authentication/concept-authentication-strengths) to require phishing-resistant authentication for employees and external users for critical apps.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/enable-cloud-protection-microsoft-defender-antivirus) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a huge majority of new and unknown variants.
- Enable [network protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/enable-network-protection) to prevent applications or users from accessing malicious domains and other malicious content on the internet.
- Turn on [tamper protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection) features to prevent attackers from stopping security services.
- Enable [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations) in full automated mode to allow Defender for Endpoint to take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.
- Run [endpoint detection and response (EDR) in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode), so that Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus doesn’t detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts detected post-breach.

Microsoft Defender XDR customers can turn on [attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction) to prevent common attack techniques:

- [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion)
- [Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-execution-of-potentially-obfuscated-scripts)
- [Block JavaScript or VBScript from launching downloaded executable content](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-javascript-or-vbscript-from-launching-downloaded-executable-content)

title: Dark Web Activity January 2025: A New Hacktivist Group Emerges
content:
#### Targeted Geolocations
- United States



#### Targeted Industries
- Energy



## Snapshot
Cyble's dark web researchers identified a new hacktivist group, "Sector 16," which allegedly has collaborated with pro-Russian hacktivist group Z-Pentest to infiltrate a SCADA system in Texas that manages oil pumps and storage tanks.

## Description
Sector 16 released a video allegedly showing unauthorized access to the Texas SCADA facility's operational data and control systems. Sector 16 also claimed access to a U.S. oil and gas production facility's control systems, demonstrating their alleged capability to monitor and manage critical infrastructure. 

Additionally, Cyble's dark web researchers reported on the dark web activities of 15 ransomware groups, including CL0P, INC Lynx, Akira, Rhysida, SafePay, RansomHub, Monti, Qilin, BianLian, Medusa, Cactus, FOG, LockBit, and BlackBasta. These groups have targeted a wide array of sectors, with CL0P alone claiming at least 115 victims by exploiting Cleo MFT vulnerabilities. The attacks have affected major ports, universities, police departments, defense contractors, government agencies, healthcare entities, and more.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
Threats to critical infrastructure, particularly in the energy sector, have become a growing concern as state-sponsored and hacktivist groups increasingly target industrial control systems (ICS) and supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems. These attacks can disrupt essential services, cause economic damage, and even pose national security risks. Adversaries often exploit vulnerabilities in outdated or poorly secured systems, leveraging tactics such as credential theft, malware deployment, and remote access to manipulate physical operations. Recent incidents, including ransomware attacks on pipelines and nation-state campaigns against power grids, underscore the evolving cyber threat landscape.

Hacktivist groups, particularly those that identify as pro-Russia and pro-Iran, have made headlines over the past year for their focus on industrial control systems (ICS) and operational technology (OT) environments, raising concerns about the security of critical infrastructure. For example, in December 2024, [Team82 researchers reported](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/5fa3e494) on custom-built malware targeting western IoT and OT devices that was linked to the pro-Iranian cyber persona Cyber Avengers. And in September 2024, [Z-Pentest claimed responsibility](https://x.com/FalconFeedsio/status/1839387180126626264) for cyberattacks against a water treatment system in Kansas. 

In May 2024, CISA issued a joint statement highlighting ongoing [pro-Russia hacktivist activity targeting ICS and small-scale OT systems](https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/resources/defending-ot-operations-against-ongoing-pro-russia-hacktivist-activity) across North American and European critical infrastructure sectors, including Water and Wastewater Systems, Dams, Energy, and Food and Agriculture. While these attacks often rely on unsophisticated techniques that create nuisance effects, investigations reveal that such actors are capable of leveraging more advanced methods to exploit insecure and misconfigured OT environments, potentially causing physical harm.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following defense strategies for organizations with both IoT and OT devices within their networks:
 
- **Adopt a comprehensive IoT and OT security solution** such as [Microsoft Defender for IoT](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/endpoint-security/microsoft-defender-iot) to allow visibility and monitoring of all IoT and OT devices, threat detection and response, and integration with SIEM/SOAR and XDR platforms such as Microsoft Sentinel and Microsoft Defender 365.
- **Enable vulnerability assessments** to identify unpatched devices in the organizational network and set workflows for initiating appropriate patch processes through [Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-vulnerability-management/defender-vulnerability-management?view=o365-worldwide) and [Microsoft Defender for Endpoint](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/endpoint-security/microsoft-defender-endpoint?rtc=1) with the [Microsoft Defender for IoT add-on](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/enable-microsoft-defender-for-iot-integration?view=o365-worldwide).
- **Reduce the attack surface** by eliminating unnecessary internet connections to IoT devices and OT control systems. Implement [Zero Trust](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/zero-trust/) practices by applying network segmentation to prevent an attacker from moving laterally and compromising assets after intrusion. IoT devices and OT networks should be isolated from IT and OT networks with firewalls. Extend vulnerability and exposure control beyond the firewall with [Microsoft Defender External Attack Surface Management](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/external-attack-surface-management/). Turn on [attack surface reduction](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?view=o365-worldwide) rules in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint to prevent common attack techniques such as those used by ransomware groups.
- **Increase network security** by enforcing multi factor authentication (MFA) methods such as Azure Active Directory MFA. Enable [network protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/enable-network-protection?view=o365-worldwide) to prevent applications or users from accessing malicious domains and other malicious content on the internet.

title: Astral Stealer Analysis
content:
## Snapshot
Researchers at CYFIRMA released a report detailing Astral Stealer v1.8, an advanced information-stealing malware written in Python, C#, and JavaScript, targeting gaming accounts (Steam, Roblox, Minecraft), browser credentials, cryptocurrency wallets, and VPNs.

## Description
It employs sophisticated evasion techniques, such as anti-debugging, VM detection, and registry modifications, to avoid detection and maintain persistence. The malware also features a fake error message tactic to distract users while executing malicious activities in the background.
 
Astral Stealer achieves persistence by modifying Windows startup settings and injecting itself into browsers and Discord to steal credentials and payment information. It manipulates Chrome extensions, alters browser shortcuts, and reinstalls itself after Discord updates to maintain access. The malware also disables Windows Defender using PowerShell commands, extracts Wi-Fi passwords, captures system information, and steals clipboard data.
 
To enhance its stealth, Astral Stealer terminates specific processes, hides its execution, and modifies system time settings to evade forensic analysis. It exfiltrates stolen data through webhooks, compressing files and sending them to remote servers. The malware has been linked to a French developer known for other infostealers, such as Yunit Stealer and Piro Sentinel.
 
Despite the takedown of most related Discord and Telegram channels, Astral Stealer remains publicly available on GitHub, with evidence of ongoing modifications by multiple contributors. According to CYFIRMA, Astral Stealer poses significant risks to individuals and organizations, particularly those involved in gaming and cryptocurrency transactions.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
Threat actors may employ information stealers to target gamers due to the high-value digital assets associated with gaming accounts, such as in-game currencies, rare items, and premium subscriptions. The gaming industry’s vast attack surface, including platforms like Steam, Epic Games, and Discord, provides numerous entry points for cybercriminals to deploy malware through phishing links, fake modifications, or malicious software disguised as cheats. 

The rise of cryptocurrency and NFTs in gaming has further incentivized attacks, as stolen crypto wallets and digital collectibles can be liquidated quickly with minimal traceability. Additionally, many gaming accounts are linked to external services like Twitch, YouTube, and social media platforms, allowing attackers to hijack multiple accounts from a single compromised credential. Credential reuse among gamers further amplifies the risk, as stolen login details can be used in credential stuffing attacks to breach additional accounts. This combination of financial incentives, widespread attack vectors, and the interconnected nature of gaming accounts makes gamers an attractive and profitable target for cybercriminals.

Recent incidents highlight how cybercriminals deploy information stealers to exploit the gaming community. In April 2024, [Proofpoint reported](https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/threat-actors-deliver-malware-youtube-video-game-cracks) that threat actors were distributing Vidar, StealC, and [Lumma Stealer](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/33933578825488511c30b0728dd3c4f8b5ca20e41c285a56f796eb39f57531ad) via YouTube, disguising them as pirated software and video game cracks to lure unsuspecting users. That same month, [McAfee researchers uncovered](https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/redline-stealer-a-novel-approach/) a new variant of RedLine Stealer masquerading as a game cheat, further demonstrating how malware authors exploit gamers' interest in game cheats. In July 2024, [CYFIRMA reported](https://www.cyfirma.com/research/kematian-stealer-a-deep-dive-into-a-new-information-stealer/) on Kematian Stealer, an information stealer with capabilities designed to extract sensitive data from gaming platforms like Minecraft, highlighting threat actors' focus on gaming-related targets.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat.

- Check your Office 365 email filtering settings to ensure you block spoofed emails, spam, and emails with malware. Use [Microsoft Defender for Office 365](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/defender-for-office-365?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for enhanced phishing protection and coverage against new threats and polymorphic variants. Configure Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to [recheck links on click](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-links-about?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) and [delete sent mail](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/zero-hour-auto-purge?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in response to newly acquired threat intelligence. Turn on [safe attachments policies](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-attachments-policies-configure?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to check attachments to inbound email.
- Encourage users to use Microsoft Edge and other web browsers that support [SmartScreen](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/web-protection-overview?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc), which identifies and blocks malicious websites, including phishing sites, scam sites, and sites that host malware.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus, or the equivalent for your antivirus product, to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown variants.
- Enforce MFA on all accounts, remove users excluded from MFA, and strictly [require MFA](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/identity-protection/howto-identity-protection-configure-mfa-policy?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) from all devices, in all locations, at all times.
- Enable passwordless authentication methods (for example, Windows Hello, FIDO keys, or Microsoft Authenticator) for accounts that support passwordless. For accounts that still require passwords, use authenticator apps like Microsoft Authenticator for MFA. [Refer to this article](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/concept-authentication-methods?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for the different authentication methods and features.
- For MFA that uses authenticator apps, ensure that the app requires a code to be typed in where possible, as many intrusions where MFA was enabled still succeeded due to users clicking “Yes” on the prompt on their phones even when they were not at their [devices](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/how-to-mfa-number-match?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc). Refer to [this article](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/concept-authentication-methods?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for an example.
- Remind employees that enterprise or workplace credentials should not be stored in browsers or password vaults secured with personal credentials. Organizations can turn off password syncing in browser on managed devices using [Group Policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/deployedge/microsoft-edge-enterprise-sync#sync-group-policies?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc).

Microsoft Defender customers can [turn on attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to prevent common attack techniques used in infostealer infections. Attack surface reduction rules are sweeping settings that stop entire classes of threats including, infostealers, credential theft, and ransomware. The following bullet points offer more guidance on specific mitigation advice:

- [Turn on PUA protection in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/detect-block-potentially-unwanted-apps-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc)
- [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion)
- [Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-execution-of-potentially-obfuscated-scripts)

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects threat components as the following malware:
 
- Trojan:Win64/AstralStealer

## References
[Astral Stealer Analysis](https://www.cyfirma.com/research/astral-stealer-analysis/). CYFIRMA (accessed 2025-01-30)
 
[Game Over: gaming community at risk with information stealers](https://blog.sekoia.io/game-over-gaming-community-at-risk-with-information-stealers/). Sekoia (accessed 2025-01-30)

title: HTTP Client Tools Exploitation for Account Takeover Attacks
content:
## Snapshot
Researchers at Proofpoint have discovered a significant trend in account takeover (ATO) attacks, where attackers exploit HTTP client tools to compromise Microsoft 365 environments.

## Description
These tools, sourced from public repositories like GitHub, are used in Adversary-in-the-Middle (AitM) and brute force attacks. A campaign utilizing the Axios HTTP client achieved a 43% success rate in compromising accounts by bypassing multifactor authentication (MFA) through precision targeting and AitM techniques. Attackers have also employed the Node Fetch client in a large-scale campaign targeting mainly the Education sector, with over 13 million login attempts but only a 2% success rate.

The attackers have adapted their strategies over time, switching between various HTTP clients such as OkHttp, Axios, Node Fetch, and Go Resty to increase the volume and diversity of attacks and evade detection. These campaigns have involved phishing threats to steal credentials, including MFA tokens, and post-compromise activities like creating mailbox rules, data exfiltration, and registering new OAuth applications with excessive permissions for persistent access. The operational patterns typically align with business hours and fluctuate based on the day of the week.

Proofpoint's analysis indicates that attackers are likely to continue adapting their strategies, leveraging new technologies and exploiting APIs to enhance their effectiveness. Specific user-agents associated with HTTP clients have been used for user enumeration and brute force attacks, and certain data center hosting services have been identified as source infrastructure for these attacks. Over 178,000 user accounts across more than 3,000 organizations have been targeted, with attackers focusing on student accounts for potential spam campaigns or resale. Despite the cessation of Go Resty based attacks in October 2024, Node Fetch based attacks persisted.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
Proofpoint’s recent analysis of HTTP client tool exploitation in account takeover attacks reinforces findings from our [Quarterly Cyber Threat Report: MITRE ATT&CK Framework Trends in OSINT (October – December 2024)](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/db42e801) regarding the dominance of Application Layer Protocols/Web Protocols in the command-and-control (C2) landscape. Adversaries continue to leverage HTTP/HTTPS not only for stealthy C2 communications but also to facilitate credential theft and session hijacking. This underscores the critical need for advanced network traffic analysis tools capable of distinguishing between legitimate web traffic and malicious activity hidden within these widely used protocols.

## Recommendations
While every situation is unique to the customer and their environment, the following recommendations are broadly applicable to help identify and mitigate cryptojacking attacks:  
 
- Separate privileged roles: Admin and user accounts should be distinct. Use [Privileged Identity Management](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/privileged-identity-management/pim-configure) or separate accounts for privileged tasks, limiting accounts with excessive permissions. Apply Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) and [Conditional Access](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/conditional-access/overview), especially for accounts with elevated roles.
- Implement MFA: Ensure comprehensive use of [MFA](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/tutorial-enable-azure-mfa), particularly for accounts with virtual machine contributor privileges. Discourage password reuse. A full list of cloud security recommendations can be found in [Security recommendations – a reference guide](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/defender-for-cloud/recommendations-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc).
- Use risk-based sign-in behaviors and conditional access policies: Monitor high Azure Active Directory risk scores and correlate risky behavior with subsequent activity. Implement conditional access policies for multifactor reauthentication, device compliance, password updates, or blocking authentication.
- Detect login anomalies: Employ standard anomaly detection methods for identifying unusual login patterns, such as proxy usage, anomalous locations, and user agents. Utilize Microsoft 365 Defender for detecting suspicious activities performed by risky users.
- Monitor external Azure IP addresses: Authentication from non-tenant IP addresses should be considered anomalous. Use the [az vm list-ip-addresses](https://learn.microsoft.com/cli/azure/vm?view=azure-cli-latest#az-vm-list-ip-addresses) command to identify allocated IP addresses within the tenant.
- Monitor quota increases: Watch for unexpected quota increases, especially across multiple regions or for rarely used resources, as they may indicate resource abuse attacks. Quota increase detections can be refined by focusing on commonly abused core types.

## References
[HTTP Client Tools Exploitation for Account Takeover Attacks](https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/http-client-tools-exploitation-account-takeover-attacks) Proofpoint (Accessed 2025-02-06)

title: Coyote Banking Trojan: A Stealthy Attack via LNK Files
content:
#### Targeted Geolocations
- Brazil



#### Targeted Industries
- Financial Services



## Snapshot
FortiGuard Labs has discovered a multi-stage operation involving the Coyote Banking Trojan, which targets users in Brazil to harvest sensitive information from financial applications and websites.

## Description
The infection begins with LNK files that execute PowerShell commands to connect to remote servers, leading to the delivery of the malware. Coyote is designed to perform keylogging, capture screenshots, and display phishing overlays to steal credentials. It establishes persistence by modifying the Windows registry and sends collected system information to a remote server, while also checking for installed antivirus products using Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI). The Trojan employs a loader DLL file and utilizes Donut to decrypt and execute the final payloads. It actively avoids detection by checking for sandbox-related usernames and virtual machine files.

Coyote has a broad scope, targeting over a thousand sites and financial agents, and monitors the active window for access to these targets. Communication with the command and control (C2) server is conducted through port 443, where it can receive instructions to perform various actions, including taking screenshots, manipulating windows, displaying fake update messages, and controlling user-visible windows. The sophistication of Coyote's infection process and its ability to adapt and expand its targets highlight the significant threat it poses to users' financial cybersecurity.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
Threat actors commonly deploy overlay attacks in banking trojan campaigns due to their effectiveness in deceiving users into divulging sensitive information. By crafting fake interfaces that closely resemble legitimate banking apps, attackers can stealthily capture login credentials, PINs, and other personal details. These attacks exploit social engineering tactics, as victims are often unaware they are interacting with a malicious interface rather than the genuine app. To learn more about the Coyote banking trojan and the growing prevalence of overlay attacks, read the Microsoft report [Recent OSINT trends in banking trojans](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/3c32651f).

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations.
 
- Configure Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to [recheck links on click](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-office-365/safe-links-about?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc). Safe Links provides URL scanning and rewriting of inbound email messages in mail flow, and time-of-click verification of URLs and links in email messages, other Microsoft 365 applications such as Teams, and other locations such as SharePoint Online. Safe Links scanning occurs in addition to the regular [anti-spam](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-office-365/anti-spam-protection-about?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) and [anti-malware](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-office-365/anti-malware-protection-about?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) protection in inbound email messages in Microsoft Exchange Online Protection (EOP). Safe Links scanning can help protect your organization from malicious links used in phishing and other attacks.
- Encourage users to use Microsoft Edge and other web browsers that support [Microsoft Defender SmartScreen](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/deployedge/microsoft-edge-security-smartscreen?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc), which identifies and blocks malicious websites, including phishing sites, scam sites, and sites that host malware.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/cloud-protection-microsoft-defender-antivirus) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attack tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown variants.
- Run [endpoint detection and response (EDR) in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc), so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus does not detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach.
- Enable [network protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-network-protection?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to prevent applications or users from accessing malicious domains and other malicious content on the internet.
- Enable [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in full automated mode to allow Microsoft Defender for Endpoint to take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.
- Turn on[potentially unwanted applications (PUA) protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/detect-block-potentially-unwanted-apps-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in block mode.

title: Rockwell Automation KEPServer
content:
#### Targeted Industries
- Critical Manufacturing



## Snapshot
Rockwell Automation reported a vulnerability in their KEPServer versions 6.0 to 6.14.263, which could lead to uncontrolled resource consumption and potentially cause the device to crash.

## Description
The vulnerability, identified as CVE-2023-3825, has a CVSS v3.1 base score of 7.5 and is exploitable remotely with low attack complexity. The issue arises from KEPServerEX's handling of OPC UA protocol, which allows for the creation of nested object types. The software does not check for recursively defined objects, enabling an attacker to send a message that could cause a stack overflow and crash the device. No public exploitation targeting this vulnerability has been reported to CISA at the time of the advisory.

## Recommendations
Rockwell Automation recommends users upgrade to KEPServer Version 6.15 or higher.

CISA recommends users take the following action to mitigate this threat:
 
- Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the Internet.
- Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.
- When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages.

## References
[Rockwell Automation KEPServer](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/ics-advisories/icsa-25-030-04). CISA (accessed 2025-02-03).

title: No need to RSVP: a closer look at the Tria stealer campaign
content:
#### Targeted Geolocations
- Malaysia  
- Brunei



## Snapshot
Researchers at SecureList have released a report detailing a malicious Android campaign targeting users in Malaysia and Brunei. The campaign, active since mid-2024, uses fake wedding invitations to trick victims into installing a malware-laced APK called "Tria Stealer."

## Description
Once installed, Tria Stealer harvests SMS messages, call logs, and data from messaging and email apps, including WhatsApp, Telegram, Gmail, and Outlook. The stolen information is exfiltrated to Telegram bots controlled by the threat actor, who then exploits it to hijack messaging accounts and impersonate victims to request money transfers from their contacts. The malware also intercepts one-time passwords (OTPs) and transaction authorization codes (TACs), allowing attackers to compromise additional online accounts.

Researchers attribute the campaign to an Indonesian-speaking threat actor based on language artifacts found in the malware. The attack method has evolved over time, with newer versions incorporating enhanced data collection capabilities. The malware spreads through compromised WhatsApp and Telegram accounts, increasing its reach.

## Recommendations
- Only install applications from trusted sources and official stores.
- If a device is no longer receiving updates, strongly consider replacing it with a new device.
- Use mobile solutions such as [Microsoft Defender for Endpoint on Android](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/microsoft-defender-endpoint-android?view=o365-worldwide)to detect malicious applications
    - Always keep Install unknown apps disabled on the Android device to prevent apps from being installed from unknown sources.
- Evaluate whether [Microsoft Defender for Internet of Things (IoT)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/defender-for-iot/organizations/overview) services are applicable to your IoT environment.

title: Malware Alert: Fake Judicial Review Emails Deliver SapphireRAT Targeting Latin American Victims
content:
## Snapshot
The Cofense Phishing Defense Center (PDC) has identified a sophisticated phishing campaign distributing SapphireRAT through emails with legal-themed lures. The attack primarily targets organizations in Latin America, particularly those handling sensitive data or critical infrastructure.

## Description
The phishing emails impersonate the Second Municipal Civil Court of Bogotá, falsely claiming the recipient owes legal penalties. Victims are instructed to review and sign attached documents, which contain a malicious link leading to a compromised website. Clicking the link initiates the download of a password-protected .rar file, which, when extracted, reveals additional compressed files containing an executable payload.
 
Once executed, SapphireRAT deploys multiple evasion techniques, including injecting code into legitimate Windows processes such as regsvr32.exe. This allows it to avoid detection while executing malicious tasks. The malware also spawns powershell.exe and conhost.exe to download and run additional payloads.
 
To maintain persistence, SapphireRAT creates an automated Windows task that repeatedly executes a malicious program stored in the AppData\Roaming directory. It also drops a .drv file to escalate privileges, ensuring long-term control over the infected system.
 
Network analysis reveals that the malware establishes connections with a remote command-and-control server, allowing attackers to issue commands, exfiltrate data, and deploy additional malware. The use of modular design enables SapphireRAT to adapt its functionality for different attack scenarios.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat.
 
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/linux-preferences) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown threats.
- Run [EDR in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode?view=o365-worldwide?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus does not detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach.
- Allow [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations?view=o365-worldwide?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in full automated mode to allow Microsoft Defender for Endpoint to take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.
- [Enable](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-controlled-folders) controlled folder access.
- Ensure that [tamper protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection#how-do-i-configure-or-manage-tamper-protection) is enabled in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Enable [network protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-network-protection) in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Follow the credential hardening recommendations in the [on-premises credential theft overview](https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/9382203e-5155-4b5e-af74-21562b1004d5/analystreport) to defend against common credential theft techniques like LSASS access.
- [Enable](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-credential-stealing-from-the-windows-local-security-authority-subsystem) LSA protection.

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects threat components as the following malware:
 
- [Trojan:MSIL/AgentTesla](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:MSIL/AgentTesla!rfn)

title: CL-STA-0048: An Espionage Operation Against High-Value Targets in South Asia
content:
#### Targeted Geolocations
- South Asia



#### Targeted Industries
- Communications Infrastructure  
- Government Agencies & Services



## Snapshot
A cyber-espionage campaign tracked as CL-STA-0048 by Palo Alto Networks has been observed targeting high-value organizations in South Asia, primarily in government and telecommunications. Palo Alto Networks researchers assess with moderately high confidence that this activity is connected to China-based threat actors.

## Description
The attackers employed rare techniques such as "Hex Staging," where malware is delivered in small encoded chunks, and exfiltration via DNS using ping. They also exploited vulnerabilities in IIS, Apache Tomcat, and MSSQL services, adapting their methods after initial failures.
 
The campaign primarily aimed to steal government employee data and sensitive organizational information, aligning with nation-state espionage motives. Investigations revealed the use of the [PlugX](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/028c3995955a4a710d67d5d4e9a5f067355bbc7ad58e5c5d1c1931e708e41b38) backdoor, [Cobalt Strike](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/fd8511c1d61e93d39411acf36a31130a6795efe186497098fe0c6f2ccfb920fc), and privilege escalation tools like SspiUacBypass and Potato Suite.
 
A distinct operational pattern emerged in the campaign, aligning with UTC+8 business hours, further supporting a connection to China. According to Palo Alto Networks, the attackers also utilized a Chinese DNS logging service and tools historically associated with groups like APT41, tracked by Microsoft as [Brass Typhoon](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/f0aaa62bfbaf3739bb92106688e6a00fc05eafc0d4158b0e389b4078112d37c6). While not definitively attributed, the tactics, tools, and victimology suggest CL-STA-0048 is part of China’s cyber espionage efforts.

## Recommendations
Apply these mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. 
 
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-cloud-protection-microsoft-defender-antivirus)and automatic sample submission on Microsoft Defender Antivirus. These capabilities use artificial intelligence and machine learning to quickly identify and stop new variants and polymorphic copies of this threat.
- Educate end users about preventing malware infections. Practice the principle of least-privilege and maintain credential hygiene. Avoid the use of domain-wide, admin-level service accounts. Restricting local administrative privileges can help limit installation of RATs and other unwanted applications.
- Turn on Microsoft Defender Firewall to prevent malware infection and stifle propagation.
- Encourage users to use Microsoft Edge and other web browsers that support SmartScreen, which identifies and blocks malicious websites, including phishing sites, scam sites, and sites that contain exploits and host malware.
- Turn on [attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction).

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects threat components as the following malware:
 
- [Trojan:Win32/Malgent!MSR](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:Win32/Malgent!MSR)

title: Hackers Attacking Windows, macOS, and Linux systems With SparkRAT
content:
## Snapshot
Researchers have discovered new developments in SparkRAT operations, highlighting its ongoing use in malicious campaigns against macOS users and government organizations. A recent report details how threat actors continue to exploit SparkRAT’s modular framework and cross-platform capabilities across Windows, macOS, and Linux, showcasing their evolving tactics.

## Description
SparkRAT, a Remote Access Trojan (RAT) first released on GitHub in 2022, is known for its adaptability, user-friendly web interface, and compatibility with Windows, macOS, and Linux. It communicates with a command-and-control (C2) server using WebSocket-based communication and HTTP POST requests for updates. The C2 servers are typically configured on port 8000, which aids in the detection of SparkRAT infrastructure..

The malware was distributed using domains disguised as meeting platforms, and scans revealed three active C2 servers hosting SparkRAT implants. Malicious files and scripts found on these servers facilitated persistence and established TCP connections with additional C2 infrastructure. An Android APK distributed on a Vietnamese gaming platform was also found initiating WebSocket connections, indicating data exfiltration and backdoor functionality. SparkRAT's infrastructure supports various malicious campaigns, from espionage to financial fraud, and its cross-platform nature increases its potential attack surface.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
Microsoft has observed a group tracked as [Storm-2077](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/7d0be221899f2b584367aba65ef2bd35efeab0b969f5b9f5f9ad486096a4ff95) utilizing SparkRAT in June of 2024. While Microsoft does not attribute the activity described in this profile to [Storm-2077](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/7d0be221899f2b584367aba65ef2bd35efeab0b969f5b9f5f9ad486096a4ff95), the group has been observed using the remote access trojan in phishing campaigns. The threat actor launched spear-phishing attacks against U.S. NGOs, the Defense Industrial Base, and sectors like IT, aviation, and finance. Emails disguised as security updates contained malicious links or password-protected ZIP files, some of which installed the remote access trojan SparkRAT.

Storm-2077, is a nation state threat actor based out of China that Microsoft began tracking in early 2024. Its techniques focus on exploiting public-facing applications, token theft, email data theft, and spear-phishing operations. This threat group is reported as TAG-100 by other security vendors.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations.
 
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-cloud-protection-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a huge majority of new and unknown variants.
- Invest in advanced anti-phishing solutions that monitor and scan incoming emails and visited websites. For example, organizations can leverage web browsers that automatically [identify and block malicious websites](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/deployedge/microsoft-edge-security-smartscreen?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc), including those used in this phishing campaign, and solutions that [detect and block malicious emails, links, and files](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/siem-and-xdr/microsoft-defender-office-365?ocid=magicti_ta_abbreviatedmktgpage).
- Turn on [Safe Links](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-office-365/safe-links-about?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) policies in Defender for Office 365 to prevent initial compromise.
- Turn on [Zero-hour auto purge (ZAP)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-office-365/zero-hour-auto-purge?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Defender for Office 365 to quarantine sent mail in response to newly-acquired threat intelligence and retroactively neutralize malicious phishing, spam, or malware messages that have already been delivered to mailboxes.
- Run [endpoint detection and response (EDR) in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can help block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus does not detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to help remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach.
- Configure [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in full-automated mode to let Microsoft Defender for Endpoint take immediate action on alerts to help resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.
- Turn on [real-time protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/configure-protection-features-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus.
- Turn on [network protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/network-protection?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Turn on the following [attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference)to block or audit activity associated with this threat:
    - [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion.](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?view=o365-worldwide#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion)
    - [Block executable content from email client and webmail.](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-executable-content-from-email-client-and-webmail)

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects threat components as the following malware:
 
- [Trojan:Win32/SparkRat](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan%3AWin32/SparkRat!MTB&threatId=-2147129710)

### Microsoft Defender for Endpoint
The following alerts associated with this activity can be triggered if Defender for Endpoint is configured to run in block mode:
