title: Security Brief: Threat Actors Take Taxes Into Account
content:
#### Targeted Geolocations
- Switzerland  
- United Kingdom  
- United States  
- Australia



#### Targeted Industries
- Financial Services



## Snapshot
Researchers at Proofpoint have detected an increase in phishing campaigns and malicious domains impersonating tax agencies and financial organizations, coinciding with tax seasons in the UK and US.

## Description
In the UK, threat actors impersonated HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) using "account update" lures to direct victims to credential harvesting sites. While in the US, hundreds of malicious tax-themed domains were used in email campaigns, including one impersonating Intuit with over 40,000 messages sent to more than 2,000 organizations. A campaign targeting Switzerland tricked users into making payments to adversary-controlled Revolut accounts under the guise of federal tax payment reminders. Australian phishing campaigns targeted myGov, the government services portal, attempting to steal multifactor authentication details and security question answers.

Additionally, tax-themed emails were used to deliver malware, such as a campaign impersonating a tax software organization to distribute Rhadamanthys malware, which subsequently downloaded and ran zgRAT. This campaign aligned with activity third-party researchers attribute to a threat actor known as Aggah. Other malware payloads delivered via tax-themed campaigns included MetaStealer, XWorm, [AsyncRAT](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/e9216610feb409dfb620b28e510f2ae2582439dfc7c7e265815ff1a776016776), and VenomRAT.

## Recommendations
Implement multifactor authentication (MFA) to mitigate credential theft from phishing attacks. MFA can be complemented with the following solutions and best practices to protect organizations:  
 
- Activate conditional access policies. [Conditional access](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/conditional-access/overview?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) policies are evaluated and enforced every time an attacker attempts to use a stolen session cookie. Conditional access policies evaluate sign-in requests using additional identity-driven signals like user or group membership, IP location information, and device status, among others, and are enforced for suspicious sign-ins. Organizations can protect themselves from attacks that leverage stolen credentials by enabling policies such as compliant devices or trusted IP address requirements.
- Configure[continuous access evaluation](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/conditional-access/concept-continuous-access-evaluation?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in your tenant.
- Invest in advanced anti-phishing solutions that monitor incoming emails and visited websites. [Microsoft Defender for Office 365](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender/microsoft-365-security-center-mdo?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) brings together incident and alert management across email, devices, and identities, centralizing investigations for threats in email. Organizations can also leverage web browsers that automatically [identify and block malicious websites](https://learn.microsoft.com/deployedge/microsoft-edge-security-smartscreen?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc). To build resilience against phishing attacks in general, organizations can use [anti-phishing policies](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/set-up-anti-phishing-policies?view=o365-worldwide) to enable mailbox intelligence settings, as well as configure impersonation protection settings for specific messages and sender domains. Enabling [SafeLinks](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-links?view=o365-worldwide) ensures real-time protection by scanning at time of delivery and at time of click.
- Continuously monitor for suspicious or anomalous activities, and search for sign-in attempts with suspicious characteristics (for example location, internet service provider \[ISP\], user agent, and use of anonymizer services). Activity can be identified and investigated with [Microsoft Defender for Identity](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender/microsoft-365-security-center-mdi?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc), which contributes identity-focused information into incidents and alerts, providing key context and correlating alerts from other products within Microsoft 365 Defender. This ensures all alerts are available in one place, and the scope of a breach can be determined faster than before.

Defenders can also complement MFA with the following solutions and best practices to further protect their organizations from such attacks.  

- Use [security defaults](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/fundamentals/concept-fundamentals-security-defaults?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) as a baseline set of policies to improve identity security posture.
- Block phishing websites and other malicious URLs and domains in the browser through [Microsoft Defender SmartScreen](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/operating-system-security/virus-and-threat-protection/microsoft-defender-smartscreen/), as well as the detection of suspicious and malicious behavior on endpoints.

Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of AsyncRAT:

- Keep software and operating systems up to date. Regularly updating software and operating systems can help prevent vulnerabilities from being exploited by attackers.
- Use anti-virus software. Anti-virus software can help detect and block malicious programs, including AsyncRAT. It is important to keep anti-virus software up to date as new threats emerge.
- Be cautious when opening emails or downloading files from unknown sources. Phishing emails and other social engineering techniques are often used to trick users into downloading malware. It is important to be cautious when opening emails or downloading files from unknown sources.
- Use strong passwords. Strong passwords can help prevent attackers from gaining access to sensitive data. Passwords should be unique and complex, and different passwords should be used for different accounts.
- Use multi-factor authentication (MFA). MFA can provide an extra layer of security by requiring users to provide additional forms of identification, such as a code sent to a mobile device, before accessing an account.
- Use a firewall. A well-configured firewall can help block unauthorized access to a network or computer.
- Regularly back up important data. Regularly backing up important data can help prevent data loss in the event of a malware infection or other security incident. It is important to store backups in a secure location, such as an offsite location or a cloud storage service.

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects threat components as the following malware:
 
- [Trojan:Win32/Rhadamanthys](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:Win32/Rhadamanthys!ic)
- [Trojan:VBS/XWorm](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:VBS/XWorm)
- [Trojan:XML/AsyncRat](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:XML/AsyncRat)
- [Backdoor:Win32/Asyncrat](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Backdoor:Win32/Asyncrat)

- [Trojan:VBA/AsyncRAT](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:VBA/AsyncRAT)
- [Trojan:MSIL/AsyncRAT](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:MSIL/AsyncRAT)
- [Backdoor:MSIL/AsyncRAT](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Backdoor:MSIL/AsyncRAT)
- [TrojanDownloader:VBS/AsyncRAT](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=TrojanDownloader:VBS/AsyncRAT)
- [TrojanDownloader:MSIL/AsyncRAT](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=TrojanDownloader:MSIL/AsyncRAT)

## Description
The investigation reveals that Phorpiex has evolved to automate the deployment of LockBit ransomware, with the botnet's successors maintaining the original code's behaviors, such as deleting Zone.Identifier files to obscure C2 metadata. The infection chain starts with spearphishing emails containing ZIP files with either an SCR file for the LockBit variant or an LNK file for the TWIZT variant. These files connect to a C2 server to download the respective ransomware or downloader variant. 

The malware employs various techniques for persistence, evasion, and defense impairment, including registry manipulation, anti-sandbox features, disabling Windows Defender, and execution flow obfuscation. The GandCrab downloader variant is also analyzed, showing similar anti-sandbox behavior and defense evasion tactics. The comparative study of downloader variants associated with LockBit, GandCrab, and Phorpiex TWIZT malware highlights shared tactics such as deleting URL cache, library obfuscation, and creating mutexes to check infection status. These variants also establish persistence by copying themselves into user directories and registering as Windows Services, while also employing masquerading techniques to disguise the true nature of files.

Phorpiex, active for over a decade, is notorious for spam campaigns, cryptocurrency mining, and malware distribution, often leveraging phishing emails with malicious attachments or compromised websites. LockBit operates on a Ransomware-as-a-Service model and is recognized for its rapid encryption and double extortion tactics.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
[Phorpiex](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/63a1bc81), also known as Trik, is a multi-part botnet that initially spread via removable USB drives and instant messaging platforms like Skype and IRC. Following the takedown of Emotet, Phorpiex has diversified its infrastructure to improve resilience, shifting some command-and-control (C2) architecture and increasing ransomware delivery on infected systems. The Phorpiex botnet has been hijacked in the past by security researchers and identified by competitor botnets as simplistic and lacking robustness. Despite this, it has been responsible for widespread infections globally, impacting enterprises significantly with static tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) that provide opportunities for interruption. The botnet's infection vectors include phishing, malware, and ransomware campaigns, with common payloads like Avaddon, Knot, BitRansomware, Nemty, GandCrab, and Pony. 

Botnets, networks of compromised devices controlled by threat actors, have cemented their place as one of the most persistent and versatile cyber threats. Botnet activity is both increasing and increasingly impactful, with a [25% year-over-year surge](https://www.ustelecom.org/research/botnets2024/) in botnet activity in 2024 and a staggering economic impact of botnet-enabled cybercrime estimated at [approximately $600 billion annually](https://kpmg.com/nl/en/home/insights/2024/08/exploring-botnets-understanding-the-threat-landscape-and-building-ethical-awareness.html). Recent developments underscore attackers’ focus on evolving evasion techniques, payload versatility, and expanded targeting—particularly across Linux and Internet of Things (IoT) systems. Read more about [recent OSINT trends in botnet threats](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/f26d000e).

## Recommendations
Apply these mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat.  
 
- Prevent threats from arriving via removable storage devices by blocking these devices on sensitive endpoints. If you allow removable storage devices, you can minimize the risk by turning off autorun, enabling real-time antivirus protection, and blocking untrusted content. [Learn about stopping threats from USB devices and other removable media](https://docs.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/device-control/control-usb-devices-using-intune)
- [Turn on PUA protection](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/threat-protection/windows-defender-antivirus/detect-block-potentially-unwanted-apps-windows-defender-antivirus). Potentially unwanted applications (PUA) can negatively impact machine performance and employee productivity. In enterprise environments, PUA protection can stop adware, torrent downloaders, and coin miners.
- Turn on [tamper protection features](https://docs.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/microsoft-defender-antivirus/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection) to prevent attackers from stopping security services.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://docs.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/microsoft-defender-antivirus/enable-cloud-protection-microsoft-defender-antivirus) and automatic sample submission on Microsoft Defender Antivirus. These capabilities use artificial intelligence and machine learning to quickly identify and stop new and unknown threats.
- Encourage users to use Microsoft Edge and other web browsers that support SmartScreen, which identifies and blocks malicious websites, including phishing sites, scam sites, and sites that contain exploits and host malware. [Turn on network protection](https://docs.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/microsoft-defender-atp/enable-network-protection) to block connections to malicious domains and IP addresses.
- Check your [Office 365 antispam policy](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/configure-your-spam-filter-policies) and your [mail flow rules](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/create-safe-sender-lists-in-office-365#recommended-use-mail-flow-rules) for allowed senders, domains and IP addresses. [Apply extra caution](https://docs.microsoft.com/exchange/troubleshoot/antispam/cautions-against-bypassing-spam-filters) when using these settings to bypass antispam filters, even if the allowed sender addresses are associated with trusted organizations—Office 365 will honor these settings and can let potentially harmful messages pass through. [Review system overrides in threat explorer](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/threat-explorer#system-overrides) to determine why attack messages have reached recipient mailboxes.

##### Attack surface reduction rules
 
These attack surface reduction rules can block, or audit activity associated with this threat:

- [Block untrusted and unsigned processes that run from USB](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/threat-protection/microsoft-defender-atp/attack-surface-reduction#block-untrusted-and-unsigned-processes-that-run-from-usb)
- [Block JavaScript or VBScript from launching downloaded executable content](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/threat-protection/microsoft-defender-atp/attack-surface-reduction#block-javascript-or-vbscript-from-launching-downloaded-executable-content)
- [Use advanced protection against ransomware](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/threat-protection/microsoft-defender-atp/attack-surface-reduction#use-advanced-protection-against-ransomware)
- [Block executable content from email client and webmail](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/threat-protection/microsoft-defender-atp/attack-surface-reduction#block-executable-content-from-email-client-and-webmail)
- [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/threat-protection/microsoft-defender-atp/attack-surface-reduction#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion)
- [Block process creations originating from PSExec and WMI commands](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/threat-protection/microsoft-defender-atp/attack-surface-reduction#block-process-creations-originating-from-psexec-and-wmi-commands)

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus incorporates next-generation antivirus capabilities, including machine learning and behavioral detection. This can result in overlapping detections, particularly of first-seen components and polymorphic variants. The detection names are listed here for reference, but related alerts are *not* actively monitored.
 
Malware implants mentioned in these campaigns can be detected as:
 
- Trojan:Win32/Phorpiex
- TrojanDownloader:Win32/Phorpiex
- Worm:Win32/Phorpiex

Associated Ransomware payloads and loaders referenced in this report most recently seen:

- Ransom:Win32/Avaddon
- TrojanDownloader:JS/Avaddon
- Ransom:Win32/KnotedCrypt

### Microsoft Defender for Endpoint
Alerts with the following titles in the security center can indicate threat activity on your network:
 
- Phorpiex Malware
- Phorpiex C2

The following alerts might also indicate threat activity associated with this threat. These alerts, however, can be triggered by unrelated threat activity and are not monitored in the status cards provided with this report.

- System file masquerade
- Fake Windows binary set to autostart
- Suspicious behavior by a svchost.exe was observed
- Possible cryptocurrency miner
- LSASS process memory modified

[Phorpiex - Downloader Delivering Ransomware](https://www.cybereason.com/blog/threat-analysis-phorpiex-downloader) Cybereason Blog (accessed 2025-01-29)

title: New TorNet backdoor seen in widespread campaign
content:
#### Targeted Geolocations
- Poland  
- Germany



## Snapshot
Cisco Talos identified an ongoing malicious campaign since at least July 2024, targeting users mainly in Poland and Germany through phishing emails impersonating financial institutions and manufacturing and logistics companies. The emails, written in Polish, German, and some in English, contain compressed attachments that, when executed, deploy various malware strains, including Agent Tesla, Snake Keylogger, and a newly discovered backdoor named TorNet.

## Description
The attackers use PureCrypter malware as a delivery mechanism, employing sophisticated techniques such as disconnecting victims from the network before payload execution to evade cloud-based security solutions.
 
Once deployed, the malware establishes persistence through Windows scheduled tasks, even ensuring execution when devices are on low battery. TorNet facilitates communication with command-and-control (C2) servers via the TOR network, helping the attackers maintain anonymity. The campaign’s infection chain involves a multi-stage process where a .NET loader decrypts and executes the payload directly in system memory, avoiding detection. Additionally, PureCrypter incorporates extensive anti-analysis techniques, checking for debugging environments, virtual machines, and security tools before launching its attack.
 
The TorNet backdoor further enhances the attack’s stealth by encrypting and transmitting data via the TOR network while allowing remote execution of arbitrary .NET code. Cisco Talos assesses with moderate confidence that the attackers' motivation is financial, judging from the phishing themes which include fake invoices and transaction confirmations.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat.
 
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/linux-preferences) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown threats.
- Run [EDR in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode?view=o365-worldwide?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus does not detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach.
- Allow [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations?view=o365-worldwide?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in full automated mode to allow Microsoft Defender for Endpoint to take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.
- [Enable](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-controlled-folders) controlled folder access.
- Ensure that [tamper protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection#how-do-i-configure-or-manage-tamper-protection) is enabled in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Enable [network protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-network-protection) in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Follow the credential hardening recommendations in the [on-premises credential theft overview](https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/9382203e-5155-4b5e-af74-21562b1004d5/analystreport) to defend against common credential theft techniques like LSASS access.
- [Enable](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-credential-stealing-from-the-windows-local-security-authority-subsystem) LSA protection.

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects threat components as the following malware:
 
- [Trojan:Win32/Wacatac](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:Win32/Wacatac.B!ml)

title: Fake installer leads to Koi Loader/Koi Stealer
content:
## Snapshot
A fake installer has been identified as the initial vector for Koi Loader/Koi Stealer malware activity.

## Description
The infection chain begins with a Windows executable installer. The initial access source is currently unknown. It is identified as "Pringle Setup" in its metadata, and is a PE32 executable for Windows. Upon execution, it initiates a series of HTTP requests, including connections to URLs and specific IP addresses. These requests deliver additional payloads and scripts, including a Windows scheduled task for persistence. The scheduled task executes a script file located at C:\ProgramData, which is an ASCII text file.
 
Files exchanged during communication with the command-and-control (C2) server include PowerShell scripts and executables associated with Koi Loader. The .NET binary used for the Koi Stealer component, also a PE32 executable, is decoded from a section within one of the PowerShell scripts.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
[In May 2024](https://redcanary.com/blog/threat-intelligence/intelligence-insights-may-2024/), Red Canary researchers highlighted Koi phishing activity, involving both Koi Loader and Koi Stealer, initially mistaken for Azorult malware. According to researchers, Koi is typically delivered via phishing emails containing ZIP files with banking-themed names, such as "Chasebank\_Statement\_May.zip." The ZIP file includes a LNK shortcut that executes curl to download a BAT script. The BAT script uses PowerShell to retrieve a JavaScript payload, which downloads additional PowerShell scripts that execute C++ code and eventually delivers the final Koi Loader PowerShell script. This script decodes and runs Koi Stealer, a .NET-based info stealer that exfiltrates sensitive data like system details, browser history, and cookies via C2 connections. Koi Loader also employs scheduled tasks to execute downloaded scripts.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of [Information Stealer](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/2296d491ea381b532b24f2575f9418d4b6723c17b8a1f507d20c2140a75d16d6) threats. 

- Check your Office 365 email filtering settings to ensure you block spoofed emails, spam, and emails with malware. Use [Microsoft Defender for Office 365](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/defender-for-office-365?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for enhanced phishing protection and coverage against new threats and polymorphic variants. Configure Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to [recheck links on click](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-links-about?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) and [delete sent mail](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/zero-hour-auto-purge?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in response to newly acquired threat intelligence. Turn on [safe attachments policies](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-attachments-policies-configure?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to check attachments to inbound email.
- Encourage users to use Microsoft Edge and other web browsers that support [SmartScreen](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/web-protection-overview?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc), which identifies and blocks malicious websites, including phishing sites, scam sites, and sites that host malware.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus, or the equivalent for your antivirus product, to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown variants.
- Enforce MFA on all accounts, remove users excluded from MFA, and strictly [require MFA](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/identity-protection/howto-identity-protection-configure-mfa-policy?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) from all devices, in all locations, at all times.
- Enable passwordless authentication methods (for example, Windows Hello, FIDO keys, or Microsoft Authenticator) for accounts that support passwordless. For accounts that still require passwords, use authenticator apps like Microsoft Authenticator for MFA. Learn [what authentication and verification methods are available in Microsoft Entra ID.](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/authentication/concept-authentication-methods)
- For MFA that uses authenticator apps, ensure that the app requires a code to be typed in where possible, as many intrusions where MFA was enabled still succeeded due to users clicking “Yes” on the prompt on their phones even when they were not at their [devices](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/how-to-mfa-number-match?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc).
- For information on password management for Microsoft Edge read ["Microsoft Edge password manager security."](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/deployedge/microsoft-edge-security-password-manager-security)

Microsoft Defender customers can [turn on attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to prevent common attack techniques used in infostealer infections. Attack surface reduction rules are sweeping settings that stop entire classes of threats including, infostealers, credential theft, and ransomware. The following bullet points offer more guidance on specific mitigation advice: 

- [Turn on PUA protection in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/detect-block-potentially-unwanted-apps-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc)
- [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion)
- [Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-execution-of-potentially-obfuscated-scripts)

title: Cobalt Strike and a Pair of SOCKS Lead to LockBit Ransomware
content:
## Snapshot
DFIR Reports threat actors infiltrated a network by executing a Cobalt Strike beacon disguised as the Windows Media Configuration Utility.

## Description
In late January 2024, a cyber intrusion commenced when a user executed a malicious file named setup\_wm.exe, disguised as the legitimate Windows Media Configuration Utility. This file was a Cobalt Strike beacon that, upon execution, established an outbound connection. Within 30 minutes, the attacker used the beacon to run discovery commands, such as nltest, to identify domain controllers. Leveraging the elevated permissions of the compromised user, the attacker deployed two proxy tools—SystemBC and GhostSOCKS—onto a domain controller via SMB and remote services. Although Windows Defender detected and blocked GhostSOCKS, the SystemBC proxy remained active, providing a command and control channel from the domain controller.
 
The attacker proceeded to execute situational awareness commands from the initial compromised host, injecting code into the WUAUCLT.exe process and extracting credentials from the LSASS process. They loaded Seatbelt and SharpView CLR modules into the process's memory space and established persistence by creating scheduled tasks to execute the SystemBC and GhostSOCKS proxies on the initial host. Approximately an hour into the intrusion, the attacker moved laterally to a file server using remote services with the same compromised account, deploying a Cobalt Strike PowerShell beacon that communicated with a different command and control server.
 
For data exfiltration, the attacker initially attempted FTP transfers, which failed, before successfully using Rclone with MEGA.io. A day later, they conducted a second successful FTP exfiltration. Throughout the environment, the attacker established multiple persistent backdoors using scheduled tasks, GhostSOCKS and SystemBC proxies, and Cobalt Strike command and control access. On the 11th day of the intrusion, LockBit ransomware was deployed across the environment, culminating the attack.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
LockBit is a prominent ransomware group that has been active since 2019, operating under a Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) model. This approach involves recruiting affiliates to conduct attacks using LockBit's tools and infrastructure, leading to a wide variation in tactics, techniques, and procedures across different incidents. 
 
Over time, LockBit has evolved its ransomware, with significant updates such as LockBit 3.0, also known as LockBit Black, introduced in July 2022. This version expanded the group's target regions by making location checks optional, aiming to appeal to a broader audience within the underground market. LockBit's operations have had a substantial global impact, with the group responsible for approximately 1,700 ransomware attacks in the United States alone between January 2020 and May 2023, resulting in $91 million in ransom payments.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat.
 
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/linux-preferences) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown threats.
- Run [EDR in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode?view=o365-worldwide?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus does not detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach.
- Allow [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations?view=o365-worldwide?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in full automated mode to allow Microsoft Defender for Endpoint to take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.
- [Enable](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-controlled-folders) controlled folder access.
- Ensure that [tamper protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection#how-do-i-configure-or-manage-tamper-protection) is enabled in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Enable [network protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-network-protection) in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Follow the credential hardening recommendations in the [on-premises credential theft overview](https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/9382203e-5155-4b5e-af74-21562b1004d5/analystreport) to defend against common credential theft techniques like LSASS access.
- [Enable](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-credential-stealing-from-the-windows-local-security-authority-subsystem) LSA protection.
- Microsoft Defender XDR customers can turn on the following [attack surface reduction rule](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction) to prevent common attack techniques used for ransomware.
- - [Block](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion) executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects threat components as the following malware:
 
- HackTool:PowerShell/DumpDBCreds.A!dha
- Trojan:Win32/Swrort
- Trojan:Win64/CobaltStrike!rfn
- Trojan:Win64/Coroxy!MTB
- Trojan:Win32/GhostSocks.MKV!MTB

## References
[Cobalt Strike and a Pair of SOCKS Lead to LockBit Ransomware](https://thedfirreport.com/2025/01/27/cobalt-strike-and-a-pair-of-socks-lead-to-lockbit-ransomware/) The DFIR Report (Accessed 2025/1/30)

title: Malware Redirects WordPress Traffic to Harmful Sites
content:
## Snapshot
Sucuri Blog researchers reported an incident where a website was redirecting visitors to a suspicious URL, prompting an investigation that revealed malicious redirect malware affecting multiple sites.

## Description
The malware was injected into the WordPress theme's functions.php file and was identified as Known JavaScript Malware: redirect?fake\_click.1 by SiteCheck. The code was designed to avoid detection by not running repeatedly in the same session and bypassing execution for logged-in WordPress users. It used complex regular expressions to filter requests and redirected visitors to a malicious domain, potentially compromising their devices with additional payloads. The malware remained undetected by filtering out bots, logged-in users, and administrators, continuously sending visitors to external malicious domains. 

While the primary payload of this malware is redirecting users, the malware could create hidden backdoors for persistent access, leak sensitive data, distribute spam, ransomware, or phishing campaigns. The site's infection could have resulted from outdated or nulled plugins or themes, poorly designed custom code, pre-existing backdoors, or compromised user accounts. The attackers' intentions could include damaging the website's reputation, impacting search rankings, exploiting traffic, or injecting spam or malware.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat:
 
- Encourage users to use Microsoft Edge and other web browsers that support [SmartScreen](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/web-protection-overview?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc), which identifies and blocks malicious websites, including phishing sites, scam sites, and sites that host malware.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus, or the equivalent for your antivirus product, to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown variants.

Microsoft Defender customers can [turn on attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to prevent common attack techniques used in infostealer infections. Attack surface reduction rules are sweeping settings that stop entire classes of threats including, infostealers, credential theft, and ransomware. The following bullet points offer more guidance on specific mitigation advice: 

- [Turn on PUA protection in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/detect-block-potentially-unwanted-apps-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc)
- [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion)
- [Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-execution-of-potentially-obfuscated-scripts)

title: FBI: North Korean IT workers steal source code to extort employers
content:
## Snapshot
The FBI has issued a new warning about North Korean remote IT workers, part of the North Korea’s IT army, who are copying company code repositories to personal accounts and potentially harvesting sensitive credentials for further compromise. Using advanced tactics like AI, face-swapping technology, and virtual desktop infrastructure (VDI), these workers evade detection while leveraging compromised accounts for financial and strategic gains.

## Description
North Korean threat actors are expanding their operations, targeting larger organizations and following through on extortion threats, with activity now spreading into Europe, according to Mandiant Principal Analyst Michael Barnhart. The FBI warns that these IT workers are exploiting remote access to steal source code from repositories like GitHub and exfiltrate sensitive data, and, after being fired, have used insider knowledge to extort their former employers. They have been known to log into company accounts from various IP addresses in a short time frame, posing a significant risk of data theft. Additionally, the FBI has observed that these IT workers use advanced tactics such as credential harvesting, session cookie theft, AI and face-swapping technology (also known as deepfake) to conceal their identities during interviews and often provide false information about their location or educational background.

The FBI's announcement also highlights risks associated with malicious activity conducted through [virtual desktop infrastructure](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/resources/cloud-computing-dictionary/what-is-virtual-desktop-infrastructure-vdi) (VDI), which some companies use to reduce costs. In the United States, authorities dismantled two laptop farms in Nashville and Arizona, which were used to impersonate U.S.-based staff. Recent indictments revealed that these schemes compromised at least sixty-four U.S. companies between 2018 and 2024.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
Threat actors are [increasingly leveraging generative AI](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/9e3529fc) to enhance cyberattacks. In North Korean remote IT workers campaign and other threat actor attacks involving impersonation, deepfakes, AI-generated videos and voices, are increasingly being used to deceive individuals into fraudulent actions. These attacks exploit the inability of [traditional methods of identifying people](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-cloud/blog/2024/10/31/ai-safety-first-protecting-your-business-and-empowering-your-people/#impersonation-using-ai), like phone or video calls, to verify identities. The [Microsoft Digital Defense Report 2024](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/security-insider/intelligence-reports/microsoft-digital-defense-report-2024) highlights multiple concerns regarding deepfakes, including their use in social engineering attacks enhanced by AI. Threat actors leverage AI to gather extensive information about targets, enabling them to craft convincing fake social media profiles or impersonate known individuals using deepfake technology. These false personas can engage targets through video calls or phone calls, with AI bots automating much of the communication before human interaction. The report warns that the sophistication of deepfakes is likely to increase, making them effective tools for fraud, identity theft, blackmail, and extortion.

[Microsoft is tackling the threat of deepfakes](https://news.microsoft.com/source/features/ai/fighting-deepfakes-with-more-transparency-about-ai/) with tools to combat deepfakes and enhance transparency in digital content, focusing on the use of AI-generated media and its potential to deceive. The Content Integrity Suite, including Content Credentials, enables creators to add certified metadata to their work, providing attribution details like who made the content, when it was made, and whether AI was used. This metadata is cryptographically attached to photos, videos, and audio, allowing for easier detection of tampering. Microsoft also offers a Content Integrity Check tool and browser extension, helping users verify content provenance, particularly on platforms like LinkedIn. These tools are part of Microsoft's broader initiative to combat deepfakes in elections and other areas.

## Recommendations
Microsoft reports how to spot deepfakes in [Fighting deepfakes with more transparency about AI](https://news.microsoft.com/source/features/ai/fighting-deepfakes-with-more-transparency-about-ai/):
 
- Know and understand the source: Look for attribution, captions and Content Credentials. Research images through a visual search. Ask yourself if the source is reputable and proceed with caution if there’s no clear source.
- Consider intent: Is the content meant to entertain, inform or persuade you? Analyzing the purpose can give you a better sense of whether someone might be trying to deceive.
- Look for inconsistencies and anomalies: AI-generated images may have misspellings, blurry figures, mismatched clothing, inconsistent lighting and odd textures.

Additionally, Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. 

- [Help prevent social engineering attacks](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/security-insider/emerging-threats/feeding-from-the-trust-economy-social-engineering-fraud?ocid=magicti_ta_blog) by not blending personal accounts with work emails or work-related tasks. Avoid opening emails, attachments, and links, including links from social networks, from suspicious sources. Ask yourself if the sender is who they say they are before clicking anything. Be wary of senders and offers. Do a search to determine if the offer is legitimate or a trap.
- Enforce MFA on all accounts, remove users excluded from MFA, and strictly [require MFA](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/identity-protection/howto-identity-protection-configure-mfa-policy?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) from all devices, in all locations, at all times.
- Activate conditional access policies. [Conditional access](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/conditional-access/overview?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) policies are evaluated and enforced every time an attacker attempts to use a stolen session cookie. Organizations can protect themselves from attacks that leverage stolen credentials by activating policies regarding compliant devices or trusted IP address requirements.
- Practice the [principle of least privilege and building credential hygiene](https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2022/05/09/ransomware-as-a-service-understanding-the-cybercrime-gig-economy-and-how-to-protect-yourself?ocid=magicti_ta_blog#defending-against-ransomware). Avoid the use of domain-wide, admin-level service accounts. Restricting local administrative privileges can help limit installation of unwanted applications.
- Software developers and publishers should ensure their [build and update infrastructure are secure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/malware/supply-chain-malware). Establish [best practices to secure software supply chain](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/nuget/concepts/security-best-practices).
- Build organizational resilience against email threats by educating users about identifying social engineering attacks and preventing malware infection. Use [Attack simulation training](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/attack-simulation-training-get-started?ocid=magicti%3cem%3eta%3c/em%3elearndoc) in Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to run attack scenarios, increase user awareness, and empower employees to recognize and report these attacks.

## References
[FBI: North Korean IT workers steal source code to extort employers](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fbi-north-korean-it-workers-steal-source-code-to-extort-employers/). BleepingComputer (accessed 2025-01-24)
 
[Emerging OSINT trends in threats leveraging generative artificial intelligence](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/9e3529fc). Microsoft (accessed 2025-01-24)
 
[AI safety first: Protecting your business and empowering your people](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-cloud/blog/2024/10/31/ai-safety-first-protecting-your-business-and-empowering-your-people/#impersonation-using-ai). Microsoft (accessed 2025-01-24)
 
[Microsoft Digital Defense Report 2024](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/security-insider/intelligence-reports/microsoft-digital-defense-report-2024). Microsoft (accessed 2025-01-24)
 
[Fighting deepfakes with more transparency about AI](https://news.microsoft.com/source/features/ai/fighting-deepfakes-with-more-transparency-about-ai/). Microsoft (accessed 2025-01-24)

title: New BackConnect Malware Linked to Qakbot Discovered
content:
## Snapshot
Researchers at Walmart Global Tech Blog have reported a resurgence of Qbot, also known as [Qakbot](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/65019ce99508dd6a7ed35ba221524b6728a564600616c7229baa0ecdec21701b) or Pinkslipbot, a modular information stealer and banking Trojan that uses Command and Control (C2) servers for payload targeting and execution.

## Description
Despite a law enforcement action on May 30th, 2024, aimed at disrupting Qbot operations, new evidence suggests the operators are active again. The researchers discovered overlaps between a sample analyzed by ZScaler, which added DNS tunneling to Zloader, and Qbot-related files. They found a ZIP file containing several DLLs and an executable, with indications that the 'winhttp.dll' is side-loaded by 'OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe', which then decrypts and loads a .dat file using a hardcoded RC4 key.

The analysis also uncovered a new backConnect malware developed by Qbot operators, which hooks into low-level createprocess and exitprocess functions and checks for a hardcoded registry key 'Software\\TitanPlus'. The malware sends information about the infected system and appears to be linked to the [BlackBasta](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/0146164ed5ffa131074fa7e985f779597d2522865baa088f25cd80c3bed8d726) ransomware operation.

## Recommendations
Apply these mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations.
 
- [Stop malicious XLM](https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2021/03/03/xlm-amsi-new-runtime-defense-against-excel-4-0-macro-malware/) or VBA macros by ensuring runtime macro scanning by AMSI is on. This feature—enabled by default—is on if the Group Policy setting for Macro Run Time Scan Scope is set to Enable for All Files or Enable for Low Trust Files.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus?view=o365-worldwide) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or its equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a huge majority of new and unknown variants.
- Turn on [tamper protection](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection?view=o365-worldwide) features to prevent attackers from stopping security services.
- Run [EDR in block mode](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode?view=o365-worldwide) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus doesn’t detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach.
- Encourage users to use Microsoft Edge or other web browsers that support [SmartScreen](https://docs.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/microsoft-defender-smartscreen/microsoft-defender-smartscreen-overview), which identifies and blocks malicious websites, including phishing sites, scam sites, and sites that contain exploits and host malware.
- Enable [network protection](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/enable-network-protection?view=o365-worldwide) to prevent applications or users from accessing malicious domains and other malicious content on the internet.
- Enable [investigation and remediation](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations?view=o365-worldwide) in full automated mode to allow Microsoft Defender for Endpoint to take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.
- Use [device discovery](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/device-discovery?view=o365-worldwide) to increase your visibility into your network by finding unmanaged devices and onboarding them to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Configure Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to [recheck links on click](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/office365/securitycompliance/atp-safe-links). Safe Links provides URL scanning and rewriting of inbound email messages in mail flow, and time-of-click verification of URLs and links in email messages and other locations. Safe Links scanning occurs in addition to the regular [anti-spam and anti-malware protection](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/anti-spam-and-anti-malware-protection?view=o365-worldwide) in inbound email messages in Exchange Online Protection (EOP). Safe Links scanning can help protect your organization from malicious links that are used in phishing and other attacks.
- Configure Exchange Online to [delete sent mail](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/office365/securitycompliance/zero-hour-auto-purge) (also known as zero-hour auto purge or ZAP) in response to newly acquired threat intelligence. ZAP retroactively detects and neutralizes malicious phishing, spam, or malware messages that have already been delivered to mailboxes.
- Use multi-factor authentication (MFA) to mitigate credential theft and prevent attacker access. Keep MFA always-on for privileged accounts and apply risk-based MFA for normal accounts. Consider transitioning to a passwordless primary authentication method, such as Azure MFA, certificates, or Windows Hello for Business.
- [Attack Simulator](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/attack-simulator?view=o365-worldwide) for Microsoft Defender for Office 365 lets you run realistic, yet safe, simulated phishing and password attack campaigns in your organization. Run spear-phishing (credential harvest) simulations to train end users against clicking URLs in unsolicited messages and disclosing their credentials.
- Check your Office 365 email filtering settings to ensure you block spoofed emails, spam, and emails with malware. Use [Office 365 security](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/office365/securitycompliance/office-365-atp) for enhanced phishing protection and coverage against new threats and polymorphic variants.
- Educate end users about identifying lures in spear-phishing emails and watering hole attacks, protecting personal and business information in social media, and filtering unsolicited communication. Encourage users to report reconnaissance attempts and other suspicious activity.

To reduce the attack surface, Microsoft 365 Defender customers can do the following:

- Turn on [attack surface reduction rules](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?view=o365-worldwide) to prevent common attack techniques used in ransomware attacks.

Attack surface reduction rules are sweeping settings that are effective at stopping entire classes of threats.

To help block the ransom and lateral movement stages:

- [Block process creations originating from PsExec and WMI commands](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction#block-process-creations-originating-from-psexec-and-wmi-commands)
- [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion)
- [Use advanced protection against ransomware](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction#use-advanced-protection-against-ransomware)
- [Block credential stealing from the Windows local security authority subsystem (lsass.exe)](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction#block-credential-stealing-from-the-windows-local-security-authority-subsystem)

To help block common techniques:

- [Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction#block-execution-of-potentially-obfuscated-scripts)

To help block common entry vectors:

- [Block Office communication application from creating child processes](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction#block-office-communication-application-from-creating-child-processes)

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects Qakbot installers as the following malware:

Qakbot downloader
 
- [TrojanDownloader:O97M/Qakbot](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=TrojanDownloader:O97M/Qakbot)

Qakbot implant

- [Trojan:Win32/QBot](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:Win32/Qbot)
- [TrojanSpy:Win32/Qakbot](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=TrojanSpy:Win32/Qakbot)
- [Trojan:Win32/Qakbot](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:Win32/Qakbot)

Qakbot behavior

- [Behavior:Win32/Qakbot.A](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/threat-search?query=Behavior:Win32/Qakbot.A)

### Microsoft Defender for Endpoint
Alerts with the following titles in the security center can indicate threat activity on your network related directly to the material in this report covering Qakbot initial infection and subsequent human-operated or ransomware activity:
 
- Qakbot malware
- Qakbot credential stealer
- Qakbot download URL
- Qakbot network infrastructure

The following alerts might also indicate threat activity associated with the Qakbot initial access component of this threat. These alerts, however, can be triggered by unrelated threat activity and are not monitored in the status cards provided with this report.

- Microsoft command-line utility Regsvr32.exe launched suspicious commands
- Process hollowing detected
- Suspicious process injection observed
- Emerging threat activity group
- Suspicious LDAP query
- Suspicious behavior by svchost.exe was observed
- Possible attempt to steal credentials
- Suspicious Remote System Discovery
- Suspicious PowerShell command line
- Outbound connection to non-standard port
- Suspicious Process Discovery
- Suspicious process launched using dllhost.exe

The following alerts might also indicate threat activity associated with the human-operated lateral movement, Cobalt Strike, and ransomware component of this threat. These alerts, however, can be triggered by unrelated threat activity and are not monitored in the status cards provided with this report.

- Connection to ransomware campaign C2
- Ransomware-linked emerging threat activity group detected
- Emerging threat activity group
- Known attack framework activity was observed
- Suspicious process launched using dllhost.exe

## References
[New BackConnect Malware Linked to Qakbot Discovered](https://medium.com/walmartglobaltech/qbot-is-back-connect-2d774052369f#new_tab). Medium (accessed 2025-01-23)
 
[Qakbot](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/65019ce99508dd6a7ed35ba221524b6728a564600616c7229baa0ecdec21701b). Microsoft (accessed 2025-01-23) 
 
[Black Basta](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/0146164ed5ffa131074fa7e985f779597d2522865baa088f25cd80c3bed8d726). Microsoft (accessed 2025-01-23)

title: Hundreds of fake Reddit sites push Lumma Stealer malware
content:
## Snapshot
Researchers at Sekoia IO reported cybercriminals have created approximately 1,000 fraudulent web pages that impersonate Reddit and the WeTransfer file sharing service to distribute the Lumma Stealer malware.

## Description
These fake pages feature a counterfeit Reddit discussion thread where users seemingly exchange help on downloading a specific tool, with one user offering a WeTransfer link to the file. However, the link directs victims to a bogus WeTransfer site that closely resembles the authentic service, where a 'Download' button delivers the Lumma Stealer payload from a deceptive domain. The malicious sites incorporate a mix of the impersonated brand's name with random characters and use ".org" or ".net" top-level domains to appear credible. Sekoia researcher crep1x discovered the scheme, identifying 529 pages mimicking Reddit and 407 posing as WeTransfer. While the initial infection vector remains unclear, the targeted topics suggest a degree of sophistication, potentially involving malvertising, SEO poisoning, or direct social media messages.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
[Lumma Stealer](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/33933578825488511c30b0728dd3c4f8b5ca20e41c285a56f796eb39f57531ad) also known as LummaC2, is an information stealer designed to extract sensitive data, such as browser session tokens, cookies, saved passwords, credit card details, and cryptocurrency wallets. The malware has been [sold as malware-as-a-service](https://darktrace.com/blog/the-rise-of-the-lumma-info-stealer) (MaaS) on underground forums since 2022, with multiple updated versions released to enhance its capabilities. In 2023, Microsoft Threat Intelligence observed Lumma being distributed via phishing emails, malvertising, drive-by downloads, and malicious tools, with notable campaigns involving Storm-1607 and Storm-0875. Once deployed, Lumma uses an AutoIT-based process to inject itself and contact its command-and-control server to download encoded configurations, which dictate the types of data to be exfiltrated. The stolen data is compressed and sent back to the C2 for monetization, typically through infostealer marketplaces or further exploitation. Recently, Lumma has been distributed through [advertisement pages](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/f4c8580a) on freeware software sites, fake [CAPTCHA](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/994ccfa2) pages, and through private [Telegram](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/f250caee) channels.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations. 
 
- Check your Office 365 email filtering settings to ensure you block spoofed emails, spam, and emails with malware. Use [Microsoft Defender for Office 365](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/defender-for-office-365) for enhanced phishing protection and coverage against new threats and polymorphic variants. Configure Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to [recheck links on click](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-links-about) and [delete sent mail](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/zero-hour-auto-purge) in response to newly acquired threat intelligence. Turn on [safe attachments policies](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-attachments-policies-configure) to check attachments to inbound email.
- Encourage users to use Microsoft Edge and other web browsers that support [SmartScreen](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/web-protection-overview), which identifies and blocks malicious websites, including phishing sites, scam sites, and sites that host malware.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus, or the equivalent for your antivirus product, to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown variants.
- Enforce MFA on all accounts, remove users excluded from MFA, and strictly [require MFA](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/identity-protection/howto-identity-protection-configure-mfa-policy) from all devices, in all locations, at all times.
- Enable passwordless authentication methods (for example, Windows Hello, FIDO keys, or Microsoft Authenticator) for accounts that support passwordless. For accounts that still require passwords, use authenticator apps like Microsoft Authenticator for MFA. [Refer to this article](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/concept-authentication-methods) for the different authentication methods and features.
- For MFA that uses authenticator apps, ensure that the app requires a code to be typed in where possible, as many intrusions where MFA was enabled still succeeded due to users clicking “Yes” on the prompt on their phones even when they were not at their [devices](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/how-to-mfa-number-match). Refer to [this article](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/concept-authentication-methods) for an example.
- Remind employees that enterprise or workplace credentials should not be stored in browsers or password vaults secured with personal credentials. Organizations can turn off password syncing in browser on managed devices using [Group Policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/deployedge/microsoft-edge-enterprise-sync#sync-group-policies).   
  
Microsoft Defender customers can [turn on attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction) to prevent common attack techniques used in infostealer infections. Attack surface reduction rules are sweeping settings that stop entire classes of threats including, infostealers, credential theft, and ransomware. The following bullet points offer more guidance on specific mitigation advice:

- [Turn on PUA protection in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/detect-block-potentially-unwanted-apps-microsoft-defender-antivirus)
- [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference)
- [Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference)

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects threat components as the following malware:  

- [Trojan:Win32/LummaCStealer](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:Win32/LummaCStealer!MTB&threatId=-2147117932)
- [Trojan:Win32/Delf](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:Win32/Delf!MSR&threatId=-2147216637)
- [PWS:Win32/Lumma](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=PWS:Win32/Lumma!MSR&threatId=-2147078266)

### Microsoft Defender for Endpoint
The following alerts might indicate threat activity associated with this threat. These alerts, however, can be triggered by unrelated threat activity and are not monitored in the status cards provided with this report.  

- Information stealing malware activity
- Octo Tempest activity group

## References

title: HellCat and Morpheus: Two Brands, One Payload as Ransomware Affiliates Drop Identical Code
content:
## Snapshot
SentinelOne discuss how affiliates across HellCat and Morpheus ransomware operations are compiling payloads that contain almost identical code.

## Description
The cyber threat landscape has seen the emergence of new ransomware groups such as FunkSec, Nitrogen, and Termite, alongside the resurgence of Cl0p and the new LockBit 4.0. Among these, the Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) offerings HellCat and Morpheus have gained prominence.

HellCat, which surfaced in mid-2024, is operated by high-profile members of the BreachForums community, targeting high-value and government entities. Morpheus, a semi-private RaaS, launched a data leaks site in December 2024 and has been targeting Italian organizations, particularly those with virtual ESXi environments, with ransom demands reaching up to 32BTC. Research revealed that an affiliate is likely involved in both HellCat and Morpheus campaigns, as evidenced by two similar ransomware payloads uploaded to VirusTotal with identical code except for victim-specific data and attacker contact details. These payloads, standard 64bit PE files, require a path as an argument for execution and exclude certain file extensions and the \Windows\System32 folder from encryption. Notably, they do not alter the file extensions of encrypted files. The ransomware uses the Windows Cryptographic API for key generation and file encryption, with no further system modifications beyond file encryption and ransom note creation. The ransom notes for both HellCat and Morpheus are nearly identical, following the same template, with differences only in the "Sources of Information" section and operation-specific contact details. While there are similarities with the ransom notes of the Underground Team RaaS, there is no evidence of a shared codebase or partnership between them. The shared codebase or builder application used by affiliates of HellCat and Morpheus suggests a level of collaboration or common source among these ransomware operations.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
HellCat and Morpheus are two ransomware groups that have recently gained attention for their similar operational tactics and shared codebase. Both operate under a Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) model, enabling affiliates to deploy ransomware attacks using their platforms. HellCat emerged in mid-2024, with its operators being prominent members of the BreachForums community, including personas like Rey, Pryx, Grep, and IntelBroker. These individuals have been linked to breaches of high-value targets and have actively engaged in publicizing their activities to establish a formidable presence in the cybercrime landscape. Morpheus, on the other hand, launched its data leak site in December 2024, with activities traceable back to at least September of the same year. Unlike HellCat, Morpheus maintains a lower public profile, operating as a semi-private RaaS. As of January 2025, Morpheus has listed victims in the pharmaceutical and manufacturing sectors, with ransom demands reaching up to 32 BTC (approximately $3 million USD).

## Recommendations
Apply these mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations.

- Educate users about [preventing malware infections](https://www.microsoft.com/security/business/security-101/what-is-malware?ocid=magicti_ta_abbreviatedmktgpage"%20\t%20"_blank), such as ignoring or deleting unsolicited and unexpected emails or attachments sent through instant messaging applications or social networks as well as suspicious phone calls.
- Invest in advanced anti-phishing solutions that monitor incoming emails and visited websites. [Microsoft Defender for Office 365](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender/microsoft-365-security-center-mdo?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) brings together incident and alert management across email, devices, and identities, centralizing investigations for email-based threats.
- Apply Microsoft’s [security best practices for Microsoft Teams](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/MicrosoftTeams/teams-security-best-practices-for-safer-messaging) to safeguard Teams users.
- Consider [blocking or uninstalling](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/client-management/client-tools/quick-assist#disable-quick-assist-within-your-organization) Quick Assist and other remote monitoring and management tools if these tools are not in use in your environment. Apply mitigations listed in [Microsoft’s technique profile on abuse of remote monitoring and management tools](https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/44b8f927-5ab5-46bb-bb79-7ca2d4e30156/overview).
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a huge majority of new and unknown variants.
- Turn on [tamper protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) features to prevent attackers from stopping security services.
- Run [EDR in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus doesn’t detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach.
- Enable [network protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-network-protection?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to prevent applications or users from accessing malicious domains and other malicious content on the internet.
- Enable [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in full automated mode to allow Microsoft Defender for Endpoint to take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.
- Use [device discovery](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/device-discovery?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to increase your visibility into your network by finding unmanaged devices on your network and onboarding them to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Refer to [Microsoft’s human-operated ransomware overview](https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/05658b6c-dc62-496d-ad3c-c6a795a33c27/analystreport) for general hardening recommendations against ransomware attacks.

Microsoft Defender XDR customers can turn on [attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to prevent common attack techniques used in ransomware attacks. Attack surface reduction rules are sweeping settings that are effective at stopping entire classes of threats:

- Ransom and lateral movement stage:
    - [Block process creations originating from PsExec and WMI commands](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-process-creations-originating-from-psexec-and-wmi-commands)
    - [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion)
    - [Use advanced protection against ransomware](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#use-advanced-protection-against-ransomware)
    - [Block credential stealing from the Windows local security authority subsystem (lsass.exe)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-credential-stealing-from-the-windows-local-security-authority-subsystem)
- Common techniques:
    - [Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-execution-of-potentially-obfuscated-scripts)
    - [Block JavaScript or VBScript from launching downloaded executable content](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-javascript-or-vbscript-from-launching-downloaded-executable-content)
- Common entry vectors:
    - [Block all Office applications from creating child processes](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-all-office-applications-from-creating-child-processes)
    - [Block Office communication application from creating child processes](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-office-communication-application-from-creating-child-processes)
    - [Block Office applications from creating executable content](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-office-applications-from-injecting-code-into-other-processes)
    - [Block Office applications from injecting code into other processes](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-office-applications-from-injecting-code-into-other-processes)

**Assess rule impact before deployment**

You can assess how an attack surface reduction rule might impact your network by opening the [security recommendation](https://security.microsoft.com/security-recommendations?ocid=magicti_ta_tvmsecreco) for that rule in threat and vulnerability management. In the recommendation details pane, check the user impact to determine what percentage of your devices can accept a new policy enabling the rule in blocking mode without adverse impact to user productivity.
