title: Sliver Implant Targets German Entities with DLL Sideloading and Proxying Techniques
content:
#### Targeted Geolocations
- Germany



## Snapshot
Cyble Research and Intelligence Labs (CRIL) has identified an ongoing cyberattack targeting organizations in Germany, employing advanced evasion techniques such as DLL sideloading, DLL proxying, and the use of the [Sliver framework](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/7b3299451d6740a9ce460a67156d8be84c0308fd6e5ccafccdb368da9f06c95c).

## Description
The attack begins with a spear-phishing email containing an archive named "Homeoffice-Vereinbarung-2025.7z," which includes a deceptive LNK file. When executed, this file uses cmd.exe to copy and run the legitimate executable wksprt.exe, which then sideloads a malicious DLL. This DLL uses proxying to maintain the host application's functionality while executing malicious shellcode that decrypts and runs Sliver, an open-source Red Team framework, establishing control over the compromised system. 

The attack unfolds entirely in memory, evading detection by security products, and the Sliver implant establishes connections to remote servers for further malicious operations. The campaign's tactics and techniques, including the use of Sliver and DLL sideloading, are consistent with those historically associated with APT29, which Microsoft tracks as Midnight Blizzard, although DLL proxying is a new addition to their known tactics. The malicious DLL has a low detection rate and acts as a proxy, forwarding function calls to a legitimate DLL while executing its own code. 

Despite the sophisticated nature of the attack and its resemblance to APT29's methods, definitive attribution to this group has not been established.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
Microsoft has observed the [Sliver command-and-control (C2) framework](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/7b3299451d6740a9ce460a67156d8be84c0308fd6e5ccafccdb368da9f06c95c) now being adopted and integrated in intrusion campaigns by nation-state threat actors, cybercrime groups directly supporting ransomware and extortion, and other threat actors to evade detection. We’ve seen these actors use Sliver with—or as a replacement for—Cobalt Strike. Given Cobalt Strike’s popularity as an attack tool, defenses against it have also improved over time. Sliver thus presents an attractive alternative for actors looking for a lesser-known toolset with a low barrier for entry.

First made public in late 2019 and advertised to security professionals, Sliver is an open-source framework that’s available on GitHub and includes many common C2 framework features such as support for multiple simultaneous operators, multiple listener types, user-developed extensions, and payload generation. Among its adopters is the prolific ransomware as service (RaaS) affiliate [Pistachio Tempest (DEV-0237)](https://aka.ms/ransomware-as-a-service#Pistachio%20Tempest%20%28DEV-0237%29). More recently, we’ve seen cybercrime actors historically tied to human-operated ransomware now deliver Sliver and various post-compromise tools. These campaigns, combined with an increasing number of Sliver C2 servers [identified by Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/b1406335), indicate that the tool is gaining in popularity with threat actors.

## Recommendations
Apply these mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. 
 
- Turn on [network protection](https://endpoint.microsoft.com/#blade/Microsoft%3cem%3eIntune%3c/em%3eDeviceSettings/DevicesMenu/configurationProfiles). Network protection helps prevent users from accessing dangerous domains and IP addresses. Check your perimeter firewall and proxy to restrict servers from making arbitrary connections to the internet to browse or download files. Such restrictions help inhibit malware downloads and C2 activity including mobile devices. Encourage users to use Microsoft Edge and other web browsers that support SmartScreen, which identifies and blocks malicious websites, including phishing sites, scam sites, and sites that contain exploits and host malware.
- Use [Microsoft Defender Firewall](https://support.microsoft.com/windows/turn-microsoft-defender-firewall-on-or-off-ec0844f7-aebd-0583-67fe-601ecf5d774f), along with your network firewall, prevents remote procedure call (RPC) and service message block (SMB) communication along endpoints whenever possible. This limits lateral movement and other attack activities. Check your perimeter firewall and proxy to restrict servers from making arbitrary connections to the internet to browse or download files. Such restrictions help inhibit malware downloads and command-and-control (C&C) activity
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/enable-cloud-protection-microsoft-defender-antivirus?view=o365-worldwide) and automatic sample submission on Microsoft Defender Antivirus. These capabilities use artificial intelligence and machine learning to quickly identify and stop new and unknown threats.
- Check your Office 365 email filtering settings to ensure you block spoofed emails, spam, and emails with malware. Use [Microsoft Defender for Office 365](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/overview?view=o365-worldwide) for enhanced phishing protection and coverage against new threats and polymorphic variants. Configure Office 365 to [recheck links on click](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-links?view=o365-worldwide) and [delete sent mail](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/zero-hour-auto-purge?view=o365-worldwide) in response to newly acquired threat intelligence.
- Educate end users about [preventing malware infections](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/threat-protection/intelligence/prevent-malware-infection). Encourage end users to practice good credential hygiene—limit the use of accounts with local or domain admin privileges and turn on Microsoft Defender Firewall to prevent malware infection and stifle propagation.

For Microsoft 365 Defender customers, follow this checklist: 

- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus?view=o365-worldwide) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a huge majority of new and unknown variants.
- Turn on [tamper protection](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection?view=o365-worldwide) features to prevent attackers from stopping security services.
- Run [EDR in block mode](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode?view=o365-worldwide) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus doesn’t detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach.
- Enable [network protection](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/enable-network-protection?view=o365-worldwide) to prevent applications or users from accessing malicious domains and other malicious content on the internet.
- Enable [investigation and remediation](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations?view=o365-worldwide) in full automated mode to allow Microsoft Defender for Endpoint to take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.
- Use [device discovery](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/device-discovery?view=o365-worldwide) to increase your visibility into your network by finding unmanaged devices on your network and onboarding them to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.

Microsoft Defender customers can turn on [attack surface reduction rules](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?view=o365-worldwide) to prevent common attack techniques used in ransomware attacks:
 
Attack surface reduction rules are sweeping settings that are effective at stopping entire classes of threats.

- Ransom and lateral movement stage:
    - [Block process creations originating from PsExec and WMI commands](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction#block-process-creations-originating-from-psexec-and-wmi-commands)
    - [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion)
    - [Use advanced protection against ransomware](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction#use-advanced-protection-against-ransomware)
    - [Block credential stealing from the Windows local security authority subsystem (lsass.exe)](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction#block-credential-stealing-from-the-windows-local-security-authority-subsystem)
- Common techniques:
    - [Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction#block-execution-of-potentially-obfuscated-scripts)
    - [Block JavaScript or VBScript from launching downloaded executable content](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction#block-javascript-or-vbscript-from-launching-downloaded-executable-content)
- Common entry vectors:
    - [Block all Office applications from creating child processes](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction#block-all-office-applications-from-creating-child-processes)
    - [Block Office communication application from creating child processes](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction#block-office-communication-application-from-creating-child-processes)
    - [Block Office applications from creating executable content](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction#block-office-applications-from-creating-executable-content)
    - [Block Office applications from injecting code into other processes](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction#block-office-applications-from-injecting-code-into-other-processes)

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects threat components as the following malware:

- [Trojan:Linux/Sliver.A](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:Linux/Sliver.A!MTB&threatId=-2147142453)
- [Trojan:Win64/Sliver.D](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:Win64/Sliver.D&threatId=-2147161988)
- [TrojanDownloader:PowerShell/Splinter.A!MTB](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=TrojanDownloader:PowerShell/Splinter.A!MTB&threatId=-2147170431)
- [Behavior:Win32/Splinter.A](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Behavior:Win32/Splinter.A!sms&threatId=-2147170366)
- [VirTool:Win32/SPLINTER.A](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=VirTool:Win32/SPLINTER.A!MTB&threatId=-2147216493)
- [VirTool:Win64/Splinter.A](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=VirTool:Win64/Splinter.A!MTB&threatId=-2147183447)

title: Attempts to carry out cyberattacks using AnyDesk, allegedly on behalf of CERT-UA
content:
#### Targeted Geolocations
- Ukraine



## Snapshot
CERT-UA warns of cybercriminals impersonating their team to gain unauthorized access to computers via the AnyDesk program. This activity is a phishing scam leveraging social engineering to exploit trust in CERT-UA's authority.

## Description
The government Computer Emergency Response Team of Ukraine (CERT-UA) has reported cases where attackers are impersonating CERT-UA to connect to victims' computers using AnyDesk, a remote access software. The attackers send requests under the guise of conducting security audits, using CERT-UA's name, logo, and a potentially changing AnyDesk identifier. While CERT-UA does use remote access tools for legitimate purposes, such actions are only performed with prior consent and through pre-approved channels. The current fraudulent activity is not related to CERT-UA's official operations but represents a social engineering attempt to exploit trust. For the attack to succeed, the victim's AnyDesk ID and active software are necessary, suggesting that the ID might have been compromised through other means.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
The abuse of remote monitoring and management (RMM) tools like AnyDesk has become a significant threat, exploited by both cybercriminals and nation-state actors. These tools, designed for legitimate remote access and system management, are increasingly leveraged for malicious purposes such as maintaining remote access, conducting reconnaissance, and deploying malware, including ransomware. [A June 2024 CrowdStrike report](https://www.csoonline.com/article/3487743/attackers-increasingly-using-legitimate-remote-management-tools-to-hack-enterprises.html) highlighted a 70% year-over-year increase in the misuse of RMM tools by adversaries. The legitimate use of these tools by managed service providers (MSPs) and IT support teams often allows them to bypass standard security measures, making their malicious use harder to detect and an attractive option for post-compromise activities. Read more about [Recent OSINT trends in abuse of remote monitoring and management tools](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/687fdb34).

Russia-based threat actors have frequently exploited RMM tools in cyber campaigns, targeting various sectors and organizations. For instance, in August 2024, [CERT-UA reported](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/560ec243) a phishing campaign using ANONVNC malware, which is based on the open-source MESHAGENT code, to target Ukrainian government bodies. Similarly, in May 2024, [CERT-UA uncovered](https://cip.gov.ua/en/news/cert-ua-poperedzhaye-pro-kiberzagrozu-cilespryamovani-ataki-z-vikoristannyam-programi-viddalenogo-dostupu-superops-rmm) Russian hackers' use of the legitimate SuperOps RMM software to access Ukrainian financial sector information systems. [Microsoft has also tracked](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/d1fba485) the Russia-based threat actor Seashell Blizzard as of February 2024, noting their use of Splashtop and Atera RMM software to establish persistence and execute commands in sophisticated attack chains. These examples underscore the strategic exploitation of RMM tools in Russian cyber operations.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. For more extensive recommendations on hunting for and defending against RMM abuse, see our [technique profile](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/9782a9ef).
 
- Use [Windows Defender Application Control or AppLocker](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/windows-defender-application-control/wdac-and-applocker-overview) to create policies to block unapproved IT management tools
    - Both solutions include functionality to block specific software publisher certificates: WDAC [file rule levels](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/windows-defender-application-control/select-types-of-rules-to-create?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#windows-defender-application-control-file-rule-levels) allow administrators to specify the level at which they want to trust their applications, including listing certificates as untrusted. AppLocker’s [publisher rule condition](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/windows-defender-application-control/applocker/understanding-the-publisher-rule-condition-in-applocker) is available for files that are digitally signed, which can enable organizations to block non-approved RMM instances that include publisher information.
    - Microsoft Defender for Endpoint also provides functionality to block specific signed applications using the [block certificate action](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/t5/microsoft-defender-for-endpoint/indicators-enhancements-allow-block-by-certificates-amp-more/ba-p/1377586).
- For approved RMM systems used in your environment, enforce security settings where possible to implement multifactor authentication (MFA).
- Consider searching for unapproved RMM software installations (see the Advanced hunting section). If an unapproved installation is discovered, reset passwords for accounts used to install the RMM services. If a system-level account was used to install the software, further investigation may be warranted.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/cloud-protection-microsoft-defender-antivirus) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a huge majority of new and unknown variants.
- Turn on the following [attack surface reduction rule](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/overview-attack-surface-reduction) to block or audit activity associated with this threat:
    - [Use advanced protection against ransomware](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#use-advanced-protection-against-ransomware)
    - [Block process creations originating from PsExec and WMI commands](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-process-creations-originating-from-psexec-and-wmi-commands). Some organizations may experience compatibility issues with this rule on certain server systems but should deploy it to other systems to prevent lateral movement originating from PsExec and WMI.

## Detections/Hunting Queries
Because organizations might have legitimate and frequent uses for RMM software, Microsoft recommends using advanced hunting queries to locate RMM software that has not been endorsed by your organization for further investigation. In some cases, these investigations might show benign activity from legitimate users. Regardless of use case, all newly installed RMM instances should be scrutinized and investigated. If a system-level account was used to install the software, further investigation might be warranted.
 
If any queries have high fidelity for discovering unsanctioned RMM instances in your environment and do not detect benign activity, you can create a [custom detection rule](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender/custom-detection-rules) from the advanced hunting query in the Microsoft Defender XDR portal.
 
[Advanced hunting queries are available on GitHub](https://github.com/jischell-msft/RemoteManagementMonitoringTools).

## References
[Attempts to carry out cyberattacks using AnyDesk, allegedly on behalf of CERT-UA](https://cert.gov.ua/article/6282069). CERT-UA (accessed 2025-01-20)

title: Threat Brief: CVE-2025-0282 and CVE-2025-0283
content:
## Snapshot
Researchers at Unit 42 investigated the exploitation of CVE-2025-0282 and CVE-2025-0283.

## Description
The attacks exploiting [CVE-2025-0282](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/CVE-2025-0282) have been observed as part of a limited campaign tracked by Unit 42 as cluster CL-UNK-0979. The exploitation involves improper handling of IFT connections, with repeated IFT error logs indicating attacker attempts. Successful exploitation allows unauthenticated attackers to gain initial access to public-facing Ivanti Connect Secure appliances, granting access to internal networks for lateral movement and other malicious activities.
 
Unit 42’s investigation revealed that attackers used Tor and Nord VPN infrastructure to conceal their activities and accessed appliances via the CVE-2025-0282 vulnerability. Once inside, they deployed a custom Perl script, `ldap.pl`, to harvest credentials from the appliance and moved laterally using these credentials via Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP). Additional tools included a memory dumping utility, `package.dll`, likely aimed at extracting credentials from LSASS process memory.
 
The attackers implemented advanced anti-forensic measures, including log tampering and the deletion of critical files such as debug logs and entries from the `/var/cores` directory. They established persistence using tools like SPAWNMOLE, SPAWNSNAIL, and SPAWNSLOTH, along with a scheduled task named `/mail` and the service DcomSrv. DLL sideloading was also utilized, leveraging malicious files `deelevator64.dll` and `vixDiskLib.dll` alongside legitimate executables `DeElevate64.exe` and `vmdisk.exe`. These DLLs beaconed to specific command-and-control (C2) servers. Additionally, process hollowing techniques were employed, with malware decrypting and injecting payloads into `svchost.exe` processes.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
Ivanti issued a security advisory addressing [CVE-2025-0282](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/CVE-2025-0282), a buffer overflow vulnerability affecting its Connect Secure, Policy Secure, and ZTA Gateway products. This vulnerability allows threat actors to exploit improperly managed memory within the software, enabling unauthenticated remote code execution on affected systems. Successful exploitation could grant attackers complete control over the target system, allowing them to execute arbitrary code or disrupt normal operations. Ivanti has released patches for affected products and strongly recommends organizations apply them promptly to mitigate the risk.

## Recommendations
Ivanti released patches for the Ivanti Connect Secure vulnerability on January 8, 2025. Ivanti will also be releasing patches for the Policy Secure and ZTA Gateways vulnerabilities on January 21, 2025. Customers who use vulnerable Ivanti products are urged to patch as soon as possible for their organization’s security. Customers are also urged to reference the Ivanti security advisory for additional recommendations related to Ivanti’s Connect Secure vulnerability.  
   
Note that applying the patch does not remediate any exploitation or post-exploitation activity that might have occurred, and additional investigation might be warranted.  
   
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations to help investigate successful exploitation.
 
- Look for newly created users on devices impacted by the vulnerability and investigate virtual private network (VPN) logs for evidence of VPN configuration modifications or sign-in activity during the possible window of compromise of unpatched devices. Applying the security patch does not remediate post-compromise activity by a threat actor with privileged access.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/enable-cloud-protection-microsoft-defender-antivirus) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attack tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a large majority of new and unknown variants.
- Run [endpoint detection and response (EDR) in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus doesn’t detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach.
- Enable [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations) in full automated mode to allow Microsoft Defender for Endpoint to take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.

Microsoft Defender customers can turn on the following attack surface reduction rule to prevent common attack techniques:

- [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference)
- You can assess how an attack surface reduction rule might impact your network by opening the [security recommendation](https://security.microsoft.com/security-recommendations) for that rule in threat and vulnerability management. In the recommendation details pane, check the user impact to determine what percentage of your devices can accept a new policy enabling the rule in blocking mode without adverse impact to user productivity.

Customers are strongly urged to keep all public-facing devices updated and to quickly implement patches when made available. Microsoft consistently observes Chinese nation-state threat actors target public facing devices across multiple vendors and products.

## References
[Threat Brief: CVE-2025-0282 and CVE-2025-0283 (Updated Jan. 17)](https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/threat-brief-ivanti-cve-2025-0282-cve-2025-0283/). Unit41 (accessed 2025-01-23).

title: Threat Bulletin: Weaponized Software Targets Chinese-Speaking Organizations
content:
#### Targeted Geolocations
- China  
- Hong Kong SAR  
- Taiwan



## Snapshot
Intezer Labs has uncovered a malware campaign targeting Chinese-speaking regions, including China, Hong Kong, and Taiwan attributed to the Silver Fox advanced persistent threat (APT) group.

## Description
The attack utilizes a multi-stage loader, dubbed PNGPlug, to deliver the ValleyRAT payload. It begins with phishing sites that lure victims into downloading a malicious MSI package disguised as legitimate software. Upon execution, the installer deploys a benign application for cover and extracts an encrypted archive containing the malware payload.
 
Key components include a padded loader (libcef.dll) to evade detection, a legitimate application (down.exe) for masking activities, and malicious payloads disguised as PNG files. The loader uses advanced techniques like memory injection, registry modification, and anti-virus detection evasion to execute ValleyRAT, a sophisticated malware associated with the Silver Fox APT group.
 
Silver Fox is a group known to conduct cybercrime and espionage campaigns, often targeting Chinese-speaking individuals and organizations. The group is known to conduct phishing activities and to deploy malware like ValleyRAT and Gh0st RAT to deploy additional payloads and monitor victim activities. 
 
ValleyRAT is designed for espionage, employing shellcode execution, obfuscation, privilege escalation, and persistence mechanisms to evade detection and maintain access. The attackers leverage phishing sites, trojanized files, and legitimate software to seamlessly deliver malware.
 
According to Intezer Labs, this campaign is notable for targeting a specific demographic—Chinese-speaking regions—and its ability to exploit operational gaps, such as reliance on free software by employees in some organizations.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat.
 
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/linux-preferences) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown threats.
- Run [EDR in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode?view=o365-worldwide?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus does not detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach.
- Allow [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations?view=o365-worldwide?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in full automated mode to allow Microsoft Defender for Endpoint to take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.
- [Enable](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-controlled-folders) controlled folder access.
- Ensure that [tamper protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection#how-do-i-configure-or-manage-tamper-protection) is enabled in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Enable [network protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-network-protection) in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Follow the credential hardening recommendations in the [on-premises credential theft overview](https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/9382203e-5155-4b5e-af74-21562b1004d5/analystreport) to defend against common credential theft techniques like LSASS access.
- [Enable](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-credential-stealing-from-the-windows-local-security-authority-subsystem) LSA protection.

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects threat components as the following malware:
 
- [Trojan:Win64/CryptInject](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:Win64/CryptInject)
- [Trojan:Win32/Malgent!MSR](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:Win32/Malgent!MSR)

## References
[Threat Bulletin: Weaponized Software Targets Chinese-Speaking Organizations](https://intezer.com/blog/malware-analysis/weaponized-software-targets-chinese/). Intezer (accessed 2025-01-17)

title: Sneaky 2FA: exposing a new AiTM Phishing-as-a-Service
content:
## Snapshot
In December 2024, Sekoia identified a new phishing kit, Sneaky 2FA, targeting Microsoft 365 accounts using an Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) approach.

## Description
This phishing kit, active since October 2024, is sold as part of a Phishing-as-a-Service (PhaaS) platform called Sneaky Log, which operates through a Telegram bot. Subscribers receive obfuscated source code to deploy independently, often on compromised WordPress websites or attacker-controlled domains.
 
Analysis revealed that Sneaky 2FA's code borrows elements from W3LL Panel OV6, another AiTM phishing kit. Its functionality includes auto-filling victims' email addresses on phishing pages, advanced obfuscation techniques, and the use of anti-analysis measures like Cloudflare Turnstile challenges. Phishing URLs feature predictable patterns, and the pages imitate Microsoft's authentication interface using blurred backgrounds and embedded HTML tricks.
 
The phishing kit’s anti-debugging mechanisms and filtering capabilities allow it to evade detection, redirecting suspicious traffic to benign destinations like Wikipedia. For successful phishing attempts, the kit communicates directly with Microsoft 365 APIs, leveraging inconsistencies in User-Agent values to execute the attack.
 
Sneaky Log's operations are fully automated via Telegram, featuring a bot for advertising and sales, a ticketing system for support, and cryptocurrency payments. Prices start at $200/month, with discounts for extended subscriptions. The platform uses mechanisms to obscure cryptocurrency transactions, suggesting potential laundering activities.
 
Approximately 100 domains hosting Sneaky 2FA campaigns have been identified, some of which were previously linked to other phishing platforms like Evilginx2. According to Sekoia, this indicates a migration of threat actors to Sneaky Log, attracted by its improved detection evasion and competitive pricing.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
Phishing kits employing adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) techniques significantly lower the barrier to entry for sophisticated phishing campaigns, enabling even low-level cybercriminals to execute attacks that bypass traditional defenses like multifactor authentication (MFA). By intercepting network traffic between the target and a device controlled by the attacker, these kits allow for the theft of session cookies and other critical credentials, effectively neutralizing MFA protections.

The phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) model further expands access to these tools, providing ready-made phishing kits complete with hosting infrastructure, email templates, and campaign management dashboards. In some cases, these kits integrate with services like Telegram, offering real-time notifications and streamlined control over campaigns. This ease of access, combined with AiTM's ability to scale attacks, makes these kits a powerful tool for cybercriminals, amplifying the risk posed to individuals and organizations alike. The integration of platforms like Telegram also enhances operational efficiency, allowing attackers to deploy, monitor, and adjust campaigns with minimal technical expertise.

To learn more about AiTM techniques, read Microsoft's threat overview detailing [adversary-in-the-middle credential phishing](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/f82cecc7).

## Recommendations
While AiTM phishing attempts to circumvent MFA, implementation of MFA remains an essential pillar in identity security and is highly effective at stopping a variety of threats. MFA is the reason that threat actors developed the AiTM session cookie theft technique in the first place. Organizations are advised to work with their identity provider to ensure security controls like MFA are in place. Microsoft customers can implement MFA through various methods, such as using the Microsoft Authenticator, FIDO2 security keys, and certificate-based authentication.
 
Defenders can also complement MFA with the following solutions and best practices to further protect their organizations from such attacks:
 
- Use [security defaults](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/fundamentals/security-defaults?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) as a baseline set of policies to improve identity security posture. For more granular control, enable conditional access policies, especially risk-based access policies. [Conditional access](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/conditional-access/overview?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) policies evaluate sign-in requests using additional identity-driven signals like user or group membership, IP address location information, and device status, among others, and are enforced for suspicious sign-ins. Organizations can protect themselves from attacks that leverage stolen credentials by enabling policies such as compliant devices, trusted IP address requirements, or risk-based policies with proper access control.
- Implement [continuous access evaluation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/conditional-access/concept-continuous-access-evaluation?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc).
- Invest in advanced anti-phishing solutions that monitor and scan incoming emails and visited websites. For example, organizations can leverage web browsers that automatically [identify and block malicious websites](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/deployedge/microsoft-edge-security-smartscreen?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc), including those used in this phishing campaign, and solutions that [detect and block malicious emails, links, and files](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/siem-and-xdr/microsoft-defender-office-365?ocid=magicti_ta_abbreviatedmktgpage).
- Continuously monitor suspicious or anomalous activities. Investigate sign-in attempts with suspicious characteristics (for example, location, ISP, user agent, and use of anonymizer services).
- Implement [Azure Active Directory passwordless sign-in with FIDO2 security keys](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/authentication/concept-authentication-passwordless#fido2-security-keys?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc).
- Enable [Zero-hour auto purge (ZAP)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-office-365/zero-hour-auto-purge) in Office 365 to quarantine sent mail in response to newly acquired threat intelligence and retroactively neutralize malicious phishing, spam, or malware messages that have already been delivered to mailboxes.

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender for Endpoint
Alerts with the following titles in the security center can indicate threat activity on your network:
 
- User compromised in AiTM phishing attack
- Possible AiTM phishing attempt

### Microsoft Defender for Office 365
Microsoft Defender for Office 365 indicates threat activity with the following alerts: 
 
- A potentially malicious URL click was detected
- A user clicked through to a potentially malicious URL
- Suspicious email sending patterns detected

## References
[Sneaky 2FA: exposing a new AiTM Phishing-as-a-Service](https://blog.sekoia.io/sneaky-2fa-exposing-a-new-aitm-phishing-as-a-service/). Sekoia (accessed 2025-01-16)

title: New Star Blizzard spear-phishing campaign targets WhatsApp accounts
content:
#### Targeted Industries
- Government Agencies & Services  
    - Diplomacy/International Relations  
    - Defense  
- Non-Government Organization  
    - Think Tank - Multi-discipline  
- Digital, Print and Broadcast Media



## Snapshot
In mid-November 2024, Microsoft Threat Intelligence observed the Russian threat actor we track as [Star Blizzard](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/e24d62ce29705358542e259267c2f18da1725bf39f10828d53c53b8cb7f3113a) sending their typical targets spear-phishing messages, this time offering the supposed opportunity to join a WhatsApp group. This is the first time we have identified a shift in Star Blizzard’s longstanding tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) to leverage a new access vector. Star Blizzard’s targets are most commonly related to government or diplomacy (both incumbent and former position holders), defense policy or international relations researchers whose work touches on Russia, and sources of assistance to Ukraine related to the war with Russia.
 
As part of our continuous monitoring, analysis, and reporting on the threat landscape, we are sharing our information on Star Blizzard’s latest activity to raise awareness of this threat actor’s shift in tradecraft and to educate organizations on how to harden their attack surfaces against this and similar activity. We also directly notify customers who have been targeted or compromised, providing them with the necessary information to help secure their environments.

## Activity Overview
In our last blog post about [Star Blizzard](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2023/12/07/star-blizzard-increases-sophistication-and-evasion-in-ongoing-attacks/?ocid=magicti_ta_blog), we discussed how the threat actor targeted dozens of civil society organizations—journalists, think tanks, and non-governmental organizations (NGOs)—between January 2023 and August 2024 by deploying spear-phishing campaigns to exfiltrate sensitive information and interfere in their activities. Since October 3, 2024, Microsoft and the US Department of Justice have seized or taken down more than 180 websites related to that activity. While this coordinated action had a short-term impact on Star Blizzard’s phishing operations, we noted at the time that after this threat actor’s active infrastructure was exposed, they swiftly transitioned to new domains to continue their operations, indicating that the threat actor is highly resilient to operational disruptions. We assess the threat actor’s shift to compromising WhatsApp accounts is likely in response to the exposure of their TTPs by Microsoft Threat Intelligence and other organizations, including national cybersecurity agencies. While this campaign appears to have wound down at the end of November, we are highlighting the new shift as a sign that the threat actor could be seeking to change its TTPs in order to evade detection.
 
Star Blizzard’s new spear-phishing campaign, while novel in that it uses and targets WhatsApp for the first time, exhibits familiar spear-phishing TTPs for Star Blizzard, with the threat actor initiating email contact with their targets to engage them before sending a second message containing a malicious link. The sender address used by the threat actor in this campaign impersonates a US government official, continuing Star Blizzard’s practice of impersonating known political/diplomatic figures, to further ensure target engagement. The initial email sent to targets contains a quick response (QR) code purporting to direct users to join a WhatsApp group on "the latest non-governmental initiatives aimed at supporting Ukraine NGOs.” This code, however, is intentionally broken and will not direct the user towards any valid domain; this is in an effort to coax the target recipient into responding.

![an email body containing text and a black square](https://cdn-riq-ti.azureedge.net/7a2f2eee-ba3e-4b96-aab3-3ebd4d122ee4)
 
*Star Blizzard initial spear-phishing email with broken QR code*

When the recipient responds, Star Blizzard sends a second email containing a Safe Links-wrapped *t\[.\]ly* shortened link as the alternative link to join the WhatsApp group.
 
![an email body containing text and a black square](https://cdn-riq-ti.azureedge.net/40d21aff-bf73-47fc-8be6-080e8ae4e7ce)

*Star Blizzard follow-on spear-phishing email with URL link*

When this link is followed, the target is redirected to a webpage asking them to scan a QR code to join the group. However, this QR code is actually used by WhatsApp to connect an account to a linked device and/or the WhatsApp Web portal. This means that if the target follows the instructions on this page, the threat actor can gain access to the messages in their WhatsApp account and have the capability to exfiltrate this data using existing browser plugins, which are designed for exporting WhatsApp messages from an account accessed via WhatsApp Web.

![screenshot of a WhatsApp webpage ](https://cdn-riq-ti.azureedge.net/c1e6a9d7-8570-4ead-b6a1-20a1bd883878)
 
*Malicious Star Blizzard phish attempt using WhatsApp linking QR code*

While this campaign was limited and appeared to have terminated at the end of November, it nevertheless marked a break in long-standing Star Blizzard TTPs and highlighted the threat actor’s tenacity in continuing spear-phishing campaigns to gain access to sensitive information even in the face of repeated degradations of their operations.
 
Microsoft Threat Intelligence recommends that all email users belonging to sectors that Star Blizzard typically targets always remain vigilant when dealing with email, especially emails containing links to external resources. These targets are most commonly related to:
 
- Government or diplomacy (incumbent and former position holders)
- Research into defense policy or international relations when related to Russia
- Assistance to Ukraine related to the ongoing conflict with Russia

When in doubt, contact the person you think is sending the email using a known and previously used email address to verify that the email was indeed sent by them.

## Attribution
Star Blizzard is a threat actor that originates from Russia, with objectives and victimology that align closely with Russian state interests. According to United States and United Kingdom government publications from December 2023, the threat actor is linked to the Russian Federal Security Service (FSB) Centre 18. The group’s targets predominately reside in the United Kingdom, United States, Europe, and Ukraine. Star Blizzard’s main effort is cloud email account credential theft achieved through spear phishing and, very rarely, using malware. The group’s motivation is typically espionage, but Star Blizzard has also been linked to hack-and-leak campaigns, where stolen and leaked data is used to shape narratives in targeted countries.

## MITRE ATT&CK Techniques observed
This Star Blizzard activity exhibits the use of the following attack techniques. For standard industry documentation about these techniques, refer to the [MITRE ATT&CK framework](https://attack.mitre.org/).
 
**Initial access**
 
- [T1566.002 Phishing: Spearphishing Link](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/002/) | Star Blizzard used a spear-phishing campaign to access targets

**Execution**

- [T1204.001 User Execution: Malicious Link](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/001/) | Star Blizzard sent a Safe Link wrapped t\[.\]ly shortened link that redirected the target to a malicious webpage

**Credential access**

- [T1555.003 Credentials from Password Stores: Credentials from Web Browsers](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/) | The QR code on the malicious webpage is used to connect the target's WhatsApp account to a linked device, allowing Star Blizzard to access and exfiltrate messages

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations.
 
- Implement [Microsoft Defender for Endpoint](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) on Android and iOS, which includes anti-phishing capabilities that also apply to QR code phishing attacks, blocking phishing sites from being accessed.
- [Enable network protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-network-protection?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint
- Ensure that [tamper protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) is enabled in Microsoft Dender for Endpoint
- Run endpoint detection and response in [block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus does not detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode.
- Configure [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in full automated mode to let Microsoft Defender for Endpoint take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.
- [Turn on PUA protection in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/detect-block-potentially-unwanted-apps-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/cloud-protection-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques.
- Turn on Microsoft Defender Antivirus [real-time protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/configure-real-time-protection-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc).
- Encourage users to use Microsoft Edge and other web browsers that support [SmartScreen](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/web-protection-overview?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc), which identifies and blocks malicious websites, including phishing sites, scam sites, and sites that host malware.
- Turn on [Safe Links](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-office-365/safe-links-about?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) and [Safe Attachments](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-office-365/safe-attachments-about?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for Office 365.
- Use the [Attack Simulator](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-office-365/attack-simulation-training-get-started?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to run realistic, yet safe, simulated phishing and password attack campaigns. Utilize the [QR code payload](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-office-365/attack-simulation-training-payloads#qr-code-payloads?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in attack simulation training scenarios to mirror Star Blizzard’s and other threat actor’s QR code spear-phishing techniques.

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender for Endpoint
The following alerts might indicate threat activity associated with this threat. These alerts, however, can be triggered by unrelated threat activity and are not monitored in the status cards provided with this report.
 
- Star Blizzard activity group

## Microsoft for XDR Advanced Hunting
**Surface events that may have communicated with the Star Blizzard C2s**. [Run query](https://security.microsoft.com/v2/advanced-hunting?query=H4sIAOVgZGcAA81WwU7CQBCdM19BeqIJevFoPBg0SqImKurBGFNKURTahoJK4sf7ZrYVSnfbbVQwzS7LdGZ23puZ7Y4poBk1aUARTcijEYV0hjkR6YG8WUDm4e2IfGrRPTn4HdEbxlj0pjSHZEZP8BXRLsYUa4fasHZgGeB_RENoz2EzgOazyCY57QdyaZ8a0AmhFWFuYLcGfKjnCJKEjrFvgNUM6-W7T4z31GuA9SW88HpBPYxYZM-IJKFHzCFkLS1iF3ocT5MuBLG9XT6WWBC_wN4XHnvQY28nEjtH5kEewFdbkC09Ks6L8bPeNfTmkPr434N-H4wGqYWj4cdBVC4s8zx2savSGGEsVvaqz60nuVMV9Js8sS7zH1vws4yhmiM77HrejvD-TXogQHXwfu9SK6-WvF1h5ornvN9ANt4wZ8X9bWrKBnNdvrqwG2KdxxXQh8QWgoWs2w-xHgh_CR6eVWSxZJ0lj2AikdOiZbRxBWlHtMKUN-69fFTlvqut1_M0AfodQRVLfstQ2cVnri0zW_VOveoYdv_oZKyqXh8ST2ozkYoyZ9uOyyUO90d9kNWyvgdu6XwtluzLZq781T5VGNUplXxbl1eqjb3CXNTsSC4j-QL7wnfGUt09yzzZdIoNivoY7E5nM-v1uqkuv9u4aRT76m-Yt-kyU7foe-uO9qDdxXMNdiLcAczZ9RHBKXSSGjeVLItsy1iHqbfpv8nUKqq2NlIb1os86vk-TuMZp7cH_Vd8lXWll0eyyW9Gcf9qNkwo9ZwonQ4GV7ztTXAbtz_bG18ZIsVBQ-Lg3hik3dBH9GX13BRNrtovArhd_G4OAAA&timeRangeId=week)
 
`let domainList = dynamic(["civilstructgeo.org", "aerofluidthermo.org"]);`
 
`union`
 
`(`
 
`DnsEvents`
 
`| where QueryType has_any(domainList) or Name has_any(domainList)`
 
`| project TimeGenerated, Domain = QueryType, SourceTable = "DnsEvents"`
 
`),`
 
`(`
 
`IdentityQueryEvents`
 
`| where QueryTarget has_any(domainList)`
 
`| project Timestamp, Domain = QueryTarget, SourceTable = "IdentityQueryEvents"`
 
`),`
 
`(`
 
`DeviceNetworkEvents`
 
`| where RemoteUrl has_any(domainList)`
 
`| project Timestamp, Domain = RemoteUrl, SourceTable = "DeviceNetworkEvents"`
 
`),`
 
`(`
 
`DeviceNetworkInfo`
 
`| extend DnsAddresses = parse_json(DnsAddresses), ConnectedNetworks = parse_json(ConnectedNetworks)`
 
`| mv-expand DnsAddresses, ConnectedNetworks`
 
`| where DnsAddresses has_any(domainList) or ConnectedNetworks.Name has_any(domainList)`
 
`| project Timestamp, Domain = coalesce(DnsAddresses, ConnectedNetworks.Name), SourceTable = "DeviceNetworkInfo"`
 
`),`
 
`(`
 
`VMConnection`
 
`| extend RemoteDnsQuestions = parse_json(RemoteDnsQuestions), RemoteDnsCanonicalNames = parse_json(RemoteDnsCanonicalNames)`
 
`| mv-expand RemoteDnsQuestions, RemoteDnsCanonicalNames`
 
`| where RemoteDnsQuestions has_any(domainList) or RemoteDnsCanonicalNames has_any(domainList)`
 
`| project TimeGenerated, Domain = coalesce(RemoteDnsQuestions, RemoteDnsCanonicalNames), SourceTable = "VMConnection"`
 
`),`
 
`(`
 
`W3CIISLog`
 
`| where csHost has_any(domainList) or csReferer has_any(domainList)`
 
`| project TimeGenerated, Domain = coalesce(csHost, csReferer), SourceTable = "W3CIISLog"`
 
`),`
 
`(`
 
`EmailUrlInfo`
 
`| where UrlDomain has_any(domainList)`
 
`| project Timestamp, Domain = UrlDomain, SourceTable = "EmailUrlInfo"`
 
`),`
 
`(`
 
`UrlClickEvents`
 
`| where Url has_any(domainList)`
 
`| project Timestamp, Domain = Url, SourceTable = "UrlClickEvents"`
 
`)`
 
`| order by TimeGenerated desc`

## Sentinel Hunting Queries
Microsoft Sentinel customers can use the TI Mapping analytics (a series of analytics all prefixed with ‘TI map’) to automatically match the malicious domain indicators mentioned in this blog post with data in their workspace. If the TI Map analytics are not currently deployed, customers can install the Threat Intelligence solution from the [Microsoft Sentinel Content Hub](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/sentinel/sentinel-solutions-deploy?tabs=azure-portal) to have the analytics rule deployed in their Sentinel workspace.
 
While the below queries are not linked to any specific threat actor, they are effective in detecting potential phishing attempts. Implementing these queries can help you stay vigilant and safeguard your organization from phishing attacks
 
- [Delivered Bad Emails from Top bad IPv4 addresses](https://github.com/Azure/Azure-Sentinel/blob/master/Solutions/Microsoft%20Defender%20XDR/Hunting%20Queries/Delivered%20Bad%20Emails%20from%20Top%20bad%20IPv4%20addresses.yaml)
- [Phishing Link Execution Observed](https://github.com/Azure/Azure-Sentinel/blob/master/Detections/MultipleDataSources/PhishinglinkExecutionObserved.yaml)
- [Successful Signin from Phishing Link](https://github.com/Azure/Azure-Sentinel/blob/master/Detections/MultipleDataSources/SucessfullSiginFromPhingLink.yaml)
- [Suspicious URL Clicked](https://github.com/Azure/Azure-Sentinel/blob/master/Hunting%20Queries/Microsoft%20365%20Defender/Initial%20access/SuspiciousUrlClicked.yaml)
- [Email Delivered to Inbox](https://github.com/Azure/Azure-Sentinel/blob/master/Solutions/Microsoft%20Defender%20XDR/Hunting%20Queries/EmailDelivered-ToInbox.yaml)

### Microsoft Security Copilot
 
Security Copilot customers can use the standalone experience to create their own prompts or run the following pre-built promptbooks to automate incident response or investigation tasks related to this threat:

- Incident investigation
- Microsoft User analysis
- Threat actor profile
- Threat Intelligence 360 report based on MDTI article

Note that some promptbooks require access to plugins for Microsoft products such as Microsoft Defender XDR or Microsoft Sentinel.

## Indicators of Compromise

| --- | --- | --- |
| civilstructgeo\[.\]org | Domain | October 2024 |
| aerofluidthermo\[.\]org | Domain | October 2024 |

- [Russian FSB Cyber Actor Star Blizzard Continues Worldwide Spearphishing Campaigns](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-341a). CISA (accessed 2025-01-13)

title: Wiz Research Identifies Exploitation in the Wild of Aviatrix Controller RCE (CVE-2024-50603)
content:
## Snapshot
Researchers at Wiz have identified active exploitation of CVE-2024-50603, a critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in Aviatrix Controller

## Description
This vulnerability, which has a CVSS score of 10.0, stems from improper neutralization of user-supplied input in the API, allowing unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary commands. The flaw impacts Aviatrix Controller versions prior to 7.1.4191 and 7.2.x before 7.2.4996. Exploitation of this vulnerability can lead to privilege escalation in AWS environments, where Aviatrix Controller is often configured with high IAM privileges by default.
 
Wiz Research has observed multiple incidents of [cryptojacking](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2023/07/25/cryptojacking-understanding-and-defending-against-cloud-compute-resource-abuse/?msockid=029395c08bc2665b315481458a11673b) and backdoor deployment via this vulnerability. Attackers have exploited publicly exposed instances, using tools like XMRig for cryptocurrency mining and deploying Sliver backdoors for persistence. While direct evidence of cloud lateral movement is lacking, researchers believe attackers could be leveraging the vulnerability to enumerate cloud permissions and potentially exfiltrate data.
 
The vulnerability was disclosed on January 7, 2025, alongside a proof-of-concept exploit, which led to widespread exploitation in subsequent days. Wiz recommends urgent patching to the fixed versions, implementing network restrictions to reduce exposure, and conducting thorough forensic investigations to identify evidence of compromise. Security teams are advised to proactively hunt for signs of exploitation, including unusual network activity, DNS requests, or AWS CloudTrail events linked to default Aviatrix roles. Proper integration of control, security, and network logs is critical for effective threat detection and mitigation. Organizations using Aviatrix Controller should take immediate action to mitigate the risks associated with CVE-2024-50603.

## Recommendations
Wiz recommends recommended the following actions to mitigate this threat: 
 
- Upgrade Aviatrix Controller to the patched version (7.2.4996)
- Implement network restrictions to prevent public access to Aviatrix Controller.
- Proactively hunt for evidence of compromise whether your environment is already patched to ensure no backdoors were left behind and no lateral movement into the cloud control plane occurred.

## Detections/Hunting Queries

title: Threat Actors Chained Vulnerabilities in Ivanti Cloud Service Applications
content:
## Snapshot
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) released a joint Cybersecurity Advisory in response to the exploitation in September 2024 of vulnerabilities in Ivanti Cloud Service Appliances (CSA): CVE-2024-8190, CVE-2024-8963, CVE-2024-9379, and CVE-2024-9380.

## Description
Threat actors exploited these zero-day vulnerabilities in two distinct chains to gain initial access, execute remote code, obtain credentials, and implant webshells. The first chain combined [CVE-2024-8963](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/cves/CVE-2024-8963/) with [CVE-2024-8190](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/cves/CVE-2024-8190/) and [CVE-2024-9380](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/cves/CVE-2024-9380/), while the second used [CVE-2024-8963](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/cves/CVE-2024-8963/) with [CVE-2024-9379](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/cves/CVE-2024-9379/). Attackers used stolen admin credentials, webshells, and reconnaissance tools like Obelisk and GoGo Scanner to maintain persistence and attempt lateral movement, including targeting a vulnerable Jenkins server. Victim organizations detected the activity through anomalous user account creation, endpoint protection alerts, and log analysis, mitigating further damage by replacing compromised virtual machines. While rapid detection prevented successful follow-on activity in most cases, the exfiltration of admin credentials highlights ongoing risks.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
In September 2024, CVE-2024-8963 and CVE-2024-8190 were added to the [Known Exploited Vulnerability (KEV) Catalog](https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog?search_api_fulltext=CVE-2024-8190&field_date_added_wrapper=all&field_cve=&sort_by=field_date_added&items_per_page=20&url=) after an exploitation was reported by [FortiGuard Labs](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/0c0e8013). Ivanti quickly released a [security advisory](https://forums.ivanti.com/s/article/Security-Advisory-Ivanti-Cloud-Service-Appliance-CSA-CVE-2024-8190?language=de) addressing CVE-2024-8190. In October 2024, Researchers at FortiGuard Labs reported their findings on the sophisticated cyberattack that exploited these vulnerabilities where the attacker gained unauthorized access, escalated privileges, and executed malicious commands while maintaining persistence by creating rogue accounts and patching the exploited vulnerabilities. Additionally, the attackers used the compromised system as a proxy for further attacks, demonstrating advanced tactics and control. Upon the discovery of the additional vulnerabilities, CVE-2024-9380 and CVE-2024-9379 were added to the KEV, and Ivanti released an additional [security advisory](https://forums.ivanti.com/s/article/Security-Advisory-Ivanti-CSA-Cloud-Services-Appliance-CVE-2024-9379-CVE-2024-9380-CVE-2024-9381?language=de).

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following actions to mitigate the risk of this threat
 
- [Upgrade to Ivanti CSA 5.0](https://forums.ivanti.com/s/article/CSA-5-0-Download). Please note that Ivanti CSA 4.6 is EOL and no longer receives patches or third-party libraries. Customers must upgrade to the latest version of the product for continued support.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus?view=o365-worldwide) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or its equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown variants.
- Turn on [tamper protection](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection?view=o365-worldwide) features to prevent attackers from stopping security services.
- Run [EDR in block mode](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode?view=o365-worldwide) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus doesn’t detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach.
- Enable [investigation and remediation](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations?view=o365-worldwide) in full automated mode to allow Microsoft Defender for Endpoint to take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.
- Use [device discovery](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/device-discovery?view=o365-worldwide) to increase your visibility into your network by finding unmanaged devices and onboarding them to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Use multi-factor authentication (MFA) to mitigate credential theft and prevent attacker access. Keep MFA always-on for privileged accounts and apply risk-based MFA for normal accounts. Consider transitioning to a passwordless primary authentication method, such as Azure MFA, certificates, or Windows Hello for Business.
- To help block lateral movements:

    - [Block process creations originating from PsExec and WMI commands](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction#block-process-creations-originating-from-psexec-and-wmi-commands)
    - [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion)
    - [Block credential stealing from the Windows local security authority subsystem (lsass.exe)](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction#block-credential-stealing-from-the-windows-local-security-authority-subsystem)

CISA and the FBI recommend the following steps to mitigate the risk of this threat: 

- Establish a baseline and maintain detailed logs of network traffic, account behavior, and software to assist in the identification of anomalies that may indicate malicious activity more quickly.
- Secure remote access tools by:
    - Implementing application controls to manage and control software execution, including allowlisting remote access programs.
    - Audit the network for systems using RDP, close unused RDP ports, and log RDP login attempts.
    - Enforce account lockouts after a specified number of attempts.
- If compromise is detected, CISA and the FBI recommend:
    - Quarantine or take offline potentially affected hosts.
    - Reimage compromised hosts.
    - Provision new account credentials.
    - Collect and review artifacts such as running processes/services, unusual authentications, and recent network connections.
    - More recommendations can be found in the original article: [Threat Actors Chained Vulnerabilities in Ivanti Cloud Service Applications.](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa25-022a)

## References
[Threat Actors Chained Vulnerabilities in Ivanti Cloud Service Applications.](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa25-022a) CISA (accessed on 2025-01-24).

title: US govt says North Korea stole over $659 million in crypto last year
content:
## Snapshot
The United States, Japan, and South Korea have reiterated warnings to the blockchain technology industry about the ongoing DPRK threat actors targeting global entities, threatening the international financial system's stability.

## Description
North Korean state-backed hacking groups remain active, having stolen over $659 million in cryptocurrency last year through a series of heists. These groups persist in using social engineering tactics to deploy malware like TraderTraitor and [AppleJeus](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/796c7ccf162d06ceaa32e04c82cd7b8025abe1d155a358319286012107a6b838), targeting blockchain companies worldwide. Notably, the July 2024 breach of WazirX, India’s largest Bitcoin exchange, resulted in a $235 million loss. Other known attacks attributed to North Korea include incidents involving [DMM Bitcoin](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/9cd8b8b5), Upbit, Rain Management, and [Radiant Capital](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/3a647a38). Chainalysis reports that North Korean hackers stole $1.34 billion in cryptocurrency across 47 cyberattacks in 2024, highlighting a continuation of their increasingly lucrative operations.
 
The statement also revisits the ongoing issue of North Korean IT workers, often referred to as "IT warriors," deceiving companies into hiring them as remote staff. Using stolen identities and AI tools, they bypass background checks and secure employment to install malware or exploit insider access for extortion. For instance, KnowBe4 recently hired a North Korean malicious actor as a Principal Software Engineer, who attempted to deploy information-stealing malware after gaining employment through fraudulent means. The U.S. State Department continues to offer rewards for information on North Korean front companies, such as Yanbian Silverstar and Volasys Silverstar, which have amassed over $88 million through illicit IT schemes over the past six years.
 
This joint statement serves as a reminder of these ongoing threats. It advises private sector entities, particularly in blockchain and freelance industries, to remain vigilant and implement measures to mitigate risks. The United States, South Korea, and Japan emphasize continued public-private collaboration, enhanced cybersecurity capacity-building across the Indo-Pacific region, and sanctions to combat these long-standing threats and protect the international financial system.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
Microsoft identifies Jade Sleet, Sapphire Sleet, and Citrine Sleet as the three primary North Korean threat groups targeting cryptocurrency organizations. According to [Microsoft's Digital Defense Report 2024](https://cdn-dynmedia-1.microsoft.com/is/content/microsoftcorp/microsoft/final/en-us/microsoft-brand/documents/Microsoft%20Digital%20Defense%20Report%202024%20%281%29.pdf), the United Nations estimates that North Korean hackers have stolen over $3 billion USD in cryptocurrency since 2017.
 
In addition to these groups, Microsoft also tracks North Korean IT remote worker activity under the designation [Storm-0287](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/29ec3550). For more information on North Korean remote IT workers and other related threat actor activities, refer to [OSINT trends of North Korean threat actors](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/87adc2a0).

## Recommendations
Government agencies have issued multiple notifications regarding DPRK IT workers, who pose an insider threat to private sector partners. The [FBI](https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2024/PSA240516) provided the following tips:

Tips to Protect Your Business  

- Implement identity verification processes during hiring, onboarding, and throughout the employment of any remote worker.
- Educate HR staff, hiring managers, and development teams regarding this threat.
- Monitor applicants for changes in addresses, particularly after being hired but before laptops are delivered to the applicant-provided address.
- Note unusual network traffic, to include remote connections to devices, and monitor environments for presence of remote desktop protocols or software that is prohibited.
- Note inconsistencies in interviews, especially applicants being unable to field questions about where they are located or key details about their past.
- Note increased noise during interviews or sounds as if an applicant is surrounded by others doing similar work.
- Verify all remote workers' identification information at E-Verify.gov.
- Note errors derived in the hiring process from the E-Verify check and request in-person or other reliable means of verification.
- Ensure that third-party staffing firms conduct robust hiring practices to fill jobs, routinely audit hiring practices, and flag changes in address or payment platforms.

Tips to Protect Yourself  

- Remain cautious regarding seemingly random outreach on job-seeking sites and social media platforms for remote positions, account sharing, and virtual assistant-type positions.
- Remain alert regarding outreach for job positions involving the receipt of packages in return for portions of proceeds derived from jobs affiliated with delivered equipment.
- If you receive a W-4, 1099-NEC, or other IRS form for a job that you did not hold, you should contact the business who provided it as well as the FBI.
- Consider placing a Self-Lock through E-Verify.gov to protect your identity from being used in employment-related identity fraud.

Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. 

- [Help prevent social engineering attacks](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/security-insider/emerging-threats/feeding-from-the-trust-economy-social-engineering-fraud?ocid=magicti_ta_blog) by not blending personal accounts with work emails or work-related tasks. Avoid opening emails, attachments, and links, including links from social networks, from suspicious sources. Ask yourself if the sender is who they say they are before clicking anything. Be wary of senders and offers. Do a search to determine if the offer is legitimate or a trap.
- Enforce MFA on all accounts, remove users excluded from MFA, and strictly [require MFA](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/identity-protection/howto-identity-protection-configure-mfa-policy?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) from all devices, in all locations, at all times.
- Activate conditional access policies. [Conditional access](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/conditional-access/overview?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) policies are evaluated and enforced every time an attacker attempts to use a stolen session cookie. Organizations can protect themselves from attacks that leverage stolen credentials by activating policies regarding compliant devices or trusted IP address requirements.
- Practice the [principle of least privilege and building credential hygiene](https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2022/05/09/ransomware-as-a-service-understanding-the-cybercrime-gig-economy-and-how-to-protect-yourself?ocid=magicti_ta_blog#defending-against-ransomware). Avoid the use of domain-wide, admin-level service accounts. Restricting local administrative privileges can help limit installation of unwanted applications.
- Software developers and publishers should ensure their [build and update infrastructure are secure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/malware/supply-chain-malware). Establish [best practices to secure software supply chain](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/nuget/concepts/security-best-practices).
- Build organizational resilience against email threats by educating users about identifying social engineering attacks and preventing malware infection. Use [Attack simulation training](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/attack-simulation-training-get-started?ocid=magicti%3cem%3eta%3c/em%3elearndoc) in Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to run attack scenarios, increase user awareness, and empower employees to recognize and report these attacks.

## References

[Joint Statement on Cryptocurrency Thefts by the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea and Public-Private Collaboration](https://www.state.gov/office-of-the-spokesperson/releases/2025/01/joint-statement-on-cryptocurrency-thefts-by-the-democratic-peoples-republic-of-korea-and-public-private-collaboration). U.S. Department of State (accessed 2025-01-15)

title: One Mikro Typo: How a simple DNS misconfiguration enables malware delivery by a Russian botnet
content:
## Snapshot
Researchers at Infoblox Threat Intel have discovered a new botnet exploiting a misconfiguration in DNS records to deliver malware through a malspam campaign. The botnet uses compromised routers, likely through a known vulnerability, to install scripts that turn the devices into SOCKS proxies. These proxies are then used for various malicious activities, including DDoS attacks, data exfiltration, phishing campaigns, and malware distribution.

## Description
The campaign was particularly sophisticated, with some emails mimicking DHL Express and delivering fake freight invoices containing a ZIP archive with a malicious JavaScript file. The zip files had consistent filenames like "Invoice 123.zip" or "Tracking 456.zip," which, when opened, triggered malware infections. The JavaScript file within these zip files is obfuscated and designed to download and execute a PowerShell script that establishes a connection to a malicious command and control (C2) server that has been previously associated with Russian-based threat actors. 

The botnet consists of approximately 13,000 hijacked MikroTik devices and leverages DNS misconfigurations in SPF records across roughly 20,000 domains, enabling unauthorized email sending and domain spoofing. The SPF misconfigurations allow any server to send emails on behalf of the domains, which should instead be restricted to specific authorized servers. The botnet's use of SOCKS proxies on the MikroTik devices allows for the masking of malicious traffic's true origin, making it harder to trace and increasing the scale of operations.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
The evolving capabilities of modern botnets highlight their ability to adapt and remain undetected while executing malicious activities. Botnet activity is both increasing and increasingly impactful, with a [25% year-over-year surge](https://www.ustelecom.org/research/botnets2024/) in 2024 and [an estimated economic impact of $600 billion annually](https://kpmg.com/nl/en/home/insights/2024/08/exploring-botnets-understanding-the-threat-landscape-and-building-ethical-awareness.html) from botnet-enabled cybercrime. Recent reports identify key trends in botnet threats, including advanced evasion techniques, payload versatility, and expanded targeting of Linux and IoT systems. Infoblox's research on this campaign reflects these trends, particularly the focus on evolving evasion tactics and broader targeting. The use of compromised MikroTik devices as SOCKS proxies not only enhances evasion but also capitalizes on the prevalence of MikroTik routers in IoT environments.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of botnets.
 
- [Restrict automatic prompts](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/automatic-file-download-notifications-in-windows-dc73c9c9-1b4c-a8b7-8d8b-b471736bb5a0) for non-user-initiated file downloads.
- [Enable Safe Links](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/exchange/enable-safelinksrule?view=exchange-ps) protection for links in email messages.
- [Enable Safe Attachments](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/exchange/set-safeattachmentrule?view=exchange-ps) in block mode.
- Enable [Zero-hour auto purge (ZAP)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-office-365/zero-hour-auto-purge) in Office 365 to quarantine sent mail in response to newly-acquired threat intelligence and retroactively neutralize malicious phishing, spam, or malware messages that have already been delivered to mailboxes.
- Run endpoint detection and response [(EDR) in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus does not detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode.

## References
[One Mikro Typo: How a simple DNS misconfiguration enables malware delivery by a Russian botnet](https://blogs.infoblox.com/threat-intelligence/one-mikro-typo-how-a-simple-dns-misconfiguration-enables-malware-delivery-by-a-russian-botnet/) Infoblox Threat Intel (accessed 2025-01-16)
 
[New Botnet Exploiting DNS Records Misconfiguration To Deliver Malware](https://gbhackers.com/dns-misconfiguration-botnet-malware/) GB Hackers (accessed 2025-01-16)
 
[MikroTik botnet uses misconfigured SPF DNS records to spread malware](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/mikrotik-botnet-uses-misconfigured-spf-dns-records-to-spread-malware/) Bleeping Computer (accessed 2025-01-16)
