title: The Hunt for RedCurl
content:
#### Targeted Geolocations
- Canada



## Snapshot
Researchers at Huntress detailed the activity impacting organizations in Canada using similar infrastructure and tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) associated with the RedCurl threat group.

## Description
This activity, observed as far back as November 2023, highlights RedCurl’s focus on cyberespionage, where they infiltrate networks to access sensitive data, such as emails and corporate documents, without demanding ransoms or encrypting systems.
 
Huntress identified suspicious activity involving the use of Windows binaries and Python scripts to create reverse proxy tunnels and exfiltrate data to cloud storage. A key discovery included the use of scheduled tasks to execute malicious binaries and scripts via pcalua.exe, a lesser-known [living-off-the-land binary](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/1543be43) (LOLBin). This binary enabled the attackers to download, unpack, and execute files using tools like PowerShell and 7zip, which were also used to archive and encrypt stolen data.
 
RedCurl's tactics in these attacks align closely with their documented behavior but also show slight variations in the infection chain and execution methods. For instance, attackers used batch scripts with embedded passwords to download and extract files from cloud storage and set up connections to command-and-control (C2) servers. Analysis revealed similarities with RedCurl modules identified in previous reports, such as RedCurl.Extractor and RPivot proxy tools.
 
The group’s reliance on legitimate tools like 7zip and PowerShell underscores the challenges of detecting such activities, as they mimic normal system administration processes. Despite these challenges, Huntress traced RedCurl’s infrastructure to domains and IPs connected to previous campaigns, reinforcing their attribution of this activity to the threat group.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
Active since 2018, [RedCurl](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1039/) is a threat actor known for engaging in corporate espionage targeting organizations across diverse industries, including finance, construction, consulting, retail, insurance, law, and travel. According to research from [Group-IB](https://www.group-ib.com/media-center/press-releases/red-curl/), RedCurl is Russian-speaking but lacks a definitive geographic connection to any specific region. Its victims are geographically distributed across countries such as Russia, Germany, Ukraine, the United Kingdom, Slovenia, Canada, Australia, and the United States.

RedCurl typically gains initial access to organizations with spear phishing emails, then executes discovery and collection commands and scripts to locate data of interest. The group then exfiltrates files to C2 servers controlled by the actor.

## Recommendations
Apply these mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations.
 
- Turn on cloud-delivered protection and automatic sample submission on Windows Defender Antivirus. These capabilities use artificial intelligence and machine learning to quickly identify and stop new and unknown threats.
- Practice the principle of least-privilege and maintain credential hygiene. Avoid the use of domain-wide, admin-level service accounts. Restricting local administrative privileges can help prevent execution of native binaries with elevated privileges.

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects threat components as the following malware:
 
- [Trojan:Win32/Wacatac](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:Win32/Wacatac.B!ml)

### Microsoft Defender for Endpoint
Alerts with the following titles in the security center can indicate threat activity on your network:
 
- Use of living-off-the-land binary to run malicious code

title: Triaging Triada: Understanding an Advanced Mobile Trojan and How it Targets Communication and Banking Applications
content:
## Snapshot
Researchers at Darktrace detailed Triada, a modular banking trojan that has been active since at least 2016.

## Description
Triada spreads through supply chain compromises, malicious app versions (e.g., YoWhatsApp), phishing campaigns, and smaller trojans like Leech, Ztorg, and Gopro. Once installed on a device, Triada collects system data and communicates with a command-and-control (C2) server to download additional malicious modules.
 
Triada’s capabilities include intercepting SMS messages (including two-factor authentication codes), stealing login credentials and payment details, creating fake accounts, and installing further malware. It can also divert in-app purchases, activate device cameras and microphones, and sign users up for paid subscriptions without consent.
 
To avoid detection, Triada embeds itself into Android’s core processes, enabling it to manipulate system functions and hide malicious modules. It can even persist after a factory reset by connecting to its C2 server upon reboot.
 
Infections have been linked to unofficial WhatsApp versions downloaded via third-party app stores. These versions allow Triada to hijack legitimate WhatsApp credentials, register fake accounts, and send device and operator data to its C2 servers. This malware’s behavior includes unusual encrypted traffic patterns, such as connections to algorithmically generated hostnames and data exfiltration through HTTP POST requests without prior GET requests.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
Banking trojans have made OSINT headlines in recent months as threat actors develop new malware and continue to enhance existing malware to conduct malicious activity. Historically, these trojans were primarily viewed as a consumer problem, focusing on harvesting banking credentials and personal financial data. However, this threat has evolved, and enterprises are now increasingly being targeted by cybercriminals. With bring your own device (BYOD) policies leading to more personal devices being connected to corporate networks, financially motivated attackers are expanding their focus to include enterprise systems, seeking to compromise valuable business data for financial gain.

To read more about banking trojan-related cyberattacks and for recommendations about defending against such threats, read [Recent OSINT trends in banking trojans](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/3c32651f).

## Recommendations
- Only install applications from trusted sources and official stores.
- If a device is no longer receiving updates, strongly consider replacing it with a new device.
- Use mobile solutions such as [Microsoft Defender for Endpoint on Android](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/microsoft-defender-endpoint-android?view=o365-worldwide)to detect malicious applications
    - Always keep Install unknown apps disabled on the Android device to prevent apps from being installed from unknown sources.
- Evaluate whether [Microsoft Defender for Internet of Things (IoT)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/defender-for-iot/organizations/overview) services are applicable to your IoT environment.

title: Ransomware abuses Amazon AWS feature to encrypt S3 buckets
content:
## Snapshot
Researchers at Halcyon identified a new ransomware campaign targeting Amazon S3 buckets, where a threat actor named "Codefinger" has encrypted the data of at least two victims using AWS's Server-Side Encryption with Customer Provided Keys (SSE-C).

## Description
The attackers gained access to AWS credentials, allowing them to use the victims' own keys to encrypt their data with the AES-256 algorithm. Since AWS does not store these keys, the victims cannot recover their data without the attacker's key.

Codefinger's method involves generating a local encryption key to encrypt the target's data and then setting a seven-day file deletion policy using the S3 Object Lifecycle Management API. Ransom notes are left in affected directories, demanding payment in Bitcoin for the decryption key and threatening to terminate negotiations if the victim attempts to change permissions or modify files.

The campaign's use of AWS native services for encryption makes the data unrecoverable without the attacker's cooperation. Halcyon has reported the issue to Amazon, who has responded by notifying customers with exposed keys and encouraging the implementation of strict security protocols. Halcyon also recommends that AWS customers set restrictive policies to prevent the use of SSE-C on their S3 buckets, disable unused keys, rotate active ones frequently, and maintain minimal account permissions.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
In addition to this campaign, threat actors exploit AWS services in various ways to conduct malicious activities while leveraging the platform’s scalability and anonymity. They often use stolen or compromised AWS accounts to launch attacks, such as hosting phishing sites, deploying malware, or setting up command-and-control (C2) servers. AWS’s elastic compute capabilities are misused for cryptojacking, where attackers mine cryptocurrency using stolen resources. Additionally, misconfigured services, such as open S3 buckets or improperly secured IAM roles, are exploited to steal sensitive data or escalate privileges. Threat actors also abuse AWS APIs for automated attacks, making detection and mitigation challenging without proper monitoring and security controls.

## Recommendations
Halcyon reccommends organizations can protect themselves by proactively hardening their AWS environments:
 
- Restrict SSE-C Usage:  

    - Use the Condition element in IAM policies to prevent the application of SSE-C to S3 buckets. Policies can be configured to restrict this feature to authorized data and users
- Monitor and Audit AWS Keys:  

    - Regularly review permissions for all AWS keys to ensure they have the minimum required access.
    - Disable unused keys and rotate active ones frequently.
- Implement Advanced Logging:  

    - Enable detailed logging for S3 operations to detect unusual activity, such as bulk encryption or lifecycle policy changes.
- Engage AWS Support:  

    - Work with AWS support to identify potential vulnerabilities and implement tailored security measures.

## References
[Ransomware abuses Amazon AWS feature to encrypt S3 buckets](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/ransomware-abuses-amazon-aws-feature-to-encrypt-s3-buckets/) Bleepingcomputer (Accessed 2025-1-17)

title: Deep Dive Into a Linux Rootkit Malware
content:
## Snapshot
Researchers at FortiGuard Labs uncovered a sophisticated Linux rootkit malware targeting CentOS systems, which allows attackers to gain full remote control of a victim's device.

## Description
The rootkit, comprising a loadable kernel module named sysinitd.ko and a user-space binary file sysinitd, is deployed using a shell script Install.sh. It establishes persistence by adding entries to startup files and hijacks inbound TCP network traffic using a Netfilter hook function. The malware creates procfs entries named "abrtinfo," "brtinfo," and "rtinfo," which facilitate input/output and control commands between the kernel module and the user-space process. The rootkit activates when it recognizes an "attack-init packet" from the attacker, which must be 13 bytes long and meet specific conditions.

After verification, the kernel module records the source and destination IP and Port, allowing subsequent traffic from the attacker to be processed. The user-space process sysinitd, disguised as a bash program to avoid detection, starts a child process that replaces its current process with "/bin/sh," granting the attacker root-level command execution. The parent process manages the child process and reads control commands to perform actions like restarting or killing the child process. The attacker's control commands are sent to the compromised system and passed to sysinitd via "/proc/rtinfo." The malware's capabilities allow the attacker to send Linux commands and retrieve results through traffic sniffing.

## References
[Deep Dive Into a Linux Rootkit Malware](https://www.fortinet.com/blog/threat-research/deep-dive-into-a-linux-rootkit-malware). Fortinet (accessed 2025-01-15)

title: DigitalPulse Proxyware Being Distributed Through Ad Pages
content:
## Snapshot
AhnLab Security Intelligence Center (ASEC) has confirmed that proxyware, identical to the DigitalPulse proxyware previously used in Proxyjacking attack campaigns, is being installed on users' systems without their consent through advertisement pages on freeware software sites.

## Description
This proxyware, signed with a Netlink Connect certificate, hijacks network bandwidth for financial gain, a technique known as proxyjacking. Users inadvertently install a disguised program called AutoClicker, which then installs the proxyware. Proxyjacking is similar to cryptojacking but uses proxyware instead of CoinMiners to profit from the infected system's resources. The malware is distributed via ad pages that pop up on freeware download sites. These sites can also redirect to pages distributing LummaC2 Malware, also known as [Lumma Stealer,](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/33933578825488511c30b0728dd3c4f8b5ca20e41c285a56f796eb39f57531ad) that uses phishing techniques to execute malicious commands.

The AutoClicker downloader malware employs analysis disruption techniques to avoid detection, including checking for virtual machine environments and web browser history file sizes. Once installed, it creates and executes a PowerShell script to install NodeJS, download malicious JavaScript, and register it in the Task Scheduler. The JavaScript malware connects to a C&C server, receives commands, and ultimately installs the proxyware, which is then registered under the name "Network Performance" in the Task Scheduler. The proxyware, DigitalPulse, has previously infected at least 400,000 Windows systems and continues to be a threat through these campaigns.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations. 
 
- Check your Office 365 email filtering settings to ensure you block spoofed emails, spam, and emails with malware. Use [Microsoft Defender for Office 365](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/defender-for-office-365) for enhanced phishing protection and coverage against new threats and polymorphic variants. Configure Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to [recheck links on click](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-links-about) and [delete sent mail](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/zero-hour-auto-purge) in response to newly acquired threat intelligence. Turn on [safe attachments policies](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-attachments-policies-configure) to check attachments to inbound email.
- Encourage users to use Microsoft Edge and other web browsers that support [SmartScreen](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/web-protection-overview), which identifies and blocks malicious websites, including phishing sites, scam sites, and sites that host malware.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus, or the equivalent for your antivirus product, to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown variants.
- Enforce MFA on all accounts, remove users excluded from MFA, and strictly [require MFA](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/identity-protection/howto-identity-protection-configure-mfa-policy) from all devices, in all locations, at all times.
- Enable passwordless authentication methods (for example, Windows Hello, FIDO keys, or Microsoft Authenticator) for accounts that support passwordless. For accounts that still require passwords, use authenticator apps like Microsoft Authenticator for MFA. [Refer to this article](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/concept-authentication-methods) for the different authentication methods and features.
- For MFA that uses authenticator apps, ensure that the app requires a code to be typed in where possible, as many intrusions where MFA was enabled still succeeded due to users clicking “Yes” on the prompt on their phones even when they were not at their [devices](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/how-to-mfa-number-match). Refer to [this article](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/concept-authentication-methods) for an example.
- Remind employees that enterprise or workplace credentials should not be stored in browsers or password vaults secured with personal credentials. Organizations can turn off password syncing in browser on managed devices using [Group Policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/deployedge/microsoft-edge-enterprise-sync#sync-group-policies).

Microsoft Defender customers can [turn on attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction) to prevent common attack techniques used in infostealer infections. Attack surface reduction rules are sweeping settings that stop entire classes of threats including, infostealers, credential theft, and ransomware. The following bullet points offer more guidance on specific mitigation advice:

- [Turn on PUA protection in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/detect-block-potentially-unwanted-apps-microsoft-defender-antivirus)
- [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference)
- [Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference)

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects threat components as the following malware:  
 
- Trojan:Win32/LummaCStealer
- PWS:Win32/Lumma

title: New Web3 attack exploits transaction simulations to steal crypto
content:
#### Targeted Industries
- Financial Services



## Snapshot
ScamSniffer has identified a new phishing technique called "transaction simulation spoofing" that has been used to steal cryptocurrency. This method exploits a feature in modern Web3 wallets that allows users to preview the outcome of a blockchain transaction before it is executed.

## Description
The attackers deceive victims by directing them to a malicious website that simulates a legitimate "Claim" function, showing the user they will receive a small amount of ETH. However, the attackers manipulate the on-chain contract state during a time delay between the simulation and the actual transaction execution. As a result, when the victim signs the transaction based on the simulated outcome, their wallet is drained, and the funds are transferred to the attacker's wallet. 

This emerging attack vector marks a notable advancement in phishing tactics. Instead of merely employing basic deception, attackers are now leveraging the trusted features of wallets that users depend on for security. This refined strategy significantly complicates the detection process. ScamSniffer's analysis of an actual case revealed that the victim lost all their assets after signing the transaction 30 seconds following the state change.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
Recent reports emphasize the escalating threats targeting Web3 wallets, which are popular tools for managing digital assets and have seen widespread adoption across the decentralized finance (DeFi) and cryptocurrency ecosystems. For example, in December 2024, the [Socket security firm highlighted](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/04dd6cf6) a supply chain attack on the popular '@solana/web3.js' library, which receives over 350,000 weekly downloads, where malicious versions were released to steal private keys. Similarly, [Cado Security Labs uncovered](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/507693d5) a phishing campaign using a fake video conferencing platform, "Meeten," designed to steal cryptocurrency and sensitive data from Web3 users through sophisticated social engineering. In another case, [ReversingLabs identified](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/86e2a9b6) a compromised npm package, '@lottiefiles/lottie-player', which included code to siphon funds from users' wallets. These examples underscore the increasing sophistication and frequency of attacks aimed at Web3 wallets, highlighting the urgent need for enhanced security measures to protect users in this rapidly evolving landscape.

## Recommendations
The source recommends the following steps to reduce the impact of this threat: 
 
- **Real-time Simulation Refresh Mechanism**: Dynamically adjust simulation refresh rates according to different blockchain block times. Ensure a mandatory refresh of simulation results before executing critical operations. Display timestamps and block heights for simulation results to enhance user awareness. Introduce prominent expiration warnings for simulation results that surpass specific age thresholds.
- **Security Service Integration**: Incorporate a phishing contract blocklist from leading security service providers. Implement real-time security checks for all interacting contract addresses and display prominent risk warnings when engaging with suspicious contracts.
- **UI/UX Improvements**: Emphasize the time-sensitivity of simulation results through clear visual indicators. Introduce additional confirmation steps for operations identified as high-risk. Provide more comprehensive transaction risk analysis and simplify the presentation of security alerts to capture user attention effectively.
- **Transaction Verification**: Always thoroughly review transaction details. Independently verify all contract interactions and maintain a healthy level of skepticism toward offers that seem too good to be true, such as "free claim" promotions.
- **Trusted Sources**: Use only trusted and verified dApps, and consider employing security tools to help identify and avoid potential threats.

## References
[New Web3 attack exploits transaction simulations to steal crypto](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-web3-attack-exploits-transaction-simulations-to-steal-crypto/). Bleeping Computer (accessed 2025-01-14)
 
[https://drops.scamsniffer.io/transaction-simulation-spoofing-a-new-threat-in-web3/](https://drops.scamsniffer.io/transaction-simulation-spoofing-a-new-threat-in-web3/) ScamSniffer (accessed 2025-01-14)

title: FunkSec: Alleged Top Ransomware Group Powered by AI
content:
## Snapshot
FunkSec, a ransomware group that emerged in late 2024, has been rapidly gaining attention due to its AI-assisted malware development and high activity, claiming over 85 victims in December alone.

## Description
The group, which presents itself as a Ransomware-as-a-Service operation, employs double extortion tactics and has no known affiliations with existing ransomware gangs. Their custom ransomware, written in Rust, encrypts files using RSA and AES encryption, deletes the originals, and appends a ".funksec" extension to the encrypted files. The malware also disables EDRs, event logging, and deletes shadow copy backups, demanding a ransom for decryption. FunkSec's operations, which include a data leak site, DDoS tool, and remote desktop management program, target countries like India and the U.S.

The group's use of AI is evident in their public scripts and ransomware source code, which feature extensive code comments in perfect English, likely generated by an LLM agent. They have also released an AI chatbot based on Miniapps to support their malicious activities. Technical analysis of FunkSec's malware shows a stripped Rust binary with redundant code and multiple calls to the same functions, using chacha20 for file encryption and generating ephemeral keys for encryption. Despite their low skill level, FunkSec has gained attention in cybercrime forums due to their Tor-based operations and low ransom demands. The group's rapid rise and the use of AI in malware development highlight the evolving landscape of cyber threats and the challenges in accurately assessing the risk posed by new ransomware groups.

## Recommendations
Apply these mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations.

- Educate users about [preventing malware infections](https://www.microsoft.com/security/business/security-101/what-is-malware?ocid=magicti_ta_abbreviatedmktgpage"%20\t%20"_blank), such as ignoring or deleting unsolicited and unexpected emails or attachments sent through instant messaging applications or social networks as well as suspicious phone calls.
- Invest in advanced anti-phishing solutions that monitor incoming emails and visited websites. [Microsoft Defender for Office 365](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender/microsoft-365-security-center-mdo?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) brings together incident and alert management across email, devices, and identities, centralizing investigations for email-based threats.
- Apply Microsoft’s [security best practices for Microsoft Teams](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/MicrosoftTeams/teams-security-best-practices-for-safer-messaging) to safeguard Teams users.
- Consider [blocking or uninstalling](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/client-management/client-tools/quick-assist#disable-quick-assist-within-your-organization) Quick Assist and other remote monitoring and management tools if these tools are not in use in your environment. Apply mitigations listed in [Microsoft’s technique profile on abuse of remote monitoring and management tools](https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/44b8f927-5ab5-46bb-bb79-7ca2d4e30156/overview).
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a huge majority of new and unknown variants.
- Turn on [tamper protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) features to prevent attackers from stopping security services.
- Run [EDR in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus doesn’t detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach.
- Enable [network protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-network-protection?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to prevent applications or users from accessing malicious domains and other malicious content on the internet.
- Enable [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in full automated mode to allow Microsoft Defender for Endpoint to take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.
- Use [device discovery](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/device-discovery?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to increase your visibility into your network by finding unmanaged devices on your network and onboarding them to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Refer to [Microsoft’s human-operated ransomware overview](https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/05658b6c-dc62-496d-ad3c-c6a795a33c27/analystreport) for general hardening recommendations against ransomware attacks.

Microsoft Defender XDR customers can turn on [attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to prevent common attack techniques used in ransomware attacks. Attack surface reduction rules are sweeping settings that are effective at stopping entire classes of threats:

- Ransom and lateral movement stage:
    - [Block process creations originating from PsExec and WMI commands](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-process-creations-originating-from-psexec-and-wmi-commands)
    - [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion)
    - [Use advanced protection against ransomware](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#use-advanced-protection-against-ransomware)
    - [Block credential stealing from the Windows local security authority subsystem (lsass.exe)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-credential-stealing-from-the-windows-local-security-authority-subsystem)
- Common techniques:
    - [Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-execution-of-potentially-obfuscated-scripts)
    - [Block JavaScript or VBScript from launching downloaded executable content](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-javascript-or-vbscript-from-launching-downloaded-executable-content)
- Common entry vectors:
    - [Block all Office applications from creating child processes](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-all-office-applications-from-creating-child-processes)
    - [Block Office communication application from creating child processes](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-office-communication-application-from-creating-child-processes)
    - [Block Office applications from creating executable content](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-office-applications-from-injecting-code-into-other-processes)
    - [Block Office applications from injecting code into other processes](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-office-applications-from-injecting-code-into-other-processes)

**Assess rule impact before deployment**

You can assess how an attack surface reduction rule might impact your network by opening the [security recommendation](https://security.microsoft.com/security-recommendations?ocid=magicti_ta_tvmsecreco) for that rule in threat and vulnerability management. In the recommendation details pane, check the user impact to determine what percentage of your devices can accept a new policy enabling the rule in blocking mode without adverse impact to user productivity.

title: RedDelta: Chinese State-Sponsored Group Targets Mongolia, Taiwan, and Southeast Asia with Evolving Cyber Threats
content:
#### Targeted Geolocations
- Mongolia  
- Taiwan  
- Ethiopia  
- Japan  
- Brazil  
- United States  
- India  
- Australia  
- Southeast Asia



## Snapshot
Between July 2023 and December 2024, the Chinese state-sponsored threat group RedDelta carried out cyber espionage campaigns targeting entities in Southeast Asia, Mongolia, and Taiwan to distribute [PlugX](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/028c3995955a4a710d67d5d4e9a5f067355bbc7ad58e5c5d1c1931e708e41b38).

## Description
Key victims included the Mongolian Ministry of Defense, the Communist Party of Vietnam, and organizations in Taiwan, Myanmar, and Cambodia. Lure documents centered on politically charged themes, such as Taiwan’s 2024 presidential candidate Terry Gou and the Vietnamese National Holiday. RedDelta’s operations extended globally, including targets in the United States, Ethiopia, Japan, Brazil, India, and Australia.
 
The group has evolved its tactics over time. In late 2023, it began delivering malware using Windows Shortcut (LNK) files through spearphishing emails. By 2024, this method shifted to using [Microsoft Management Console (MSC)](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/5b8609f0) files and remotely hosted HTML files on Microsoft Azure. RedDelta relied on the Cloudflare content distribution network to obfuscate command-and-control (C2) traffic and evade detection, a tactic also seen in other state-sponsored campaigns.
 
RedDelta’s activities align with China’s strategic goals, particularly focusing on governments and diplomatic organizations in Southeast Asia and Mongolia. Its attacks reflect a return to its historical focus on Asia after targeting European entities in 2022. According to Insikt Group, RedDelta has a long history of adapting its techniques in response to geopolitical events, including prior operations against Catholic organizations during China-Vatican talks and ongoing campaigns targeting Mongolian NGOs, Buddhist activists, and academic professionals.
 
RedDelta’s use of advanced techniques, such as DLL hijacking and proxying C2 traffic through Cloudflare, underscores the group’s sophistication and its commitment to furthering China’s strategic objectives in the region.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
Insikt Group's reporting on Red Delta closely overlaps with activity attributed to [Twill Typhoon](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/01aef6bb1a4cd12178aca7fceb848002164b83bf375fa33699ed4c5523b4fd3c) by Microsoft. Twill Typhoon is is a nation-state activity group based out of China. Twill Typhoon focuses on espionage and is known to primarily target government-related organizations located around the world, such as in Europe, East Asia, and Africa. Twill Typhoon is known to use either malware on removable media or spearphishing emails with malicious links or attachments as an initial access vector to deliver a remote access trojan (RAT), typically [PlugX](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/028c3995955a4a710d67d5d4e9a5f067355bbc7ad58e5c5d1c1931e708e41b38) or UDiskShell.

In May 2024, Microsoft observed spear-phishing activity targeting government agencies and services and non-governmental organizations in different regions, including Central Asia, Eastern Europe, North America, Northern Europe, South Asia, Southeast Asia, and Western Europe. The spear phishing emails included content pertaining to current events in East Asia and a hyperlink that downloaded a Microsoft Management Console (MSC) file. The MSC file installed the remote access trojan (RAT) PlugX. Read [Twill Typhoon spear phishing campaign abuses MSC files](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/9c46f395) to learn more about the group's recent activity.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. 
 
- Windows 11 (Consumer) users may enable the [Smart App Control feature](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/apps/develop/smart-app-control/overview) to prevent opening potentially dangerous file types from untrusted origins. Smart App Control in Windows 11 will block opening any *.msc* file from an Internet source.
- Invest in advanced anti-phishing solutions that monitor and scan incoming emails and visited websites. For example, organizations can leverage web browsers that automatically [identify and block malicious websites](https://learn.microsoft.com/deployedge/microsoft-edge-security-smartscreen?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc), including those used in this phishing campaign, and solutions that [detect and block malicious emails, links, and files](https://www.microsoft.com/security/business/siem-and-xdr/microsoft-defender-office-365?ocid=magicti_ta_abbreviatedmktgpage).
- Refer to Microsoft’s human-operated ransomware overview for general hardening recommendations against ransomware attacks.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a huge majority of new and unknown variants.
- Turn on the following [attack surface reduction rule](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/overview-attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc)to block or audit activity associated with this threat:
    - [Use advanced protection against ransomware](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#use-advanced-protection-against-ransomware)
    - [Block process creations originating from PsExec and WMI commands](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-process-creations-originating-from-psexec-and-wmi-commandshttps://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-process-creations-originating-from-psexec-and-wmi-commands). Some organizations may experience compatibility issues with this rule on certain server systems but should deploy it to other systems to prevent lateral movement originating from PsExec and WMI.
    - [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?view=o365-worldwide#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion)

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects threat components as the following malware:
 
- Backdoor:Win32/Doplugs
- [Trojan:Win32/WinLNK](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:Win32/WinLNK!MSR)
- [Trojan:Win32/Korplug](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:Win32/Korplug!MSR)
- [Trojan:Win32/Malgent](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:Win32/Malgent!MSR)

title: Russian ISP confirms Ukrainian hackers "destroyed" its network
content:
#### Targeted Geolocations
- Russia



#### Targeted Industries
- Information Technology



## Snapshot
Ukrainian hacktivists from the Ukrainian Cyber Alliance group claimed responsibility for a cyberattack on Russian internet service provider Nodex, which resulted in the exfiltration of sensitive documents and the wiping of the ISP's systems.

## Description
The attack left Nodex's network destroyed, as confirmed by the company in a VKontakte post, where they informed customers of the destruction of their network infrastructure, presumably by an attack originating from Ukraine. The ISP's efforts to restore services from backups were underway, with no specific timeline provided for full recovery. NetBlocks observed a collapse in connectivity on Nodex's network following the cyberattack. 

The Ukrainian Cyber Alliance has a history of targeting Russian organizations since 2016 and has claimed numerous breaches against Russian entities, including the Russian Ministry of Defense and other government and military targets. In a recent operation in October 2023, the group also targeted and wiped the servers of the Trigona ransomware gang.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
Pro-Ukraine hacktivism has become a significant component of the ongoing cyber conflict between Russia and Ukraine, with groups like the Ukrainian Cyber Alliance (UCA) leading numerous cyberattacks against Russian entities. Formed in 2016 as a coalition of various hacker groups, UCA has consistently targeted Russian organizations, including governmental, military, and financial institutions, as part of its cyber warfare strategy. These cyber activities have intensified alongside the physical conflict, reflecting the evolving nature of warfare in the digital age.
 
The recent attack on Nodex by UCA exemplifies the scale and impact of pro-Ukraine hacktivism. This incident is part of a broader pattern where Ukrainian hacktivists retaliate against Russian cyber aggressions, such as the December 2023 [breach of Ukraine's top telco, Kyivstar](https://therecord.media/russians-infiltrated-kyivstar-months-before), by Russian hackers. In response, Ukrainian groups have launched significant cyber offensives, including the January 2024 [attack on M9com](https://therecord.media/ukraine-blackjack-hackers-sbu-claim-breach-russia-M9com), which disrupted internet services in Moscow. Additionally, pro-Ukrainian hacktivists have claimed responsibility for a [cyberattack on Russian security company Doctor Web](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/b7f1454e) (Dr.Web) that occurred in September 2024. The breach led Dr.Web to disconnect its internal servers and halt virus database updates during their investigation. These actions highlight the escalating cyber warfare and the strategic use of digital attacks to weaken the opponent's critical infrastructure, communications, and services.

## References
[Russian ISP confirms Ukrainian hackers "destroyed" its network](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-isp-confirms-ukrainian-hackers-destroyed-its-network/) Bleeping Computer (accessed 2025-01-09)

title: Black Basta’s Tactical Evolution: Deploying Zbot, DarkGate, and Bespoke Malware
content:
## Snapshot
Researchers at SocRadar report Black Basta, a notorious ransomware group, employs advanced malware like Zbot for credential theft and DarkGate for data exfiltration and ransomware deployment, leveraging sophisticated evasion and infiltration tactics.

## Description
Black Basta, a ransomware group known for its sophisticated tactics, has been observed deploying custom malware like Zbot and DarkGate in its campaigns. These operations often start with phishing emails and social engineering tactics to establish initial access. Zbot, a variant of the infamous Zeus malware, is designed primarily for credential theft and enabling lateral movement within networks. It captures sensitive information such as login credentials, paving the way for deeper infiltration.
 
DarkGate, another bespoke tool in Black Basta’s arsenal, serves as a multi-functional malware with capabilities for data exfiltration, ransomware deployment, and system manipulation. It employs advanced evasion techniques like process hollowing and encrypted payloads to avoid detection by security systems. These tools, combined with remote access solutions such as AnyDesk and TeamViewer, allow Black Basta to execute highly coordinated and effective attacks, targeting organizations across critical sectors.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
Black Basta, a ransomware group that emerged in early 2022, has evolved its attack methods to include sophisticated social engineering tactics and the deployment of advanced malware such as Zbot and DarkGate.  Their campaigns often begin with email bombing, where targeted users are inundated with numerous emails to overwhelm their inboxes. Subsequently, the attackers impersonate IT staff or support personnel on platforms like Microsoft Teams to gain the trust of victims. Once trust is established, they persuade users to install legitimate remote access tools like AnyDesk or TeamViewer, which are then used to deploy malware payloads.This strategic combination of social engineering and malware deployment has enabled Black Basta to effectively infiltrate and compromise targeted networks across various sectors.

Read more about Microsoft's coverage of [Black Basta here.](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/0146164ed5ffa131074fa7e985f779597d2522865baa088f25cd80c3bed8d726)

## Recommendations
Apply these mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations.

- Educate users about [preventing malware infections](https://www.microsoft.com/security/business/security-101/what-is-malware?ocid=magicti_ta_abbreviatedmktgpage"%20\t%20"_blank), such as ignoring or deleting unsolicited and unexpected emails or attachments sent through instant messaging applications or social networks as well as suspicious phone calls.
- Invest in advanced anti-phishing solutions that monitor incoming emails and visited websites. [Microsoft Defender for Office 365](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender/microsoft-365-security-center-mdo?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) brings together incident and alert management across email, devices, and identities, centralizing investigations for email-based threats.
- Apply Microsoft’s [security best practices for Microsoft Teams](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/MicrosoftTeams/teams-security-best-practices-for-safer-messaging) to safeguard Teams users.
- Consider [blocking or uninstalling](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/client-management/client-tools/quick-assist#disable-quick-assist-within-your-organization) Quick Assist and other remote monitoring and management tools if these tools are not in use in your environment. Apply mitigations listed in [Microsoft’s technique profile on abuse of remote monitoring and management tools](https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/44b8f927-5ab5-46bb-bb79-7ca2d4e30156/overview).
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a huge majority of new and unknown variants.
- Turn on [tamper protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) features to prevent attackers from stopping security services.
- Run [EDR in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus doesn’t detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach.
- Enable [network protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-network-protection?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to prevent applications or users from accessing malicious domains and other malicious content on the internet.
- Enable [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in full automated mode to allow Microsoft Defender for Endpoint to take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.
- Use [device discovery](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/device-discovery?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to increase your visibility into your network by finding unmanaged devices on your network and onboarding them to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Refer to [Microsoft’s human-operated ransomware overview](https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/05658b6c-dc62-496d-ad3c-c6a795a33c27/analystreport) for general hardening recommendations against ransomware attacks.

Microsoft Defender XDR customers can turn on [attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to prevent common attack techniques used in ransomware attacks. Attack surface reduction rules are sweeping settings that are effective at stopping entire classes of threats:

- Ransom and lateral movement stage:
    - [Block process creations originating from PsExec and WMI commands](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-process-creations-originating-from-psexec-and-wmi-commands)
    - [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion)
    - [Use advanced protection against ransomware](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#use-advanced-protection-against-ransomware)
    - [Block credential stealing from the Windows local security authority subsystem (lsass.exe)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-credential-stealing-from-the-windows-local-security-authority-subsystem)
- Common techniques:
    - [Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-execution-of-potentially-obfuscated-scripts)
    - [Block JavaScript or VBScript from launching downloaded executable content](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-javascript-or-vbscript-from-launching-downloaded-executable-content)
- Common entry vectors:
    - [Block all Office applications from creating child processes](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-all-office-applications-from-creating-child-processes)
    - [Block Office communication application from creating child processes](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-office-communication-application-from-creating-child-processes)
    - [Block Office applications from creating executable content](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-office-applications-from-injecting-code-into-other-processes)
    - [Block Office applications from injecting code into other processes](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-office-applications-from-injecting-code-into-other-processes)

**Assess rule impact before deployment**

You can assess how an attack surface reduction rule might impact your network by opening the [security recommendation](https://security.microsoft.com/security-recommendations?ocid=magicti_ta_tvmsecreco) for that rule in threat and vulnerability management. In the recommendation details pane, check the user impact to determine what percentage of your devices can accept a new policy enabling the rule in blocking mode without adverse impact to user productivity.

![Graphical user interface, text, applicationDescription automatically generated](https://cdn-riq-ti.azureedge.net/2981805b-00f5-4cb1-a694-a49c40d865b6)

*Security recommendations in threat and vulnerability management*

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects Qakbot downloaders, implants, and behavior as the following malware: 
 
- [TrojanDownloader:O97M/Qakbot](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=TrojanDownloader:O97M/Qakbot)
- [Trojan:Win32/QBot](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:Win32/Qbot)

**Shared malware and generic detections**

Microsoft Defender Antivirus incorporates next-generation antivirus capabilities, including machine learning and behavioral detection. title: Recruitment Phishing Scam Imitates CrowdStrike Hiring Process
content:
## Snapshot
On January 7, 2025, CrowdStrike identified a phishing campaign that used its recruitment branding to deliver malware.

## Description
The attackers use a phishing email that impersonates CrowdStrike's recruitment process to lure victims to a malicious website, cscrm-hiring\[.\]com, which offers a fake "employee CRM application" for download. This application is a Windows executable written in Rust that serves as a downloader for the XMRig cryptominer. The executable performs environment checks to evade detection, such as detecting debuggers, counting active processes and CPU cores, and scanning for malware analysis tools. If the system passes these checks, it displays a fake error message and proceeds to download XMRig using configuration information from a text file. The malware establishes persistence by creating a batch script in the Start Menu Startup directory and a new Windows registry logon autostart key. It operates in the background, using minimal CPU resources to avoid detection.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
Threat actors, including North Korean groups, actively exploit fake job lures to compromise victims, as seen in the [Contagious Interview campaign](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/b739abca) targeting tech job seekers with cross-platform malware. [In September 2024](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/4cb94d70), Trend Micro identified more\_egg attacks where threat actors posed as job applicants on LinkedIn. They linked this activity to FIN6, tracked by Microsoft tracks as Storm-0538, a group that uses job application platforms to deploy payloads like Terrapreter and Cobalt Strike. [By October 2024](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/611c1b09), Proofpoint observed a surge in cryptocurrency fraud scams enticing victims with fake job offers. As [AI continues to enhance](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/9e3529fc) the sophistication of these campaigns, organizations might consider prioritizing [attack simulation training](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/attack-simulation-training-get-started?ocid=magicti%3Cem%3Eta%3C/em%3Elearndoc) and encouraging employees to separate personal accounts from work-related tasks.

## Recommendations
Apply these mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat.
 
- Build organizational resilience against email threats by educating users about identifying social engineering attacks and preventing malware infection. Use [Attack simulation training](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/attack-simulation-training-get-started?ocid=magicti%3Cem%3Eta%3C/em%3Elearndoc) in Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to run attack scenarios, increase user awareness, and empower employees to recognize and report these attacks.
- [Help prevent social engineering attacks](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/security-insider/emerging-threats/feeding-from-the-trust-economy-social-engineering-fraud?ocid=magicti_ta_blog) by not blending personal accounts with work emails or work-related tasks. Ask yourself if the sender is who they say they are before clicking anything. Be wary of senders as well as offers that are too good to be true. Do a search to determine if the offer is legitimate or a trap.
- Invest in advanced anti-phishing solutions that monitor incoming emails and visited websites. [Microsoft Defender for Office](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender/microsoft-365-security-center-mdo?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) 365 brings together incident and alert management across email, devices, and identities, centralizing investigations for threats in email. Organizations can also leverage web browsers that automatically [identify and block malicious websites](https://learn.microsoft.com/deployedge/microsoft-edge-security-smartscreen?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc). To build resilience against phishing attacks in general, organizations can use [anti-phishing policies](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/set-up-anti-phishing-policies?view=o365-worldwide) to enable mailbox intelligence settings, as well as configure impersonation protection settings for specific messages and sender domains. Enabling [SafeLinks](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-links?view=o365-worldwide) ensures real-time protection by scanning at time of delivery and at time of click.
- Continuously monitor for suspicious or anomalous activities, and search for sign-in attempts with suspicious characteristics (for example location, internet service provider \[ISP\], user agent, and use of anonymizer services). title: PHP Servers Vulnerability Exploited To Inject PacketCrypt Cryptocurrency Miner
content:
## Snapshot
A server-side vulnerability in PHP servers is being exploited to inject a PacketCrypt cryptocurrency miner. .

## Description
Attackers are executing multiple commands through PHP's system() function to download a malicious executable named "dr0p.exe" from a remote server. This executable acts as a downloader, fetching "pkt1.exe" from a US-based server hosting the EvilBit Block Explorer. The malware then launches "packetcrypt.exe," which is a cryptocurrency miner, and supplies a PKT Classic wallet address as an argument. The PKT Classic wallet associated with the attack has accumulated approximately 5 PKTC, valued at roughly 0.0021785 USDT. The vulnerability exploited may be CVE-2024-4577 or due to misconfigurations allowing public access to php-cgi.exe. The malicious IP address 23.27.51.244 is identified as distributing the malware, which is linked to the PKTC wallet address pkt1qxysc58g4cwwautg6dr4p7q7sd6tn2ldgukth5a.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
CVE-2024-4577 is a critical remote code execution vulnerability affecting PHP running on Windows. It enables unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code via the PHP-CGI process, exploiting a flaw in how the system handles specific Unicode characters in certain locales. This vulnerability bypasses mitigations for [CVE-2012-1823](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/cves/CVE-2012-1823/) by leveraging the Windows operating system's ["best-fit" Unicode mapping](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/openspecs/windows_protocols/ms-ucoderef/d1980631-6401-428e-a49d-d71394be7da8), which can convert less-common characters into metacharacters recognized as commands by PHP. Exploitation is most likely in locales like Japanese, Simplified Chinese, or Traditional Chinese, though other locales could also be vulnerable.
 
PHP addressed this issue on June 6, 2024, in versions 8.3.8, 8.2.20, and 8.1.29. Versions prior to these remain exposed. DEVCORE detailed the flaw the same day, while[watchTowr released a proof-of-concept (POC) exploit](https://labs.watchtowr.com/no-way-php-strikes-again-cve-2024-4577/) on June 7, demonstrating how crafted HTTP requests could leverage the vulnerability. [Subsequent scanning and exploit activity](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/8635c515), including those linked to the [TellYouThePass ransomware](https://www.imperva.com/blog/update-cve-2024-4577-quickly-weaponized-to-distribute-tellyouthepass-ransomware/), began almost immediately. [Symantec](https:/.security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/82e132cc) reported the exploitation of CVE-2024-4577 as the initial access vector for a campaign that leveraged Backdoor.Msupedge in an attack against a university in Taiwan. 
 
Notably, financially motivated and nation-state actors were observed exploiting this flaw starting June 7. Microsoft identified exploitation techniques involving `mshta.exe` to execute malicious HTA files, further implicating this vulnerability in broader campaigns. When the goal of the threat actors is to use the victim's device for crypto-mining, this is called cryptojacking and can result in financial  loss to the victim due to the compute fees.

## Recommendations
This sources recommends "regular security patching and auditing of web servers to mitigate vulnerabilities and prevent performance issues caused by threats like crypto miners."

[PHP released patches for this issue on June 6, 2024](https://www.php.net/ChangeLog-8.php). Customers who have not patched to do so as soon as possible for their organization’s security.

Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations.
 
- Enable [Network Protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/network-protection).
- Microsoft Defender customers can turn on [attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction) to prevent common attack techniques:  

    - [Block](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference) executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion.
- Run endpoint detection and response (EDR) in block [mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode).

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects threat components as the following malware: 
 
- [Exploit:PHP/CVE-2024-4577](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Exploit:PHP/CVE-2024-4577!MSR&threatId=-2147054383)
- [Exploit:Python/CVE-2024-4577](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Exploit:Python/CVE-2024-4577!MSR&threatId=-2147054386)

### Microsoft Defender for Endpoint
The following alerts might also indicate threat activity associated with this threat. These alerts, however, can be triggered by unrelated threat activity and are not monitored in the status cards provided with this report. 
 
- Possible PHP-CGI vulnerability exploitation
- Suspicious mshta process launched
- Suspicious behavior by an HTML application was observed
- File downloaded from an untrusted source

### Microsoft Defender XDR
Look for command line activity started by the PHP server process that includes the distinctive arguments in Figure 1. This might indicate exploitation of the PHP-CGI process. [Run query in the Microsoft 365 Defender](https://security.microsoft.com/v2/advanced-hunting?query=H4sIAO23cWYAA61VTU_CQBCds4n_oXKhJKLikcSDAU1IDCHGewNtwSrQhhYR44_3zdvV8lWpjdm0LLPz8ebN7LQrobxJJD5-B7KQmLsU6w7yUOaSYX8qJ_IpjqzkGbIFHkd6OItwGsmQ77lMdjzcQzrFvg-NGW1usBypSwI_iTShOYHOBc7e8dRxdok1hK8A-2J7H_-DDbtq-DrYz7BMvAfqqOUzJKl4eE-xHHERwexjRPBkCS9T_Kq-j90S1iGQtaB3TnxDyDJoe8hS0SRkMsD_sc3pxnLQZsbqKaFNXRo_2bzAg544lLh8O3Z1N-rWx5MBWYxYr3t1-7bY5ecWtspLDN0nWRNjzrCyN8LZkrg71FJ2chu195lbhndgq1AU7YG8K4s9VCGPd2bjaWUiIB_Sm_HVwEnM_Dez7SHWoXoH1lbxabd4kETge8z6pcQeMxtTpSerl8JC-yspkLaIY2Q5Dsmt9kQTJ1fYXWA53OeVS8Gb6SzN6oP4dD8Bqhlr6paOr9JH8qz1zZj_IVmDUu06tV3YjneJ4pV8pMzB3btXandN_OV9lLlJVfxu90kVD3-fS7tRqk6OlPfnv1D-H6fHYw3YnWZqHGMnny_agWN7_-bWlwfcA-gYJvaxGKw-kbhS27rZxd-fNnzVful6g68Muj7wVUNXPGWL0bW28OkUWf8yzfRrltkvxbFMTAYGt8cpbaayW7I-5bnKp1rC-rzYr0ATLK3wrEv3RPmYX9_gnpSWCAAA&timeRangeId=month)

title: Formbook Phishing Campaign with old Payloads
content:
## Snapshot
Seqrite Labs recently uncovered a phishing campaign distributing Formbook, an information stealer, via email attachments.

## Description
Formbook, active since 2016, has evolved significantly with enhanced stealth features and evasion techniques. Sold as Malware-as-a-Service (MaaS) on hacking forums, this malware employs multiple layers of obfuscation and memory-only payload loading to avoid detection. A notable feature is its use of steganography, embedding malicious files within images to decrypt and execute payloads in memory.
 
This attack campaign begins with spear-phishing emails containing ZIP file attachments. Upon extraction, a single executable (e.g., PurchaseOrder.exe) launches a multi-stage infection process. The initial stage decrypts and loads the second stage (Arthur.dll) into memory, while Arthur.dll decrypts and executes the third stage (Montero.dll). Each stage incorporates delays and obfuscation to evade sandbox analysis and security tools.
 
Montero.dll introduces advanced tactics, including configuration decryption, mutex creation to prevent multiple instances, and exploitation of system features like exclusion paths and scheduled tasks for persistence. It also supports additional payload downloads and process hollowing, targeting processes like MSBuild.exe, vbc.exe, or RegSvcs.exe.
 
The final payload, a MASM-compiled binary, is heavily obfuscated and employs sophisticated techniques for execution, such as memory-only decryption and process hollowing. By leveraging these multi-layered strategies, threat actors behind this campaign ensure high levels of stealth, persistence, and adaptability in their attacks.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations.

- Check your Office 365 email filtering settings to ensure you block spoofed emails, spam, and emails with malware. Use [Microsoft Defender for Office 365](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/defender-for-office-365?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for enhanced phishing protection and coverage against new threats and polymorphic variants. Configure Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to [recheck links on click](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-links-about?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) and [delete sent mail](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/zero-hour-auto-purge?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in response to newly acquired threat intelligence. Turn on [safe attachments policies](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-attachments-policies-configure?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to check attachments to inbound email.
- Encourage users to use Microsoft Edge and other web browsers that support [SmartScreen](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/web-protection-overview?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc), which identifies and blocks malicious websites, including phishing sites, scam sites, and sites that host malware.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus, or the equivalent for your antivirus product, to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown variants.
- Enforce MFA on all accounts, remove users excluded from MFA, and strictly [require MFA](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/identity-protection/howto-identity-protection-configure-mfa-policy?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) from all devices, in all locations, at all times.
- Enable passwordless authentication methods (for example, Windows Hello, FIDO keys, or Microsoft Authenticator) for accounts that support passwordless. For accounts that still require passwords, use authenticator apps like Microsoft Authenticator for MFA. [Refer to this article](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/concept-authentication-methods?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for the different authentication methods and features.
- For MFA that uses authenticator apps, ensure that the app requires a code to be typed in where possible, as many intrusions where MFA was enabled still succeeded due to users clicking “Yes” on the prompt on their phones even when they were not at their [devices](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/how-to-mfa-number-match?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc). Refer to [this article](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/concept-authentication-methods?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for an example.
- Remind employees that enterprise or workplace credentials should not be stored in browsers or password vaults secured with personal credentials. Organizations can turn off password syncing in browser on managed devices using [Group Policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/deployedge/microsoft-edge-enterprise-sync#sync-group-policies?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc).

Microsoft Defender customers can [turn on attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to prevent common attack techniques used in infostealer infections. Attack surface reduction rules are sweeping settings that stop entire classes of threats including, infostealers, credential theft, and ransomware. The following bullet points offer more guidance on specific mitigation advice:

- [Turn on PUA protection in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/detect-block-potentially-unwanted-apps-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc)
- [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion)
- [Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-execution-of-potentially-obfuscated-scripts)

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects threat components as the following malware:
 
- [Trojan:Win32/Formbook](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:Win32/Formbook)
- [Trojan:MSIL/FormBook](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:MSIL/FormBook)

### Microsoft Defender for Endpoint
Alerts with the following titles in the security center can indicate threat activity on your network:
 
- Information stealing malware activity

title: ASEC December 2024 Threat Trend Report on APT Attacks (South Korea)
content:
#### Targeted Geolocations
- Korea



## Snapshot
In December 2024, AhnLab monitored APT spear-phishing attacks that targeted entities in Korea, distributing LNK files designed to deceive recipients into believing they were from trusted sources.

## Description
One type of attack involved LNK files that executed a malicious PowerShell command to extract and decompress a CAB file containing multiple scripts on the victim's PC. These scripts can exfiltrate information and download additional malware. File names associated with this attack included "Bithumb Korea\_Contract.docx.lnk" and "Report on Trading Details of Virtual Assets.hwp.lnk" among other names, with decoy documents used to disguise the malicious activity.
 
Another type of attack executed RAT malware through LNK files, which contained malicious PowerShell commands. In addition to leveraging the Dropbox API and Google Drive to download malware, the LNK files also created additional script files and deployed an obfuscated RAT in the TEMP or PUBLIC folders during execution. The RATs, such as XenoRAT and [RoKRAT](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/8fcae4db5ec22dcdd4b6a41896def195417e2a706e3a82a6b2a3d50220ea89f8), were capable of keylogging and taking screenshots. File names in this type of attack included "January Issue-Open Page.lnk" and "241205 Full Text from Japan to Mongolia.lnk," with various decoy files used to mislead the victims.

## Recommendations
Implement multifactor authentication (MFA) to mitigate credential theft from phishing attacks. MFA can be complemented with the following solutions and best practices to protect organizations: 

- Activate conditional access policies. [Conditional access](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/conditional-access/overview?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) policies are evaluated and enforced every time an attacker attempts to use a stolen session cookie. Conditional access policies evaluate sign-in requests using additional identity-driven signals like user or group membership, IP location information, and device status, among others, and are enforced for suspicious sign-ins. Organizations can protect themselves from attacks that leverage stolen credentials by enabling policies such as compliant devices or trusted IP address requirements.
- Configure [continuous access evaluation](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/conditional-access/concept-continuous-access-evaluation?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in your tenant.
- Invest in advanced anti-phishing solutions that monitor incoming emails and visited websites. [Microsoft Defender for Office](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender/microsoft-365-security-center-mdo?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) 365 brings together incident and alert management across email, devices, and identities, centralizing investigations for threats in email. Organizations can also leverage web browsers that automatically [identify and block malicious websites](https://learn.microsoft.com/deployedge/microsoft-edge-security-smartscreen?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc). To build resilience against phishing attacks in general, organizations can use [anti-phishing policies](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/set-up-anti-phishing-policies?view=o365-worldwide) to enable mailbox intelligence settings, as well as configure impersonation protection settings for specific messages and sender domains. Enabling [SafeLinks](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-links?view=o365-worldwide) ensures real-time protection by scanning at time of delivery and at time of click.
- Continuously monitor for suspicious or anomalous activities, and search for sign-in attempts with suspicious characteristics (for example location, internet service provider \[ISP\], user agent, and use of anonymizer services). Activity can be identified and investigated with [Microsoft Defender for Identity](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender/microsoft-365-security-center-mdi?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc), which contributes identity-focused information into incidents and alerts, providing key context and correlating alerts from other products within Microsoft 365 Defender. This ensures all alerts are available in one place, and the scope of a breach can be determined faster than before.

Defenders can also complement MFA with the following solutions and best practices to further protect their organizations from such attacks. 

- Use [security defaults](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/fundamentals/concept-fundamentals-security-defaults?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) as a baseline set of policies to improve identity security posture.
- Block phishing websites and other malicious URLs and domains in the browser through [Microsoft Defender SmartScreen](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/operating-system-security/virus-and-threat-protection/microsoft-defender-smartscreen/), as well as the detection of suspicious and malicious behavior on endpoints.

## Detections/Hunting Queries

- [Trojan:MSIL/XenoRat](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:MSIL/XenoRat.SG!MTB&ThreatID=2147900905)
