title: Dark Web Profile: Kairos Extortion Group
content:
#### Targeted Geolocations
- United States  
- Australia  
- Taiwan  
- Canada  
- Germany



#### Targeted Industries
- Healthcare & Public Health  
- Critical Manufacturing  
- Financial Services



## Snapshot
Researchers from SOCRadar released a report detailing Kairos, a new extortion group that began operations in late 2024.

## Description
Notably, the group does not use ransomware. Instead, Kairos focuses on data theft and extortion without encrypting files. The group targets sensitive information within organizations, demanding payment to prevent public exposure. Since its inception, Kairo has been attributed to 14 attacks.
 
Kairos demonstrates a selective and calculated approach, focusing on sectors such as healthcare, business services, manufacturing, education, and technology. The group has focused its efforts in the United States, but also impacted organizations in Australia, the United Kingdom, Canada, and Taiwan. Kairos' ability to infiltrate critical infrastructure and businesses across diverse sectors underscores a broad and strategic operational scope.
 
According to SOCRadar, the group relies heavily on Initial Access Brokers (IABs) to purchase entry into corporate networks, bypassing the complexities of initial compromise. Once inside, the group exfiltrates sensitive data, including personal, financial, and medical information, and uses threats of exposure on data-leak sites to pressure victims into paying ransoms.
 
Kairos’s methods are streamlined and precise, focusing on high-value targets and leveraging data-leak platforms to maximize reputational and financial damage threats. As the group refines its tactics, Kairos is expected to broaden its reach and evolve its extortion strategies, posing an ongoing threat to organizations globally.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat.
 
- Harden internet-facing assets and identify and secure perimeter systems that attackers might use to access the network. Public scanning interfaces, such as [Microsoft Defender External Attack Surface Management](https://www.microsoft.com/security/business/cloud-security/microsoft-defender-external-attack-surface-management), can be used to augment data. The Attack Surface Summary dashboard surfaces assets such as Exchange servers which require security updates as well as provides recommended remediation steps.
- As more organizations move to the cloud, it is important to continue to protect Active Directory resources through credential hardening during this transition. Threat actors are motivated by easy access and continue to look for easy paths to acquire domain administrator privileges. Microsoft provides some steps organizations can take to build credential hygiene in our [on-premises credential theft threat overview](https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/9382203e-5155-4b5e-af74-21562b1004d5/analystreport).
- Enforce multifactor authentication (MFA) on all accounts, remove users excluded from MFA, and strictly require MFA from all devices, in all locations, at all times.
- Enable passwordless authentication methods (for example, Windows Hello, FIDO keys, or Microsoft Authenticator) for accounts that support passwordless. For accounts that still require passwords, use authenticator apps like Microsoft Authenticator for MFA. Refer to this article for the different authentication methods and features.
- [Protect user identities and credentials](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-for-identity/what-is?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) using Microsoft Defender for Identity, a cloud-based security solution that leverages on-premises Active Directory signals to monitor and analyze user behavior to identify suspicious user activities, configuration issues, and active attacks.
- Windows administrators can perform the following to further harden the LSASS process on their devices:   

    - [Configure Protected Process Light (PPL) for the LSASS process](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows-server/security/credentials-protection-and-management/configuring-additional-lsa-protection). For new, enterprise-joined Windows 11 installations (22H2 update), this is already enabled by default.
    - [Use Windows Defender Credential Guard](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/identity-protection/credential-guard/credential-guard-manage#enable-windows-defender-credential-guard). This is also now included by default for organizations using the Enterprise edition of Windows 11.
    - Use [restricted admin mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/archive/blogs/kfalde/restricted-admin-mode-for-rdp-in-windows-7-2008-r2) for RDP.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown variants.
- Turn on [tamper protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection) features to prevent attackers from stopping security services.
- Run [endpoint detection and response (EDR) in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode) so that Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus does not detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts detected post-breach.
- Enable [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations) in full automated mode to allow Defender for Endpoint to take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.

Microsoft Defender customers can turn on [attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction) to prevent common attack techniques:

- [Block credential stealing from the Windows local security authority subsystem (lsass.exe)](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?view=o365-worldwide#block-credential-stealing-from-the-windows-local-security-authority-subsystem)
- [Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-execution-of-potentially-obfuscated-scripts)
- [Block process creations originating from PSExec and WMI commands](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-process-creations-originating-from-psexec-and-wmi-commands)
- [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion)

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender for Endpoint
The following alerts might indicate activity associated with this threat. These alerts, however, can be triggered by unrelated threat activity.
 
- Renaming of legitimate tools for possible data exfiltration
- Suspicious process transferring data to external network
- Possible exfiltration of archived data

title: Cerberus Unchained: The Multi-Stage Trojan Banking Campaign Targeting Android Devices
content:
## Snapshot
Researchers have identified a resurgence of the Cerberus Android banking trojan in a sophisticated multi-stage attack campaign targeting Android users' banking credentials, SMS data, and contact lists. Known for its deceptive overlay attacks, Cerberus disguises itself as legitimate apps to trick users into entering sensitive information on fake, but convincing, screens.

## Description
Originally discovered in 2019, Cerberus has evolved with advanced features like keylogging, remote access, and the use of Domain Generation Algorithms (DGAs) for dynamic, encrypted Command and Control (C2) communications. This adaptability is evident in its use of droppers, native libraries, and encrypted payloads, which help it bypass Android security measures.
 
Distributed via Google Play and third-party app stores, the malware poses a persistent threat to various sectors. Once installed, it conducts reconnaissance by identifying installed apps, gathering system information, and capturing screen and audio data. Cerberus remains a notable example of malware leveraging multi-stage techniques to infiltrate and exploit devices while evading detection.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
Banking trojans have made OSINT headlines in recent months as threat actors develop new malware and continue to enhance existing malware to conduct malicious activity. Historically, these trojans were primarily viewed as a consumer problem, focusing on harvesting banking credentials and personal financial data. However, this threat has evolved, and enterprises are now increasingly being targeted by cybercriminals. With bring your own device (BYOD) policies leading to more personal devices being connected to corporate networks, financially motivated attackers are expanding their focus to include enterprise systems, seeking to compromise valuable business data for financial gain.

To read more about banking trojan-related cyberattacks and for recommendations about defending against such threats, read [Recent OSINT trends in banking trojans](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/3c32651f).

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat.
 
###   
Strengthen Microsoft Defender for Endpoint configuration
 
- Ensure that [tamper protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#how-do-i-configure-or-manage-tamper-protection) is enabled in Microsoft Dender for Endpoint.
- Enable [network protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/enable-network-protection?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Run [Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus does not detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach.
- Configure [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in full automated mode to let Microsoft Defender for Endpoint take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.

### Strengthen Microsoft Defender Antivirus configuration

- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/enable-cloud-protection-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus, or the equivalent for your antivirus product, to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown variants.
- Enable Microsoft Defender Antivirus scanning of [downloaded files and attachments](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-advanced-scan-types-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc).
- Enable Microsoft Defender Antivirus [real-time protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/configure-real-time-protection-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc).

### Strengthen Microsoft Office 365 configuration

- Turn on [Safe Links](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-office-365/safe-links-about?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) and [Safe Attachments](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-office-365/safe-attachments-about?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for Office 365.
- Enable [Zero-hour auto purge (ZAP)](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-office-365/zero-hour-auto-purge?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Office 365 to quarantine sent mail in response to newly acquired threat intelligence and retroactively neutralize malicious phishing, spam, or malware messages that have already been delivered to mailboxes.

### Strengthen Microsoft Defender for Office 365 configuration

- Invest in [advanced anti-phishing](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-office-365/anti-phishing-protection-about?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#additional-anti-phishing-protection-in-microsoft-defender-for-office-365) solutions that monitor incoming emails and visited websites. [Microsoft Defender for Office 365](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender/microsoft-365-security-center-mdo?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) merges incident and alert management across email, devices, and identities, centralizing investigations for email-based threats. Organizations can also leverage web browsers that automatically [identify and block](https://learn.microsoft.com/deployedge/microsoft-edge-security-smartscreen?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) malicious websites, including those used in this phishing campaign.
- Configure Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to [recheck links on click](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-office-365/safe-links-about?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc). Safe Links provides URL scanning and rewriting of inbound email messages in mail flow, and time-of-click verification of URLs and links in email messages, other Microsoft 365 applications such as Teams, and other locations such as SharePoint Online. Safe Links scanning occurs in addition to the regular [anti-spam](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-office-365/anti-spam-protection-about?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) and [antimalware](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-office-365/anti-malware-protection-about?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) protection in inbound email messages in [Microsoft Exchange Online Protection (EOP)](https://products.office.com/exchange/exchange-email-security-spam-protection?ocid=magicti_ta_abbreviatedmktgpage). Safe Links scanning can help protect an organization from malicious links used in phishing and other attacks.
- Use the [Attack Simulator](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-office-365/attack-simulation-training-get-started?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to run realistic, yet safe, simulated phishing and password attack campaigns. Run spear-phishing (credential harvest) simulations to train users against clicking URLs in unsolicited messages and disclosing credentials.

### Strengthen operating environment configuration

- Use a vulnerability management system, such as [Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-vulnerability-management/defender-vulnerability-management?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc), to manage vulnerabilities, weaknesses, and remediation efforts across your environment's operating systems, software inventories, and [network devices](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/network-devices?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc).
- Require [multifactor authentication (MFA)](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/admin/security-and-compliance/set-up-multi-factor-authentication?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc). While AiTM phishing attempts to circumvent MFA, implementation of MFA remains an essential pillar in identity security and is highly effective at stopping a variety of threats.  

    - Leverage [phishing-resistant authentication methods](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity/authentication/concept-authentication-methods?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) such as FIDO Tokens, or [Microsoft Authenticator](https://www.microsoft.com/security/mobile-authenticator-app?ocid=magicti_ta_abbreviatedmktgpage) with passkey. Avoid telephony-based MFA methods to avoid risks associated with SIM-jacking.
- Implement Entra ID [Conditional Access authentication strength](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/concept-authentication-strengths?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to require phishing-resistant authentication for employees and external users for critical apps.
- Encourage users to use Microsoft Edge and other web browsers that support [Microsoft Defender SmartScreen](https://learn.microsoft.com/deployedge/microsoft-edge-security-smartscreen?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc), which identifies and blocks malicious websites, including phishing sites, scam sites, and sites that host malware.
- Organizations can also use [Microsoft Defender External Attack Surface Management (EASM)](https://www.microsoft.com/security/business/cloud-security/microsoft-defender-external-attack-surface-management?ocid=magicti_ta_abbreviatedmktgpage), a tool that continuously discovers and maps the digital attack surface to provide an external view of your online infrastructure. EASM leverages vulnerability and infrastructure data to generate Attack Surface Insights, reporting that highlights key risks to a given organization.

### Strengthen mobile device security

- Only install applications from trusted sources and official stores.
- If a device is no longer receiving updates, strongly consider replacing it with a new device.
- Use mobile solutions such as [Microsoft Defender for Endpoint on Android](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/microsoft-defender-endpoint-android?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to detect malicious applications
- Always keep *Install unknown apps* disabled on the Android device to prevent apps from being installed from unknown sources.
- Evaluate whether [Microsoft Defender for IoT](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/defender-for-iot/organizations/overview?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) services are applicable to your Internet of Things (IoT) environment.

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects threat components as the following malware:
 
- [HackTool:Win32/AutoKMS](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=HackTool:Win32/AutoKMS)
- [Program:AndroidOS/Multiverze](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Program:AndroidOS/Multiverze!pz)

## References
[Cerberus Unchained: The Multi-Stage Trojan Banking Campaign Targeting Android Devices](https://socradar.io/cerberus-multi-stage-trojan-banking-campaign/). SOC Radar (accessed 2025-01-06)

title: “Can you try a game I made?” Fake game sites lead to information stealers
content:
## Snapshot
Researchers at Malwarebytes observed a new malicious campaign targeting users through Discord, email, and text messages. Victims are approached with an offer to beta test a new video game, often presented as a personal request from the "developer." Those who express interest receive a download link to an archive hosted on platforms like Dropbox, Catbox, or Discord’s CDN, often shared from compromised accounts for added credibility.

## Description
Instead of a legitimate game, victims unknowingly install an information-stealing Trojan. The campaign delivers various stealers, including Nova Stealer, Ageo Stealer, and Hexon Stealer. These tools extract browser credentials, Discord tokens, cryptocurrency wallet data, and more. Nova Stealer, part of a Malware-as-a-Service model, even uses Discord webhooks to alert operators of stolen data in real time. Hexon Stealer, a newer variant, expands its capabilities to exfiltrate 2FA codes, credit card details, and browser autofill data.
 
The attackers frequently target Discord credentials to compromise more accounts, leveraging social engineering to spread malware through trusted contacts. The overarching goal is monetary gain, whether through cryptocurrency theft, selling credentials, or expanding their network of compromised users. Fake game websites, often hosted on unresponsive or protected platforms, serve as another avenue to distribute malware, with some campaigns even using Blogspot as a delivery method.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
Cybercriminals are increasingly using messaging apps like Discord and Telegram as private communication channels, to spread information stealers like Nova Stealer, and exfiltrate targeted data. These platforms offer a combination of simplicity, security, and anonymity that allows cybercriminals to communicate easily, either in private chats or public channels, without the oversight common in traditional underground forums. 

Additionally, these platforms support features like webhooks and bots, which are exploited by attackers to distribute malware and conduct phishing attacks. For instance, Discord’s webhooks, initially designed for notifications, can be misused to exfiltrate data collected by information stealers by sending it to attacker-controlled channels through HTTPS requests. This misuse of webhooks complicates monitoring and blocking efforts due to their integration with various apps and the encryption used. Discord's content delivery network (CDN) is also exploited by cybercriminals to host malware payloads, making it an effective distribution tool. As these platforms offer both robust automation capabilities and discreet communication options, they have become increasingly attractive to cybercriminals looking to bypass traditional security measures and reach a wider audience.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations.

- Check your Office 365 email filtering settings to ensure you block spoofed emails, spam, and emails with malware. Use [Microsoft Defender for Office 365](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/defender-for-office-365?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for enhanced phishing protection and coverage against new threats and polymorphic variants. Configure Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to [recheck links on click](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-links-about?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) and [delete sent mail](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/zero-hour-auto-purge?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in response to newly acquired threat intelligence. Turn on [safe attachments policies](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-attachments-policies-configure?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to check attachments to inbound email.
- Encourage users to use Microsoft Edge and other web browsers that support [SmartScreen](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/web-protection-overview?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc), which identifies and blocks malicious websites, including phishing sites, scam sites, and sites that host malware.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus, or the equivalent for your antivirus product, to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown variants.
- Enforce MFA on all accounts, remove users excluded from MFA, and strictly [require MFA](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/identity-protection/howto-identity-protection-configure-mfa-policy?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) from all devices, in all locations, at all times.
- Enable passwordless authentication methods (for example, Windows Hello, FIDO keys, or Microsoft Authenticator) for accounts that support passwordless. For accounts that still require passwords, use authenticator apps like Microsoft Authenticator for MFA. [Refer to this article](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/concept-authentication-methods?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for the different authentication methods and features.
- For MFA that uses authenticator apps, ensure that the app requires a code to be typed in where possible, as many intrusions where MFA was enabled still succeeded due to users clicking “Yes” on the prompt on their phones even when they were not at their [devices](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/how-to-mfa-number-match?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc). Refer to [this article](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/concept-authentication-methods?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for an example.
- Remind employees that enterprise or workplace credentials should not be stored in browsers or password vaults secured with personal credentials. Organizations can turn off password syncing in browser on managed devices using [Group Policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/deployedge/microsoft-edge-enterprise-sync#sync-group-policies?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc).

Microsoft Defender customers can [turn on attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to prevent common attack techniques used in infostealer infections. Attack surface reduction rules are sweeping settings that stop entire classes of threats including, infostealers, credential theft, and ransomware. The following bullet points offer more guidance on specific mitigation advice:

- [Turn on PUA protection in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/detect-block-potentially-unwanted-apps-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc)
- [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion)
- [Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-execution-of-potentially-obfuscated-scripts)

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender for Endpoint
Alerts with the following titles in the security center can indicate threat activity on your network:
 
- Information stealing malware activity

## References
[“Can you try a game I made?” Fake game sites lead to information stealers](https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/news/2025/01/can-you-try-a-game-i-made-fake-game-sites-lead-to-information-stealers). Malwarebytes (accessed 2025-01-06)

title: EAGERBEE, with updated and novel components, targets the Middle East
content:
#### Targeted Geolocations
- Middle East



#### Targeted Industries
- Government Agencies & Services  
- Information Technology  
    - Internet Routing, Access & Connection



## Snapshot
Researchers at Kaspersky have uncovered the deployment of the EAGERBEE backdoor targeting ISPs and governmental entities in the Middle East.

## Description
The malware leverages a unique service injector to embed itself into running services. EAGERBEE utilizes a dynamic link library (DLL) file, “tsvipsrv.dll”, and payload file, “ntusers0.dat”, to install the backdoor via the SessionEnv service. Once installed, the backdoor gathers system information such as NetBIOS names, OS details, IP addresses, and processor architecture. It uses this data to establish a connection with its command-and-control (C2) server, employing SSL/TLS encryption if necessary.
 
The EAGERBEE backdoor operates continuously, retrieving configurations stored in public directories or embedded in its binary, which are decoded using XOR keys. Communication with the C2 server facilitates the download of the Plugin Orchestrator module, which manages additional plugins for malicious activities. These plugins include components for file system manipulation, process management, remote access, network connection listing, and service management.
 
Kaspersky’s analysis revealed that the backdoor injects malicious code into legitimate processes like the Themes service, allowing it to evade detection. The Plugin Orchestrator collects additional information, such as memory usage and process details, before executing commands and injecting plugins into memory. The plugins support tasks like file and process manipulation, remote shell execution, and service control, providing attackers with extensive capabilities.
 
The researchers noted overlaps between EAGERBEE and the CoughingDown threat group, including code similarities and shared C2 infrastructure. Some instances of EAGERBEE were deployed through the ProxyLogon vulnerability (CVE-2021-26855) in Exchange servers, emphasizing the importance of patching known exploits. In one case, attackers used legitimate Windows services like MSDTC and IKEEXT to load malicious DLLs. However, researchers were unable to identify the group responsible and assessed with medium confidence a relation between EAGERBEE and the CoughingDown threat group.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
[CVE-2021-26855](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/CVE-2021-26855) is a server-side request forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in Microsoft Exchange Server. It allows attackers to send arbitrary HTTP requests and authenticate as the Exchange Server's computer account. This authentication bypass affects Microsoft Exchange Server versions 2013, 2016, and 2019. Although [Salt Typhoon](https://.security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/97d973d15f12895b3f1627cc441d5810903223c6c607da5500d370cc8b0c1632) was the threat actor behind the earliest exploitation of this vulnerability in March 2021, its use has expanded, with a growing number of actors, including financially motivated cybercriminals to state-sponsored groups, leveraging it.

## Recommendations
Apply these mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. 
 
- Apply the [corresponding security updates for Exchange Server](https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/releaseNote/2021-Mar), including applicable fixes for [CVE-2021-26855](https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/vulnerability/CVE-2021-26855), While it is important to prioritize patching of internet-facing Exchange servers to mitigate risk in an ordered manner, unpatched internal Exchange Server instances should also be addressed as soon as possible.
    - For Exchange Server instances in Mainstream Support, critical product updates are released for the most recently released CU and for the immediately previous CU. For Exchange Server instances in Extended Support, critical product updates are released for the most recently released CU only.
    - If you don't have a supported CU, Microsoft is producing an additional series of security updates (SUs) that can be applied to some older and unsupported CUs to help customers more quickly protect their environment. For information on these updates, see [March 2021 Exchange Server Security Updates for older Cumulative Updates of Exchange Server](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/t5/exchange-team-blog/march-2021-exchange-server-security-updates-for-older-cumulative/ba-p/2192020).
    - Installing the updates is the only complete mitigation for these vulnerabilities and has no impact on functionality. If threat actor has exploited these vulnerabilities to install malware, installing the updates will not remove implanted malware or evict the actor.
- Apply the following interim mitigations if you are unable to apply security updates to Exchange Server 2013, 2016, and 2019. For detailed guidance, read the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) blogpost [Microsoft Exchange Server Vulnerabilities Mitigations March 2021](https://msrc-blog.microsoft.com/2021/03/05/microsoft-exchange-server-vulnerabilities-mitigations-march-2021/).

    - **Apply IIS rewrite rule mitigating CVE-2021-26855 SSRF**. Apply this [PowerShell](https://github.com/microsoft/CSS-Exchange/tree/main/Security#backendcookiemitigationps1)-based mitigation to filter HTTPS requests that contain malicious *X-AnonResource-Backend* and malformed *X-BEResource* cookies observed in the server-side request forgery (SSRF) attacks in the wild. This will help defend against the known attack patterns, but not the SSRF as a whole. (***Note**:* This IIS rewrite rule will be removed if Exchange Server is upgraded. You will need to reapply this mitigation if the security patch has not been installed.)
    - **Run Nmap script to scan for CVE-2021-26855**. Use [this script](https://github.com/microsoft/CSS-Exchange/blob/main/Security/http-vuln-cve2021-26855.nse) to detect whether a specified Exchange Server is vulnerable to the Exchange Server SSRF vulnerability (CVE-2021-26855). This can be used to validate patch and mitigation state of exposed servers. See the MSRC blogpost for implementation and rollback instructions.
- In some scenarios, Exchange Server deployments have highly privileged access to Active Directory, which could be used for the lateral movement opportunities further into organizations. Organizations should determine if they have rerun Exchange Setup with the */PrepareAD* parameter since [February 2019's quarterly Exchange updates](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/t5/exchange-team-blog/released-february-2019-quarterly-exchange-updates/ba-p/609061), which decreases Exchange rights in Active Directory.
- Consider only presenting Exchange web services, such as Outlook on the web and Exchange ActiveSync, directly to the internet where necessary. For example, if you have devices with Virtual Private Network (VPN) capabilities, you can restrict access to this Exchange role to the VPN service.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://docs.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/microsoft-defender-antivirus/enable-cloud-protection-microsoft-defender-antivirus) and automatic sample submission on Microsoft Defender Antivirus. These capabilities use artificial intelligence and machine learning to quickly identify and stop new and unknown threats.
- Utilize the Microsoft Defender Firewall and your network firewall to prevent RPC and SMB communication among endpoints whenever possible. This limits lateral movement as well as other attack activities.

## References
[EAGERBEE, with updated and novel components, targets the Middle East](https://securelist.com/eagerbee-backdoor/115175/). Kaspersky (accessed 2025-01-06). 
 
[CVE-2021-26855 - Microsoft Exchange Server Remote Code Execution Vulnerability](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/CVE-2021-26855). Microsoft (accessed 2025-01-06).

title: North Korean Hackers Wipe Cryptocurrency Wallets via Fake Job Interviews
content:
## Snapshot
GBHackers discovered a new wave of cyberattacks targeting cryptocurrency wallets linked to the North Korean threat actors’ campaign "[Contagious Interview](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/9ce29d67)."

## Description
The Contagious Interview campaign affects multiple operating systems, including Windows, macOS, and Linux, and utilizes cross-platform tools like Golang. Attackers use sophisticated phishing tactics, posing as recruiters on LinkedIn, and direct victims to fraudulent websites that mimic legitimate recruitment platforms like Willo, a candidate screening site. Victims are tricked into downloading a malicious "fix" that delivers malware designed to drain cryptocurrency wallets. The malware used in recent attacks, often in a ZIP file named VCam\_intel.zip, includes shell scripts and Golang-based programs to deploy a backdoor and credential-stealing mechanisms. For macOS, it uses a fake Chrome update process, *ChromeUpdateAlert.app*, to steal credentials and employ a persistent service to maintain control over the system. The malware can exfiltrate sensitive files, execute shell commands remotely, modify Chrome preferences, and extract Chrome cookies, passwords, and macOS Keychain data. The primary goal is to steal cryptocurrency by targeting wallets like MetaMask, aligning with North Korea's broader campaigns to fund their regime through cybercrime. Security researchers have identified malicious domains and hashes associated with this campaign, noting the malware's sophisticated capabilities, including architecture detection and cross-platform compatibility. The Golang code contains advanced features like a persistent backdoor, targeting of Chrome user data, and multilevel commands for data theft and system control.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
This latest report on the Contagious Interview campaign, alongside previous [OSINT reporting](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/87adc2a0), highlights the evolving threat of North Korean cyber activity. These operations are driven by tailored social engineering campaigns across platforms, using fraudulent remote employment. Since initially reported in November 2023 by Unit 42 and attributed by Microsoft to [Storm-1877](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/038db949), the Contagious Interview campaign has been documented multiple times involving fake recruiters and various malware updates. [In October 2024](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/9ce29d67), Unit 42 observed Contagious Interview targeting tech industry jobs seekers via multiple video call applications, delivering cross-platform versions of the BeaverTail and InvisibleFerret malware to steal cryptocurrency wallets and browser passwords. [That same month](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/839e57f8), DataDog Security Research discovered related activity targeting software developers with malicious npm packages. [By November 2024](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/9a2e8410), Unit 42 observed domains linked to the campaign in what they dubbed "Wagemole Campaign," highlighting how North Korean IT workers use fake or stolen identities to secure remote jobs. Most recently, [in December 2024,](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/b5a152a8) NTT Security Japan reported the deployment of a new malware, 'OtterCookie,' as part of the Contagious Interview campaign.

In 2024 alone, North Korean threat actors stole hundreds of millions in cryptocurrency while expanding their operations. The ongoing Contagious Interview campaign illustrates the persistence and adaptability of their operations heading into this year.

## Recommendations
*GBHackers highlight the importance of maintaining strong security practices, including scrutinizing unexpected permission requests and keeping security tools updated*:

- Exercise Caution in Job Offers: Verify the authenticity of recruiters and job interviews, especially when asked to download files or share sensitive information.
- Update Antivirus Solutions: Ensure all systems and antivirus software are up to date to detect and mitigate such threats.
- Avoid Running Unknown Commands: Be wary of commands or fixes suggested in emails or messages from unknown sources.
- Use MultiFactor Authentication (MFA): Secure cryptocurrency wallets and other sensitive accounts with MFA.

Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of these type of threats.

- Avoid opening emails, attachments, and links, including links from social networks, from suspicious sources. Ask if the sender is who they say they are before clicking anything. Be wary of senders as well as offers that are too good to be true. Do a search to determine if the offer is legitimate or a trap.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc)  in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a huge majority of new and unknown variants.

Implement MFA to mitigate credential theft from phishing attacks. MFA can be complemented with the following solutions and best practices to protect organizations: 

- Activate conditional access policies. [Conditional access](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/conditional-access/overview?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) policies are evaluated and enforced every time an attacker attempts to use a stolen session cookie. Organizations can protect themselves from attacks that leverage stolen credentials by activating policies regarding compliant devices or trusted IP address requirements.
- Configure [continuous access evaluation](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/conditional-access/concept-continuous-access-evaluation?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in your tenant.
- Invest in advanced anti-phishing solutions that monitor incoming emails and visited websites. [Microsoft Defender for Office](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender/microsoft-365-security-center-mdo?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) 365 brings together incident and alert management across email, devices, and identities, centralizing investigations for threats in email. Organizations can also leverage web browsers that automatically [identify and block malicious websites](https://learn.microsoft.com/deployedge/microsoft-edge-security-smartscreen?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc), including those used in this phishing campaign. To build resilience against phishing attacks in general, organizations can use [anti-phishing policies](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/set-up-anti-phishing-policies?view=o365-worldwide) to enable mailbox intelligence settings, as well as configure impersonation protection settings for specific messages and sender domains. Enabling [SafeLinks](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-links?view=o365-worldwide) ensures real-time protection by scanning at time of delivery and at time of click.
- Monitor for suspicious or anomalous activities, and search for sign-in attempts with suspicious characteristics (for example location, internet service provider \[ISP\], user agent, and use of anonymizer services). Activity can be identified and investigated with [Microsoft Defender for Identity](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender/microsoft-365-security-center-mdi?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc), which contributes identity-focused information into incidents and alerts, providing key context and correlating alerts from other products within Microsoft 365 Defender. This ensures all alerts are available in one place, and the scope of a breach can be determined faster than before.
- Additionally, block phishing websites and other malicious URLs and domains in the browser through [Microsoft Defender SmartScreen](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/operating-system-security/virus-and-threat-protection/microsoft-defender-smartscreen/), as well as the detection of suspicious and malicious behavior on endpoints.
- Continuously monitor suspicious or anomalous activities. Investigate sign-in attempts with suspicious characteristics (for example, location, ISP, user agent, and use of anonymizer services).

Microsoft Defender customers can turn on [attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti%3cem%3eta%3c/em%3elearndoc) to prevent common attack techniques:

- [Block process creations originating from PsExec and WMI commands](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti%3cem%3eta%3c/em%3elearndoc#block-process-creations-originating-from-psexec-and-wmi-commands)
- [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion)

title: Nuclei flaw lets malicious templates bypass signature verification
content:
## Snapshot
Researchers at Wiz discovered a vulnerability in the open-source vulnerability scanner Nuclei, specifically tracked as [CVE-2024-43405](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/cves/CVE-2024-43405/), which could allow attackers to bypass signature verification and inject malicious code into templates. Nuclei, developed by ProjectDiscovery, uses over 10,000 YAML templates to scan for vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and other security issues.

## Description
These templates include a code protocol for executing commands locally, and each template is signed with a digest hash to ensure integrity. The vulnerability stems from a discrepancy between Go's regex-based signature verification and the YAML parser's handling of line breaks. Go does not recognize carriage returns (\r) as line breaks, while the YAML parser does, creating an opportunity for attackers to insert a second "# digest:" line with malicious code that bypasses the signature check but is executed by the YAML parser. Additionally, Nuclei only checks the first occurrence of "# digest:" in a template, ignoring any subsequent ones, which could be exploited with malicious payloads.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
Open source software, like Nuclei, is widely regarded as secure due to the constant scrutiny from its extensive community of contributors. However, its popularity and accessibility make it an attractive target for cybercriminals, especially those seeking to exploit the software supply chain. This risk is exemplified by recent incidents, such as the [malicious npm package "ethereumvulncontracthandler,"](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/792148c9) which posed as a vulnerability detection tool but instead deployed the Quasar RAT onto developers' systems. Such cases highlight a troubling trend where tools designed—or purporting to be designed—to detect vulnerabilities can themselves become sources of exploitation. With Nuclei’s more than 50 million monthly scans, the potential impact of any vulnerabilities in such widely used tools is significant, emphasizing the importance of vigilance in the open source community.

## Recommendations
The source recommends:

- **Update Nuclei to version 3.3.2 or later to address the patched vulnerability.**Updating to the latest version, released on September 4, mitigates the risk posed by this flaw. Organizations should prioritize upgrading to ensure their systems are secure against exploitation.
- **For those unable to upgrade immediately, disable custom code templates.**As a temporary measure, disabling the execution of custom code templates helps reduce exposure to the vulnerability. This workaround is essential for users who cannot update promptly.
- **Use only trusted, verified templates if applying the patch is delayed.**To minimize risk, organizations should refrain from using custom templates and instead rely on trusted, verified ones until the patch can be implemented. This practice ensures that only secure, validated templates are in use, reducing the potential for exploitation.

## References
[Nuclei flaw lets malicious templates bypass signature verification](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/nuclei-flaw-lets-malicious-templates-bypass-signature-verification/) Bleeping Computer (accessed 2025-01-07)

title: Malicious Obfuscated NPM Package Disguised as an Ethereum Tool Deploys Quasar RAT
content:
## Snapshot
Cybersecurity researchers have identified a malicious npm package named "ethereumvulncontracthandler", which poses as a tool for detecting vulnerabilities in Ethereum smart contracts. Published on December 18, 2024, by a user named "solidit-dev-416," this package is designed to deploy the Quasar RAT, an open-source remote access trojan, onto developers' systems.

## Description
Upon installation, a malicious script is retrieved from a remote server and is executed silently in order to deploy the RAT on Windows systems. The package employs multiple layers of obfuscation, including Base64 and XOR encoding, as well as minification, to conceal its malicious code. The malware also performs checks to avoid running in sandboxed environments before fetching and executing a second-stage payload from a remote server. This script runs PowerShell commands to initiate the execution of Quasar RAT. 

Once installed, Quasar RAT establishes persistence through Windows Registry modifications and contacts a command-and-control server to receive further instructions, enabling it to gather and exfiltrate information. The threat actor uses this server to catalog infected machines and manage multiple compromised hosts simultaneously, potentially as part of a botnet infection. 

This recent reporting highlights the broader risks of malicious packages in open-source ecosystems, where threats like Quasar RAT leverage deceptive tactics and unreliable metrics, such as fake GitHub stars, to enhance their reach and compromise systems. A study by Socket and academic partners reveals a rise in fake GitHub stars used to boost the popularity of malware-hosting repositories, often disguised as pirated software or cryptocurrency bots. Black market vendors, like Baddhi Shop, sell stars to inflate metrics. While GitHub actively removes fake accounts, researchers stress that star count is an unreliable quality metric and suggest weighted metrics to better assess repository credibility.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat.
 
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/linux-preferences) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown threats.
- Run [EDR in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode?view=o365-worldwide?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus does not detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach.
- Allow [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations?view=o365-worldwide?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in full automated mode to allow Microsoft Defender for Endpoint to take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.
- [Enable](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-controlled-folders) controlled folder access.
- Ensure that [tamper protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection#how-do-i-configure-or-manage-tamper-protection) is enabled in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Enable [network protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-network-protection) in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Follow the credential hardening recommendations in the [on-premises credential theft overview](https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/9382203e-5155-4b5e-af74-21562b1004d5/analystreport) to defend against common credential theft techniques like LSASS access.
- [Enable](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-credential-stealing-from-the-windows-local-security-authority-subsystem) LSA protection.
- Microsoft Defender XDR customers can turn on the following [attack surface reduction rule](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction)to prevent common attack techniques used for ransomware.
    - [Block](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-executable-content-from-email-client-and-webmail) executable content from email client and webmail
    - [Block](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion) executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion

## References
[Malicious Obfuscated NPM Package Disguised as an Ethereum Tool Deploys Quasar RAT](https://thehackernews.com/2025/01/malicious-obfuscated-npm-package.html). The Hacker News (accessed 2025-01-03)

title: Advancing Through the Cyberfront, LegionLoader Commander
content:
## Snapshot
Researchers at TRAC Labs detailed LegionLoader, a downloader malware written in C/C++ that first surfaced in 2019.

## Description
Also known as Satacom, RobotDropper, or CurlyGate, LegionLoader delivers malicious payloads, including Chrome extensions like CursedChrome. These extensions can alter email content, capture browser activity, withdraw cryptocurrency, and manage balances in platforms like Facebook and Coinbase. Since mid-2024, it has also distributed stealer malware such as LummaC2 and StealC.
 
LegionLoader typically spreads through drive-by downloads and fake installers hosted on compromised websites. It uses a multi-stage process, beginning with an MSI binary that communicates with a server to obtain a password for decrypting an embedded malicious ZIP archive. The malware employs side-loading techniques, previously using rnp.dll but more recently switching to steamerrorreporter64.exe to inject payloads via the process hollowing technique.
 
The payloads undergo layered encryption, including Base64, RC4, and XTEA algorithms, to evade detection. After decrypting, LegionLoader injects its core payload into legitimate processes like explorer.exe. It communicates with a command-and-control (C2) server using Base64-encoded and RC4-encrypted configurations, enabling the delivery of additional malicious files and commands.
 
LegionLoader’s modular configuration allows attackers to tailor its operations, specifying payload types (.dll, .exe, or .bat) and execution methods. It leverages tools like Mersenne Twister to generate file names and paths dynamically, adding another layer of obfuscation. The malware also targets Chrome credentials stored in user data, further enhancing its capability for credential theft.
 
This adaptive malware remains a persistent threat, evolving its techniques to bypass detection and increase payload delivery efficiency. According to TRAC Labs, its use of encrypted communications and modular design highlights the importance of robust endpoint protection and monitoring solutions.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat.
 
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/linux-preferences) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown threats.
- Run [EDR in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode?view=o365-worldwide?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus does not detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach.
- Allow [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations?view=o365-worldwide?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in full automated mode to allow Microsoft Defender for Endpoint to take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.
- [Enable](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-controlled-folders) controlled folder access.
- Ensure that [tamper protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection#how-do-i-configure-or-manage-tamper-protection) is enabled in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Enable [network protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-network-protection) in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Follow the credential hardening recommendations in the [on-premises credential theft overview](https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/9382203e-5155-4b5e-af74-21562b1004d5/analystreport) to defend against common credential theft techniques like LSASS access.
- [Enable](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-credential-stealing-from-the-windows-local-security-authority-subsystem) LSA protection.

## References

title: 36 Chrome Extensions Compromised in Supply Chain Attack
content:
## Snapshot
Researchers at Cyberhaven identified a supply chain attack that compromised 36 Google Chrome browser extensions, impacting around 2.6 million users.

## Description
Although initial reports focused on Cyberhaven's security-focused extension, subsequent investigations revealed that the same code had been injected into at least 35 extensions collectively used by roughly 2,600,000 people.

The attackers injected data-stealing malware into these extensions, including one from Cyberhaven itself, which was designed to protect against insider threats. The infiltration occurred when a Cyberhaven employee was tricked by a phishing attack, resulting in a malicious update to their extension (version 24.10.4) during December 25-26, 2024.

The attackers exploited a legitimate Google authorization process to trick developers into authorizing a malicious OAuth application named "Privacy Policy Extension," which circumvented multifactor authentication and facilitated the upload of the malware-infected extensions. The primary goal of the malware was to steal Facebook account passwords. Cyberhaven has updated the compromised extension to eliminate the malicious code and has also released open-source tools on GitHub to assist in detecting such attacks. The phishing campaign began around December 5, targeting developers listed as public contacts for Chrome extensions with emails from fake addresses, leading to malicious sites that mimicked Chrome policy violation notices. Other affected extensions include Internxt VPN, VPNCity, Uvoice, and ParrotTalks, and a command-and-control server IP address has been identified for monitoring purposes. Cyberhaven has advised users to change their passwords and check for any suspicious activity on their accounts.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
Read more about inital [reporting of this threat here.](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/8d2371e6) Cyberhaven and ExtensionTotal have put together a live site to track and report any further updates to this incident, which can be [found here.](https://www.extensiontotal.com/cyberhaven-incident-live)

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations for related threats.

- Establish [best practices to secure software supply chain](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/nuget/concepts/security-best-practices).
- Conduct an [audit for packages and dependencies](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/nuget/concepts/auditing-packages), analyzing the security of packages included in software projects.
- Configure [continuous access evaluation](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/conditional-access/concept-continuous-access-evaluation?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in your tenant.
- Invest in advanced anti-phishing solutions that monitor incoming emails and visited websites. [Microsoft Defender for Office](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender/microsoft-365-security-center-mdo?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) 365 brings together incident and alert management across email, devices, and identities, centralizing investigations for threats in email. To build resilience against phishing attacks in general, organizations can use [anti-phishing policies](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/set-up-anti-phishing-policies?view=o365-worldwide) to enable mailbox intelligence settings, as well as configure impersonation protection settings for specific messages and sender domains. Enabling [SafeLinks](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-links?view=o365-worldwide) ensures real-time protection by scanning at time of delivery and at time of click.
- Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management Admins can conduct their own [Browser extensions assessment](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-vulnerability-management/tvm-browser-extensions).

Defenders can also complement MFA with the following solutions and best practices to further protect their organizations from such attacks. 

- Use [security defaults](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/fundamentals/concept-fundamentals-security-defaults?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) as a baseline set of policies to improve identity security posture. For more granular control, enable conditional access policies. [Conditional access](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/conditional-access/overview?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) policies evaluate sign-in requests using additional identity-driven signals like user or group membership, IP location information, and device status, among others, and are enforced for suspicious sign-ins. Organizations can protect themselves from attacks that leverage stolen credentials by enabling policies such as compliant devices or trusted IP address requirements.
- Invest in advanced anti-phishing solutions that monitor and scan incoming emails and visited websites. For example, organizations can leverage web browsers that automatically [identify and block malicious websites](https://learn.microsoft.com/deployedge/microsoft-edge-security-smartscreen?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc), including those used in this phishing campaign, and solutions that [detect and block malicious emails, links, and files](https://www.microsoft.com/security/business/siem-and-xdr/microsoft-defender-office-365?ocid=magicti_ta_abbreviatedmktgpage). Additionally, block phishing websites and other malicious URLs and domains in the browser through [Microsoft Defender SmartScreen](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/operating-system-security/virus-and-threat-protection/microsoft-defender-smartscreen/), as well as the detection of suspicious and malicious behavior on endpoints.

Microsoft Defender customers can [turn on attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc). 

    - [Turn on PUA protection in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/detect-block-potentially-unwanted-apps-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc)
    - [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion)
    - [Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-execution-of-potentially-obfuscated-scripts)

title: New DoubleClickjacking attack exploits double-clicks to hijack accounts
content:
## Snapshot
Cybersecurity expert [Paulos Yibelo](https://www.paulosyibelo.com/) has discovered a new web attack technique called "DoubleClickjacking," which exploits the timing of mouse double-clicks to deceive users into performing unintended actions on websites.

## Description
This method is a variation of [clickjacking](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-pages/security/faq#how-does-power-pages-help-to-protect-against-clickjacking--), or UI redressing, where attackers overlay a legitimate webpage in a hidden iframe with a page they control, aligning buttons and links to trick users into clicking on elements that perform malicious actions, such as authorizing an OAuth application or accepting a multifactor authentication request. However, DoubleClickjacking bypasses existing clickjacking defenses by not using an iframe or trying to pass cookies to another domain. Instead, it operates directly on legitimate sites. 

In a DoubleClickjacking attack, a user is lured to click a button on a malicious site, which then opens a new window with another lure. It exploits the brief gap between two clicks by swapping a legitimate window, like a CAPTCHA, with a sensitive one, such as an OAuth prompt, just before the second click. The attack leverages the [mousedown](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element/mousedown_event) event, which triggers faster than the [onclick](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element/click_event) event, making it effective regardless of click speed. As the user attempts to solve the captcha by double-clicking, the overlay quickly closes, causing the second click to land on an authorization button or link on the legitimate site that's been swapped into the background by JavaScript. Yibelo demonstrated the effectiveness of this attack by taking over accounts on platforms such as Shopify, Slack, and Salesforce. He also noted that the technique could be adapted for browser extensions, potentially authorizing web3 transactions or disabling VPNs, and could even be used on mobile devices by prompting users to "Double-Tap."

## Recommendations
To counter this threat, Yibelo suggested the following:
 
- Adding JavaScript to webpages to disable sensitive buttons until a gesture is made
- Propose a new HTTP header to limit or block rapid context-switching during double-click sequences or expand CSP headers to cover such scenarios
- Developers may implement the protective library on sensitive pages

## References
[New DoubleClickjacking attack exploits double-clicks to hijack accounts](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-doubleclickjacking-attack-exploits-double-clicks-to-hijack-accounts/). BleepingComputer (2024-12-06)
 
[DoubleClickjacking: A New Era of UI Redressing](https://www.paulosyibelo.com/). Paulos Yibelo (2024-12-06)

title: NonEuclid RAT
content:
## Snapshot
Researchers at CYFIRMA released a report detailing NonEuclid, a remote access trojan (RAT), being advertised and sold in underground forums.

## Description
Developed in C#, NonEuclid RAT is highly sophisticated, offering features such as antivirus bypass, privilege escalation, and ransomware encryption for critical files. NonEuclid employs stealth techniques like dynamic DLL loading, anti-VM checks, and AES encryption, making it both versatile and difficult to detect. Further, NonEuclid’s promotion and use are widespread, with its developer actively advertising it on underground forums, Discord, and YouTube.
 
The malware leverages advanced mechanisms to ensure persistence and evade detection, including modifying Windows Defender exclusions, using mutex controls to avoid duplicate instances, and implementing anti-process monitoring to terminate security tools like Task Manager. NonEuclid also includes UAC bypass and registry modifications to escalate privileges and maintain persistence. Additionally, it employs ransomware capabilities, encrypting files with AES and appending the “.NonEuclid” extension.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat.
 
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/linux-preferences) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown threats.
- Run [EDR in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode?view=o365-worldwide?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus does not detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach.
- Allow [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations?view=o365-worldwide?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in full automated mode to allow Microsoft Defender for Endpoint to take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.
- [Enable](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-controlled-folders) controlled folder access.
- Ensure that [tamper protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection#how-do-i-configure-or-manage-tamper-protection) is enabled in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Enable [network protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-network-protection) in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Follow the credential hardening recommendations in the [on-premises credential theft overview](https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/9382203e-5155-4b5e-af74-21562b1004d5/analystreport) to defend against common credential theft techniques like LSASS access.
- [Enable](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-credential-stealing-from-the-windows-local-security-authority-subsystem) LSA protection.
- Microsoft Defender XDR customers can turn on the following [attack surface reduction rule](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction) to prevent common attack techniques used for ransomware.

- - [Block](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-executable-content-from-email-client-and-webmail) executable content from email client and webmail
    - [Block](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion) executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion

title: Seeing is Deceiving | Analysis of Fake Zoom Meeting Phishing Attack
content:
## Snapshot
SlowMist, a blockchain security firm, analyzed phishing attacks that impersonated Zoom meeting links, leading to the installation of malware and the theft of cryptocurrency assets worth millions. The attack employed a fake domain and malicious software to collect sensitive information and siphon funds to controlled wallets.

## Description
SlowMist's analysis revealed a phishing campaign using a fake Zoom domain, "app\[.\]us4zoom\[.\]us," which mimicked legitimate Zoom meeting links. Clicking the "Launch Meeting" button prompted users to download a malicious installation package named “ZoomApp\_v.3.14.dmg,” containing an executable file named ".ZoomApp." Upon execution, the malware collected system information, browser data, KeyChain credentials, and cryptocurrency wallet details, which were sent to a server located in the Netherlands. Decryption of the phishing domain's monitoring logs revealed that the attackers used the Telegram API, with the language used in the script identified as Russian. Researchers traced stolen funds linked to the threat actor's address, discovering profits exceeding $1 million, with transactions involving ETH and other cryptocurrencies funneled through platforms like ChangeNOW, Gate.io, and Binance.

## Recommendations
Implement multifactor authentication (MFA) to mitigate credential theft from phishing attacks. MFA can be complemented with the following solutions and best practices to protect organizations: 

- Configure [continuous access evaluation](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/conditional-access/concept-continuous-access-evaluation?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in your tenant.
- Invest in advanced anti-phishing solutions that monitor incoming emails and visited websites. [Microsoft Defender for Office](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender/microsoft-365-security-center-mdo?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) 365 brings together incident and alert management across email, devices, and identities, centralizing investigations for threats in email. Organizations can also leverage web browsers that automatically [identify and block malicious websites](https://learn.microsoft.com/deployedge/microsoft-edge-security-smartscreen?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc), including those used in this phishing campaign. To build resilience against phishing attacks in general, organizations can use [anti-phishing policies](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/set-up-anti-phishing-policies?view=o365-worldwide) to enable mailbox intelligence settings, as well as configure impersonation protection settings for specific messages and sender domains. Enabling [SafeLinks](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-links?view=o365-worldwide) ensures real-time protection by scanning at time of delivery and at time of click.
- Monitor for suspicious or anomalous activities, and search for sign-in attempts with suspicious characteristics (for example location, internet service provider \[ISP\], user agent, and use of anonymizer services). Activity can be identified and investigated with [Microsoft Defender for Identity](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender/microsoft-365-security-center-mdi?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc), which contributes identity-focused information into incidents and alerts, providing key context and correlating alerts from other products within Microsoft 365 Defender. This ensures all alerts are available in one place, and the scope of a breach can be determined faster than before.

Defenders can also complement MFA with the following solutions and best practices to further protect their organizations from such attacks. 

- Use [security defaults](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/fundamentals/concept-fundamentals-security-defaults?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) as a baseline set of policies to improve identity security posture. For more granular control, enable conditional access policies. [Conditional access](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/conditional-access/overview?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) policies evaluate sign-in requests using additional identity-driven signals like user or group membership, IP location information, and device status, among others, and are enforced for suspicious sign-ins. Organizations can protect themselves from attacks that leverage stolen credentials by enabling policies such as compliant devices or trusted IP address requirements.
- Invest in advanced anti-phishing solutions that monitor and scan incoming emails and visited websites.
- Additionally, block phishing websites and other malicious URLs and domains in the browser through [Microsoft Defender SmartScreen](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/operating-system-security/virus-and-threat-protection/microsoft-defender-smartscreen/), as well as the detection of suspicious and malicious behavior on endpoints.
- Continuously monitor suspicious or anomalous activities. Investigate sign-in attempts with suspicious characteristics (for example, location, ISP, user agent, and use of anonymizer services).
- Only install apps from trusted sources and official stores.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc)  in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a huge majority of new and unknown variants.

## References
[Seeing is Deceiving | Analysis of Fake Zoom Meeting Phishing Attack](https://slowmist.medium.com/seeing-is-deceiving-analysis-of-fake-zoom-meeting-phishing-attack-3b0138e13e49). Medium (accessed 2025-01-02)
