title: Likely China-based Attackers Target High-profile Organizations in Southeast Asia
content:
#### Targeted Geolocations
- Southeast Asia



#### Targeted Industries
- Government Agencies & Services  
- Transportation Systems  
    - Aviation  
- Communications Infrastructure



## Snapshot
Researchers at Symantec detailed an espionage campaign, active since at least October 2023, likely conducted by China-based threat actors. The campaign targeted organizations in a number of industries, including government, telecommunications, and aviation.

## Description
The attackers employed a mix of open-source (e.g., Dismap, [Impacket](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/19a4861eb55c4c074ab0a8c6f58738d8f50dda8badf96695758399e3d826dda6), and FastReverseProxy) and living-off-the-land (e.g., PowerShell, Reg.exe, and Windows Management Instrumentation) tools in their attacks. Many of these tools have been previously observed in attacks attributed to Chinese actors including Rakshasa, a tool previously used by Earth Baku and SharpNBTScan, a .NET application previously used by Mustang Panda (tracked by Microsoft as [Twill Typhoon](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/01aef6bb1a4cd12178aca7fceb848002164b83bf375fa33699ed4c5523b4fd3c)). 

The operations focused on exfiltrating data of interest, including credentials, from targeted organizations. The threat actors maintaining prolonged access to target environments, allowing them to map the network and identify systems of interest. According to Symantec, data was exfiltrated using WinRAR to gather and compress files of interest into password-protected archives. These archives were then uploaded to cloud storage platforms like File.io, allowing the attackers to discreetly transfer the data.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
Microsoft attributes this malicious activity to [Antique Typhoon](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/b66b85c00a4caf612f122cb818e0a4c54afa5af2397e06d6c743a8f939476a0c?tab=description&) based on the tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) and IOCs reported by SentinelOne. Active since late 2020, Antique Typhoon is a China-based threat actor known to primarily target national government agencies, telecommunications, media, information technology, education, and non-governmental organizations. Most targets are in Western Europe and the Americas, with some observed in Eastern Europe, Southeast Asia, and West Asia. Antique Typhoon's operations focus on data theft and credential access. 

Most Chinese threat activity is for intelligence collection purposes and, as represented in Microsoft Threat Intelligencce nation-state notification (NSN) data, especially prevalent in Association of Southeast Asian Nations countries around the South China Sea. To learn more about Chinese cyber threat activity in and around the South China Sea, read [Microsoft's most recent Digial Defense Report](https://cdn-dynmedia-1.microsoft.com/is/content/microsoftcorp/microsoft/final/en-us/microsoft-brand/documents/Microsoft%20Digital%20Defense%20Report%202024%20%281%29.pdf).

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. 
 
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown variants.
- Turn on [tamper protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection) features to prevent attackers from stopping security services.
- Run [endpoint detection and response (EDR) in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode) so that Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus does not detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts detected post-breach.
- Enable [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations) in full automated mode to allow Defender for Endpoint to take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects threat components as the following malware:
 
- [Trojan:Win32/LotusBlossom](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:Win32/LotusBlossom!MTB)

title: Attack Exploiting Legitimate Service by APT-C-60
content:
#### Targeted Geolocations
- Japan



## Snapshot
The JPCERT Coordination Center (JPCERT/CC) released a report detailing an attack by APT-C-60 against an organization in Japan during August 2024.

## Description
The attacker used a phishing email disguised as a job application to lure the victim into downloading malware via a Google Drive link. The malicious file, a VHDX virtual disk image, contained LNK files and decoy documents. Upon execution, the LNK file triggered a series of actions, including creating a downloader, SecureBootUEFI.dat, which was made persistent through COM hijacking.
 
SecureBootUEFI.dat communicated with legitimate services Bitbucket and StatCounter, using the latter to identify infected devices by encoding unique device information into StatCounter’s referrer data. The downloader subsequently fetched additional payloads, Service.dat, which in turn retrieved and decoded further malware components, cn.dat and sp.dat, storing them in the system. 
 
The backdoor used in the attack, dubbed SpyGlace by ESET, is a well-documented tool with advanced functionality, including encrypted communication and modular execution. The backdoor has been observed in attacks attributed to APT-C-60, notably in similar campaigns reported between August and September 2024 targeting East Asian countries.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
[APT-C-60](https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/actor/apt-c-60) is a South Korea-linked cyberespionage group that focuses its targeting in East Asian countries, active since at least December 2021. In August, [ESET researchers observed](https://www.eset.com/int/about/newsroom/press-releases/research/eset-research-spy-group-exploits-wps-office-zero-day-analysis-uncovers-a-second-vulnerability/) the group exploiting a remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in WPS Office for Windows ([CVE-2024-7262](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/cves/CVE-2024-7262/)) to deploy its custom backdoor, SpyGlace, to impact users in East Asia. Previously, [the group was observed](https://threatbook.io/blog/Military-Topics-in-Focus:-APT-C-60-Threat-Continues-to-be-Exposed) using military-themed lures in phishing campaigns to gain access to victim enviornments.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat.
 
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/linux-preferences) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown threats.
- Run [EDR in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode?view=o365-worldwide?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus does not detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach.
- Allow [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations?view=o365-worldwide?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in full automated mode to allow Microsoft Defender for Endpoint to take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.
- [Enable](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-controlled-folders) controlled folder access.
- Ensure that [tamper protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection#how-do-i-configure-or-manage-tamper-protection) is enabled in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Enable [network protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-network-protection) in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Follow the credential hardening recommendations in the [on-premises credential theft overview](https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/9382203e-5155-4b5e-af74-21562b1004d5/analystreport) to defend against common credential theft techniques like LSASS access.
- [Enable](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-credential-stealing-from-the-windows-local-security-authority-subsystem) LSA protection.

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects threat components as the following malware:
 
- [Trojan:Win32/Malgent](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:Win32/Malgent!MSR)

[Attack Exploiting Legitimate Service by APT-C-60](https://blogs.jpcert.or.jp/en/2024/12/APT-C-60.html). JPCERT/CC (accessed 2024-12-12)

title: Radiant links $50 million crypto heist to North Korean hackers
content:
## Snapshot
Mandiant attributes the $50 million USD cryptocurrency heist from Radiant Capital, which occurred [in October 2024](https://medium.com/@RadiantCapital/radiant-post-mortem-fecd6cd38081), to North Korean state-affiliated threat actor UNC4736.

## Description
Threat actors used sophisticated malware to target three trusted developers at Radiant, a decentralized finance (DeFi) platform. They compromised the developers' devices to execute unauthorized transactions, exploiting the multi-signature process and stealing funds from Arbitrum and Binance Smart Chain markets. The initial infiltration began on September 11, 2024, when a Radiant developer was tricked into downloading a malicious ZIP file via a Telegram message that appeared to be from a former contractor. The contractor said they were pursuing a new career opportunity and asked for feedback on an alleged endeavor. The message included a ZIP file that contained a decoy PDF and a macOS malware payload named 'InletDrift,' which established a backdoor on the infected device. Radiant Capital stated that requests to review PDFs are routine in professional settings, and that, post compromise, the devices showed only minor glitches and error messages during signing, typical for hardware wallets and Safe. Additionally, the domain sent with the ZIP file had spoofed the former contractor’s actual website.
 
Despite Radiant's security measures, including transaction simulations and verification layers, the attack went undetected as it was designed to display benign transaction data on the interfaces while signing malicious transactions in the background. Mandiant, assisting in the ongoing investigation, assesses with high confidence that UNC4736 (tracked by Microsoft as [Citrine Sleet](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/740afa51582ebef367a7120efe99a535ba803f2169356580369a0fd680137145)) is behind the attack. Radiant is working with United States law enforcement and zeroShadow to recover the stolen funds and is emphasizing the need for more robust device-level security solutions to prevent such sophisticated attacks in the future. [ZeroShadow](https://x.com/zeroshadow_io/status/1865839771798429699) also attributes with high confidence this incident to the DPRK.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
In a related observation, Microsoft first identified atokyonews\[.\]com in November 2023 and attributed the domain to Citrine Sleet. This threat actor primarily targets financial institutions and, using social engineering, conducts thorough reconnaissance of the cryptocurrency industry and associated individuals. Additionally, Citrine Sleet has previously used registered domain names for social engineering, malware hosting, and command-and-control (C2).

## Recommendations
[Radiant Captial provided the following preventative recommendations](https://medium.com/@RadiantCapital/radiant-post-mortem-fecd6cd38081):
 
- Implement a governance layer where, if one or more signers encounter issues or anomalies, the process is halted for further verification before proceeding.
- Utilize an uncompromised, independent device to verify transaction data before signing.
- Avoid using blind signing for critical transactions.
- Integrate a mechanism where recurring transaction errors or glitches automatically trigger a full audit of the transaction before additional signing attempts can be made.
- Manually review transaction payloads.

Microsoft recommends the following to reduce the risk of these threats.

- [Help prevent social engineering attacks](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/security-insider/emerging-threats/feeding-from-the-trust-economy-social-engineering-fraud?ocid=magicti_ta_blog) by not blending personal accounts with work emails or work-related tasks. Avoid opening emails, attachments, and links, including links from social networks, from suspicious sources. Ask yourself if the sender is who they say they are before clicking anything. Lastly, don’t overshare online. If threat actors can find your personal details from your social media profiles, they can use it to help make their scams appear more legitimate.
- Protect sensitive data using [data security solutions](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/security-101/what-is-data-security "https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/security-101/what-is-data-security"). Use [data protection](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/security-101/what-is-data-protection "https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/security-101/what-is-data-protection") tools like [Microsoft Purview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/purview/information-protection "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/purview/information-protection") to [discover, classify, and protect sensitive information](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/purview/information-protection "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/purview/information-protection"), and to manage and mitigate [risks posed by insiders](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/security-101/what-is-insider-threat "https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/security-101/what-is-insider-threat"). 
    - [Create and Deploy data loss prevention (DLP) policies](https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/compliance/dlp-create-deploy-policy%22%20/t%20%22_blank "https://docs.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/compliance/dlp-create-deploy-policy%22%20/t%20%22_blank") to automatically detect and protect sensitive data across emails, documents, and conversations. Deploy [DLP solutions](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/security-101/what-is-data-loss-prevention-dlp "https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/security-101/what-is-data-loss-prevention-dlp") to monitor and prevent unauthorized data access and leaks.
    - Configure insider risk management with [Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/risk-management/microsoft-purview-insider-risk-management "https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/risk-management/microsoft-purview-insider-risk-management"). [Turn on Microsoft 365 audit logs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/purview/audit-log-enable-disable?tabs=microsoft-purview-portal "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/purview/audit-log-enable-disable?tabs=microsoft-purview-portal") to stay informed of actions taken by the insider risk management features. Additionally, attackers may attempt to hide evidence of the breach by disabling auditing features, clearing logs, or manipulating log files. Therefore, [verify the auditing status for your organization](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/purview/audit-log-enable-disable?tabs=microsoft-purview-portal#verify-the-auditing-status-for-your-organization "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/purview/audit-log-enable-disable?tabs=microsoft-purview-portal#verify-the-auditing-status-for-your-organization") or [employ audit logging](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/compliance/assurance/assurance-audit-logging "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/compliance/assurance/assurance-audit-logging") detection, and view [best practices for managing auditing and security logging](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/security-policy-settings/manage-auditing-and-security-log "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/security-policy-settings/manage-auditing-and-security-log").
    - Separate privileged roles. Admin and user accounts should be distinct. Use [Privileged Identity Management](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/privileged-identity-management/pim-configure "https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/privileged-identity-management/pim-configure") or separate accounts for privileged tasks, limiting accounts with excessive permissions. Apply [Conditional Access](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/conditional-access/overview "https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/conditional-access/overview"), especially for accounts with elevated roles. [Adaptive Protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/purview/insider-risk-management-adaptive-protection?tabs=purview-portal "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/purview/insider-risk-management-adaptive-protection?tabs=purview-portal") can automatically apply strict security controls on high-risk users and minimize impact of potential data security incidents.
- Implement [strong access controls](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/security-101/what-is-access-control "https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/security-101/what-is-access-control") to secure sensitive information, detect if a breach has already occurred or is currently in action by suspicious [login security](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/security-101/what-is-login-security "https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/security-101/what-is-login-security") activity, and adopt [Zero Trust principles](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/security-101/what-is-zero-trust-architecture "https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/security-101/what-is-zero-trust-architecture") to reduce time in breach detection. [Zero trust](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/security/zero-trust/zero-trust-overview "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/security/zero-trust/zero-trust-overview")assumes that threats could be both external and internal and require verification at every access attempt. 
    - Use [Microsoft Entra ID Protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/id-protection/overview-identity-protection "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/id-protection/overview-identity-protection") to help detect, investigate, and remediate identity-based risks like leaked credentials.
- Educate employees on the importance of data security through data handling best practices and provide regular security training for employees to recognize and respond to threats.
    - [Use Microsoft curated resources and training.](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/cybersecurity-awareness "https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/cybersecurity-awareness")
    - Deploy the [phishing risk-reduction tool](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/threat-protection/attack-simulation-training "https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/threat-protection/attack-simulation-training") to empower employees through simulations and targeted training.
- Monitor for suspicious or anomalous activities, and search for sign-in attempts with suspicious characteristics (for example location, internet service provider \[ISP\], user agent, and use of anonymizer services). Activity can be identified and investigated with [Microsoft Defender for Identity](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender/microsoft-365-security-center-mdi?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc "https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender/microsoft-365-security-center-mdi?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc"), which contributes identity-focused information into incidents and [alerts](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-for-identity/alerts-overview "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-for-identity/alerts-overview"), providing key context and correlating alerts from other products within Microsoft 365 Defender. This ensures all alerts are available in one place, and the scope of a breach can be determined faster than before. For example, add [persistence and privilege escalation alerts](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-for-identity/persistence-privilege-escalation-alerts "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-for-identity/persistence-privilege-escalation-alerts") to assist in identifying attacker access in your network.
- Use Azure [encryption to protect data both in transit and at rest](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/security/fundamentals/encryption-overview "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/security/fundamentals/encryption-overview") and [apply data masking techniques](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dynamics365/customer-service/administer/data-masking-settings "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dynamics365/customer-service/administer/data-masking-settings") to obscure sensitive information.
- Utilize [AI and machine learning technologies](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/security-101/what-is-ai-for-cybersecurity "https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/security-101/what-is-ai-for-cybersecurity") for advanced data security. Ensure that the right people, machines, and software components get access to the right resources at the right time with [Identity and Access Management (IAM).](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/fundamentals/introduction-identity-access-management "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/fundamentals/introduction-identity-access-management") Many [IAM systems](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/security-101/what-is-identity-access-management-iam "https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/security-101/what-is-identity-access-management-iam") are AI-enabled and capable of detecting and stopping attacks before they become bigger problems.

## References
[Radiant links $50 million crypto heist to North Korean hackers](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/radiant-links-50-million-crypto-heist-to-north-korean-hackers/). BleepingComputer (accessed 2024-12-10)
 
[Radiant Capital Post-Mortem](https://medium.com/@RadiantCapital/radiant-post-mortem-fecd6cd38081). Medium (accessed 2024-12-10)
 
[Radiant Capital Incident Update](https://medium.com/@RadiantCapital/radiant-capital-incident-update-e56d8c23829e). Medium (accessed 2024-12-10)

title: Threat Actor Targets the Manufacturing industry with Lumma Stealer and Amadey Bot
content:
#### Targeted Industries
- Critical Manufacturing



## Snapshot
Cyble Research and Intelligence Labs (CRIL) uncovered a sophisticated cyberattack campaign targeting the manufacturing sector through malicious LNK files disguised as PDF documents.

## Description
The attack likely begins with spear-phishing emails, leading victims to download a shortcut file hosted on a remote WebDAV share. Once executed, the LNK file initiates a multi-stage process involving legitimate Windows tools like ssh.exe, powershell.exe, and mshta.exe, enabling the download and execution of additional malicious payloads.
 
The attackers employ techniques such as DLL sideloading and Living-off-the-Land Binaries (LOLBins) to evade detection. Using tools like the [Lumma stealer](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/33933578825488511c30b0728dd3c4f8b5ca20e41c285a56f796eb39f57531ad) and Amadey bot, they exfiltrate sensitive information and establish persistence on compromised systems. The campaign leverages Google AMP URLs combined with shortened links to bypass traditional URL scanning, and the payloads are hosted on platforms like Pastebin.
 
By utilizing encrypted and obfuscated scripts, the attackers execute payloads directly in memory, avoiding file-based detection. They also employ advanced evasion techniques, such as modifying legitimate DLL files and injecting malicious code into processes like msiexec.exe and explorer.exe.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
Cyble has [previously reported](https://cyble.com/blog/lummac-stealer-leveraging-amadey-bot-to-deploy-sectoprat/) campaigns in which Lumma Stealer and Amadey Bot were deployed together to conduct malicious activities. In August 2023, the company documented the malwares' use in delivering SectopRAT, a remote access trojan (RAT) with extensive capabilities. SectopRAT can steal browser data, including cryptocurrency wallet details, and create a hidden secondary desktop to monitor and manipulate browser sessions. Further, it employs advanced anti-virtual machine (Anti-VM) and anti-emulator techniques, making it challenging to analyze and detect during malware research.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations.

- Check your Office 365 email filtering settings to ensure you block spoofed emails, spam, and emails with malware. Use [Microsoft Defender for Office 365](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/defender-for-office-365?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for enhanced phishing protection and coverage against new threats and polymorphic variants. Configure Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to [recheck links on click](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-links-about?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) and [delete sent mail](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/zero-hour-auto-purge?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in response to newly acquired threat intelligence. Turn on [safe attachments policies](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-attachments-policies-configure?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to check attachments to inbound email.
- Encourage users to use Microsoft Edge and other web browsers that support [SmartScreen](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/web-protection-overview?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc), which identifies and blocks malicious websites, including phishing sites, scam sites, and sites that host malware.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus, or the equivalent for your antivirus product, to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown variants.
- Enforce MFA on all accounts, remove users excluded from MFA, and strictly [require MFA](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/identity-protection/howto-identity-protection-configure-mfa-policy?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) from all devices, in all locations, at all times.
- Enable passwordless authentication methods (for example, Windows Hello, FIDO keys, or Microsoft Authenticator) for accounts that support passwordless. For accounts that still require passwords, use authenticator apps like Microsoft Authenticator for MFA. [Refer to this article](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/concept-authentication-methods?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for the different authentication methods and features.
- For MFA that uses authenticator apps, ensure that the app requires a code to be typed in where possible, as many intrusions where MFA was enabled still succeeded due to users clicking “Yes” on the prompt on their phones even when they were not at their [devices](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/how-to-mfa-number-match?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc). Refer to [this article](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/concept-authentication-methods?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for an example.
- Remind employees that enterprise or workplace credentials should not be stored in browsers or password vaults secured with personal credentials. Organizations can turn off password syncing in browser on managed devices using [Group Policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/deployedge/microsoft-edge-enterprise-sync#sync-group-policies?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc).

Microsoft Defender customers can [turn on attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to prevent common attack techniques used in infostealer infections. Attack surface reduction rules are sweeping settings that stop entire classes of threats including, infostealers, credential theft, and ransomware. The following bullet points offer more guidance on specific mitigation advice:

- [Turn on PUA protection in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/detect-block-potentially-unwanted-apps-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc)
- [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion)
- [Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-execution-of-potentially-obfuscated-scripts)

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects threat components as the following malware:
 
- [Trojan:Win32/CoinMiner](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:Win32/CoinMiner.AQ)
- [HackTool:Win32/AutoKMS](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=HackTool:Win32/AutoKMS)
- [Trojan:Win32/Killav](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:Win32/Killav.DR)

## References
[Threat Actor Targets the Manufacturing industry with Lumma Stealer and Amadey Bot](https://cyble.com/blog/threat-actor-targets-manufacturing-industry-with-malware/). Cyble (accessed 2024-12-06)

title: Crypto-stealing malware posing as a meeting app targets Web3 pros
content:
## Snapshot
Cado Security Labs uncovered a cybercriminal campaign targeting individuals in the Web3 space with a fraudulent video conferencing platform named "Meeten," which has been active since September 2024.

## Description
The malware, with versions for both Windows and macOS, aims to steal cryptocurrency assets, banking information, web browser data, and Keychain credentials (on Mac). Cado Security Labs warns that the threat actors behind Meeten have used various names for the fake software, such as Clusee\[.\]com, Cuesee, Meeten\[.\]gg, Meeten\[.\]us, Meetone\[.\]gg, and Meetio. The threat actors bolster the scams legitimacy with official-looking websites and social media accounts, including Twitter and Medium, filled with AI-generated content. Victims are lured to these sites through phishing or social engineering and are tricked into downloading the [Realst stealer](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/107ad21a) malware. The fraud often starts with contact on platforms like Telegram, where the attackers impersonate known contacts of the victim to discuss fake business opportunities. In one report, the threat actor sent an investment presentation from the victim's company to them, indicating a level of sophistication. The Meeten websites also host JavaScript code designed to steal cryptocurrency directly from web browsers. 
 
For macOS users, the malware is disguised as a package named 'CallCSSetup\[.\]pkg,' with other file names used in the past, and prompts users for their system password, leading to privilege escalation. It then displays a decoy message while stealing data in the background, including Telegram credentials, banking card details, and browser information from various web browsers, as well as Ledger and Trezor wallet details. The stolen data is zipped and sent to a remote server with device information such as build name, version, and system information.
 
The Windows variant of Realst, distributed as 'MeetenApp\[.\]exe,' uses a stolen digital certificate and contains a 7zip archive and an Electron application that downloads additional malware components. This version collects similar information as the macOS variant but features a more sophisticated delivery mechanism, better evasion techniques, and persistence through registry modification. The application is said to be built on an Electron framework, which is used to develop cross-platform desktop applications with web languages like Javascript. Cado reports there's been increased use by threat actors creating malware with Electron applications.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
Threat actors have [previously used](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/038db949) fake video conference applications to carry out [supply chain attacks](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/malware/supply-chain-malware) targeting software developers and suppliers, aiming to infect legitimate applications and updates to distribute malware. They exploit unsecure network protocols, server infrastructure, and coding practices. Attackers might alter source code and hide malicious code within build and update processes, which can run with the same trust and permissions as the legitimate application.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following to reduce the risk of these threats.
 
- [Help prevent social engineering attacks](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/security-insider/emerging-threats/feeding-from-the-trust-economy-social-engineering-fraud?ocid=magicti_ta_blog) by not blending personal accounts with work emails or work-related tasks. Avoid opening emails, attachments, and links, including links from social networks, from suspicious sources. Ask yourself if the sender is who they say they are before clicking anything. Do a search to determine if the offer is legitimate or a trap.
- Practicing the [principle of least privilege and building credential hygiene](https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2022/05/09/ransomware-as-a-service-understanding-the-cybercrime-gig-economy-and-how-to-protect-yourself?ocid=magicti_ta_blog#defending-against-ransomware), [preventing cloud identity abuse](https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/4e5f51c4-244f-47ab-a097-6800ce820c26/analystreport), and using [SmartScreen](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/web-protection-overview?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) and [Safe Links](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/web-protection-overview?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) can significantly limit the impact of these attacks on your network.
- Enforce MFA on all accounts, remove users excluded from MFA, and strictly [require MFA](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/identity-protection/howto-identity-protection-configure-mfa-policy?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) from all devices, in all locations, at all times.
- Remind employees that enterprise or workplace credentials should not be stored in browsers or password vaults secured with personal credentials. Organizations can turn off password syncing in browser on managed devices using [Group Policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/deployedge/microsoft-edge-enterprise-sync#sync-group-policies?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc).
- Implement [conditional access authentication strength](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/concept-authentication-strengths?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to require phishing-resistant authentication for employees and external users for critical apps.
- Implement [conditional access app control in Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-cloud-apps/proxy-intro-aad?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for users connecting from unmanaged devices.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/enable-cloud-protection-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a huge majority of new and unknown variants.
- Turn on [tamper protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) features to prevent attackers from stopping security services.
- Run [endpoint detection and response (EDR) in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus doesn’t detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode.
- Additional layers of protection can be applied with intrusion detection and prevention systems ([IDPS](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/firewall/premium-features?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#idps)) using Azure Firewall Premium. [Perform network intrusion detection by using Azure Network Watcher and open-source tools](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/network-watcher/network-watcher-intrusion-detection-open-source-tools?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc). Use Azure Web Application Firewall ([WAF](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/web-application-firewall/overview?WT.mc_id=AZ-MVP-5000120)) to provide centralized protection of your web applications from common exploits and vulnerabilities.
- Check your Office 365 email filtering settings to ensure you block spoofed emails, spam, and emails with malware. Use [Microsoft Defender for Office 365](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/defender-for-office-365?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for enhanced phishing protection and coverage against new threats and polymorphic variants. Configure Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to [recheck links on click](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-links-about?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) and [delete sent mail](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/zero-hour-auto-purge?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in response to newly acquired Threat Intelligence. Turn on [safe attachments policies](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/safe-attachments-policies-configure?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to check attachments to incoming emails. Keep [Microsoft Purview auditing](https://learn.microsoft.com/purview/audit-solutions-overview?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) set up so that audit records can be investigated when needed.

Microsoft Defender customers can [turn on attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to prevent common attack techniques. Attack surface reduction rules are sweeping settings that stop entire classes of threats including, infostealers, credential theft, and ransomware. The following bullet points offer more guidance on specific mitigation advice: 

- - [Block process creations originating from PsExec and WMI commands](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-process-creations-originating-from-psexec-and-wmi-commands). Some organizations may experience compatibility issues with this rule on certain server systems but should deploy it to other systems to prevent lateral movement originating from PsExec and WMI.
    - [Turn on PUA protection in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/detect-block-potentially-unwanted-apps-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc)
    - [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion)

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
- [Behavior:MacOS/Realst.A](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Behavior:MacOS/Realst.A&ThreatID=2147895181)

title: Romania's election systems targeted in over 85,000 cyberattacks
content:
#### Targeted Geolocations
- Romania



#### Targeted Industries
- Government Agencies & Services



## Snapshot
Romania's election infrastructure faced over 85,000 cyberattacks, with threat actors gaining access to election-related websites and leaking credentials on a Russian hacker forum shortly before the presidential elections. Additionally, Romanian intelligence agencies have highlighted a potential state-backed influence campaign targeting the presidential election, where TikTok influencers with millions of followers promoted candidate Calin Georgescu using coordinated messages and hashtags.

## Description
The Romanian Intelligence Service (SRI) reported that the Permanent Electoral Authority's IT infrastructure was compromised on November 19, with a server containing mapping data being targeted. This server was connected to both the public web and the Authority's internal network. The leaked credentials pertained to several Romanian election sites, and the attackers obtained these by either targeting legitimate users or exploiting vulnerabilities in a training server for voting section operators. 

The attacks, which originated from over 33 countries, continued until the night after the first presidential election round on November 25th. The attackers aimed to access and compromise the election infrastructure, alter public election information, and deny system access. They attempted breaches using SQL injection and cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerabilities. The SRI warned that the infrastructure still harbors vulnerabilities that could allow attackers to move laterally within the network and establish persistence. 

Additionally, the SRI described an influence campaign targeting the Romanian presidential election, where over 100 TikTok influencers with a collective following of over 8 million were paid to promote presidential candidate Calin Georgescu. The Ministry of Internal Affairs observed a sharp increase in the visibility of these videos, which shared [similarities with content promoting a pro-Russian candidate in Moldova](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/05cff118). The SRI noted that Georgescu's campaign was supported by a sudden increase in activity from 25,000 TikTok accounts, with 800 of them created in 2016 and becoming active just before the election. While the SRI did not directly attribute the attacks and influence campaign to Russia, the Romanian Foreign Intelligence Service highlighted Russia's history of election interference and its perception of Romania as an enemy state due to its NATO alliance.

As of December 6, the Constitutional Court of Romania (CCR) [annulled the presidential elections](https://www.ccr.ro/comunicat-de-presa-6-decembrie-2024/) based on findings that the first round of elections was affected by a Russian influence campaign and decided that new elections will be held.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
Russia targets Romania for influence operations in part due to Romania's strategic role on NATO’s eastern flank, its energy initiatives, and its position on the Black Sea. Romania hosts key NATO infrastructure, including the Aegis Ashore missile defense system. Additionally, Romania’s efforts to reduce reliance on Russian energy through projects like the BRUA pipeline challenge Moscow’s influence in the region. Situated on the Black Sea, Romania plays a critical role in regional security and economic dynamics that are vital to Russia’s geopolitical interests. To undermine Romania's alignment with NATO and the EU, Russia employs disinformation campaigns that exploit domestic issues and regional tensions, seeking to weaken trust in democratic institutions and disrupt Western cohesion.

## References
[Romania's election systems targeted in over 85,000 cyberattacks](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/romanias-election-systems-targeted-in-over-85-000-cyberattacks/). Bleeping Computer (accessed 2024-12-09)

title: Snowblind: The Invisible Hand of Secret Blizzard
content:
#### Targeted Geolocations
- Pakistan  
- Afghanistan  
- India



## Snapshot
Researchers at Lumen's Black Lotus Labs, in collaboration with Microsoft's Threat Intelligence Team, have uncovered that the Russian cyber-espionage group Turla, tracked by Microsoft as [Secret Blizzard](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/01d15f655c45c517f52235d63932fb377c319176239426681412afb01bf39dcc), has been hijacking the infrastructure of the Pakistani threat actor Storm-0156 since December 2022. Secret Blizzard infiltrated 33 command-and-control (C2) nodes belonging to Storm-0156, leveraging this access to deploy its own malware and gather intelligence.

## Description
Initially targeting Storm-0156's C2 infrastructure, Secret Blizzard deployed malware, including "TwoDash" and "Statuezy," into Afghan government networks, using the Pakistani group’s prior foothold. In mid-2023, they further infiltrated the workstations of Storm-0156 operators, enabling them to exfiltrate sensitive data, including credentials, stolen files, and malware used in Indian government and military networks. By mid-2024, Secret Blizzard began utilizing additional malware, such as CrimsonRAT, appropriated from the compromised Pakistani infrastructure.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
Microsoft has observed that Secret Blizzard has used the tools and infrastructure of at least six other threat actors during the past seven years. While not unique, leveraging the access of other adversaries is a somewhat unusual attack vector for threat actors in general. Microsoft Threat Intelligence partnered with Black Lotus Labs to confirm that Secret Blizzard command-and-control (C2) traffic emanated from Storm-0156 infrastructure, including infrastructure used by Storm-0156 to collate exfiltrated data from campaigns in Afghanistan and India.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence tracks Secret Blizzard campaigns and, when we are able, directly notifies customers who have been targeted or compromised, providing them with the necessary information to help secure their environments. Read Microsoft's blog on [Secret Blizzard compromising Storm-0156 infrastructure for espionage](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2024/12/04/frequent-freeloader-part-i-secret-blizzard-compromising-storm-0156-infrastructure-for-espionage/) for further information on this campaign.

## Recommendations
### Strengthen Microsoft Defender for Endpoint configuration
 
- Microsoft Defender XDR customers can implement [attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-deployment-implement) to harden an environment against techniques used by threat actors
    - [Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-execution-of-potentially-obfuscated-scripts)

    - [Block process creations originating from PSExec and WMI commands](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-process-creations-originating-from-psexec-and-wmi-commands)

    - [Block executable files from running](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?view=o365-worldwide#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion) unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion

    - [Block abuse of exploited vulnerable signed drivers](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-abuse-of-exploited-vulnerable-signed-drivers)

    - [Block Webshell creation for Servers](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-webshell-creation-for-servers)
- [Enable network protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/enable-network-protection) in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint
- Ensure [tamper protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection#how-do-i-configure-or-manage-tamper-protection) is enabled in Microsoft Dender for Endpoint
- Run endpoint detection and response in [block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts even when your non-Microsoft antivirus does not detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode
- Configure [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations) in full automated mode to let Microsoft Defender for Endpoint take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume

### Strengthen Microsoft Defender Antivirus configuration

- [Turn on PUA protection in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/detect-block-potentially-unwanted-apps-microsoft-defender-antivirus) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/cloud-protection-microsoft-defender-antivirus) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving threat actor tools and techniques
- Turn on Microsoft Defender Antivirus [real-time protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/configure-real-time-protection-microsoft-defender-antivirus)

### Strengthen operating environment configuration

- Encourage users to use Microsoft Edge and other web browsers that support [SmartScreen](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/web-protection-overview) which identifies and blocks malicious websites, including phishing sites, scam sites, and sites that host malware. Implement [PowerShell execution policies](https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/scripting/security/security-features?view=powershell-7.4#execution-policy) to control conditions under which PowerShell can load configuration files and run scripts
- Turn on and monitor PowerShell [module and script block logging](https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/scripting/security/security-features?view=powershell-7.4#module-and-script-block-logging)
- Implement [PowerShell execution policies](https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/scripting/security/security-features?view=powershell-7.4#execution-policy) to control conditions under which PowerShell can load configuration files and run scripts.
- Turn on and monitor PowerShell [module and script block logging](https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/scripting/security/security-features?view=powershell-7.4#module-and-script-block-logging).

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects this threat as the following malware: 
 
- [Backdoor:Win64/Wainscot](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Backdoor:Win64/Wainscot.A!dha "https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?name=backdoor:win64/wainscot.a!dha")
- [Backdoor:MSIL/CrimsonRat.A](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Backdoor:MSIL/CrimsonRat.A "https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?name=backdoor:msil/crimsonrat.a")
- [Backdoor:MSIL/CrimsonRat.B](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Backdoor:MSIL/CrimsonRat.B!MTB "https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?name=backdoor:msil/crimsonrat.b!mtb")
- TrojanSpy:MSIL/CrimsonRat.A
- [TrojanDownloader:Win64/TwoDash](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=TrojanDownloader%3AWin64/TwoDash!dha&threatId=-2147125841 "https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?name=trojandownloader%3awin64/twodash!dha&threatid=-2147125841")
- [Trojan:MSIL/ReverseRAT](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:MSIL/ReverseRat.CCBH!MTB "https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?name=trojan:msil/reverserat.ccbh!mtb")
- Trojan:Win32/TinStrut.A
- Trojan:Win64/TinyTurla.A
- Trojan:Win64/TinyTurla.B
- Trojan:Win32/MiniPocket.A
- TrojanDownloader:Win64/TwoDash.A
- Trojan:Win64/TwoDash.B
- Trojan:Win64/PostGallery.A
- Trojan:Win32/Statuezy.B
- Trojan:Win32/TinyTurla

### Microsoft Defender for Endpoint
The following Microsoft Defender for Endpoint alerts can indicate associated threat activity:

The following alerts might also indicate threat activity related to this threat. Note, however, these alerts also can be triggered by unrelated threat activity.

title: U.S. Organization in China Targeted by Attackers
content:
## Snapshot
Researchers at Symantec identified a four-month-long intrusion targeting a large U.S. organization with a significant presence in China, likely conducted by a China-linked threat actor.

## Description
The attack, which spanned from April to August 2024, involved lateral movement across the network and compromised multiple computers, including Exchange Servers, indicating an intent to harvest emails for intelligence gathering. The attackers deployed exfiltration tools, suggesting that data was stolen from the organization. The threat actors utilized DLL-sideloading techniques, leveraging legitimate applications such as GoogleToolbarNotifier.exe and iTunesHelper.exe to load malware. They also used [Impacket](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/19a4861eb55c4c074ab0a8c6f58738d8f50dda8badf96695758399e3d826dda6) for network protocol manipulation, FileZilla for FTP transfers, and PSCP for secure file copying. Living-off-the-land tactics were employed, including the use of WMI, PsExec, and PowerShell for executing commands, moving laterally, and reconnaissance.

The initial infection vector is unknown, but the first signs of malicious activity were detected on April 11, 2024, with the use of WMI to execute suspicious commands. The attackers performed credential dumping, Kerberoasting to steal service account credentials, and used PowerShell to download files and query Active Directory. They also targeted specific domain groups, such as "Exchange Servers," and used PsExec to execute commands on remote systems.

Evidence suggests a connection to the China-linked groups [Daggerfly](https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/daggerfly-espionage-updated-toolset) and [Crimson Palace](https://news.sophos.com/en-us/2024/06/05/operation-crimson-palace-sophos-threat-hunting-unveils-multiple-clusters-of-chinese-state-sponsored-activity-targeting-southeast-asia/), known for targeting entities in Southeast Asia. According to Symantec, the attackers' use of known tools and tactics, such as DLL sideloading and living-off-the-land techniques, aligns with methods favored by Chinese threat actors.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat.
 
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/linux-preferences) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown threats.
- Run [EDR in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode?view=o365-worldwide?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus does not detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach.
- Allow [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations?view=o365-worldwide?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in full automated mode to allow Microsoft Defender for Endpoint to take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.
- [Enable](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-controlled-folders) controlled folder access.
- Ensure that [tamper protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection#how-do-i-configure-or-manage-tamper-protection) is enabled in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Enable [network protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-network-protection) in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Follow the credential hardening recommendations in the [on-premises credential theft overview](https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/9382203e-5155-4b5e-af74-21562b1004d5/analystreport) to defend against common credential theft techniques like LSASS access.
- [Enable](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-credential-stealing-from-the-windows-local-security-authority-subsystem) LSA protection.

## Detections/Hunting Queries

### Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects threat components as the following malware:
 
- [Trojan:Win32/Malgent!MSR](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan:Win32/Malgent!MSR)

title: Solana Web3.js library backdoored to steal secret, private keys
content:
## Snapshot
Attackers temporarily compromised the Solana JavaScript SDK, specifically the '@solana/web3.js' library, in a supply chain attack, releasing two malicious versions aimed at stealing cryptocurrency private keys. The @solana/web3.js library receives more than 350,000 weekly downloads on npm.

## Description
Socket security firm reported that versions 1.95.6 and 1.95.7 of the library contained code designed to exfiltrate private and secret keys, which could allow attackers to drain funds from wallets. The attack is believed to be the result of a social engineering/phishing attack targeting maintainers of the official Web3.js open-source library maintained by Solana. The firm said that an account with publish-access was compromised, enabling the attacker to publish these unauthorized versions. The malicious activity was identified within hours, and the affected versions were unpublished. DataDog researcher Christophe Tafani-Dereeper discovered that the threat actors added a malicious "addToQueue" function to the compromised library versions, which was designed to send stolen keys to the attacker's server using CloudFlare headers. BleepingComputer reported five key locations within the library where calls to the [addToQueue](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-apps/developer/data-platform/webapi/reference/addtoqueue?view=dataverse-latest) function that legitimately access private keys. The compromised functions include "fromSecretKey()," "fromSeed()," "createInstructionWithPublicKey()," "createInstructionWithPrivateKey()," and the account constructor. The stolen keys were sent to the attacker's endpoint at "https://sol-rpc\[.\]xyz/api/rpc/queue." The attack has been linked to a specific Solana address, which at the time of reporting contained 674.86 Solana and various tokens.

## Recommendations
Solana advised developers who might have been compromised to update to the latest version, v1.95.8, and to rotate any keys that could be affected.

Socket suggests developers take immediate action:
 
- Check Dependencies: Audit your projects for any usage of @solana/web3.js and identify if versions 1.95.6 or 1.95.7 are in use.
- Rollback or Update: Downgrade to a safe version prior to 1.95.6 or update to version 1.95.8, which was released to remove the injected code.
- Verify Code: Manually inspect your node\_modules directory and dependency trees for suspicious modifications.
- Revoke Access: Regenerate compromised keys and revoke permissions as needed.

Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat.

- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus, or the equivalent for your antivirus product, to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown variants.
- Remind employees that enterprise or workplace credentials should not be stored in browsers or password vaults secured with personal credentials. Organizations can turn off password syncing in browser on managed devices using [Group Policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/deployedge/microsoft-edge-enterprise-sync#sync-group-policies?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc).
- Educate end users about [preventing malware infections](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/malware/prevent-malware-infection). Practicing the [principle of least privilege and building credential hygiene](https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2022/05/09/ransomware-as-a-service-understanding-the-cybercrime-gig-economy-and-how-to-protect-yourself?ocid=magicti_ta_blog#defending-against-ransomware). Avoid the use of domain-wide, admin-level service accounts. Restricting local administrative privileges can help limit installation of unwanted applications.
- Software developers and publishers should ensure their [build and update infrastructure are secure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/malware/supply-chain-malware). Establish [best practices to secure software supply chain](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/nuget/concepts/security-best-practices).
- Conduct an [audit for packages and dependencies](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/nuget/concepts/auditing-packages), analyzing the security of packages included in software projects.

Microsoft Defender customers can [turn on attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to prevent attack techniques.

title: Venom Spider Spins Web of New Malware for MaaS Platform
content:
## Snapshot
Researchers at Zscaler ThreatLabz have identified new malware tools added to the arsenal of a known threat actor operating a malware-as-a-service (MaaS) platform, Venom Spider (also known as Golden Chickens).

## Description
These campaigns introduced two new malware families, RevC2 and Venom Loader.The first campaign, active from August to September, used an API documentation lure to deliver RevC2, a backdoor for stealing sensitive data. RevC2, distributed via VenomLNK files, ensures execution only under specific conditions, avoiding detection. It uses WebSockets for command-and-control (C2) communication and can execute commands, steal data, and log processes. The second campaign, from September to October, employed a cryptocurrency transaction lure to deliver Venom Loader, which deployed a More\_eggs lite backdoor variant. More\_eggs lite is a variant of [more_eggs](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/4cb94d70) but contains only the capability to perform remote code execution (RCE) and is used as a loader. Venom Loader loads More\_eggs lite by decoding encoded payloads and establishes persistence via registry modifications. More\_eggs lite communicates with its C2 server using HTTP POST requests, enabling remote code execution (RCE) capabilities. Zscaler noted that RevC2 and Venom Loader appear to be early-stage malware with potential for further development.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. 

- Encourage users to use Microsoft Edge and other web browsers that support [SmartScreen](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/web-protection-overview?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc), which identifies and blocks malicious websites, including phishing sites, scam sites, and sites that host malware.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus, or the equivalent for your antivirus product, to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown variants.
- Enforce MFA on all accounts, remove users excluded from MFA, and strictly [require MFA](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/identity-protection/howto-identity-protection-configure-mfa-policy?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) from all devices, in all locations, at all times. For MFA that uses authenticator apps, ensure that the app requires a code to be typed in where possible, as many intrusions where MFA was enabled still succeeded due to users clicking “Yes” on the prompt on their phones even when they were not at their [devices](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/how-to-mfa-number-match?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc). Refer to [this article](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/active-directory/authentication/concept-authentication-methods?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) for an example.

Microsoft Defender customers can [turn on attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) to prevent common attack techniques used in infostealer infections. Attack surface reduction rules are sweeping settings that stop entire classes of threats including, infostealers, credential theft, and ransomware. The following bullet points offer more guidance on specific mitigation advice: 

- [Turn on PUA protection in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/detect-block-potentially-unwanted-apps-microsoft-defender-antivirus?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc)
- [Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-executable-files-from-running-unless-they-meet-a-prevalence-age-or-trusted-list-criterion)
- [Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc#block-execution-of-potentially-obfuscated-scripts)

title: New "CleverSoar" Installer Targets Chinese and Vietnamese Users
content:
#### Targeted Geolocations
- China  
- Vietnam



## Snapshot
Researchers from Rapid7 Labs identified a new malware installer, dubbed CleverSoar, being used to impact Chinese and Vietnamese-speaking victims.

## Description
The installer deploys advanced malicious tools, including the Winos4.0 framework and the Nidhogg rootkit, enabling activities such as data theft, keystroke logging, and bypassing security measures. The malware is distributed via fake .msi installers disguised as gaming or software-related applications. It selectively targets systems based on language settings, terminating its process if the language is not Chinese or Vietnamese, indicating a region-specific espionage motive.
 
Rapid7 observed sophisticated anti-detection methods in CleverSoar, such as firmware-level anti-virtual machine (VM) checks, Windows Defender evasion, and anti-debugging techniques. The malware also employs persistence mechanisms like scheduled tasks and rootkit installations, ensuring it remains active on compromised systems. Interestingly, the malware disables antivirus tools, turns off the firewall, and customizes its payload to avoid detection.
 
Although attribution remains uncertain, similarities to prior campaigns suggest links to the same group behind the ValleyRAT malware. CleverSoar’s intricate design and focus on espionage underscore the importance of proactive defense, particularly for users in the affected regions.

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat.
 
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/linux-preferences) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown threats.
- Run [EDR in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode?view=o365-worldwide?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus does not detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach.
- Allow [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations?view=o365-worldwide?ocid=magicti_ta_learndoc) in full automated mode to allow Microsoft Defender for Endpoint to take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.
- [Enable](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-controlled-folders) controlled folder access.
- Ensure that [tamper protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection#how-do-i-configure-or-manage-tamper-protection) is enabled in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Enable [network protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/enable-network-protection) in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
- Follow the credential hardening recommendations in the [on-premises credential theft overview](https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/9382203e-5155-4b5e-af74-21562b1004d5/analystreport) to defend against common credential theft techniques like LSASS access.
- [Enable](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-credential-stealing-from-the-windows-local-security-authority-subsystem) LSA protection.

title: Threat Assessment: Howling Scorpius (Akira Ransomware)
content:
## Snapshot
Researchers at Unit 42 have been monitoring the Howling Scorpius ransomware group, which they suspect is behind the Akira ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) and its new strain, Megazord.

## Description
According to Palo Alto, Howling Scorpius, emerging in early 2023, has targeted small to medium-sized businesses in North America, Europe, and Australia, using a double extortion tactic by stealing data before encrypting it. They have developed encryptors for Windows, Linux, and specifically for ESXi hosts.

Initial access is gained through various methods, including exploiting vulnerable VPN services, purchasing valid accounts, targeting external-facing services like RDP, and spear phishing campaigns, with known exploits of CVE-2020-3259 and CVE-2023-20269. The group uses tools like Mimikatz and LaZagne for credential access, focusing on Active Directory databases, and employs lateral movement techniques involving RDP and SMB. They evade defenses by terminating antimalware processes, creating new domain accounts, and sometimes setting up their own VMs to bypass host security tools. Data exfiltration is carried out using WinRAR, WinSCP, RClone, and FileZilla through FTP.

The Akira ransomware variants use a hybrid encryption approach, with the Windows variant employing the ChaCha20 algorithm and RSA, and the Linux/ESXi variant using several symmetric encryption algorithms. The Megazord strain, written in Rust, requires a password for execution and has distinct file extensions and ransom note, indicating possible different operators within the group.

A new variant, Akira\_v2, has been identified with expanded capabilities and command-line arguments, targeting virtual machine files and able to shut down running VMs. This variant, along with the original Akira ransomware, avoids encrypting certain system-critical files and directories but targets a wide range of file extensions associated with databases and virtual machines. The ransomware has been spotlighted by several cybersecurity research entities, highlighting its significant threat and the active development of new strains and capabilities by Howling Scorpius, which is now among the top five most active ransomware groups.

## Microsoft Analysis and Additional OSINT Context
Prior to ransomware deployment, attackers often take multiple steps to move laterally, acquire credentials, and exfiltrate data. For a holistic guide on securing your organization from ransomware threats, refer to the [Ransomware-as-a-Service](https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2022/05/09/ransomware-as-a-service-understanding-the-cybercrime-gig-economy-and-how-to-protect-yourself/#defending-against-ransomware) blog.

[Akira Ransomware Attacking Airline Industry With Legitimate Tools](https://security.microsoft.com/intel-explorer/articles/53f413f8)

## Recommendations
Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations.  
 
- Read our [ransomware as a service blog](https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2022/05/09/ransomware-as-a-service-understanding-the-cybercrime-gig-economy-and-how-to-protect-yourself/#defending-against-ransomware) for advice on developing a holistic security posture to prevent ransomware, including credential hygiene and hardening recommendations.
- Turn on [cloud-delivered protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/configure-block-at-first-sight-microsoft-defender-antivirus) in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a huge majority of new and unknown variants.
- Turn on [tamper protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/prevent-changes-to-security-settings-with-tamper-protection) features to prevent attackers from stopping security services.
- Run [endpoint detection and response (EDR) in block mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode) , so that Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus doesn’t detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts detected post-breach.
- Enable [investigation and remediation](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/automated-investigations) in full automated mode to allow Defender for Endpoint to take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume.   
  
Microsoft Defender customers can turn on [attack surface reduction rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction) to prevent common attack techniques used in ransomware attacks. Attack surface reduction rules are sweeping settings that are effective at stopping entire classes of threats.

- Ransom and lateral movement stage:

-[Block process creations originating from PsExec and WMI commands](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#block-process-creations-originating-from-psexec-and-wmi-commands)

-[Use advanced protection against ransomware](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference#use-advanced-protection-against-ransomware)

## Detections/Hunting Queries
